events.title: Starbucks says it is not buying Chipotle after takeover speculation
events.summary: "Starbucks is not buying Chipotle," a Starbucks spokesperson told CNBC's Jim Cramer. The denial follows days of rumors that Starbucks was trying to acquire the fast-casual chain. The deal rumors sent shares of Chipotle higher, while Starbucks stock fell on the reports. Starbucks on Monday denied that it is considering acquiring Chipotle Mexican Grill in what would be the biggest-ever restaurant takeover. Chipotle's stock was down more than 4% in morning trading Monday following the statement, while Starbucks shares were more than 1% higher. The coffee giant's denial comes after days of rumors about a potential megadeal between the two restaurant companies. On Thursday, the Financial Times reported that Starbucks has been working with advisors on a Chipotle takeover proposal in recent months. The newspaper cited people familiar with the matter. Earlier in October, Semafor reported that Chipotle had hired advisors to defend against activist investors or an unwanted takeover bid. The fast-casual chain is trying to recover from a rocky 2025 , when traffic to its restaurants fell. Chipotle shares are down about 20% over the last year, making it a cheaper target. Chipotle investors were looking forward to a potential reunion with Brian Niccol, who previously led Chipotle and is now CEO of Starbucks. But Starbucks shareholders were largely concerned about an expensive distraction while the coffee chain is in the middle of its own turnaround.

events.title: Smart ring maker Ultrahuman to roll out biological-age model across UAE
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Ultrahuman , a Bengaluru-based health tech startup best known for its smart rings, has partnered with Abu Dhabi health authorities to develop a biological-age model that it says will eventually be made available to people across the United Arab Emirates. On Monday, Ultrahuman announced that it had signed a two-year memorandum of understanding with the Abu Dhabi Public Health Center (ADPHC) to develop and validate the model, which will combine clinical biomarkers with data from wearable devices. The partnership aims to use these signals to estimate how quickly an individual is aging and identify factors — including sleep, activity, cardiovascular health, and metabolism — that may be accelerating or slowing that process. The partnership marks Ultrahuman’s latest effort to go beyond selling wearable hardware and deploy its health algorithms at a much larger scale. The startup increasingly sees itself as a health-data company, with its smart ring serving as one way to collect information that can underpin algorithms spanning aging, longevity, and other areas of health, CEO Mohit Kumar said in an interview. “If you look at Ultrahuman as a company, we obviously have the Ultrahuman Ring, which is a way to acquire data from the human body,” Kumar told TechCrunch. “But truly, what we care about is not just the form factor, the ring, but what do we do with this data?” Working with a government gives Ultrahuman the opportunity to apply its algorithms to a far broader population than its own customer base, Kumar said. The startup has sold around 800,000 smart rings globally so far. The Abu Dhabi partnership is Ultrahuman’s first step toward deploying a health algorithm at a national scale, with the health age model eventually intended to be available to people across the UAE, according to the company. Even though Ultrahuman is known for its smart rings, Kumar said the biological-age model is being designed to be wearable-agnostic, allowing data from rings, wrist-worn devices, straps, and patches to feed into the system alongside clinical biomarkers. Individuals will eventually be able to access their health age through government digital-health platforms including TAMM and Sahatna, the startup said. Ultrahuman and ADPHC will spend the next two years working on research and clinical validation of the model. Kumar told TechCrunch that the broader rollout will happen in phases, but did not provide a timeline. The UAE is already among Ultrahuman’s 10 largest markets and accounts for about 4% to 5% of its overall revenue, Kumar said. The startup has operated in the market for nearly five years and sees about 25% higher retention there compared with its other markets, he noted. Ultrahuman’s existing customer base gives it a narrower view of the population than a government health system. Its typical users are between 25 and 43 years old, Kumar said, while deploying the model across the UAE would expose it to a much broader range of age groups. The underlying biological-age model was developed using Ultrahuman’s existing data, combining users’ chronological ages with wearable signals and, for some users, blood-test markers, Kumar told TechCrunch. That allows the startup to track how health markers typically change with age and identify deviations from those patterns. Kumar stressed the model will not be trained on data from the UAE. “We will deploy an algorithm on the UAE data,” he said, adding that Ultrahuman will not have access to personally identifiable information through the program. Ultrahuman is not the only smart-ring maker working with Abu Dhabi on preventive health. In May, the Department of Health – Abu Dhabi announced a partnership with Ultrahuman arch-rival Oura to combine the company’s wearable data with the emirate’s longitudinal health data, initially focusing on women’s health and cardiometabolic risk. Kumar told TechCrunch that Ultrahuman is not aware of another company working with Abu Dhabi authorities on the health age model specifically. While he acknowledged that the government works with multiple health-tech companies, he declined to comment on the scope of Oura’s work with Abu Dhabi. The parallel partnerships come as Ultrahuman and Oura compete in the smart-ring market while looking to push their businesses beyond wearable hardware and deeper into preventive health. The work with the Abu Dhabi authorities also comes as Ultrahuman is looking to build a smart ring that can run software on the device and even power everything from AI interactions to games . events.title: Nobel prize in economics awarded to Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford
events.summary: Hall and Woodford were jointly awarded for their contribution to the "microeconomic foundations" needed to create macroeconomic stability. Their has looked beyond macroeconomic variables and showed how individual households and businesses collectively shape the economy. The economics memorial prize is the last to be announced, following the original Nobel Prizes in physiology or medicine, physics, chemistry, literature and peace. Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford were on Monday awarded the Nobel memorial prize in economics for work that underpins the models used by central banks and governments to "smooth out" periods of boom and bust. The U.S.-born pair were jointly awarded for their contribution to the "microeconomic foundations" that contribute to macroeconomic stability. The Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel was established by Sweden's central bank in 1968. The winners will split a 12 million Swedish kronor ($1.2 million) prize. Hall, born in California, is a professor at Stanford University, while Massachusetts-born Woodford is a professor at Columbia University. "With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume," John Hassler, chair of the Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences, said in a statement. During the stagflationary oil crises of the 1970s, widely accepted Keynesian models — which prescribed cutting interest rates and increasing government budget deficits to tackle recessions — seemed to "no longer work," the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said. To revitalize these models, the economists' separate work has looked beyond macroeconomic variables such as inflation, production and consumption and showed how individual households and businesses collectively shape the economy through decision-making based on their expectations for the future, the academy said. Their work has shown the importance of central banks and governments communicating their policy plans, which can "influence this view of the future and move the economy in the right direction," it said. "On the basis of these models, well-timed fiscal and monetary policy measures can reduce the economy's peaks and troughs," the academy added. "Since the new models' introduction, they have been extremely helpful in dealing with the economic downturns that have affected us." This year's laureates include Navanethem "Navi" Pillay, who was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize on Friday for her work promoting peace and international law, and Canadian poet and writer Anne Carson, who won the literature prize for a "bold and inventive oeuvre."

events.title: Microsoft to rely more on homegrown AI chips, reducing dependence on Nvidia
events.summary: Microsoft said it will eventually have multiple gigawatts worth of its Maia AI chips. The company intends to make Maia its primary architecture for running AI models. The next-generation Maia 300 chip enters production in 2027. Microsoft will ramp up use of its homegrown artificial intelligence chips after years of reliance on Nvidia's graphics processing units, as the software giant attempts to bolster its AI stack. Starting with its third-generation Maia AI accelerator, unveiled on Monday, Microsoft said it will mainly rely on its own silicon to handle incoming requests. Microsoft's greatest strength in AI has been its Azure cloud, which runs a series of models for clients. Its Microsoft 365 Copilot and GitHub Copilot offer AI-powered services to software engineers and other office workers. And the company develops in-house models, though they've yet to make a big splash in a market dominated by OpenAI , Anthropic and Google . The emerging opportunity in chips stems from unrelenting demand for advanced processors and a desire in the market for choice. Nvidia's GPUs have been the standard for AI workloads and models, and they fill Microsoft's existing data centers, while also serving to train models from OpenAI and Anthropic. But as demand keeps growing, the model leaders have embraced a variety of silicon from companies including Amazon , Advanced Micro Devices , Cerebras , Google and, in recent months, Microsoft. For general-purpose use, Microsoft already taps its own central processing units as well as silicon from Intel and AMD . Finance chief Amy Hood said at a Goldman Sachs conference last month that use of its own chips has helped with "margin improvement over the course of a decade." Microsoft introduced its inaugural AI chip, the Maia 100, in 2023 . It touted the Maia 200 this past January , and CEO Satya Nadella told analysts in July that Maia 200 "delivers 30% better performance per dollar than the latest generation hardware in our fleet" and said it was handling OpenAI models. Production of the Maia 300 starts in 2027. Microsoft is targeting multi-gigawatt deployments of chips in the Maia family, according to a blog post from Executive Vice President Scott Guthrie. But Alistair Speirs, a general manager, declined to provide a timeline. "We reserve a little bit of optionality there, because this is an industry that's changing very fast, and we want to deploy the right silicon for the right models that we're using at the right time as well," Speirs said. AI's quiet safety gatekeepers are stepping into the spotlight Microsoft's Nadella says AI needs an 'emergency brake' that humans control Nvidia GPUs are everywhere. Here are the ways companies are accessing them Hollywood takes on Zuckerberg, Musk and Altman amid widespread anxiety over AI Microsoft expects to pack 96 Maia 300 chips into each data center rack, double the number for the Maia 200. The new version can run through up to seven times more AI tokens per rack, with 40% more tokens per megawatt when compared with GPUs. "We need new architectures that will give us essentially better performance, better use of the power that we have," Speirs said. "You can think of power translating pretty directly into operational cost for something like a data center as well." Parts of Microsoft 365 Copilot should speed up with Maia 300, said Jim Kleewein, a technical fellow at the company. In a note distributed to clients on Wednesday, Evercore ISI analysts estimated that Maia will represent about 10% of Microsoft's spending on AI chips by the first quarter of 2027. The analysts recommend buying Microsoft shares. Nvidia will still be a big part of the equation. CEO Jensen Huang spoke at an event last week where Microsoft announced a Surface laptop containing an Nvidia processor. And when it comes to training models, Microsoft partners with Nvidia and AMD, Speirs said. Unlike Google's tensor processing units or Amazon's Inferentia and Trainium, Microsoft's accelerators can't be rented by the hour to other companies. "Nobody has tested them outside of Microsoft yet," said Patrick Moorhead, CEO of advisory firm Moor Insights and Strategy. WATCH: Melissa Otto: Nvidia is the bellwether of the AI trade

Text of this article October 12, 2026 UPDATE App Store Indie Games Week kicks off today Seven acclaimed indie games, including Sifu, Vampire Crawlers, and No Man’s Sky, make their App Store debut Today, Indie Games Week lights up the App Store with a celebration of the incredible catalog of imaginative games made by independent teams with big dreams. Players worldwide can jump into their next adventure with seven highly acclaimed indie games, available for download or pre-order on iPhone and iPad. All week, the App Store will spotlight these indie gems with daily features and curated collections. “Indie games are constantly pushing the boundaries of creativity to deliver unique gameplay experiences to Apple users, and we wanted to take a moment to celebrate these games and the teams that take creative risks to push gaming forward,” said Carson Oliver, Apple’s head of App Store Worldwide. “Whether from a solo developer or a growing studio, the App Store gives bold ideas a global stage — turning daring visions into worldwide hits. We’re thrilled with the incredible games launching on the App Store this week and amazed by their breathtaking artistry, brilliant design, and deeply moving stories.” There are whole new worlds to discover during Indie Games Week, from building empires, to brawling through cinematic combat, to getting lost in another universe entirely. With the critically acclaimed Sifu , Indie Games Week puts the art of combat front and center. This stylish third-person brawler follows a young kung fu student on a relentless path of revenge. Battles are ferocious and unforgiving, with enemies attacking simultaneously, forcing players to parry strikes, chain combos, and weaponize everything around them. Sifu arrives fully adapted for iPhone and iPad, with custom-tuned touch controls, a reworked camera system, and full controller support. For players looking for quick bursts of strategy mixed with dark humor, Vampire Crawlers is an invitation to rough up skeletons, bats, and other nefarious creeps in a gothic card battler. The spin-off of the smash hit Vampire Survivors cleverly trades dodging bullets for tactical deck building. Players conquer chaotic dungeon runs by discovering game-changing card combos, uncovering secret relics, and mastering the luck of the draw. After celebrating a decade of continuous evolution, Hello Games’ groundbreaking space odyssey No Man’s Sky makes its mobile debut on iPhone and iPad on October 28. The game includes every major content expansion to date, including the most recent Cosmos update, where players can command their own space stations. Set in an infinite, procedurally generated universe rendered entirely at runtime, No Man’s Sky lets players explore, trade, fight, and survive across an interconnected galaxy — all in the palm of their hands. Also this week, players can guide a curious feline through an open-world metropolis in Little Kitty, Big City , assemble card armies to conquer royal adversaries in the strategic kingdom builder 9 Kings , dig deep to fend off foes in the alien mining simulator Dome Keeper , or grapple with agonizing moral choices to save a crumbling empire in Yes, Your Grace 2: Snowfall . All will be featured throughout Indie Games Week and are available now to download on the App Store. events.title: Microsoft bets on home-grown AI chip to challenge Nvidia
events.summary: By making the chips the main hardware for running AI across its products, Microsoft’s reliance on Nvidia could be reduced. SAN FRANCISCO – Microsoft said on Oct 12 it will roll out its in-house Maia artificial intelligence chips on a massive scale starting in 2027, making them the main hardware for running AI across its products – a move that could reduce its reliance on Nvidia. Chips like Maia are the technology inside the vast data centres powering the AI boom, and Microsoft plans to deploy enough of them to draw several gigawatts of electricity – roughly the output of several large nuclear reactors. Nvidia has held a near-lock on the chips used to train AI models, but tech giants and rival chipmakers are now racing to stake out positions in inference – the work of running those models to answer questions and carry out tasks once they are up and running. That market is expanding fast as companies roll out AI assistants and so-called agents that perform multi-step jobs on their own, with Nvidia, AMD, Amazon and Google all pushing out new products in the space. “Today marks a new phase for Microsoft’s AI infrastructure,” Microsoft executive vice-president Scott Guthrie wrote in a blog post announcing the plans. The company said the Maia 200 chip is already operational, including for the Microsoft 365 Copilot assistant, while a more powerful successor, the Maia 300, will launch in 2027. Maia 200 runs models from OpenAI, Microsoft’s own in-house MAI models and leading open-source models. The chip is deployed in the United States, Europe and Australia, and delivers up to 1.7 times more output per watt than leading GPU-based systems for AI features built into Teams and Copilot, according to the company. Microsoft said the Maia 300 will squeeze 40% more AI work out of the same amount of electricity than leading systems, and more than twice as much as its own previous chip. Energy efficiency has become a central concern for tech companies racing to build data centres, as the electricity demands of AI strain power grids and drive up costs. Each server rack, a cabinet-sized unit in a data centre, will hold 96 of the chips, twice as many as before, and handle up to seven times the workload, the company said. The new chip’s computing components will be manufactured by Taiwan’s TSMC. In a separate post, Microsoft engineers said a big focus was cutting the power wasted moving data back and forth inside the machines, a growing problem as AI tools handle more complex tasks. The systems are mostly cooled with liquid, but Microsoft said they can also run in older data centres cooled by air. AFP

events.title: We were scared of living too far from our aging parents. Instead of either of us moving home, we found a compromise.
events.summary: Direct flights have made it easier to go back to our hometowns and for our parents to visit us in Vancouver, too. Courtesy of Susanna Kelly-Shankar My husband and I loved living in Munich, though his parents were in Australia and mine in Alaska. As our parents got older, we wanted visiting them to be easier, but neither of us wanted to go home. We settled on Vancouver, which offers decent flight options to where our parents reside. Alaska is a bucket-list travel destination for many. For me, it's the place I call home, but I found myself itching to leave as an adult. After years of traveling, I felt like I was changing, while my hometown stayed frozen in time. I was ready for a permanent adventure abroad, and so I set my sights on moving to Europe. Then one fateful evening, while climbing the corporate ladder to finance my European dream, I met a traveling Australian who shared a similar vision of life abroad — it felt like kismet. Through distance, we stayed connected, fantasizing about a move. One day, I finally took the leap, packed my life into a few suitcases, and moved halfway across the world to Munich, taking the chance on an exciting new relationship and life in Germany . The first few months were tough. Our days were full of navigating visas, cultural differences, bureaucracy, language learning, and apartment hunting — but the challenges delivered big rewards. Over six transformative years, Munich became our home. We built lifelong friendships and discovered a healthy work-life balance. Our relationship became rock-solid, and we flew to Las Vegas to get married. Not long after, we were granted permanent residency. People asked us why we chose to move to Germany . Our answer felt easy: Europe was a dream, but logistically, it was a sort of middle ground between the United States and Australia, a place where we both had to start over on equal footing. I often joked that I was a German at heart, and living in Munich felt like a homecoming in many ways, so I never saw myself leaving after working so hard to get here. It was the perfect halfway point — until it wasn't. While looking for a compromise, we set our sights on Vancouver Although we loved Munich, we didn't feel we could stay so far from our parents. Courtesy of Susanna Kelly-Shankar The COVID-19 pandemic brought our lives and global travel to a screeching halt. Seemingly overnight, our idyllic place between Sydney and Eagle River felt impossibly far away. With our parents in a high-risk group, I had anxiety every time my phone rang, wondering if it would be the kind of news that would call me home. But in Munich, where traveling to Anchorage would take me about a day, I might not be able to get home in time. Living half a world away from our aging parents went from being an exciting life adventure to a stressful and agonizing distance. That was when we started having the conversation about moving home. It was hard to walk away from everything we built in Germany, but in our heart of hearts, we knew it was time to be closer to our loved ones. My partner and I had wedding celebrations in three different places. Courtesy of Susanna Kelly-Shankar But where is home when you're a multinational couple ? How could we choose between his parents in Sydney and my parents in Alaska? To make matters more complicated, neither of us was ready to return to our home countries. We started exploring a compromise that might allow us to support both families. I have dual Canadian citizenship through my dad, and Vancouver, Canada, shot to the top of our shortlist because of its frequent flights year-round to Sydney and seasonal direct flights to Anchorage. (Offseason, I could fly home via Seattle with a quick stopover.) Once the world reopened, we began the big international move process all over again, navigating visas, friendships, pet relocation, and apartment hunting. It didn't take long for our move to pay off We've been settling into our life in Canada. Courtesy of Susanna Kelly-Shankar The moment I landed in Vancouver, my heart ached for life in Munich. I wasn't sure I could adjust to both the culture shock of living in Canada and the reverse culture shock of being back in North America. Our decision paid off almost immediately, and any fears I had over making the right choice disappeared. Shortly after moving, my dad had a sudden cardiac arrest while playing ice hockey. Within hours, I was on a direct three-hour flight home and by his side in the hospital, able to support him and my mom during his long recovery. Now, it doesn't take too long for me to fly back to Alaska. Courtesy of Susanna Kelly-Shankar Similarly, my partner has made relatively quick-turnaround trips to Sydney, like when he went home to help his dad through a double knee-replacement surgery. His options now include daily direct flights that take about 15 hours — a significant reduction from the previous 22-plus-hour indirect options from Munich. It's been nice to be able to visit my hometown, Eagle River, more easily. Courtesy of Susanna Kelly-Shankar As time goes on and our parents continue to age, being as close as we can to our families has been a true privilege and blessing. We went from seeing our families once every few years to several times a year. Six years away in Munich, both my partner and I realized how much time we lost with our parents; the years of aging suddenly seemed to hit all at once. Apart from being there for the lows, I get to be there for the highs, too. I've been around for more birthdays, more celebrations, and more stories parents can pass on face-to-face Making memories with our parents while we still have them is more important than living out our dream in Germany. Over time, I have found immense happiness in Canada, where, surrounded by mountains and ocean, I get the raw, rugged nature I miss so much about Alaska, the freedom to work for myself, and the benefits of living in such a multicultural city with my partner. We certainly plan to stay a while. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Israeli academic and Al Jazeera contributor Ori Goldberg dies at 50
events.summary: Goldberg, a regular Al Jazeera contributor, died after a long battle with colon cancer, his family says in a statement. Israeli academic and independent analyst Ori Goldberg has died at the age of 50, his family has said. His eldest daughter Avigail confirmed his death after a long battle with colon cancer in a statement on Goldberg’s X account on Sunday. “In one sentence, he was the best dad in the world. But you can’t really describe him in one sentence, and I don’t think I’ll have the courage to try,” she wrote. In a separate post on Goldberg’s X account, his eldest son, identified as Dave, said his father was “the light where things looked dark”. Goldberg was a frequent contributor to Al Jazeera’s website where his opinion pieces focused on Middle East affairs. In his final piece for the Qatar-based media network last month, he wrote about Israeli authorities’ reaction to the award-winning documentary NAZA , by Yuval Avraham and Rachel Szor. In a memorable piece titled Israel is imploding in December 2025, he explored whether Israel could be losing its status as regional hegemon while the Israeli state and society become increasingly dysfunctional. “An international coalition, led by the United States with the participation of Qatar, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye, is gradually removing Gaza from Israel’s control, as well as pressuring Israel out of its territorial escapades in Syria and Lebanon,” he wrote. In another piece from the same month titled Netanyahu will win again he explained why the Israeli prime minister’s supporters would likely vote for him in a 2026 election. “He is ‘their’ man, the one who represents them against the elites who feel the country is theirs by right. He alone, through his audacity and cunning, took the fight to Israel’s enemies and brought them to their knees.” he wrote. “[Netanyahu] is the one who broke the paradigm that put Israel at the mercy of the world. Israel now does as it wishes, and those desires are for Israel alone to articulate”. Goldberg also appeared regularly on Al Jazeera English news and current affairs shows including Inside Story. He received a PhD in History from Tel Aviv University in 2008 and wrote his dissertation on the role of religious experience in the creation and application of Iranian Shia revolutionary discourse during the second half of the 20th century. He received many awards and scholarships, including a fellowship at the Mellon Foundation from 2013 to 2015.

events.title: What are the key matches to watch as the UEFA Champions League returns?
events.summary: Atletico vs Man United and Man City vs PSG headline the Champions League match day two action as the competition returns. The UEFA Champions League (UCL) 2026-27 enters its second round of matches this week, with 36 teams in action across Europe as clubs return to the elite football competition. After the first set of league fixtures, two-time title holders Paris Saint-Germain lead the points table with three points, followed by six-time champions Bayern Munich and five-time winners Barcelona, who also won their opening matches. list 1 of 4 Barcelona beat Getafe as Gordon scores his first goal list 2 of 4 Lionel Messi returns from Argentina farewell as Inter Miami face DC United list 3 of 4 Mohamed Salah sets Turkish Super Lig record for Trabzonspor list 4 of 4 Man City beat 10-man Liverpool 3-0 in first game after guilty verdict The competition’s league phase format, now in its third year, started in September and runs until January 2027. It will be followed by the knockout rounds, with the champions crowned in early June. Here’s all you need to know about this year’s competition: The Champions League is an annual club competition that features the best teams from across Europe. This season marks the third time that 36 teams will participate in the main round, an increase from 32 under the old format. What is the 2026-27 Champions League format? Since 2003, the UCL has featured 32 clubs split into eight groups of four, with the top two from each section advancing to the last 16. That has changed radically in recent years. From the 2024-25 season, the 36 clubs are pooled into a single league in a “Swiss system” more commonly associated with chess. Earlier, participating teams played six games in the group stage, facing each opponent home and away. Now, each club plays eight games, one each against eight different opponents. How does the Champions League knockout format work? At the end of the league phase, the top eight qualify directly for the knockouts, while those between the ninth and 24th places have to compete in two-legged knockout-phase playoffs. Teams ranked 25th and below are eliminated. The UCL knockout format is straightforward – it begins with the round of 16, followed by the quarterfinals, semifinals and the final. When are the league phase and knockout matches? The league phase matches are scheduled for: The knockout phase matches are scheduled for (all dates in 2027): Playoffs: February 16, 17 and 23, 24 Round of 16: March 9, 10 and 16, 17 Quarterfinals: April 6, 7 and 13, 14 Semifinals: April 27, 28 and May 4, 5 Which are the best Champions League matches to watch? The key matches to follow on matchdays two and three are as follows: Top five UCL matches to watch this week Arsenal vs Lille , Tuesday 19:00 GMT Atletico vs Manchester United , Tuesday 19:00 GMT Galatasaray vs Barcelona , Tuesday 19:00 GMT Manchester City vs PSG , Wednesday 19:00 GMT AS Roma vs Real Madrid , Wednesday 19:00 GMT Top five Champions League matches to watch next week: PSG vs Barcelona , October 20, 19:00 GMT Liverpool vs Villarreal , October 20, 19:00 GMT Como vs Manchester United , October 21, 16:45 GMT Bayern Munich vs Arsenal , October 21, 19:00 GMT Real Madrid vs RB Leipzig , October 21, 19:00 GMT What are the key UCL storylines to follow? Man City’s home clash with PSG headlines the upcoming round of matches, marking the troubled Etihad club’s first Champions League match since an independent commission found them guilty of breaking more than 100 Premier League financial rules . Elsewhere, City’s crosstown rivals, under-fire Man United, are also in action this week. They head to Madrid to face an in-form Atletico, hoping to register just their third win this season. Meanwhile, manager Jose Mourinho will face his former club AS Roma when Real travel to the Italian capital. Who are the top players to watch in the Champions League? PSG’s Ferran Torres, who scored a hat-trick in the first UCL match, is a joint top scorer in this year’s UCL alongside Ermedin Demirovic of Stuttgart. Also watch out for Man City’s Erling Haaland, Bayern Munich’s talented Michael Olise and PSG forward Ousmane Dembele, all of whom scored two goals in their respective UCL openers.

events.title: Nobel prize for economics awarded to two Americans, Hall and Woodford, for work on New Keynesian models – business live
events.summary: Nobel Prize for Economics awarded to Hall and Woodford Newsflash: The Nobel Prize for economics has been awarded to Robert E Hall and Michael Woodford, for their work on the “microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation”. [Reminder: As we flagged earlier , Woodford was among the predicted winners – he’s one of the architects of modern forward guidance, the idea that central banks can control the economy through influencing public expectations about inflation, rather than just through interest rates.] The S veriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel is worth 12 million Swedish kronor (£900,000), plus the glory of course, and the knowledge that every pronouncement you make now comes with the authority of a Nobel Prize winner. 44m ago HMV to quit historic Oxford Street store, again.... 3h ago Just three women have ever won Nobel economics prize 3h ago Praise for Woodford and Hall is starting to pour in 4h ago How Hall created the fresh-water and salt-water economic divide 4h ago Who are our latest Nobel Economics laureates?.... 4h ago How Hall and Woodford's work on microfoundations won Nobel Prize 4h ago Nobel Prize for Economics awarded to Hall and Woodford 5h ago Watch the Nobel economics prize announcement here 5h ago AFP: Nobel watchers guess who gets economics' top prize 6h ago EU sets cap on imports of hybrid EVs from China 7h ago IFS warns UK faces £35bn budget shortfall 8h ago Who might win the Nobel prize for economics today? 8h ago Introduction: UK business inflation pressures hits three-year high; The euro is having a bad day, dropping to a 16-month low against the pound. Expectations that the Bank of England will raise interest rates next month appear to have lifted the pound to €1.1836, the highest since June 2025. Enrique Díaz-Alvarez , chief economist at global financial services firm Ebury , says: “The sterling rally against the common currency continues to hit fresh 16-month highs, with the pound also stabilising against the US dollar. “As in the previous week, this was more about the euro’s troubles than about any good news in Britain. Markets increasingly expect the Bank of England to raise rates at its 5th November meeting and we concur, though we still see this as no more than a one off insurance hike. We will this week hear from MPC members Mann, Greene and Pill - the three members who voted for a hike in September. Back in the financial markets, the oil price is pushing higher after Saudi Arabia was hit by new attacks. Brent crude is now up 2% at $106.80 a barrel, after Saudi Arabia said it was facing a new barrage of incoming fire on Monday. Riyadh airport remains shut after a deadly missile strike on a departure terminal on Saturday, that was claimed by Yemen’s Iran-allied Houthis. HMV to quit historic Oxford Street store, again.... Away from the Nobel economics prize announcement….HMV is preparing to exit its London flagship on Oxford Street in March - just over three years after reopening there with great fanfair – as the landlord proposed doubling the rent. The entertainment retailer said it was now seeking alternative sites on the capital’s main high street, or another central location, as it had been trading strongly, my colleague Sarah Butler reports. The latest closure comes after HMV returned to the site in November 2023 after closing in 2019 leaving the store empty for an extended period before a brief stint housing one of many American candy stores that popped up on Oxford Street during the pandemic. HMV , which currently has 114 stores under its own brand across the UK and a further six Fopp sites, said a proposed increase in rent which is already understood to be well over £1m a year – coupled with a requirement to fund substantial renovation works on the Oxford Street building – would make the store “commercially unsustainable”, leaving it with no choice but to seek an alternative site. The store was HMV’s very first, and was opened in 1921 by Sir Edward Elgar , the British composer. Since then it has played host to a number of British bands, including a rooftop gig by Blur in 1995 and the Spice Girls’ Christmas lights switch-on the following year. It is understood the Hong Kong-based landlord has signed a lease with an alternative tenant. Phil Halliday , managing director of HMV , said: “This is a special store, it’s where we began 100 years ago and bringing it back to life in 2023 was a big moment in our recent history. It’s frustrating that it has been made commercially unviable. However, we are looking ahead, and our focus is now on what we do to make exciting steps for hmv in 2027.” He said sales were up by a quarter year-on-year at the Oxford Street store and 15% at established UK stores in the first nine months of 2026 as sales of both vinyl records and CDs continued to sell well and more shoppers came into stores. “We have put together an offer that works across a number of generations,” Halliday added.

events.title: OPay readies $4B New York IPO
events.summary: The News OPay, the Lagos-based fintech firm backed by Softbank and Chinese billionaire Zhou Yahui, more than doubled its revenue in the first half of 2026 as lending overtook payments as its top source of income, according to a filing ahead of a planned New York listing likely set for next month. The company has applied to trade under the ticker OPAY, with a potential Nigerian secondary listing to follow. The filing lays out a business growing rapidly after jumping 137% to $467 million in revenue in the first half of 2026 while net income rocketed by over 300% to $91 million. OPay launched in Nigeria as a payments company in 2018 backed by Chinese investors and later funded by venture investors led by Softbank. OPay hadn’t disclosed an IPO price range or a listing date as Semafor was going to press but based on the normal sequence of filings and roadshows, investors will be expecting pricing to be revealed in mid-November. Previous reports have put the initial valuation estimates around $4 billion. The fintech firm also outlined plans for a secondary listing on the Nigeria Stock Exchange after the NYSE debut to give local investors an opportunity to buy into a business that drives nearly nine-tenths of its revenue from Nigeria. But the F-1 filing warned investors that shares traded in Lagos may not be exchangeable for the New York-listed American depositary shares, potentially limiting liquidity and allowing prices to diverge. Know More A key part of the IPO is a broader strategic relationship with Standard Bank Group, Africa’s largest lender by assets. Its subsidiary, Stanbic Africa Holdings, has agreed to invest up to $200 million, subject to a formula that caps its stake at 4.99% of OPay after the offering. Standard Bank’s Africa head Lungisa Fuzile is expected to join OPay’s board following the IPO. The two companies have also signed a non-binding memorandum of understanding to explore partnerships spanning payments, merchant acquisition, lending, remittances and the distribution of selected banking and financial products. OPay suggested in the filings that it will use Standard Bank’s infrastructure, regulatory expertise and presence to expand across Africa. Step Back OPay took off in 2019 in Nigeria with ambitions to be a super app that offered various features, including motorcycle taxi bookings, food deliveries, and quick loans. But it narrowed its focus to financial services in recent years and raised $570 million in venture funds between 2018 and 2021. A handful of African tech companies have successfully listed in the US, notably e-commerce platform Jumia and telecom towers provider IHS but have had mixed performances. An OPay listing in the US would be the first by a fintech company with a mostly Nigerian customer base.

events.title: Feds search Rep. Ilhan Omar's home in immigration probe
events.summary: Federal agents conducted a pre-dawn search Monday at the Washington home of Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.) as part of an ongoing immigration probe, a DOJ spokesperson confirmed to Axios. Why it matters: Searching Omar's home marks a substantial escalation of the Trump administration's fight with the outspoken progressive, who has condemned the immigration crackdown in her state. Driving the news: Fox News first reported that Homeland Security Investigations agents conducted the search, citing a Justice Department statement. A DOJ spokesperson confirmed to Axios that DHS agents "executed a judicially authorized search warrant secured by the Department of Justice" as part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation. DHS referred Axios to the DOJ. Rep. Omar's office immediately responded to Axios' requests for comment. Last month, border czar Tom Homan confirmed an ongoing criminal probe into Omar, though he declined to offer details. Fox reported Monday that the search was tied to a fraud investigation into Omar's immigration paperwork. The Somali native came to the U.S. in 1995 as a 12-year-old refugee. The intrigue: President Trump has made Minnesota's Somali community one of the most frequent targets of his anti-immigration rhetoric, and Omar the face of those attacks. Just last week, he called on Minnesotans to " fight back " against the state's Somalian population. He's also specifically demanded that Omar leave the country, or that she be deported . events.title: FAA warns U.S. airlines of safety risks over Saudi Arabia after attacks
events.summary: The FAA warned U.S. airlines about safety risks flying in or near Saudi Arabia after attacks on one of the country's biggest airports. Delta Air Lines is scheduled to launch its first nonstop flight between Atlanta and Riyadh later this month, but said it hasn't decided whether it will go ahead. The Federal Aviation Administration told U.S. airlines to exercise caution when flying in or around Saudi Arabia after deadly attacks claimed by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis, which have shut down the airport in the Saudi capital. King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, remains closed as of Monday after strikes that started last week. The attacks escalated Saturday, when a projectile struck a passenger terminal at the airport, officials said, killing at least 12 people and wounding more than 300. Airlines suspended flights to the airport, some for the rest of the week. The U.S., Australia and other countries advised citizens against travel to the region. The FAA late Sunday said pilots should "exercise caution" in or around Saudi Arabia "due to safety-of-flight risks associated with ongoing military activities" and navigation systems. It said the threats could be a potential risk "to aircraft at all altitudes." The FAA's warning is in effect until Dec. 10. Most U.S. airlines don't fly to Saudi Arabia. Delta Air Lines is scheduled to launch its first nonstop flight from Atlanta to Riyadh on Oct. 23. CEO Ed Bastian said in an interview Thursday, before the Saturday missile attack, that "safety is going to make the call" on whether to operate the flight as planned. As of Sunday night, Delta hadn't changed its plans, a spokeswoman said. events.title: Banks are set to report this week. Here's what the options market expects
events.summary: Bank earnings kick off this week with no fewer than seven of the biggest names set to report. With the S&P 500 near all-time highs, the results could provide a significant market catalyst. Financials are the third-worst performing S&P 500 sector in 2026. Despite being flat on the year, the options market is pricing in some big moves as investor weigh the impact of higher rates and stretched consumer. Here's what the options market sees, according to the latest Cboe LiveVol data. Goldman Sachs - Tuesday, Oct. 13 The options market is pricing in a 2.84% move for Goldman Sachs after it reports earnings. Across the last eight reported quarters, the stock has moved just about 2% on average. Only three of those quarters have seen a negative stock reaction, with the most recent being a 1.87% move lower in April. The stock rallied a whopping 9% after July's Q2 report, which is the largest post-earnings move since January, 2019. JPMorgan - Tuesday, Oct. 13 Options are pricing in a move similar to Goldman Sachs for JPMorgan, with a 2.5% implied move inline with its past eight quarter average of 2.22%. Unlike Goldman, JPMorgan's recent reports haven't been met with much positivity. The stock's 2.5% move higher following July's report was its first positive reaction since April, 2025, when it jumped 4% higher. Odeh said the explosion had “mobilised” Israel’s political echelons, with the Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu heading to the area, and the Israeli minister of National Security National Ben Gvir canceling a political engagement that was on his agenda.

events.title: Meet the scrappy entrepreneurs getting their piece of the AI buildout pie
events.summary: National Jobsite Catering serves about 1,500 meals on an average day at each of its dozen data center construction sites. Jason Andrew for BI At 5 a.m. in Northern Virginia , chefs are already preparing chicken and chile roja enchiladas, fried shrimp tacos, and big batches of rice and beans to feed thousands of data center construction workers. By late morning, a crew brings the food from the off-site kitchen to a break tent where workers can pick up lunch without leaving the worksite. They don't pay: The Big Tech companies spending billions on AI infrastructure foot the bill. On an average day, National Jobsite Catering serves about 1,500 meals at each of its dozen data center construction sites across Northern Virginia, Texas, Ohio, Louisiana , Nevada, and Georgia, founder Scott Kaplan tells me. The busiest sites serve twice as many. After one to three years, the crews wrap up and move on. Kaplan, whose business used to consist of a fleet of food trucks catering one-off events along the East Coast, designed a venture that can follow them. If you build it, they will cook. Local restaurants and caterers partner with National Jobsite Catering to scale up and serve an influx of workers. Jason Andrew for BI National Jobsite Catering is part of the economic ecosystem being generated by America's data center boom. The tech giants leading the AI buildout are expected to spend more than $5 trillion on technology and data centers through 2030, with more than 1,500 data centers already in the works in the US. The room where a worker sleeps , the gym he hits before his shift, his parking spot, his lunch — these are all provided by a growing network of businesses. Local firms in the suburban and rural areas where the bulk of data centers are being built can get a windfall from a single project, but a more lasting proposition is the opportunity to serve site-to-site as construction crews move around. Whether that translates into lasting benefits for host towns is at the heart of growing pushback against the wave of data centers popping up across the country. Kaplan recognized the new opportunity a few years ago when a hyperscaler hired him to bring trucks to a site outside Philadelphia to feed 2,500 workers. "Literally the town that it was in had one restaurant — and it was in a strip club," he says. To avoid a lunch-hour bottleneck, Kaplan proposed preparing meals in a temporary kitchen and bringing them to the site. After replicating this model for other projects, his company now has 20 full-time employees and partners with established local vendors, helping them add equipment and plan production. He estimates a project can employ about 15 local people in kitchen, delivery, and distribution roles. Studies of data center job creation show a drop-off when construction is complete. Jason Andrew for BI "They know what they're doing," Kaplan says of the local partners. "But they've never cooked for 1,000 to 3,000 people." Since pivoting to data centers exclusively four years ago, revenue has gone up 10X, Kaplan says. Before thousands of construction workers can arrive on-site, they need somewhere to leave their cars — a logistical challenge that's creating a new market. WhereiPark began as a marketplace for city parking spots, but its fastest-growing business now comes from leasing lots near data center construction sites. General contractors have asked WhereiPark to find as many as 2,000 spaces for a project. A church lot used mainly on Sundays might work, as might a struggling shopping center or a nearby fairground or casino. In more remote locations, a contractor may need to grade and stripe land. Local landowners, meanwhile, earn temporary income from unused space without selling the farm . "If there's nowhere for the construction workers to park, the thing doesn't get built," says Joshua Eisen, WhereiPark's chief revenue officer. A team in Toronto does much of the search via property data, calls, and emails; a partner or the general contractor then inspects a prospective lot locally. The company also partners with shuttle operators to ferry workers between the lots and construction sites. For a builder juggling several projects, that means one contact and billing relationship instead of a new search and lease negotiation in every town. A completed facility the size of a Walmart might have just 50 spaces, so most lots return to their previous use. WhereiPark can repeat the search around another project without owning land. With global AI investment expected to exceed a trillion dollars in 2026 alone, companies of all sizes are getting in on the gold rush. Food services and facilities management giant Aramark launched a new division called Nexus earlier this year, which offers hotel-like amenities, fitness centers, and recreation to help attract skilled workers. The company noted that Nexus contracts carry higher-than-average profit margins. Executives projected that three initial data center sites could each generate Aramark about $150 million in annualized revenue once fully running. Data center construction is creating a gold rush for businesses wanting to get in on the action. Jason Andrew for BI The data center housing business has a precedent in the oil patch, where companies have long followed temporary crews from project to project. Target Hospitality , a $1.8 billion company that has housed oilfield workers and operated two Texas detention centers for ICE, is building and operating accommodations for data center construction crews, including a $550 million deal for a 4,000-bed facility in North Texas. The company advertises furnished bedrooms equipped with small fridges and microwaves, as well as communal dining, gyms, and WiFi. Its modular assets can be redeployed elsewhere. In August, the company said it has secured contracts representing more than 9,000 beds and $1.4 billion since January. Facing growing opposition, hyperscalers have pitched the AI buildout as an engine of economic development , promising spillover benefits for local areas. Microsoft's "community-first" promise cited its experience in Washington state to estimate that for every direct construction job created, another is generated in sectors including security, maintenance, retail, and food service. While spillovers certainly occur, the exact level varies project to project. To capitalize on that before-and-after job creation , Salute sells data center clients security, safety oversight, and technical support during construction and facility management after it opens. The company, which has worked exclusively with data centers since its founding in 2013, brings in experienced staff to get sites running while recruiting and training locally. It tends to employ veterans and oil and gas workers accustomed to remote job sites, and hopes those who relocate will put down roots. events.title: AI minister warns 'likely' UK's cyber defences will be breached
events.summary: Published 12 October 2026, 13:11 BST The UK's AI minister has warned it is "likely, if not inevitable" the country's cyber defences will at some point be breached. Speaking at a press conference, Kanishka Narayan pointed to an incident of a rogue OpenAI agent hacking an Australian government website in June. He said while no medical records are known to have been accessed in the attack, the incident should still "concern us". Narayan said the government plans to put advanced AI to work to combat the threat, as he set out how the government plans to prepare for any serious future incidents. The minister said the move would build on two existing pilots which have helped identify and fix over 1,000 vulnerabilities across government systems. He said his message to the largest companies behind the world's most powerful AI systems was: "Listen when your scientists warn of serious dangers. Investigate unexpected behaviour. And if you cannot adequately control the risks, do not release the system." In his speech, Narayan also confirmed scientists at the UK's AI watchdog, the AI Security Institute (AISI), were conducting "rigorous evaluations" of the latest generation of advanced AI models to "identify risks early" and "to test robust safeguards to help keep people safe". AISI began evaluating risks of the latest frontier AI models, prior to their public release, shortly after it was established in November 2023. But it was reported in September , external that the White House had asked some leading US labs not to share their models with the research organisation until its own tests were completed. The move was viewed at the time as a blow to AISI - which has been championed by the UK government and its partners for advancing open, constructive and collaborative AI testing. Microsoft president Brad Smith recently told the BBC the institute had helped cement the UK as the country best-placed to drive forward global regulation. On Monday, Narayan said that in the last few weeks, the government had worked with the US "to retain access for Britain's AISI to the most powerful AI models before they are released". He also said the UK would also look into creating stronger protections through the Cyber Security and Resilience bill, particularly at how serious AI incidents can be identified and reported. The announcement follows a series of incidents involving AI agents across major firms such as OpenAI and Anthropic acting outside human control and hacking into external systems. On 9 September, Evan Hubinger, a top safety researcher at Anthropic, warned in a post on X that AI is advancing so quickly he believed there is a greater than 10% chance it "could kill all humans" within the next decade. The bosses of the US-based AI giants such as Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind have all backed the idea of an AI development slowdown . However, there are currently no global safety rules in place to regulate the companies and their technology. Meanwhile, President Trump has called for the sector to regulate itself so that US firms do not lose out to Chinese rivals. events.title: Americans Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford win Nobel memorial prize in economics
events.summary: STOCKHOLM -- American economists Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford won the Nobel Memorial Prize in economics Monday for their work on models that have helped governments and central banks manage economic shocks, such as energy crises and inflation. The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the winners in Stockholm, noting that their work created the theoretical foundation to better understand how consumers decide whether to save or spend, insights that make it easier for policymakers worldwide to stabilize economies after fluctuations. “The laureates’ research has made it possible to manage major macroeconomic crises far more effectively than before,” the Nobel committee wrote. “It has been hugely beneficial during the pandemic and the energy crises of recent years." Hall is affiliated with Stanford University in California, and Woodford with Columbia University in New York. Woodford spoke to the committee by phone from New York: “It’s a tremendous honor. It’s a surprise." For decades, governments responded to economic shocks by following the Depression-era prescriptions of the British economist John Maynard Keynes: Intervene in the economy by lowering taxes and hiking government spending, thereby encouraging consumers and businesses to spend and invest and help restart growth. “This is the Keynesian recipe and it worked well — until it didn’t,’’ said Timo Boppart of the Nobel economics committee. Policymakers had thought economic management involved simple trade-offs — unemployment, for instance, would stay low at a time of high inflation and rise when inflation fell. But the “ stagflation ’’ of the 1970s — when the world economy experienced simultaneous high inflation and high unemployment — proved the formula was simplistic. Some economists argued that government attempts to intervene in the economy were doomed to fail. But Hall and Woodford, in separate contributions, set about improving the Keynesian model to take into account how consumers and businesses actually make decisions about whether to invest and spend. “Economic outcomes are the result of millions of decisions made at the microlevel by households and businesses,’’ the Nobel committee wrote. “Using models based upon this approach, rather than simply studying the economy from a macro perspective, like a bird’s eye view," Hall and Woodford’s research "generated a paradigm shift in the theory of stabilization policy.’’ Hall studied the way that consumer decisions about whether and how much to spend depend on what they expect their future income to be. “If they are optimistic, they will consume more than if they are pessimistic,’’ the committee wrote. But consumer expectations can change unexpectedly as new information about the economy comes in. And some households are so poor they can’t borrow or tap savings in response to economic changes. In a 1982 paper with the economist Fredric Mishkin, Hall found that around 80% of households made spending decisions based on their expectations for the future “while the rest lived hand to mouth,’’ the committee wrote. “The prize is for research that pushes our understanding of macroeconomics from the bottom up, from families and firms making decisions over time, while looking ahead,” Ivan Werning, an economist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, said in an email. During the phone call broadcast at a news conference, Woodford said his work has stressed “the understanding of the people who are in the markets and making decisions about spending.” The economics prize is formally known as the Bank of Sweden Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel. The central bank established it in 1968 as a memorial to Nobel, the 19th-century Swedish businessman and chemist who invented dynamite and established the five Nobel Prizes. events.title: Intel, Broadcom CEOs warn capital crunch could become AI's biggest bottleneck
events.summary: Intel and Broadcom warned that access to capital could emerge as a major constraint on the artificial intelligence boom. "[What] I think might be the biggest constraint is capital," Hock Tan said at the DBS Asia Future Forward Conference in Singapore on Monday. SINGAPORE — The chief executives of Intel and Broadcom warned that access to capital could emerge as a major constraint on the artificial intelligence boom, even as demand for computing infrastructure continues to outstrip supply. Broadcom CEO Hock Tan said financing could become a bigger obstacle to AI expansion than shortages of semiconductors, memory chips or electricity, as the industry races to build the infrastructure needed to power increasingly sophisticated models. Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan echoed concerns about financing, pointing to the rising cost of capital and questions over whether companies investing heavily in AI will eventually generate sufficient returns. "If there's any challenge in the front, it's capital and the cost of capital, and then the other part is in the longer run, people want to see the ROI," he said. Their remarks highlight an emerging challenge for the AI industry, which has poured enormous sums into data centers, advanced chips and power infrastructure in anticipation of surging demand for computing capacity. The warnings come as rising borrowing costs threaten to complicate financing for technology companies investing heavily in AI infrastructure. Higher bond yields could make it more expensive to fund data center construction and chip purchases, potentially putting pressure on the economics of projects that may take years to generate returns. AI's quiet safety gatekeepers are stepping into the spotlight Microsoft's Nadella says AI needs an 'emergency brake' that humans control Nvidia GPUs are everywhere. Here are the ways companies are accessing them Hollywood takes on Zuckerberg, Musk and Altman amid widespread anxiety over AI Hock Tan said the industry has repeatedly encountered supply bottlenecks over the past two years, but expects some of those constraints to ease as production capacity expands. "[In the] last two years we have seen a series of bottlenecks that keep coming out, but then we overcome it," he said. "Memory shortage today might not be that way a year from now." He suggested that wafer shortages could ease by 2028 or 2029, while power availability could also improve as new infrastructure comes online. Despite the financing concerns, both executives remained bullish on near-term demand for AI computing infrastructure. "There is more demand for compute infrastructure than we can supply," Hock Tan said, adding that the imbalance could persist through 2029 and potentially into 2030. Intel’s Tan similarly said the industry was unlikely to experience a significant slowdown over the next two to three years, citing growing adoption of AI applications and demand for computing power. But sustaining that growth beyond the next few years will depend on how quickly businesses adopt AI and whether the technology delivers meaningful economic benefits, the executives said. Broadcom’s Tan cautioned that demand for computing infrastructure could slow if the adoption of advanced AI models disappoints or improvements in their capabilities begin to plateau. Lip-Bu Tan, meanwhile, emphasized that companies would increasingly need to demonstrate tangible returns from AI investments through improved efficiency and new business models.

events.title: BYD plans hiring spree to bolster European workforce to 40,000
events.summary: BYD executive vice-president Stella Li said the company’s workforce in Europe would be “absolutely over 40,000 in 2030”. PARIS – BYD said it is planning to go on a hiring spree in Europe and increase its workforce there to about 40,000 people by the end of the decade as the Chinese automotive giant seeks to evolve from a simple exporter to a major car producer in the region. “BYD’s commitment in Europe is very deep, and it is long term,” executive vice-president Stella Li, who heads the company’s overseas business, said in an interview at the Paris Motor Show with Bloomberg TV on Oct 12. Asked specifically about BYD’s European employment plans, Li said separately that its workforce there would be “absolutely over 40,000 in 2030”. The company will soon have more than 10,000, she said. That would make BYD one of the biggest non-European automotive employers in the region. The company, the world’s largest maker of electric vehicles, is deepening its investments there as Chinese exporters face increasing scrutiny from European authorities. BYD plans to recruit from the auto industry and beyond, including workers potentially laid off by European companies, she said. Talks between China and the European Union last week ended with a broad agreement that included curbs on the number of hybrid vehicles that would be imported from the Asian country. BYD is still assessing the implications of the EU’s new restrictions as the company did not yet have sufficient details, Li said. Meanwhile, the Shenzhen-based company is in the final stages of preparations for its first European factory, located in Hungary, aiming for mass production to begin in the fourth quarter, she said. Then the company will probably build its next couple of factories elsewhere in the region, with France and Spain being on the shortlist, Li said. BLOOMBERG

events.title: McKinsey: Automation could absorb half of U.S. work hours by 2035. The bigger challenge is skills
events.summary: Good morning. AI could automate more than half of U.S. work hours over the next decade. But that doesn’t mean half the workforce will disappear. That’s a key finding of new research from the McKinsey Global Institute (MGI). The report estimates that technological and economic changes could reduce labor demand by the equivalent of 36 million jobs over the next decade. At the same time, economic growth, including growth in AI-related industries and services, could create demand for about 41 million jobs. The U.S. could have more jobs in 2035 than today, even as technology changes how people work and the skills they need. The challenge is that new jobs may require skills that many workers don’t currently have. In fields such as management and law, where judgment, coordination and accountability matter, AI is more likely to help people do their jobs than replace them outright, according to the report. It may also create new responsibilities that require training, from checking AI-generated work to ensuring its responsible use and redesigning workflows. Office and administrative support roles face particular exposure to automation, with roughly 80% of current work hours potentially automated by 2035. That doesn’t mean 80% of jobs will disappear, but it signals how significantly these roles could change. For some workers, adapting will mean moving into entirely different occupations. MGI estimates that about 11 million Americans may need to leave declining occupations for new ones. Others may be able to stay in their fields as their work evolves. Still, roughly 770,000 workers a year may need to change occupations over the next decade—about 3.6 times the historical rate, according to McKinsey senior partners Eric Kutcher, the firm’s former CFO, and Tanguy Catlin, director of MGI. Credentials present another hurdle. About 85% of growing employment requires a credential or certification. For 38% of those jobs, the credential is legally required; for another 47%, employers prefer it. The research suggests companies could widen their talent pools by rethinking which qualifications are essential and giving greater weight to proven skills and experience. MGI recommends tracking whether employees move into new roles, whether companies fill more positions internally and how workers fare, not just AI-related cost savings. Finance leaders could examine how employees use the time AI frees up. Is it used to improve customer service, develop new ideas, grow the business or tackle more complex work? Or does it simply reduce the time spent on existing tasks? The key question isn’t just how much work AI can take on. It’s what the business does with the time it saves. events.title: Former Plaud exec raises $26M for AI app that listens to you in the background

One of the core promises of AI is that the more it knows about a person, the better it will be able to assist them with tasks and make appropriate suggestions, which, if you’ll believe the tech companies, requires apps and devices to listen, watch or record users’ activity all the time and gather all possible context. There’s obviously privacy and data security concerns with anything that’s collecting data about you continuously. But startups are building such apps undeterred anyway, arming themselves with the belief that the market for personalized assistance is big enough to swallow such concerns. Former Plaud exec Peter Mo is building Ambi to do something similar. The app aims to provide real-time intelligence and insights to people by listening to them all the time. The company said on Monday that it has raised $26 million across multiple funding rounds led by Luminous Ventures, which has backed companies like Meituan and Unitree Robotics, and Original Design Manufacturer (ODM) Huaqin. Ambi is also releasing apps for iPhones, Macs and Apple Watch. These apps act like meeting note-takers, but users can choose to have them listening so they can capture context all day. Meeting note-taking companies have been working to automate tasks that follow once calls are done, based on the summaries and action items they gather during the conversation, and using multitudes of connectors to software systems. Ambi wants to take this a step further by having its agent start the work during the meeting itself. The company’s promise is that its AI agent can proactively give you suggestions or surface relevant knowledge while you are in a meeting, based on your calendar, meetings, knowledge base, and web data. Users can also start a task on one device and continue it on another. “The way we interact with intelligence is limited. Often the intelligence is trapped on the screen, and if you use hardware like Plaud, you need to wait for recording to transfer to the phone, upload to the cloud, and get intelligence after processing. That’s why we are building Ambi to use AI anytime and anywhere,” the company’s co-founder and CEO, Mo, told TechCrunch. The company has ambitions to capture more information. Its upcoming desktop app will be able to look at the work that users do and store important parts in its memory to give more personalized suggestions. Apps like Littlebird or Minimi already do something similar. The startup is also planning to launch its own hardware device, which will have a screen, a speaker, a camera, and microphones to capture context and display information. Ambi’s launch comes amidst growing concerns around AI devices that don’t have enough indicators to suggest they are capturing data on people around the user. It is not clear if Ambi’s apps or its upcoming device will have enough indicators to alert third-parties that their conversations are being recorded if the user doesn’t disclose their use of Ambi’s tech. Some meeting note-takers have even been sued because their tech recorded people’s conversation and data without their consent. Plus, the recent release of Apple’s Voice Intelligence feature, which transcribes speech continuously, has raised privacy concerns . Mo said that users can turn off ambient data capture on Ambi’s apps and devices at any time, and the feature is off by default. The startup said it doesn’t store any recordings of users and encrypts the data, but it didn’t specify what kind of encryption it uses. Despite these measures, the onus of declaring ambient capture is still on the users. He classified this as an industry-wide problem. “We have to inform our users that they have to tell others about ambient capture. We, as an industry, haven’t solved this problem [of disclosure]. We have tried to put the information about disclosure in every place possible, but if users try to hide the capture, we can’t just solve the problem,” he said. Ambi currently has over 50 staff across offices in San Francisco, Beijing, Shanghai and Shenzhen. events.title: What happens if a rogue AI agent goes on a spending spree? Mastercard is preparing for that risk
events.summary: AI agents are already defying instructions and taking actions their creators never intended. Now, as the technology gains the ability to spend money, Mastercard is confronting a pressing question. How do you keep autonomous software under control? The risks are increasingly tangible. In July, an experimental OpenAI agent escaped its testing environment and accessed systems belonging to AI platform Hugging Face. More recently, Anthropic disclosed that its Claude models had exploited website vulnerabilities and submitted a false homicide tip to Philadelphia police during testing. For Mastercard president and chief technology officer Ed McLaughlin, these concerns are especially relevant as the payments giant prepares for a future in which AI agents can independently make purchases and transact with other machines. “This probably is what I’m most excited about,” McLaughlin said in an interview with Fortune Next to Lead . Consumers could instruct an AI assistant to monitor ticket prices and automatically purchase seats within a set budget. Mastercard’s Agent Pay technology is designed to facilitate those transactions, while Agent Pay for Machines allows autonomous systems to transact with one another within defined parameters. But giving AI agents the authority to spend money also means giving them the power to make costly mistakes. An agent could book a nonrefundable flight for the wrong date while staying within its authorized budget. That raises a thornier question for Mastercard and the broader financial industry. Who is responsible when an AI agent follows the rules but makes the wrong decision? That challenge reflects a dilemma facing business leaders today as AI agents move from assisting employees and consumers to making decisions on their behalf. How much independence should companies give these systems, and what safeguards need to be in place before they act? McLaughlin says the key is knowing which AI agent is making a purchase, who permitted it, and what it’s allowed to buy. ‘”Part of it is bringing humans back into the loop,” he said. “So even if the agent goes rogue and tries to do something, you can say no.” Whether those safeguards will persuade consumers to hand over their purchasing power remains to be seen. McLaughlin, however, expects agentic commerce to follow the trajectory of online shopping and mobile payments, which initially faced skepticism before becoming routine as consumers experienced their convenience firsthand. As companies give AI agents more authority, executives face a new responsibility: leaders must decide what those systems can do, when humans should intervene, and who answers when something goes wrong. McLaughlin says that at Mastercard, whose network spans 3.7 billion accounts worldwide, those controls are essential to moving quickly. His guiding philosophy is a pointed departure from Silicon Valley’s longstanding mantra: “Move fast and don’t break things.” Ruth Umoh ruth.umoh@fortune.com This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Zelenskyy accuses Russia of violating Trump’s energy ceasefire as drone attacks continue
events.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy welcomed the U.S.-brokered "energy ceasefire" but warned that Moscow must do the same. "All morning today, more and more Russian jet-powered shaheds have continued to enter our skies over Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities," Zelenskyy said Monday. The Kremlin said that contacts are ongoing regarding an energy ceasefire, and that they would provide more information in due course. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy welcomed the U.S.-brokered "energy ceasefire" but warned Monday that Kyiv would retaliate if Moscow failed to comply, as fresh Russian drone attacks targeted Ukraine's energy infrastructure just hours after President Donald Trump announced the agreement. "If the Americans need it, we are ready to sign these guarantees to make sure they can be trusted, and it's important that we all see this situation in the same way," he said, addressing the Warsaw Security Forum via video link. "All morning today, more and more Russian jet-powered shaheds have continued to enter our skies over Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities. We shoot down many of them, and if we didn't, there would clearly be even more damage to our energy infrastructure," he said. "For now, this is Putin's answer to Trump." He added: "If Russia does not agree to an energy ceasefire, we will respond." It comes after Zelenskyy lamented Russia's continued drone attacks on Ukrainian energy targets on Sunday, including an attack on a power plant in Kharkiv in Eastern Ukraine close to the Russian border. Overnight, Russia attacked state-owned Ukrainian energy company Naftogaz's gas production infrastructure in Kharkiv region, the company said. No one was injured in the strike by the jet-powered drone, which caused a fire at the facility, it added. "Critical equipment was damaged in the attack," said Naftogaz's Acting CEO Sergii Fedorenko in a statement. Earlier on Sunday, Trump announced an "energy ceasefire" to lower fuel costs ahead of the U.S. midterm elections. "Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!" Trump wrote on social media on Sunday. The Kremlin said on Monday that contacts are ongoing on an energy ceasefire and that it would provide more information in due course, Reuters reported. It declined to comment on whether any deal would be limited to oil refineries. Russia's presidential office didn't immediately respond to a CNBC request for further information. Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, ceasefires have repeatedly proved fragile. Trump has tried several times to broker an end to the war, but none have succeeded so far. "We've been here many times before over the last four and a half years, so I don't think we should build our hopes up too much," former IEA head of oil Neil Atkinson told "Squawk Box Europe" on Monday. On Friday, Trump said he had made a deal with President Vladimir Putin in which Russia would supply more than 4 million tons of diesel to global markets. "The reality of it is that the volumes talked about are very small," said Atkinson, who is also a visiting fellow at the National Center for Energy Analytics. "The deal that's been agreed is not really market moving in any significant way." According to Trump, Russia will supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel immediately, followed by 500,000 tons in November, and then another 4 million tons of diesel based on the condition of Russia's refineries. EU top diplomat Kaja Kallas welcomed an energy ceasefire but said, "This is not the time to ease pressure on Russia." "Suspending sanctions on Russian diesel provides Moscow with more revenues to wage war," she said in a statement Saturday. EU's foreign ministers are due to meet in Luxembourg on Monday morning to discuss the Russia-Ukraine war, among other things. The EU will adopt nearly 1,600 new sanctions listings targeting Russia's military-industrial complex, in the single largest expansion of our sanctions list since Russia started its war, Kallas said ahead of the meeting. Oil prices turned positive after Zelenskyy's Monday comments, after trading about 1.5% lower earlier in the session. Brent crude futures with December delivery were up 1.24% to $106.02 a barrel at 8:15 a.m. ET, while West Texas Intermediate futures for November ticked 1.56% higher to $93.28 per barrel.
