events.title: Psychedelic medicine is approaching a turning point. The U.S. needs the right infrastructure to be ready
events.summary: On September 14, the FDA set aside four hours and invited more than 80 speakers to consider how psychedelic therapies might work in regulated settings. The discussion reflected growing interest from regulators, physicians, patients, and veterans’ organizations in how these potential treatments may offer relief to those living with mental illness. But it also revealed a gap beyond rescheduling or reclassification: the infrastructure needed to deliver these therapies safely and at scale. It’s clear there is a significant patient need. More than 62 million American adults live with mental illness, and tens of millions have few, if any, treatments that work. Nearly one in three patients treated for major depressive disorder sees no meaningful relief from medication, and first-line post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) treatments carry an average nonresponse rate of 40%. Psychedelic therapies could provide one of the solutions to this crisis. Findings from a 2022 trial published in the New England Journal of Medicine showed a single 25 mg dose of psilocybin, with psychological support, significantly reduced depressive symptoms in treatment-resistant patients. Similarly, Oregon Health & Science University published findings from the largest real-world U.S. study of psilocybin, including 346 people and 24 licensed service centers, with participants reporting reduced symptoms of depression, anxiety, and PTSD. Nearly two-thirds ranked the session among the most meaningful experiences of their lives. Today’s psychedelics bear little resemblance to their 1970s counterparts. These medicines undergo rigorous clinical trials and licensed manufacturing processes to preserve safety, chain of custody, and their therapeutic effect. The clinical foundation has been established, and now the U.S. needs the operational foundation to act on it. For these psychedelic therapies to reach patients and make an impact, more is involved than rescheduling and FDA approval. The commercial architecture – including manufacturing standards, licensed supply chains, clinical administration protocols, and trained practitioners – to deliver them safely and at scale has to be created. As CEO and co-founder of Optimi Health, a Canada-based manufacturer and drug developer of pharmaceutical-grade psychedelic compounds for research and clinical use, I not only have a stake in this discussion, but also a unique understanding of how this can be achieved in real-world settings. Our company has spent several years manufacturing and exporting pharmaceutical-grade psychedelic therapies for clinical settings in Australia, Canada, and the United Kingdom. Australia’s model offers key insights into how therapeutic delivery can work inside a national framework. There, when a patient with treatment-resistant depression sees an authorized psychiatrist, the psychiatrist then prescribes a pharmaceutical-grade dose from a licensed manufacturer. The patient then takes it under physician supervision and the chain of custody is documented at every step. There is no ambiguity about what was administered, at what dose, or by whom. Optimi has supported dozens of clinics in Australia, with no serious adverse events reported. And to-date we have supplied more than 5,000 doses of psychedelic therapies globally for patients and clinical research. The recent FDA hearing and efforts from the Administration show that the U.S. is asking the right questions, and there’s an opportunity to build on this progress. The framework required to bring these therapies to American patients can be adapted from working models, with Canada and Australia already demonstrating that psychedelic medicines can be manufactured, distributed, and administered responsibly. As the largest and most innovative pharmaceutical market in the world, and with the American psychedelic drugs market forecasted to reach $3.60 billion by 2032, the U.S. has what it needs to build its own model and lead in this space. A great patient need can be met if pharmaceutical companies, and the government, are willing to take the next steps. Veterans and millions of other Americans living with treatment-resistant mental illness are looking for solutions. The time is now for the U.S. to approve and reschedule psychedelic therapies and, most importantly, lay the right foundation for the next chapter in American mental healthcare and pharmaceutical industry innovation. events.title: Nobel economics prize awarded to Robert Hall and Michael ⁠Woodford
events.summary: The Swedish academy says the academics’ models are ‘now used by central banks and ​governments around the world’. The ⁠2026 Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences has been awarded to US academics Robert Hall and Michael ⁠Woodford for their work on how monetary and fiscal policy can help stabilise fluctuations in the economy, according to the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences. The winners of the prestigious award, formally known ⁠as the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel and the final prize to be given out this year, were announced on Monday. list 1 of 4 Canadian Anne Carson wins 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature list 2 of 4 Who is Navi Pillay, winner of the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize? list 3 of 4 US sanctions International Criminal Court in major escalation list 4 of 4 Why is the US sanctioning the International Criminal Court? The two laureates developed new macroeconomic models that improve people’s ability to implement effective stabilisation policies, enabling fiscal and monetary policy measures that can reduce damaging swings in the economy. “The laureates’ work has provided us ‌with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world,” John Hassler, chair of the Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences, said in a statement. “With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume.” During the oil crises in the 1970s, the existing Keynesian models used to determine when and how measures should be implemented to tackle recessions or other economic fluctuations stopped working. Hall and Woodford then developed new tools to understand what policy responses could be the most effective. “Rather than basing the models on statistical links between macroeconomic variables, such as inflation, production and consumption, they chose to build them on a microeconomic foundation,” the academy said. “This encompasses an understanding of how the total mass of individual households and businesses affect the economy through their actions.” The economics prize, first awarded ⁠in 1969, is not part of the five original awards ⁠created in the 1895 will of industrialist and dynamite inventor Alfred Nobel, but was instead established by Sweden’s central bank. The majority of previous laureates have been from the United States. Only three women have ⁠ever won, most recently Claudia Goldin in 2023 for her work on how gender has affected pay and employment over time ⁠in the US. Last year’s winners – Joel Mokyr, Philippe Aghion and Peter Howitt – won for ‌their work on “creative destruction” and how new technology and production methods can boost growth and living standards. Like the other Nobel awards, the economics prize consists of a diploma, a gold medal, and a $1.2m cheque. The Nobel prizes for medicine , physics, chemistry, literature and peace were announced last ‌week, with South African jurist Navi Pillay and Canadian writer Anne Carson among the winners.

events.title: The annoying scam that may be hiding in your work calendar
events.summary: That meeting on your calendar might not be what it seems. Getty Images; Rebecca Zisser/BI The only thing worse than a meeting that should've been an email? A meeting that's a scam. Calendar phishing is on the rise. Here's why your work schedule is a target. One victim learned she'd been hacked when her contacts received a bogus calendar invite from her. When Pete Thomas spots a meeting on his calendar that he doesn't remember scheduling, the startup executive launches a mini investigation. He searches his inbox for the sender's name, and if that fails, he tries LinkedIn. If Thomas still comes up empty or senses tomfoolery, he'll scan the invitation's contents for odd URLs or other red flags before hitting delete. He's received several in recent months that failed those checks. "It's a distraction," said Thomas, CTO of Kapwork, a fintech firm in Los Angeles. "You always have to look for context." As if email and text message scams weren't enough, workers are contending with a growing wave of phishing attempts arriving through their calendars. In August, calendar-led attacks surged more than tenfold from July, according to a recent study from email security firm Sublime, while a midyear report from Microsoft found that such attacks nearly quadrupled in June from May. Cybersecurity pros say calendars offer attackers advantages over more traditional avenues, and that AI is helping to make the schemes more convincing. They also warn that AI agents could give attackers a leg up by accepting fraudulent invitations on workers' behalf. "You suddenly have new and interesting opportunities because of these personal agents," said Hugh Thompson, program chair of RSAC, an annual cybersecurity conference, and former chief technology officer of software firm Symantec. Risky business The goal of most calendar scammers, digital safety experts say, is to lure victims to phishing sites or deploy social engineering attacks that trick people into revealing sensitive information. The tactic is especially problematic for workers in jobs that rely on regularly meeting with strangers online, such as sales, recruiting, consulting, and other client-facing roles. Aman Gairola, cofounder of Indian design agency Say Design, thought he'd landed a potential client in June when someone booked a meeting on his calendar through his company's website. The invitation included a link to what appeared to be a Google Drive folder containing a project brief. Gairola said he clicked the link and landed on a page that looked like Google Drive, but something felt off. He checked the URL, saw the site was fake, and stopped short of opening any files. "If I have to rate this, how convincing it is, I would rate it a 9.5 out of 10," said Gairola, adding that Say Design is considering removing the option to book intro calls directly through its website and switching to a form-based approach. "It has definitely added a layer of scrutiny to the invites that we get." Attractive vehicles Calendar invitations are attractive vehicles for scammers in part because they create a sense of urgency, said Mark Beare, an executive at cybersecurity firm Malwarebytes. Workers are common targets since many are used to receiving meeting invitations from colleagues , clients, and partners, he added. Another allure is that calendar invites are processed differently from standard email attachments, according to the Microsoft report. Malicious links can land on users' calendars without requiring them to explicitly open an attachment, the software giant said. Calendar invitation scams often take one of two forms. In one, an invitation includes a compromised meeting link, or a form designed to collect credentials or prompt someone to download malware, said Ron Kerbs, CEO of Kidas, which develops tools to detect scams and deepfakes in voice calls. In the other, he said, a victim joins what appears to be a legit video call, only to encounter a scammer posing as someone they have reason to trust, such as an employee at a real company. The impersonator might use the name of an actual staffer, but a fake email address, as well as AI-generated audio or video to make the ruse more convincing, he said. "They're using deepfake technology to look the same as the guy from IT," Kerbs said. Double whammy Sometimes, the sender really is someone you know. Scores of Jenn Drummond's contacts recently received an unexpected calendar invitation from her email address, warning that they had been served with a court summons. The invitation, which was sent after Drummond's email account was hacked while she was boarding a flight, linked to a fake legal notice requesting their financial information. Drummond, a world-record-setting mountaineer and keynote speaker, said that even if the majority of recipients knew it was a scam, she still feels embarrassed that some people might think she's suing them or that she was hacked in the first place. "What are people going to think? I'm not trustworthy — and your brand is what you build trust on," Drummond said. "I was sick to my stomach." Protecting yourself Cybersecurity veterans say there are limits to what people can reasonably expect to catch. Mathew Woodyard, director of threat intelligence at identity and access management company Okta, said that the burden of securing users mostly falls on the businesses that operate the services. "The strongest mitigation isn't user education about 'spotting a fake invite,' since the invites increasingly look identical to legitimate ones," he said. "It's giving users something that can't be phished in the first place." Woodyard said that passkeys can help solve the problem. Because they're created for a specific page, they only work on the authentic website, rather than a mock-up. That removes the need for people to make a judgment call when logging in, Woodyard said. "Until phishing-resistant factors like passkeys become the default rather than an opt-in afterthought, phishing attacks will keep working," Woodyard said. events.title: Trump thinks Ukraine needs a new president. Who could replace Zelenskyy?
events.summary: Popular former general Zaluzhnyi leads potential challengers, alongside intelligence chief Budanov and reformer Fedorov. Kyiv, Ukraine – The White House wants Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy gone. “I think it’s ⁠⁠time for Ukraine to get a new president,” United States President Donald Trump told reporters on Saturday, claiming that Zelenskyy’s months-long strikes on Russian refineries had hurt global diesel supplies. list 1 of 4 Trump calls for Ukraine election, says Zelenskyy failed to end war list 2 of 4 Oval Office spat to public rebukes: A timeline of Trump-Zelenskyy ties list 3 of 4 Zelenskyy says Russia violated energy truce announced by Trump list 4 of 4 Ukraine’s Zelenskyy accuses Russia of violating Trump’s ‘energy ceasefire’ But Trump’s wish is not Ukraine’s command. Even though Zelenskyy’s five-year presidential term expired in 2024, Ukraine’s constitution and martial law grant him a wartime extension. Many Ukrainians want their political establishment to be renewed, but are reluctant to see a presidential vote before the four-and-a-half year war is over. In response to Trump’s remarks, Zelenskyy proposed holding a vote if Russian President Vladimir Putin guaranteed a 60-day ceasefire. However, if the elections are held in the near future, who could compete with Zelenskyy? “If the elections are held fast, one of the former military [commanders] is Zelenskyy’s most probable rival,” Kyiv-based analyst Igar Tyshkevych told Al Jazeera. Meanwhile, old political heavyweights such as former President Viktor Poroshenko, who lost the 2019 presidential vote to Zelenskyy, and former Prime Minister Yulia Tymoshenko, who is being investigated for corruption, do not stand a chance, he said. Valerii Zaluzhnyi: ‘Most probable alternative’ Ukraine’s former top general and current ambassador to the United Kingdom tops the lists of Zelenskyy’s rivals. “At least since 2023, and especially since 2024, after his resignation, the most probable alternative to Zelenskyy, his most dangerous competitor who can defeat him in the election is Valerii Zaluzhnyi,” Volodymyr Fesenko, head of the Kyiv-based Penta think tank, told Al Jazeera. Almost two-thirds of Ukrainians – 64 percent – trust him, according to an October 8 poll by the Rating Group, a Kyiv-based pollster, and only 25 percent “distrust” him. This trust is rooted in his 2022 military triumphs. After defending Kyiv in the early weeks of Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion, Zaluzhnyi led counteroffensives that returned 40 percent of Russian-controlled territory to Ukraine. He was fired in 2023 after a long-anticipated summer counteroffensive yielded no results. Zaluzhnyi remains a man of mystery when it comes to the most pressing postwar matters. Burly and imposing, the 53-year-old is deliberately taciturn, leaving the public guessing about his views on Ukraine’s economic restoration, crippling demographic crisis or push to join the European Union. He does not take part in talk shows, barely talks to journalists and occasionally publishes opinion pieces with detailed analyses of war-related problems and general statements about securing lasting peace and security guarantees from Ukraine’s Western partners. The former comedian was elected in 2019 with 73 percent of the vote, the highest result in Ukraine’s post-Soviet history. Despite a string of corruption scandals in his inner circle, the 48-year-old is popular enough to take another swing at a presidency. More than half of Ukrainians – 53 percent – trust him, although 40 percent do not, according to the Rating Group’s poll. However, Trump’s renewed animosity may benefit Zelenskyy again. After his February 2025 row with Trump in the Oval Office, Zelenskyy’s approval ratings hit a wartime high of 67 percent. However, Zelenskyy may have ruined his own chances with his appointment policies. “He came to power under the slogans of resetting the power, of picking the most competent, not the most trusted” ministers or advisers, analyst Tyshkevych said. Kyrylo Budanov: Trusted by more than half of Ukrainians Lt. Gen. Kyrylo Budanov is the second most popular and charismatic military leader who has a shot at becoming Ukraine’s president. The 40-year-old former top military intelligence officer was appointed head of Zelenskyy’s administration in January. Budanov led daring operations against Russia, including a raid on Russian-annexed Crimea in 2016 to plant explosives at a military airfield. In 2020, Zelenskyy appointed him head of the defence ministry’s intelligence directorate (GUR), which became an aggressive, tech-driven special forces service. The GUR’s sea drone attacks damaged Russia’s Black Sea Fleet, forcing it to retreat from annexed Crimea to the Russian port of Novorossiysk. Budanov is trusted by 53 percent of Ukrainians and mistrusted by 31 percent, according to the Rating Group’s poll. Mykhailo Fedorov: Young, popular, daring At 35, Fedorov is the youngest person on the list of potential presidents.

events.title: Which banners did Liverpool fans display at Anfield against Man City?
events.summary: From creative wordplay on song lyrics to simply calling Man City ‘cheats’, the Reds fans went all out at Anfield. It was billed as one of the most emotionally charged club football matches in recent years with Liverpool’s historically vocal and disapproving fans promising a hostile reception for Manchester City as the Blues played their first match after being found guilty of breaching the Premier League’s financial rules. In the end, Manchester City walked away from it with three points in the bag and smiles on their faces but not without facing scorn from the Reds’ supporters at their famed Anfield Stadium in Liverpool. The Blues evaded a much-anticipated “ Anfield welcome ” by avoiding the route usually taken by team buses driving into the venue. Instead, City’s bus was driven into the stadium via a different route and entrance, usually reserved for service vehicles on match days. While Enzo Maresca’s team avoided the flares, pyrotechnics and attacks on the bus that were meted out to City during their visit to Anfield for a UEFA Champions League match eight years ago, there was no escaping the chants and banners inside the stadium. The creativity of Liverpool fans was displayed on the streets lined with thousands of Reds fans before kickoff and inside Anfield once they unfurled their scathing banners in the stands. Here’s a selection of the best banners and signs displayed inside Anfield on Sunday: The most direct attacks since the Premier League’s independent commission’s guilty verdict was announced have focused on the finding that City “arranged ‘sham’ contracts” with a number of its commercial partners. Man City were found guilty of 114 of the 115 charges, giving Liverpool fans the chance to create a wide, strip-like banner that carried the word “cheats” but with the British pound sign replacing the “e” 115 times. The banner was held across the stand behind City’s goal. Liam Gallagher, lead vocalist of the British rock band Oasis, is a self-admitted lifelong Man City fan. Gallagher has been vocal in his support for City despite the charges and was among the travelling Blues supporters at Anfield. Liverpool fans picked on lyrics from some of Oasis’s biggest hits and creatively used them to mock City. The banner above takes a line from the hit song Stop Crying Your Heart Out. A little creativity was needed for this banner, which carried a stanza from the song Where Did It All Go Wrong? A number of the titles that City won during the charged 2009-2018 period were with teams built around global football stars. Liverpool’s supporters were among many in the Premier League who felt “cheated” during the years that City piled up domestic football trophies. They made no secret of their feelings when given the chance at Anfield against Man City. Liverpool fans mocked the empire built by City’s former manager Pep Guardiola, who signed some of the biggest names during his decade-long run at the helm, which brought 20 trophies. Manchester City fans had their own way of mocking Liverpool. They waved inflatable bananas at the away end, a reference to a decades-long tradition when a City fan took a blow-up banana to a game in 1987. It also served as a dig at then-Liverpool captain Steven Gerrard, who slipped during a match against Chelsea in the 2013-2014 season when the 0-2 loss to the London club set off a series of results that saw City clinch a come-from-behind Premier League title.

events.title: Turmoil within Dolly Parton’s estate underscores the precariousness of family businesses after founders die
events.summary: Dolly Parton waves to her fans at Dollywood in Pigeon Forge, Tenn., in March 2024. Amy Harris/Invision via AP Dolly Parton’s nephew Bryan Seaver announced the legendary singer’s death on Aug. 25, 2026, in a prerecorded video. Seaver, the son of one of Parton’s 11 siblings , had been her head of security for many years. But Seaver is currently embroiled in a messy dispute with She’s Alive LLC, the company Parton established to manage her business assets after her death . This unusually acrimonious fight highlights some of the business succession problems that can arise when the founder of a company dies but wants its other leaders to keep it going. Parton, a legendary American singer, actress, entrepreneur and philanthropist, left behind an estimated US$450 million estate . She’s Alive LLC terminated Seaver’s involvement with the business, and a court has issued a restraining order against him. Seaver is accused of engaging in “ an obscene, deliberate and escalating campaign of threats” against Parton’s estate . He denies the allegations. As professors who research and teach topics related to inheritance law, we are fascinated by the Parton case. It illustrates some of the pitfalls of planning for the transition of a privately held business after the founder’s death – a concern for celebrity and noncelebrity estates alike. Following Dolly Parton’s death, there has been turmoil in her management involving her nephew Bryan Seaver. Managing celebrity estates after death Celebrity estates, like Parton’s, are distinct because they often contain valuable intellectual property. This includes copyrights, which protect creative works , such as songs and recordings, including Parton’s catalog of hits. Another valuable asset in these estates are publicity rights , which protect the use of the celebrity’s name or likeness, such as the use of Parton’s face on a T-shirt sold for profit. These rights can be enormously valuable long after the celebrity has died. Without careful planning beforehand and appropriate management after death, the estate may never get the full value of these property interests. Prince, for example, died in 2016 without a will or any formal estate plan. The twice-divorced Minneapolis pop star had no surviving children. His estate passed to his siblings, who were his sole heirs . It took more than six years to administer his complicated $156 million estate , which concluded with the heirs establishing corporate entities to manage his intellectual property rights. One of those entities, Prince Legacy LLC, recently became embroiled in litigation when some of Prince’s heirs sought to fire the managers who had been hired to manage their share of the intellectual property rights. Marilyn Monroe, who died in 1962, also without any children, left behind a professionally drafted will under which her longtime acting coach, Lee Strasberg (and his then-wife) inherited most of her publicity rights. But Strasberg remarried, and his widow – a woman whom Monroe never met – hired various professional managers, including a company known as CMG Worldwide , which specializes in the management, marketing and promotion of publicity rights associated with dead celebrities. Because of the successful management of her estate’s publicity rights, Monroe became known as one of the highest-paid dead celebrities – with large sums enriching a woman she’d never met. Marilyn Monroe’s will is seen on display at Julien’s Auctions in Beverly Hills, Calif., in 2012. Joe Klamar/AFP via Getty Images Should a founder’s relatives remain in charge? Many much-less famous family businesses face similar questions about how to keep their profits and revenue flowing and who should manage the company after the founder of a family business dies. A continuation of business operations may have many benefits for a deceased founder’s family. The founder may have relayed their succession plans to them. Relatives often have institutional knowledge and loyalties that can enhance the value of the business and make it last longer. Studies have not conclusively shown, however, whether continuing a business within the family is clearly better or worse for its bottom line than having outsiders manage it. As one study found, family managers often have a “ sense of kinship obligation ” and enjoy “personal and social fulfillment” from working together in the business. That, in turn, creates incentives to manage the firm carefully with an eye toward long-term survival. By contrast, another study of small and medium-size businesses after the sudden death of a CEO-owner found that, in the short run, nonfamily successors are better equipped to run the company . Relatives, by contrast, may be hampered by grief and the emotional impact of the death. But the study also found that in the long run, family members may be more successful in managing the business because they “are likely to view the firm’s survival as a way to stay connected with the deceased family member and keep their memory alive. In turn, this is expected to inspire great stewardship towards the firm.” Other studies, however, have found that maintaining family control over the management of a company after its founder’s death can hurt its performance. Restricting the pool of potential managers to relatives excludes better-qualified candidates who can bring expertise and experience that members of the family lack. Research has shown that hiring pros tends to be best for the business . Death can be bad for business When the owner of a privately held business dies, their assets, including real property, intellectual property and investments, will pass to others according to the estate plan, if the owner created one. But in many cases, the true value of a business is more than just the sum of all its assets. Some of the value may reside in the owner’s talent, knowledge and business acumen. In some cases, the owner maintained personal relationships with employees or customers that may have played a key operational role. In others, the owner may have relied upon unique personal qualities to achieve success in business. Parton herself, for example, was likely the most significant driver of value for her business because of her creativity and star power. According to a 2022 study by economists who studied what happened to startups following the death of nearly 1,500 business founders, growth and profitability fell after the founder’s death. Smaller companies are at risk of having to close altogether. The study found that the negative effects on business continuity “appear to be driven by entrepreneur specialness rather than leadership transition,” which suggests that the founder’s unique contributions to the business can be difficult to replicate after death even with excellent transition planning. events.title: Health insurance open enrollment: Use this 'algorithm' to pick a plan, financial advisor says
events.summary: Open enrollment for health insurance is fast approaching for people who get plans through their employers or the Affordable Care Act marketplace. Consumers may have to make financial trade-offs amid soaring premiums, experts said. There are two questions consumers should generally consider when shopping for health plans, one advisor said. Open enrollment season is upon us — and that means millions of Americans will soon need to pick their health insurance plan for 2027. The choice can have big financial consequences for households, which, with a few exceptions, are generally locked into their insurance plan for a year before being able to switch. But choosing a health insurance plan isn't always a straightforward decision, experts said. Consumers who buy insurance through an employer or on the Affordable Care Act marketplace may have a hodgepodge of plans to choose from, with different premiums, cost-sharing provisions, doctor networks and other factors to consider. Households are grappling with such choices amid soaring healthcare costs , in some cases forcing them to make difficult financial trade-offs during open enrollment, experts said. "Employers are passing through the costs more and more in different ways to employees, so it's important for employees to have their thinking cap on when deciding how to choose their benefits," said Carolyn McClanahan, a physician and certified financial planner based in Jacksonville, Florida. She said she recommends consumers use a two-question "algorithm" when determining which plan is right for them. Here are some important things to consider during open enrollment this year. Open enrollment is the period during which people can enroll in, renew or change their health plans for the coming year. Most Americans under age 65 — about 166 million people — get health insurance via employer-sponsored health plans. Employers have flexibility to set their own open enrollment periods, but typically hold them in the fall and for about a month, said JoAnn Volk, founder and co-director of the Center on Health Insurance Reforms at Georgetown University. An additional 19.2 million Americans were enrolled in a health insurance plan through the Affordable Care Act marketplace for 2026, according to figures published by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services in June. Participants are typically self-employed, gig workers, early retirees, small business owners and others who don't get health insurance at work, or through federal programs such as Medicare or Medicaid. Social Security claiming ages may soon get new names. What retirees need to know The SALT deduction limit is $40,400 for 2026. Here's how to maximize it CNBC's No. 1 financial advisor takes a family-office approach Trump Accounts hit 70 million enrolled and can now accept stock donations CNBC's Financial Advisor 100: Best financial advisors, top firms for 2026 ranked CNBC Elite Advisors: Top ultra-high net worth wealth management firms for 2026 In states that use the federal ACA marketplace, open enrollment runs from Nov. 1, 2026, to Jan. 15, 2027. Consumers must enroll by Dec. 15 in order for coverage to start at the beginning of 2027. Coverage starts Feb. 1 for those who enroll in or change their plans from Dec. 16 through Jan. 15. Certain states run their own marketplaces rather than relying on the federally run marketplace. Those states' open enrollment periods may differ: For example, they may allow signups later into December to still get coverage that starts Jan. 1, run longer enrollment windows or start earlier than Nov. 1, Volk said. Idaho's open enrollment starts Oct. 15 and Connecticut's starts Oct. 23 , for example. Consumers can shop for health plans on healthcare.gov and navigate to their respective state marketplace to enroll. Volk said she recommends consumers type the URL to directly navigate to healthcare.gov rather than using a search tool such as Google to look for terms like "ACA marketplace" or "Obamacare." A study published in August by Georgetown University's Center on Health Insurance Reforms found that consumers who searched for coverage online via tools such as Google were "frequently routed towards products not regulated by the ACA" with fewer consumer protections. What to consider during open enrollment Here are the two questions that McClanahan, the founder of Life Planning Partners and a member of CNBC's Financial Advisor Council , said she recommends considering when comparing options during open enrollment: 1. Is choice or cost more important to you? The answer to this question will help consumers pick from among the alphabet soup of health plan types: HMO, EPO, PPO and POS plans, for example. If consumers have a lot of health problems or get sick often, and they want ample leeway to see a broad roster of doctors, a preferred provider organization, or PPO, plan might be best, McClanahan said.

events.title: Business faces a more interventionist Washington post-midterms
events.summary: Both parties will be pressured to intervene more in markets after the midterms as economic frustration animates the new Congress, according to an FGS Global sketch of 2027 Washington scenarios, shared first with Axios. Why it matters: In a Trump-dominated Washington, Congress ceded much of its power and relevance. That'll change three weeks from Tuesday if Democrats win the House, as expected, and perhaps the Senate in the midterms. The new analysis by FGS , a worldwide strategic leadership advisory with huge clients, is a sequel to a popular FGS report that Jim VandeHei and I used as the basis for a series of popular "Behind the Curtain" columns before the 2024 elections. FGS bills "Alternative Futures: Beyond November" as a framework for processing the epic battles ahead: how power will get used, how both parties will evolve, and how business leaders can navigate the uncertainty. "The 2026 midterms will begin — not end — a 27-month period of unusually high strategic uncertainty," the report says. Zoom in: Michael Feldman — FGS partner and co-chairman, North America — tells me that for Republicans, "intervention may mean tariffs, industrial policy, domestic manufacturing incentives, and other measures aimed at strengthening U.S. production capacity, economic security, and competitiveness." "For Democrats, intervention may mean affordability policies, labor protections, antitrust enforcement, plus regulation designed to reduce costs, curb concentrated corporate power and address inequality." "Everyone is focused on who controls Congress," Feldman added. "We think the more important question for business is what happens next. The midterms are the beginning, not the end, of a period of significant political and policy uncertainty." Left: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) campaigns in Linden, N.J., last year. Right: House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) campaigns in Davenport, Iowa, last week. Photos: Getty Images Zoom out: Three structural shifts will drive the post-midterm operating environment for businesses of all sizes, FGS warns. " Voter dissatisfaction may be the most important force pushing both parties away from established policy orthodoxies. A frustrated electorate could push both parties toward more populist, interventionist and less predictable approaches to business." "Technological disruption could reshape the political agenda as profoundly as traditional partisan conflict. AI and related technologies are becoming a political variable — not merely a sector-specific policy issue." "Generational turnover will weaken established political assumptions even where ideology remains unchanged. The next generation of leaders may inherit existing parties without inheriting their relationships, orthodoxies or governing style." The bottom line: "Divided government does not necessarily mean lower political/legislative risk," FGS writes. "It may mean that policy/political conflict moves in less predictable ways." Get the 16-page FGS report .

events.title: The Eurosummer season is getting longer and more popular. These 4 charts show how and where Americans are vacationing.
events.summary: Naples, Italy, has seen the fastest growth in flight capacity from North America over the past three years. Alessandro Tortora/Getty Images More North Americans are flocking to Europe for summer vacation. Business Insider analyzed flight data to identify the trendiest, most popular destinations. Over 1.5 million seats were added on flights to Italy, while capacity doubled for Czechia and Croatia. Whether it's eating gelato under the Mediterranean sun or exploring a medieval city, North Americans can't get enough of summer trips to Europe . Business Insider analyzed data from Cirium, an aviation analytics firm, to create four charts that show how Eurosummer is on the rise — and which destinations are the trendiest. We looked at the number of seats on flights from North America to Europe. Unlike just measuring the number of flights, this also accounts for the airplanes' capacity. Airlines scheduled 69% more seats in July 2026 than in July 2010. Meanwhile, the number of flights went up 59%, from roughly 15,700 to 24,900. As the data is based on flight schedules rather than border crossings, it does not necessarily reflect tourists' final destinations. Even so, passenger demand still informs where airlines send their fleets and launch new routes. Cirium's data also show that airlines are adding more seats in summer than in winter. In 2026, there were 77% more seats from North America to Europe in July than in January. In 2010, there was a 50% gap between those months. However, there is also some country-level data showing that the summer travel season is getting longer, as more people choose to fly later in the year. Spanish government statistics show that 57% more Americans arrived in the country in October 2025 than in October 2019. Overall arrivals during the summer months of 2019 and 2025 increased by a quarter. Which countries are becoming more popular? The UK has long been the most popular transatlantic market — its 15 million annual seats are nearly double those of France and Germany — due to strong business links and airline partnerships that make it a useful hub connecting to destinations elsewhere in Europe. To find where more North Americans are flocking, we focused on changes in flight capacity between the years ending in July 2023 and July 2026. This also helps minimize the fluctuation in recovery times from the pandemic. That expansion has not been spread evenly across Europe. Only four countries saw fewer seats across the period. There are no longer any flights to Ukraine due to the war. Norway and Sweden both saw their seats drop by more than half, and Belgium dipped by 3%. Three countries saw over 1 million seats added in that time. Unsurprisingly, they are already Europe's most popular for tourists: Italy, Spain, and France. However, percentage growth shows that the fastest-growing markets are not all traditional hot spots. We excluded destinations with fewer than 10,000 scheduled seats in the year ending July 2023, so that small base numbers wouldn't skew the results relative to busier destinations. It is clear that tourists are besotted with Italy. Airlines added more seats there than to any other European country, and it ranked fourth for proportional increase — up 52%. Czechia and Croatia stand out as the only two countries where airlines are sending at least double the capacity they had in the year ending July 2023. Over the past year, airlines have relaunched routes to Prague, known for its striking medieval Gothic architecture. Croatia also offers a dose of historic attractions plus a host of beaches on the Adriatic Sea. While the UK as a whole saw only a 4% increase in the number of seats, capacity on flights to Scotland increased by 70%. As well as the Highlands' mountainous vistas, Edinburgh attracts visitors from across the world for its performing-arts festival in August. Ireland also continues to rise in popularity. Dublin and Shannon are the only European airports where you can cross the American border before taking off for the US. Denmark is propping up travel to Scandinavia, thanks to fashionable Copenhagen and new flights to Billund, home of Lego. Which European cities are the trendiest? The picture gets more specific when you zoom into the airport level. We excluded airports that weren't served pre-pandemic or had fewer than 10,000 seats in the year ending July 2023. Flights to Naples, Italy, now have room for more than five times as many passengers as in the year ending July 2023. In the past few years, United Airlines, American Airlines, Delta Air Lines, and Air Canada have all launched new routes to the home of pizza and the gateway to the picturesque Amalfi Coast . Dubrovnik, a coastal Croatian city known for its medieval walls, found fame in the 2010s as a filming location for "Game of Thrones," but it has continued to soar in popularity. While flights to France as a whole saw only a 16% increase in capacity, three French airports made the top 10. Portugal is also proving popular, with two cities on the list. Last summer, United launched flights from Newark to Faro, the capital of Portugal's seaside Algarve region. And in August, American Airlines said it will start flying to Porto for the first time ever, starting March 2027. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Far right surges as crises threaten Sanchez: Could Vox lead Spain?
events.summary: Snap vote could bring PP and Vox to power as polls show falling support for Sanchez, one of Europe’s last leftist leaders. Madrid, Spain – “What I really hate about [Prime Minister Pedro] Sanchez is how keen he is to allow more migrants into our country,” said Alberto Munoz, who wears the red and gold wristband of Vox party supporters. The 24-year-old computer programmer from Barcelona is among a growing group of young Spanish people who are attracted to the far-right, anti-immigration party. list 1 of 4 Spain calls snap election amid housing crisis list 2 of 4 How will Spain’s housing crisis affect elections? list 3 of 4 Graffiti artist honours Spain’s housing rights figure ‘Maricarmen’ list 4 of 4 Ceuta or Sebta? Why one city has two names and a disputed status Eight years ago, Vox was a tiny party on the fringes of Spanish politics. But polls suggested it is getting closer to power as Spain heads to snap elections on November 29. To reach a parliamentary majority, 176 seats are needed. According to a recent survey by the leading centre-left newspaper El Pais, the conservative People’s Party (PP) and Vox – whose support is predicted to double from the last elections in 2023 – would secure 198 seats. If the PP forms a coalition with Vox, it would be the first time the hard right would return to power in Spain since the death of Francisco Franco in 1975. In the most recent elections in 2023, the PP won the most votes but not enough to lead on its own, and it did not enter a coalition with Vox. Sanchez of the Socialist Workers’ Party instead formed a government with the help of the Catalan nationalist party, Together for Catalonia. Since then, the PP has formed four regional governments with Vox, and the parties share power in about 100 councils. A coalition between them now would likely see Sanchez defeated. “There is hope for Spain with these elections. We will fight for victory and to convince Spaniards we are worth voting for,” Jose Antonio Fuster, national spokesman for Vox, told Al Jazeera. “But the PP cannot make the same mistakes as 2023 and must not start dividing up ministries until we have won.” Sanchez’s party is predicted to win 112 seats in November, down from 121 three years ago. If the Socialists lose, it would spell the end of one of the last left-wing governments left in Europe after advances for the far right in France, Germany, Italy, Austria and Finland as populism sweeps Europe. Steven Forti, an expert in the far right who lectures in contemporary history at the Autonomous University of Barcelona, said, like other far-right parties in Europe and Latin America, Vox distances itself from the Franco dictatorship. Santiago Abascal, the Vox leader, once told the Spanish parliament that Sanchez’s government was the “worst for the past 80 years” – implying the Franco dictatorship was better. “It is dog whistle politics – you do not make an explicit reference to the dictatorship. Vox is like other far-right parties in that respect,” Forti told Al Jazeera. “Young people are attracted to Vox by a feeling of rebellion against the established parties, nationhood and antimigrant feeling. If the polls are right, they will be in power with the PP, but what matters is what ministries they control.” Vox is the only party that has substantially increased its support. A survey for RTVE, the state broadcaster, projected that the far-right party would increase its seats in parliament from 33 to 65 while it indicated the PP’s support had not risen and all left-wing parties had lost support. Antonio Alonso, a lecturer in international relations at the University CEU San Pablo in Madrid, said right-wing parties were more stable than their badly divided opponents. “What is key is that the far left is split into so many different groups and it will be hard to mobilise them as one front together. Meanwhile, the right with the PP and Vox is more unified,” he told Al Jazeera. Alberto Nunez Feijoo, the PP leader, plans to play on voters’ anger over corruption scandals that have hit Sanchez. “This is an election between corruption and decency, between decline and prosperity, between a government that aspires only to survive and a country that is thinking about its future,” he told reporters after Sanchez announced the snap elections. He also pledged to build 200,000 homes each year and cut taxes. Fired up by a housing crisis that has seen tens of thousands of people protest across Spain, Sanchez called the vote in an audacious gamble to rally support and confound the polls. It was the eviction of 87-year-old Maria del Carmen Abascal from her Madrid home, a flat she had lived in for seven decades, which inflamed public opinion and prompted activists to camp out in central Madrid and other cities. Known across Spain as Maricarmen, she died this month after the protests.

events.title: Beckham, Yao Ming attend NBA China Games in a boost to Macao's live events
events.summary: The NBA China Games help attract new tourists to Macao for reasons unrelated to gambling. Macao is spending billions to diversify tourism offerings beyond casinos. Live events are projected to bring in nearly $2.8 trillion globally by 2032. When Dallas resident Barrington Traille read about the NBA China Games in his local newspaper, he said he knew it was the perfect 53rd wedding anniversary present for his wife. "I follow the Mavericks… and she follows the Rockets," he said from The Venetian Macao, which hosted the games on Oct. 9 and 11. "I decided, hey, I'm going to give you a treat. We are going to China." They planned the trip, their first to Asia, less than a week before tip-off and brought along their son Dominic. The two Texas teams squared off in a pair of pre-season games over the weekend at the NBA China Games 2026, the second in a five-year deal to hold the event in Macao. The decision made the Traille family a part of one of the fastest-growing trends in the travel industry: live event tourism, which includes traveling to attend music concerts, sporting events and business conferences. The NBA China Games 2026 combined all three, blending professional basketball games, fan events featuring K-pop performances and an off-court summit with speakers ranging from Alibaba Chairman Joe Tsai to sports stars Yao Ming and David Beckham. When Taylor Swift's Eras Tour ended in 2024, live events were valued at $1.5 trillion, according to a report from the consulting firm Kearney. Come 2030, the sector is expected to reach nearly $2.8 trillion , it said. For the NBA, the games are a chance to grow international fanbases in China, where basketball has long ranked among the nation's top sports . The game was boosted by the success of former players Yao Ming and Jeremy Lin, and more recently by current Chinese players, like Portland Trail Blazers' Yang Hansen. And that fandom attracts dollars that travel beyond the NBA into the broader international sports ecosphere, from the growing collectibles industry to partnerships abroad. In 2025, Luckin Coffee, China's largest coffee chain, became the official coffee sponsor of the Portland Trail Blazers, following previous affiliations with the NBA China Games and the Houston Rockets. "It's not just about media exposure," Chairman David Li told CNBC Thursday. "Sports embody discipline, professionalism (and) healthy living. These are very much intrinsic to Luckin's brand DNA." With trillions on the global table, an intense battle for live events is happening off the court too, as countries vie for hosting rights that bring international cash and cachet to their cities. Winning events can involve coordinating national visa policies, city-level infrastructure spending and ensuring expertise in the private hospitality sector. The pay-off can be massive in terms of income and international attention. The 2025 Australian Grand Prix generated more than $300 million in revenue for Melbourne, while the 2025 Singapore Formula One race reached more than 2 billion social media users, according to Kearney. For Macao, the benefit of hosting the NBA China Games from 2025 to 2030 furthers the special administrative region's efforts to diversify beyond gaming. "Gaming is important," said Maria Helena de Senna Fernandes, the director of Macao's Government Tourism Office. "But at the same time, we also need to develop other activities and other kinds of industries, so that we don't put our eggs just in one basket." The six gaming operators in Macao are part of a push for non-gaming to comprise 60% of its GDP by 2030. When new gaming concessions were awarded in 2022, the six operators collectively pledged to invest 118.8 billion Macanese patacas ($14.7 billion), with more than 90% earmarked to explore new overseas markets and non-gaming projects , such as live music and sports events. The Trailles are glad they came to Macao. "It's great," said Barrington. "It's Little Las Vegas." Dominic, who works in the hotel industry in Texas, echoed that sentiment. "There's a lot of money here," he noted.

events.title: Trump privately expresses doubts about livestreaming execution
events.summary: President Trump has privately shared misgivings about livestreaming the firing-squad execution of a former Army major who murdered 13 people at Fort Hood in Texas, according to four people who have spoken with the president. Why it matters: Trump has been deluged with "negative input" about the idea from a bipartisan chorus of lawmakers as well as advisers inside and outside of his White House, a senior administration official said. A livestream of former Army Maj. Nidal Hasan's execution on Dec. 3 "might not happen," Trump told one confidant, who doesn't work in the administration and shared the comment with Axios. "He didn't sound particularly enthusiastic" about webcasting the execution, the source said. "That's why he's calling around, doing the Trump thing, asking people what they think." Zoom in: Hasan faces a firing squad at Fort Hood, where he went on his murderous shooting rampage 17 years ago. He would be the first person in the U.S. whose execution would be livestreamed. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced the norm-shattering idea Thursday on Real America's Voice. "We'll make sure that people are able to watch it — that it's public — because people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things," Hegseth said. Zoom out: The idea was roundly condemned domestically and internationally . In the ensuing days, Trump started to publicly shift his positions: At first, Trump was full-throated in his support. "Absolutely, I approve," Trump told reporters early Friday evening. Later that night, Trump was more nuanced : "They want to do that because they want to set an example. I wasn't involved in that decision, but I understand the decision." On Saturday, Trump took control by telling reporters he would have the final say: "There are two thoughts: Don't show it and show it. 'Cause you know, by showing it, maybe other people won't be doing what he did. So I'll make a decision, ultimately. I know what the military would like to do, but we'll make a decision," the president told reporters at the White House. Behind the scenes: Vice President Vance has signaled where he thinks the president is going with the decision, according to a source. "I don't know if that's actually going to happen," Vance, speaking off the cuff, told reporters Friday. He has privately repeated that to others. "I'm not going to be watching it," Vance said. Between the lines: Trump, Vance and everyone else in the administration is clear about supporting Hasan's execution. But the president is grappling with competing pressures. "The president wants the bastard to pay, and a public execution might be that extra humiliation [Hasan] deserves," another confidant who spoke with the president said. "At the same time, he doesn't want to make the guy a martyr." Said another: "This is an old dude in a wheelchair we're shooting. We want to livestream that?" (Hasan, 56, was permanently injured when he was shot during his capture.) Friction point: The divide in opinion over livestreaming the execution is another point of disagreement between Vance and Hegseth. They've been on opposite sides when it comes to the use of military force in Yemen and Iran , to the leadership of the Army . Advisers say the men have a good relationship. Context: Whether at the state or federal level, executions often are witnessed only by family members or select media. They haven't been livestreamed. Executions used to be viewed in public squares, but that practice was discontinued in the 1930s, according to NPR . Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh's 2001 execution was viewable to loved ones and bombing survivors via a private closed-circuit telecast. Flashback: Yelling "Allahu Akbar!" Hasan fatally shot 13 people — including a pregnant woman — and wounded 32 others on Nov. 5, 2009, when they lined up for medical checks at Fort Hood's Soldier Readiness Processing Center. The rampage was the worst terrorist attack on U.S. soil since 9/11. A special Senate Homeland Security and Government Affairs Committee report criticized the military for "political correctness" that blinded authorities to the major's increasingly clear Islamist radicalization. The bottom line: Hasan will be executed unless something unexpected happens. The only real doubt is whether private citizens with no attachment to the case will be able to witness it. "If I had to bet, I would bet the president doesn't authorize this," said one administration official. "But I'm not gonna get ahead of the boss and try to predict what he'll do." "Hasan will be executed for his crimes," the official said, "and that's what matters."

events.title: Azerbaijan’s school hijab ban: What’s behind it, and what’s next?
events.summary: Protests have broken out as some schools begin preventing students and teachers from attending classes. An Azerbaijan government decision to indirectly prohibit students and staff from wearing the hijab in schools has sparked protests. The amendment approved last month stopped short of explicitly banning the Muslim headscarf but barred clothing in schools that the government said violates the “principle of secularism”. list 1 of 3 Things are not going so well for Russia list 2 of 3 Pashinyan’s pro-Europe party wins Armenia election list 3 of 3 After Nagorno-Karabakh, Armenians vote for peace over nationalism The decision has sparked protests as some schools began preventing students and teachers from attending classes. Teacher Zahra Hasanova told Al Jazeera that she was informed she could no longer wear the hijab at school. “To be honest, I am a little emotional. I am hurt,” she said. “[The hijab] is a personal choice, and if one day I want to take it off, that should be my choice too.” The state-run Azerbaijani Press Agency (APA) said the amendment to the Descriptions of Uniforms for Students of State General Education Institutions aimed to ensure a unified dress code that reflects the country’s “secular principle”. About 96 percent of Azerbaijan’s population identifies as Muslim. Its constitution defines the country as secular while also guaranteeing religious freedom. The APA added that clothes that reflect the “history, culture, and national and moral values of the Azerbaijani people” may be worn for celebrations pending approval by the Pedagogical Council, which operates under the Ministry of Science and Education. Such clothing ensures that teachers reflect “professional standards” and will have positive effects on the “school’s public reputation”, it said. The measure has sparked protests and a social media campaign in Azerbaijan. Videos circulated showing students hugging their teachers and crying as they were turned away from schools. Local media outlets reported that students in at least two schools in Azerbaijan boycotted classes in protest against the restrictions. Imprisoned journalist Polad Aslanov, who is serving a 113-year prison sentence after being convicted of high treason in 2020, launched a hunger strike over the new requirements. “Despite being in prison, I am raising my voice against the trampling of our constitutional rights by employing the only means of struggle available to me – a hunger strike!” Aslanov wrote in a message posted on Facebook by his wife, Gulmira Aslanova. Reports of internet blackouts have not been confirmed by data from watchdogs, including Open Observatory of Network Interference and NetBlocks. A social media campaign followed by protests also spread to Turkiye. Some have drawn parallels between the developments in Azerbaijan and Turkiye’s “post-modern coup” in 1997 when women wearing headscarves were banned from attending university classes and dismissed from their civil service jobs or were forced to resign. Demonstrators last week gathered outside Azerbaijan’s consulate in Istanbul to protest the restrictions affecting Muslim women, calling on authorities in Baku to reconsider the decision. Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev issued a veiled criticism of Turkiye, a strong ally of Azerbaijan, for the protests. In a speech at his New Azerbaijan Party congress, Aliyev warned not to “interfere with our lifestyle” without directly mentioning Turkiye. Authorities in Ankara did not officially respond to Aliyev’s comment. Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, however, mentioned in his September 23 address at the United Nations General Assembly that Muslim women were facing increasing discrimination.

events.title: Israel mints tech unicorns. Can it keep them from leaving for New York?
events.summary: The Scene Israel has produced more tech unicorns per citizen than any country in the world, twice as many as the US. Ittai Ben-Zeev’s job is getting them to stay there. The CEO of the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange is tasked with convincing the next Wiz, Monday.com, and Fiverr, which all went public in New York or sold to US rivals, to list at home instead. He’s also courting global investors whose money will help boost trading and valuations. His biggest tailwind, he said, is the takeover of US markets by a handful of AI giants. Israeli startups worth a few billion dollars can’t get the attention of investors rhapsodizing about trillion-dollar IPOs from SpaceX, Anthropic, and OpenAI. “New York is no longer an option,” said Ben-Zeev, the exchange’s CEO since 2016. After the Oct. 7 attacks, 7% of its workforce was called up for military service and the bear case for its stock market was obvious. Since Oct. 8, 2023, the TA-125 has beaten the S&P 500 by 50 percentage points and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite by 23. The country is on track this year for a record 30 IPOs . Foreign holdings of Israeli shares more than doubled from September 2023 to the beginning of this year. Ben-Zeev dismissed wartime nationalism as a reason for Israeli founders to list at home, or for Israeli investors to buy their shares. “Israelis will be patriotic about certain issues, but that’s not the way they view the exchange,” he said. But he said the Jewish diaspora has increased its investments. Bill Ackman and his Israeli-born wife, Neri Oxman, bought 4.9% of the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange in 2024 after a 45-minute meeting with management, Ackman said in an interview. “Owning a stock exchange is the purest way to bet on a country,” he said, taking a minute to run the numbers: His $23 million investment is worth $230 million today. He said AI’s productivity-enhancing potential will overcome Israel’s economic weakness, its small population. “There will be a trillion-dollar company coming out of Israel, and that value will be shared among a tiny country.” The war also gave TASE cover to move its Sunday-to-Thursday trading to Monday through Friday. It wasn’t an easy pitch in a country that takes Shabbat seriously, but a way “to signal the world that we are part of it” and gain entry into global indexes that have long snubbed it, Ben-Zeev said. Anti-Israel sentiment and antisemitism are fueling campaigns at many US institutions to divest from Israel. Politicians will politick, he said, but “investors, at the end of the day, want to make a return.” Q&A Liz Hoffman: Israel has produced more tech unicorns per capita than any other country in the world, but they all want to go public in New York. How do you hold onto them? Ittai Ben-Zeev: It used to be that a tech company with $100 million [in annual revenue] could IPO in New York. That’s no longer the case. The $100 million became $500 million. And because of the gigantic IPOs that are coming, for most Israeli tech companies, New York is no longer an option. Six or seven years ago, if an Israeli company couldn’t do an IPO on Nasdaq or NYSE, they were looking at Singapore, Toronto, Australia. We managed to change the perception. And I believe that in 2027, maybe before the end of 2026, we’ll start seeing global investment banks leading global IPO offerings on TASE, and only for TASE. I’m mindful, speaking to you the week of the anniversary of Oct. 7 — is patriotism part of the pitch? No. Post-Oct. 7, I see a genuine change in the way that Jewish people in the diaspora, especially in the States, want to invest in Israel, not only to make a return but also to get a broader connection to Israel. But that’s not the case with the Israeli entrepreneurs. Israelis, I have to tell you, will be patriotic about certain issues, but that’s not the way they view the exchange. Then what’s the pitch? You are Israeli. You don’t understand the American mentality. The American market can be brutal. You miss your estimates by one cent, your share price goes down, and then what? Start in the Israeli market and, once you’re ready, you can always do a dual listing. Think about TASE as a stop on the way to New York. You’ve also courted global companies to dual-list in Tel Aviv. Palo Alto Networks did that after buying [Israeli startup] CyberArk, but why would most companies bother? We have data that shows you get more liquidity and more demand for your shares. You can argue that it’s not significant enough, but it’s a free option. And not too many people are aware of it, but if you look at the amount of money Israelis have in cash deposits in Israeli banks and you compare it to GDP, we are No. 1 of any western society. That’s money that is just ready to be invested. You’re in New York this week, selling the Israeli economy to investors. But the Middle East is a volatile place to invest right now, and there are big anti-Israel divestment campaigns at some US institutions. In the old days, people would ask me: What will happen to Israel if something happens in Iran? I remember being in New York a couple of years ago, telling one of those American investors that if something happened in Iran, you should be more worried about your American portfolio than your Israeli portfolio. Israel is more well-positioned than it used to be, and I’m not sure that everybody fully understands it. In terms of BDS [the push for boycotts, divestment, and economic sanctions against Israel], there are politicians all over the world. Investors, at the end of the day, want to make a return. And the Israeli market is a good marketplace to make a return. Also, I think Israel can do a better job of PR. This is part of what we tell companies: You need to know how to sell the pitch. It’s not only about facts; it’s also about storytelling. As a country, this is something we need to do better. You shifted trading from Sunday to Thursday to Monday to Friday. Was that a hard sell? We were in the middle of a war. Everybody understood that it’s important for us to signal the world that we are part of it. We needed to get aligned to global standards, and this is what we did this year. What’s it like having Bill Ackman on your cap table? For sure it has helped change the perception. Israeli tech guys, they look to New York. When they will read what you’re writing, they will give it much more credit than what the Israeli newspaper writes. So a very successful businessman like Bill talking about the Israeli economy, putting faith in the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange, helps my pitch.

events.title: Saudi Arabia’s resolve, and fears of a ‘forever war’
events.summary: The Scene Riyadh Season — the Saudi capital’s biggest suite of events that had been key to its tourism push — opens next week with concerts, UFC, the Epcot-esque Boulevard World, and the world’s top ranked tennis players set to compete at the Six Kings Slam. Since 2019, it has been the capital’s answer to anyone asking whether Riyadh is the place to be. After the Houthi strikes over the weekend, residents are asking themselves the same question. Traffic on King Fahd Road is lighter and some companies — mostly those based in the King Abdullah Financial District — told staff to work from home on Sunday. Schools in the city have moved to remote learning for the week, with no clear date yet on when students will return to class. When I ask Saudis — friends, relatives, and sources — how they are doing, most say: , thanks to God, the catchall for everything from the greatest blessings to the mantra mourners repeat when family members die. It’s the same expression they used in March when Iranian missiles first reached the capital, but the tone now is different after more than a dozen people were killed and hundreds wounded in attacks on King Khalid International Airport. Fear is breaking through. Social media and WhatsApp group chats have been filled with eulogies for Captain Hamoud Alkalthami, the Saudia Airlines pilot killed on Thursday, and for Saturday’s dead — eight of them foreign residents from countries including Bangladesh, Egypt, and Sudan. People are posting about and queuing to donate to blood banks. The crown prince himself did so last week, part of an annual campaign, and that image was used to spur urgently needed donations. The captain’s death in particular has become a symbol for many Saudis: The war now has a martyr, with a name and face that looks like theirs. Manal’s view Saudis broadly trust their government. When they wrap themselves in the flag, or share statements of solidarity after attacks (at least for those who use their real names), it’s genuine and reflects how people speak in private. But there has been a shift. Some are talking about leaving, which a few months ago would have been seen as a betrayal. Most are still confident and say the kingdom has come through worse. What’s pretty universal is the desire for the disruption to be over and to get back to living. While the conflict with Iran was clear — we have been told to be wary of the Islamic Republic from the time we understood what an enemy was — the confrontation with the Houthis is more complex. Riyadh has tried a mix of strikes and diplomacy for more than a decade, and the UN-brokered truce in 2022 held long enough for people to stop thinking about the issue. It’s clear now that it’s a forever war, and few people I speak to can describe what winning would look like. Without public polls, it’s impossible to gauge exactly what the Saudis think. Speaking to more than 25 people this weekend showed a split. One camp wants the Houthis finished for good, whatever that may meanOthers worry about the toll on Yemenis, our poorer neighbors, who make up the kingdom’s largest foreign community and share ties of kinship and history with Saudis. Over the past six months, those who lived through the 1991 Gulf War used it to explain why they weren’t worried. Those six weeks of Iraqi strikes had one Saudi business leader “ more frightened of the uncertainty of the Scud than anything else. ” Uncertainty is again, 35 years later, the greatest fear. Notable The strikes sharply raise the risk of Saudi Arabia being drawn into a wider war, after a decade in which Riyadh worked to contain the Yemen conflict rather than escalate it , Bloomberg reported. Eulogies for the 12 killed in Saturday’s strike filled Saudi social media, among them a Flynas flight attendant killed on duty and a university student in her final year , Arab News reported.

events.title: I want our $1 billion business to stay in the family, but that doesn't mean I'll automatically hire my kids
events.summary: Tricia Wallwork is now the CEO of her family business. Courtesy of Tricia Wallwork Tricia Wallwork is the CEO of Milo's Tea, founded by her grandfather in 1946. She's grown the brand exponentially, and recently surpassed $1 billion in retail sales. She's learned about family governance from other family-owned companies, she says. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Tricia Wallwork , CEO and Chair of the Board at Milo's Tea . It has been edited for length and clarity . When my grandad Milo returned from World War II , he married my grandma, Bea, the very next week. He likes to say he only had $20 and a footlocker, but he also had a vision: for a hamburger stand serving burgers, fries, pies, and sweet tea to Atlanta's steelworkers. That was the beginning of Milo's Tea. Since then, the business has had three distinct iterations: the initial burger stand, franchise restaurants that my dad and stepmother ran, and now the tea company that I operate. Tricia Wallwork's grandfather started the family company when he came back from war. Courtesy of Tricia Wallwork Through them all, we've been guided by my grandparents' founding values: listening to customers, using real ingredients , and treating people well. I became a lawyer, then joined the family business I never wanted to work at the family business , so I became a lawyer. I thought I would save the world, but really, I was just writing letters and representing companies. It wasn't what I had envisioned, so I traded my high heels for steel-toed boots and started working at Milo's. My dad and stepmom had noticed a trend: people would drive through their restaurants just to order sweet tea . Running a hamburger joint is difficult, so they decided to sell the franchise company and use the proceeds to start the first version of our tea plant. I saw them constantly figuring things out on the fly — like using pantyhose to filter tea. Things are much more sophisticated today, but I still have that entrepreneurial spirit. I've grown the company drastically over 14 years I became CEO of Milo's Tea in 2012, and since then, our growth has been like a hockey stick. In 2012, we did about $30 million in retail sales. In September, we surpassed $1 billion in retail sales, ahead of our projections. It's a very unusual situation to be in as a third-generation business owner . I've tried to find mentors to help me get ahead of things and manage this rocket ship. I've surrounded myself with great advisors, who have helped me and the rest of the board (including my dad, stepmother, and stepsister) be very intentional about family governance. We've created a family mission statement and set a goal of remaining 100% family-owned. That allows us to take a long-term view of how we invest in the company. We have protocols for the next generation While I hope my children own the company one day, I don't pressure them to work here. I don't want them to feel a duty to work at Milo's Tea, because that becomes a burden. I would rather them see it as an opportunity to do something remarkable. We have regular family meetings for the next generation to learn about Milo's and a framework for getting involved. After they've attended college, they can attend shareholder meetings. After two shareholder meetings, they can attend a board meeting. There's no pressure to engage, just opportunity. So far, both my kids have taken advantage. We've also created an internship program, where our kids can learn about Milo's by working an hourly job. If they want to get hired here, they need to work somewhere else for at least three years and get promoted before they can apply. I like to say merit, not inheritance. Sometimes, in family business, you see the older generation hanging on until the end. My parents and grandparents weren't like that. They've done a good job of supporting the next generation while also getting out of the way so management and the board can really drive growth. That combination of honoring legacy while driving forward has made Milo's what it is today. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Vance says Microsoft replaced laid-off workers with foreign hires. Here’s what the visa data shows
events.summary: The Trump administration suspended Microsoft, Adobe and six IT services firms from PERM, the Labor Department program that lets employers sponsor foreign workers for green cards. Vice President JD Vance accused Microsoft of replacing laid-off American workers with foreign hires. Data shows two-thirds of Microsoft's H-1B approvals went to people already working at the company. Amazon and Meta, the nation's two largest H-1B work visa sponsors, were not suspended. As the Trump administration announced Thursday that it suspended eight tech companies from sponsoring foreign workers for green cards, Vice President JD Vance singled out Microsoft , claiming it replaced the 6,000 workers it laid off in 2025 with people on H-1B work visas. The suspension of the Labor Department's PERM program for green cards, which grant permanent residency to immigrants, doesn't affect H-1Bs, which are temporary work permits, but H-1B approval data shows how heavily these companies rely on foreign workers. Data from the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services' H-1B Employer Data Hub also shows that Amazon and Meta were the biggest sponsors of H-1B visas, and neither was suspended. The crackdown went beyond tech. At the same news conference Thursday, the Labor Department's inspector general, Anthony D'Esposito, announced an investigation into alleged J-1 visa fraud involving nine major American universities. Trump supporters have long argued that these programs undercut American workers by incentivizing employers to hire from abroad. All eight suspended companies rank among the nation's top 50 H-1B sponsors. Most are IT services and consulting firms. Adobe is the smallest, at No. 45. The biggest sponsor wasn't suspended Amazon, with 19,178 H-1B approvals in fiscal 2025, and Meta, with 6,294, were the top two sponsors, and neither was suspended. Microsoft was a close third with 6,258, according to the USCIS data hub. Microsoft out-sponsored Amazon for years. Amazon passed Microsoft in 2017 and now gets about three times as many approvals. The numbers cut both ways. Microsoft did receive more than 6,000 H-1B approvals last year, as Vance said. But 2 in 3 went to people already working there. Amazon, which brought in nearly four times as many H-1B workers new to the company, was not on the suspension list.
