events.title: Palantir CTO says some AI researchers are taking up smoking because they expect AI to cure cancer
events.summary: Palantir's CTO Shyam Sankar said taking up smoking has become a way for AI researchers to show how much they believe in AI. Tom Brenner/Bloomberg via Getty Images Some AI researchers are picking up cigarettes, Palantir's CTO said. Why? They think AI is going to cure cancer anyway, Shyam Sankar said. Lighting up is their way of showing others that their AI "chips are all in," he said. Forget sleepmaxxing and cold plunging: smoking is the new lifestyle flex among AI researchers. At least, that's according to Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar , who said some AI researchers are taking up smoking to signal their belief that AI will eventually cure cancer . "So many AI researchers have started smoking as a way of signaling to other researchers how much they believe in AI," Sankar said in an interview on CBS News' "Face the Nation" on Sunday. The logic, he said, is: "I believe so much in AI that it's going to cure cancer. So I'm showing you my chips are all in." Sankar did not name any researchers or provide evidence for the claim. Smoking remains a major cause of preventable illness and death, and no AI breakthrough has eliminated the health risks associated with cigarettes. But the Palantir executive's remarks echo a countercurrent already visible in parts of the tech industry. As Business Insider's Henry Chandonnet reported last month, a small group of founders, engineers, and investors has embraced cigarettes in a sector otherwise known for optimizing their health with cold plunges, sleep tracking, and peptide treatments . For some of them, a cigarette break is an opportunity to meet people and network. For others, it's a way to come across as more relaxed and less polished than the typical startup founder. And some AI believers expect the technology to make smoking-related health risks a thing of the past. "By the time you do get lung cancer, our AI robots are supposed to have cured that," Avi Schiffmann, the founder of AI wearable startup Friend, previously told Business Insider. 'The machine god of AGI' In the CBS News interview, Sankar raised the smoking anecdote while criticizing what he called Silicon Valley's "mass psychosis" and "social delusion" around AI. He has been outspoken in his criticism of AI safety advocates , whom he accused in the interview of treating artificial general intelligence as a "machine god." Invoking philosopher Blaise Pascal's idea that humans have a "God-shaped hole" in their hearts, Sankar said that some people in Silicon Valley have placed quasi-religious faith in AGI. "I think it's important to understand that many of these folks in Silicon Valley who are building this technology have filled that hole with the machine god of AGI," Sankar said. events.title: ‘Energy ceasefire’: What’s behind Trump’s love-hate ties to Russian oil?
events.summary: Trump’s energy truce sparks criticism over aiding Russia’s war finances amid diesel shortages and rising consumer costs. US President Donald Trump has announced an immediate “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine, days after easing sanctions on Russian fuel to tackle soaring domestic and global fuel prices. The energy truce, announced on Sunday, marks another shift in Washington’s approach to Russian energy, as the Iran-US war and recent Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy facilities disrupted global oil supplies and pushed up fuel prices. Trump has even asked Ukraine not to attack Russian oil facilities, as Moscow remains a major exporter of diesel. list 1 of 3 Trump calls on Ukraine to replace Zelenskyy amid tensions over Russia deal list 2 of 3 Hormuz attacks intensify as efforts to end war on Iran stall list 3 of 3 Oval Office spat to public rebukes: A timeline of Trump-Zelenskyy ties The spike in diesel prices in recent weeks has particularly put pressure on Trump’s Republican Party ahead of November’s midterm elections. Surveys show Americans hold the Trump administration responsible for the soaring fuel prices amid the unpopular US war on Iran. “Attacks on refineries and energy facilities have taken capacity out of an already stretched global fuel market, pushing up costs for transport, agriculture and businesses, with the pain ultimately passed on to consumers,” Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, told Al Jazeera, referring to the mutual attacks on energy sites by Ukraine and Russia. “A genuine ceasefire could help protect supplies and ease some of that pressure, particularly as winter approaches.” However, she warned it was too early to call it a “diplomatic breakthrough”, citing Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s statement that the energy truce came as a surprise to him. Trump’s decisions have drawn criticism from US politicians and European allies, who warn that allowing Russian fuel back into global markets could provide Moscow with new revenue to finance its war in Ukraine. In March, the Trump administration gave a sanctions waiver to Russian seaborne oil. So, why has Trump repeatedly changed his position on Russian energy, and what is behind his latest decisions? What is the ‘energy ceasefire’ Trump announced? On Sunday, Trump said Russia and Ukraine had agreed to immediately stop attacking each other’s energy infrastructure. “Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” he wrote on Truth Social, without providing further details. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he was not aware of the energy truce, saying the deal was “news to me” but welcomed the announcement nonetheless. However, he said Russian drones continued targeting Ukrainian energy facilities, including a power plant in Kharkiv, after Trump’s statement. “We are waiting for the details of the conditions between the Americans and Russians, ⁠⁠⁠⁠and we are waiting ⁠⁠⁠⁠to see one specific step the Americans are ready to take,” Zelenskyy said on Monday during a video address to a security conference in Warsaw. “This ⁠⁠⁠⁠energy ceasefire, it can work, and it can become a major step towards ending ‌‌‌‌the war if the Americans truly step in now and make ‌‌‌‌sure ‌‌‌‌Russians respect it.” Ukraine has repeatedly targeted Russian oil refineries, arguing that energy revenues help fund Moscow’s war . Russia, meanwhile, has attacked Ukraine’s electricity and heating infrastructure throughout the four-year conflict. Academic Alexey Muriaev has urged caution over Trump’s announcement, questioning whether an agreement has actually been reached, and if so, what it entails. “Is it about suspending attacks on oil refineries? And if that’s the case, then the situation would be inadequate, because Ukraine’s oil refineries have already been taken out by Russia’s strikes beforehand,” Muraviev, senior research fellow in Defence and Strategic Studies at Edith Cowan University, told Al Jazeera. “So, in this sense, it would mean effectively Ukraine suspending unilateral action against Russia’s oil refinery facilities.” Muriaev also linked the announcement to Trump’s diesel agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin, suggesting it may be a signal to Zelenskyy. “Attacking Russian oil refinery capability would probably be interpreted by Washington as an attack on US economic interests,” he said, referring to the agreement on diesel exports through April 2027. What’s the state of global oil prices? The ongoing conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine have continued to keep global oil markets under pressure. On Monday, Brent crude, the international benchmark, fell to about $103.04 a barrel following Trump’s ceasefire announcement and Russian diesel deal, while US West Texas Intermediate crude traded at about $90.96.

events.title: Giants Brigades lead southern Yemen fightback against the Houthis
events.summary: Yemen’s Southern Giants Brigades have emerged as one of the leading forces against the Houthis. On October 5, groups linked to the former Southern Transitional Council (STC), including the powerful Southern Giants Brigades , and troops of the internationally recognised government of Yemen, launched a major offensive against the Houthis near the strategically important Bab al-Mandeb strait. It was part of a nationwide military campaign aimed at driving the Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah or Supporters of God, out of territories under their control, including the vital coastline region seized by the Iran-linked group in September. list 1 of 3 Yemen forces claim key gains near Bab al-Mandeb: What’s the latest? list 2 of 3 What would it take for the Yemen offensive to succeed? list 3 of 3 Yemen’s government is on the attack against the Houthis. What has changed? By Monday afternoon, the pro-government force, led by the Giants Brigade, said they had managed to cut off the main road linking the Red Sea port city of Mocha with the Bab al-Mandeb, a vital waterway for energy supplies. This effectively gave the anti-Houthi forces one of their first major military gains in years and followed an announcement by Rashid al-Alimi, chairman of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council (PLC), of a major offensive against the Iran-backed group. It also highlighted the effectiveness of anti-Houthi forces – which include units with contrasting political goals – when working together. This has seen STC-affiliated groups, some of whom seek independence for the south, ally with pro-government national forces against the Houthis. The collaboration between these two factions follows a high-profile conflict in southern Yemen in January , when Saudi-aligned Yemeni government forces defeated the United Arab Emirates-backed STC, resulting in the relative centralisation of anti-Houthi forces. Among the leading formations in the recent government offensive led by this alliance are the Giants Brigades, which have their roots in the southern separatist movement. The force is commanded by Abd al-Rahman Abu Zaraa al-Muharrami , a Salafi who studied at the ultraconservative Dammaj religious school in the northern governorate of Saada. Formed largely by Salafi fighters during the battle against the Houthis in the southern city of Aden in the first half of 2015, the Giants Brigades have become one of Yemen’s most formidable military forces during the war. The brigades, believed to have been armed, trained and funded by the UAE, rose to prominence in 2017, leading an offensive that captured large swaths of Yemen’s western coast from the Houthis. The advance was eventually halted on the outskirts of the Red Sea port city of Hodeidah following the United Nations-brokered Stockholm Agreement in late 2018. In January 2022, the Giants Brigades achieved another major victory against the Houthis, seizing three districts in the southern governorate of Shabwa and advancing deeper into neighbouring Marib. Their offensive came to a halt after the Houthis launched an attack on Abu Dhabi on January 17, 2022. Al-Muharrami had no known military background before the war, which began with the Houthis’ capture of Sanaa in September 2014, and the group has largely stayed out of infighting between anti-Houthi forces. He joined Yemen’s eight-member PLC in April 2022, around the time his forces adopted the name Southern Giants Brigades, signalling their growing southern political identity. The formation later joined the STC, further strengthening the brigades’ ties with the southern separatist movement. When STC forces collapsed following the Yemeni government offensive in January, al-Muharrami flew to Riyadh and voiced support for the Saudi-led initiative to unify southern forces. The Giants Brigades’ involvement in the war against the Houthis is now seen as a test of its political allegiance, with some observers arguing that it remains fundamentally a separatist force. Some believe that the Giants Brigades’ previous advances against the Houthis into Hodeidah suggest that the group does not necessarily have a separatist agenda. They have also pointed to the group’s spearheading of the latest military offensive against the Houthis beyond southern Yemen, where many former STC units have remained confined, as another sign of its stronger commitment to national unity. Fathi bin Lazraq, editor of the Aden Al-Ghad newspaper and an outspoken critic of southern separatists, believes that the Giants Brigades would be willing to fight the Houthis anywhere in Yemen. “These forces are part of the contingent that has been fighting the Houthis since 2015, having been formed in Yemen following the collapse of the Yemeni army,” he told Al Jazeera. “They engage the Houthis from military, political, civil and religious standpoints.

events.title: EU to limit Chinese hybrid vehicle imports to 350,000 a year
events.summary: Brussels uses WTO rules to quickly impose quota, which will halve Chinese market share to 3% VW boss backs EU plan to bolster domestic industry The EU is to limit the number of hybrid electric vehicles imported from China to 350,000 cars a year, the European Commission has confirmed. Imports have been soaring in the past two years; about 800,000 battery and plug-in hybrids are likely to be sold this year. The EU expects that the quota, which will come into force in December, will halve China’s market share, which now stands at 6% in a landmark four-year agreement made in Beijing last week . The annual limit on imports of hybrids will be taken under the World Trade Organization safeguard measures, which mean it can be implemented swiftly without the type of investigations needed in anti-dumping measures. Any cars imported above the quota level will not be subject to tariffs, but will remain blocked in customs at docks in Europe. Chinese vehicles assembled within the EU, such as those made in Hungary or, in future, Spain, will not be subject to the quota, officials have confirmed, but EU companies making cars in China will. China’s exports of hybrids to the EU tripled to €6.7bn (£5.7bn) in the first half of this year, from €2.2bn a year earlier, according to Chinese customs data. As part of the deal, China has also agreed to drop some tariffs on auto parts and cut duties by half on footwear, olive oil and ice-cream from the EU. Officials stressed that the quota is fully supported by China, and further dialogue on cars and other imports including chemicals, renewable energy and furniture is continuing. “We will continue the dialogue on some products … this is by no means the end of the story,” an official said. Last month, the EU called for feedback on a new rule that could oblige companies to diversify their supply chains while the “Made in Europe” legislation would do the same in public procurement. On Thursday, EU leaders will discuss a French-German proposal for a “kill switch” or new instrument that would allow Brussels to block access to the single market for certain goods in the event of any harmful development, such as a ban on rare earths crucial for the tech and automotive industries. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning The deal on hybrid EVs comes amid mounting concern over the £1bn-a-day trade deficit the EU is now running with China. Up until recently, the EU’s strategy for tackling what it says is an “unsustainable” trade imbalance has been to seek to increase exports to China. Sources said there has been “a paradigm shift” with concerns of deindustrialisation and job losses in the industrial heartlands forcing a renewed focus on curbing imports rather than increasing exports. “We are closely surveilling, our imports. We know what’s coming in. We know where there’s a surge, and we know what hits the hardest in terms of our deindustrialisation,” said an official. Andrew Small, the director of the Asia programme at the European Council for Foreign Relations, said China was likely to “suck the EU into drawn-out negotiations” on other sectors but the mood had changed in the EU. “I think if China had offered a deal like this earlier in the year, say in spring, it would have been much easier to take the heat out. My sense is that things have now moved somewhat too far politically,” he said. Electric, hybrid and low-emission cars

events.title: U.S. private equity deal value was down 14.1% in Q3, PitchBook says
events.summary: Private equity has been in a low-grade slowdown for years, locked in a Groundhog Day loop. “You hear it every year now,” said Kyle Walters, PitchBook analyst. “You heard it in 2023, where private equity said: ‘It could come back this year.’ Then, you get to 2024, and 2024 is going to be a different year. Then, you get to 2025 and 2025 was a bit better, and people say ‘maybe this is the year.’” U.S. private equity—with more than $3 trillion in assets under management—has been locked in a cycle of geopolitical uncertainty and possible rate hikes, along with the challenges of a rapidly concentrating market with limited exits. This was true in Q3 2026: Exit value for the quarter was down 14.1% year-over-year and deal value was down 13.6% year-over-year, according to PitchBook data.  “AUM for the asset class isn’t growing nearly like it used to,” said Walters. “A 12% annual growth rate over the last ten, 15 years. We’re closer to half that now… This is the new norm, putting capital to work with headwinds in the market, and bringing companies to market with unresolved issues.”  Fundraising, Walters pointed out, is especially tough and has “definitely gotten harder over the last 18 to 24 months,” he said.  “Part of that is because of limited exits,” Walters told Fortune . “If you’re not getting distributions from your GPs, you have less capital to deploy, so you have to concentrate on fewer managers. That’s what we’re seeing take shape. But that’s not to say there are fewer managers raising capital. It’s that fewer managers are crossing the finish line, they’re fighting over scraps of the fundraising pie.” This isn’t true of everyone, of course. The biggest firms remain massive. Take KKR , which hit its $300 billion fundraising goal (originally slated for three years, the raise took 30 months). However, a possible set of new interest rate hikes (even before the end of the year) could throw the sector into even more turmoil. “[If there’s a rate hike] instead of some gradual recovery I’ve been imagining, you probably get a Q4 that looks a lot like Q3,” said Walters. “That’s not bad, it’s not at 2025 levels but still above the doldrums you saw in 2022 and 2023 where activity wasn’t really happening at all. PE has penciled a lot of this in, so they’ve kind of broadly accepted that there’s a rate hike coming. So, if it doesn’t, it’s a pleasant surprise. You’ll still see transactions take place—it’s just not going to be at the scale we hoped for coming into the year.”  As the weather forecast in Groundhog Day goes: “It’s going to be cold, it’s going to be gray, and it’s going to last you the rest of your life.”  See you tomorrow, Allie Garfinkle X: @agarfinks Email: alexandra.garfinkle@fortune.com Submit a deal for the Term Sheet newsletter here . events.title: When I thought of 'success,' I pictured a thriving career and high-achieving children. Then my daughter was born with complex medical needs.
events.summary: The author's definition of success changed when her daughter was born. Courtesy of Jamie Davis Smith When I was younger, I viewed success through the lens of typical milestones. I pictured a career as a lawyer, a family, and kids who would go on to their own thriving careers. When my daughter was born with complex medical needs and disabilities, my perspective changed. When I was younger, I pictured a career as an attorney and a family with high-achieving children who would one day build successful careers of their own. I built my life around these goals. I went to law school , got married, and let my job dictate when I started a family. For a while, everything seemed to be going according to plan. I had a thriving career as a civil rights lawyer that I loved, and I got pregnant right on schedule. Almost as soon as I saw two pink lines, I dove headlong into planning my child's future . I made a mental list of the activities she would need to be well-rounded and, laughably, even considered how the right preschool could eventually propel her into one of the country's best colleges. I planned to return to my full-time job a few months after giving birth and assumed that would go according to plan, too. However, my priorities shifted abruptly when my daughter was unexpectedly born with complex medical needs and disabilities. The author's daughter was born with complex medical needs and disabilities. Courtesy of Jamie Davis Smith My daughter's disabilities forced me to reconsider how I approached life I thought my first days as a new mother would be spent blissfully tracking feedings, tracking milestones, and joyfully putting my plans for my little family's future into place. However, instead of worrying about when my daughter would crawl, walk, and talk, I wondered whether she would live or die. That put her life, and mine, sharply into focus. At first, I still hoped our plans were only briefly derailed and that the vision I had for my family's future could still come to fruition. But when my daughter eventually came home from the neonatal intensive care unit, tethered to oxygen and monitors that beeped constantly, I realized that I needed to let go of the pressure and expectation that a successful life meant wealth, a professional career, and good schools . The author now has four kids, and thinks about their future differently. Courtesy of Jamie Davis Smith Leaning out was a necessity Changing my approach to life wasn't a choice at first. With a significantly disabled child who needed round-the-clock nursing-level care, working outside the home was impossible. I mourned the life I had lost: a job I loved that allowed me to help people, an active social life with friends I held dear, and frequent travel. As time passed, the extent of her disabilities and medical needs revealed themselves as even more severe than I had first realized. It became clear that she would never speak or perform basic tasks, such as feeding herself. She needed a wheelchair to get around and constant doctor's appointments and therapies to stay healthy. I mourned the life I had imagined for my daughter, too, one that involved playgrounds, dance classes, and eventually living independently. However, I slowly started focusing more on happiness and living in the present rather than keeping up with my law school classmates and their typically developing kids. My definition of success shifted from a big house and nice car to truly enjoying myself and living to the fullest each day. I changed what success meant for my kids, too. Instead of worrying about whether my kids would get into Harvard, I celebrated my daughter taking her first steps at age seven and learning to use an assistive communication device to make basic requests like asking for a cup of water. I now have three other kids who are typically developing. While I could easily have slid back into my original parenting mindset of pressuring them to have high-paying careers , I now emphasize the importance of happiness and making time for people and activities that bring them joy every day. I now know, starkly, that life can change in an instant and tomorrow isn't promised to anyone. Now, she is more focused on thriving than surviving. Courtesy of Jamie Davis Smith Now I focus on thriving rather than surviving I realized that before my daughter was born, many days were about survival. I was focused on achieving the next goal, the next milestone. While planning for a better future, I had practically forgotten how to focus on the here and now. My daughter showed me how necessary and important it is to find happiness each day. Although I left my full-time job out of necessity, it was the right call for several reasons. I now have flexible jobs as an adjunct professor and a freelance writer. While I don't have the prestige and paycheck that I once did, I have more flexibility to spend time with my daughter and her three younger siblings. I can fit in walks with friends while the kids are at school and find time to decompress with a book and a cup of hot tea when I need to. It's not the type of life I imagined, but I am grateful every day that my daughter taught me why it's so important to just survive, but thrive. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Two U.S. professors win Nobel prize in economics
events.summary: Stanford University's Robert E. Hall and Columbia University's Michael Woodford won the Nobel Prize in economics for research on how policymakers can stabilize economies , the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said on Monday. Why it matters: Their work helped shape how central banks set interest rates and communicate policy. The win comes as those institutions fight energy-driven inflation and risks to economic growth. Zoom out: For decades, policymakers relied on economic models that linked higher inflation with lower unemployment. But that framework broke down during the 1970s stagflation when both prices and joblessness surged at the same time. "The solution by Robert Hall and Michael Woodford was to build a new framework ground up," Timo Boppart, a member of the Nobel economics prize committee, said on Monday. What they're saying: Woodford, who called into Monday's press conference hosted by the committee, said he was "elated" by the win. " It's a tremendous honor. It's a surprise — but I'm feeling very good about it," Woodford said. The intrigue : Asked by a reporter about the threat to the global economy, Woodford said the Middle East conflict has disrupted energy markets and driven price changes with consequences far beyond the region. He pointed to the 2008 financial crisis as a key test of his research, when central banks cut interest rates to near zero but struggled to revive economic activity. His framework helped explain how other tools, including forward guidance and asset purchases, could support the economy. Zoom in: In research culminating in a landmark 2003 book, Woodford developed a framework linking businesses' pricing decisions to inflation and monetary policy. Hall — a Stanford professor who chaired the committee that dates U.S. recessions for 46 years — showed in a 1978 paper how consumers' spending decisions reflect expectations about future income. Of note: The prize comes with an award of 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million), up from 11 million kronor last year, to be divided between the two winners. Flashback: Recent economics Nobels have recognized research on technological progress, economic prosperity and labor markets. Last year's prize went to Joel Mokyr, Philippe Aghion and Peter Howitt for their work explaining how innovation drives economic growth. In 2024, Daron Acemoglu, Simon Johnson and James Robinson won for their research on how institutions shape economic prosperity. Harvard economist Claudia Goldin won in 2023 for research that advanced the world's understanding of women's labor market outcomes.

events.summary: A New York federal judge ordered the Trump administration to immediately stop airing government-funded ads criticized as propaganda and aimed at influencing the midterm election. The temporary restraining order by Judge Jennifer Rochon also bars the Department of Homeland Security from spending any more of the $20 million set aside for the TV ad campaign. President Donald Trump said on Oct. 5 he would pay for the ads going forward. The White House said the president would not reimburse the federal government for the cost of the already aired ads. A federal judge in New York ordered the Trump administration Sunday night to immediately stop airing controversial government-funded television ads featuring President Donald Trump that critics call political propaganda intended to influence the November midterm election. The temporary restraining order by Judge Jennifer Rochon in Manhattan federal court also bars the Department of Homeland Security from spending any more of the $20 million allocated for the ad campaign. About $19 million of that allocation has already been spent on the ads. The order came a day after the Manhattan U.S. Attorney's Office, which is defending the Trump administration in a lawsuit challenging the ads, told Rochon the ads would not continue airing past Sunday. Rochon's order, which lasts 14 days unless extended, directs the Trump administration to cancel all scheduled ads, including those due to air on Sunday evening. The ads have included the caption "Paid for by the U.S. Government" since they began being aired. The Manhattan U.S. Attorney's Office declined to comment. "Instead, much of Defendants' opposition boils down to a single premise: it is too late for the Court to act. That is not because Defendants have stopped airing the ads," the plaintiffs said. events.title: Ray Dalio and billionaire F1 boss Toto Wolff traded tips on how to get the best out of staff using 'tough love'
events.summary: Ray Dalio and Mercedes F1 boss Toto Wolff discussed why high-pressure leadership only works when it is matched with genuine care for a team. Jakub Porzycki/NurPhoto via Getty Images/Dia Dipasupil/Getty Images Billionaire Ray Dalio says a balance of high standards and genuine care is a recipe for happy staff. Meaningful work and relationships create stronger teams, Dalio said at a conference in Singapore. Dalio's comments were echoed by fellow panelist Toto Wolff, the boss of the Mercedes F1 team. Investing and F1 may not share obvious similarities at first glance, but when it comes to managing people, some lessons cross disciplines. During a recent conference appearance, Bridgewater Associates founder Ray Dalio and Toto Wolff, the billionaire CEO of Mercedes F1, agreed that demanding leaders need to pair high standards with genuine care for their teams. As Dalio put it, management needs to implement "tough love." "My mantra is meaningful work and meaningful relationships," Dalio said on a panel at the Milken Institute Asia Summit in Singapore last week. "When I say tough love, there’s the tough, but there’s also that element of love, that element of mutual caring." Dalio, who built Bridgewater into the world’s largest hedge fund, said leaders need a clear mission and have to hold people accountable for delivering on it. But he argued that pressure without a sense of shared purpose can undermine a team. "You want tough love with your kids; you want tough love with everything because tough makes you stronger," he said. "And then also when you have a team, you have to make that team successful." Wolff offered a case study in how that balance can be difficult to get right. He recalled putting "pressure and pressure" on a senior Mercedes technical leader during a disappointing season, after the team’s run of eight straight constructors’ championships ended. After Wolff publicly said Mercedes’ car did not deserve to win a race, the executive told him he was considering leaving because he could no longer handle the pressure. Wolff said he ultimately changed course. At a dinner intended to resolve the dispute, he offered the executive a contract allowing him to leave on one month’s notice, far shorter than the usual notice period for senior technical staff, and told him to set his own salary and bonus. "Fundamentally, I had to change," Wolff said. "I couldn’t continue what I thought was my modus operandi over 30 years." Dalio said that kind of mutual care matters beyond compensation. While money is important, he said, employees and leaders alike are motivated by connection, purpose, and a sense of belonging to a community. Dalio’s comments echoed an earlier point Wolff made: that workers are not motivated by pay alone. The Mercedes boss said leaders who understand employees' personal priorities, whether that is recognition, time with family, or room for a hobby, are better placed to keep them. Dalio took that idea further, arguing that once people have enough money to meet their needs, happiness is no longer closely tied to wealth. "The greatest determinant of happiness is a sense of community," he said. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Current price of oil as of October 12, 2026
events.summary: As of 6:45 a.m. Eastern Time today, oil sold for $108.04 per barrel (using Brent as the benchmark, which we’ll get into momentarily). That’s $2.32 higher than yesterday morning and approximately a $44.50 rise over the past year. Oil price per barrel % Change Price of oil yesterday $105.72 +2.19% Price of oil 1 month ago $106.02 +1.90% Price of oil 1 year ago $63.49 +70.16% Will oil prices go up? It’s impossible to predict the future of oil prices. Several factors determine the movement of oil, but it ultimately boils down to supply and demand. Again, when threats of economic downturn, war, etc. are high, the oil trajectory can turn rapidly. How oil prices translate to gas pump prices When you pay for gas at the pump, you’re paying for more than just the crude oil itself; you’re also springing for links along the chain, such as the refineries and wholesalers—not to mention taxes and local gas station markups. Still, the crude oil aspect affects the final price most dramatically, as it typically accounts for more than half the price per gallon. When oil prices spike, so do gas prices. And frustratingly, when oil prices drop, gas prices tend to take their time drifting down to the lower price (sometimes referred to as “rockets and feathers”). The role of the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve In case of emergency, the U.S. has a store of crude oil known as the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. Its primary purpose is energy security in case of disaster (think sanctions, severe storm damage, even war). But it can also go a long way toward softening crippling price hikes during supply shocks. It’s not a long-term answer—more of an immediate relief to assist the consumer and keep critical parts of the economy running, like key industries, emergency services, public transportation, etc. How oil and natural gas prices are linked Oil and natural gas are both major energy fuels. A big change in oil prices can affect natural gas by extension. For example, if oil prices increase, some industries may swap natural gas for some segments of their operations where possible—which increases demand for natural gas. Historical performance of oil When examining oil’s performance, there are generally two major benchmarks: Brent crude oil is the main global oil benchmark. West Texas Intermediate (WTI) is the main benchmark of North America. Between the two, Brent better represents global oil performance because it prices much of the world’s traded crude. And, it’s often the best way to track historical oil performance. In fact, even the U.S. Energy Information Administration now uses Brent as its primary reference in its Annual Energy Outlook. Looking at the Brent benchmark across several decades, oil has been anything but steady. It’s seen spikes due to factors such as wars and supply cuts, and it’s also seen crashes from global recessions and an oversupply (called a “glut”). For example: The early 1970s brought the first big oil shock when the Middle East cut exports and imposed an embargo on the U.S. and others during the Yom Kippur War. Prices dropped in the mid-1980s for reasons such as lower demand and more non-OPEC oil producers entering the industry. Prices spiked again in 2008 with increased global demand, but it soon plummeted alongside the global financial crisis. During the 2020 COVID lockdown, oil demand collapsed like never before—bringing prices below $20 per barrel. All to say, oil’s historical performance has been anything but smooth. Again, it’s hugely affected by wars, recessions, OPEC whims, evolving energy initiatives and policies, and much more. Energy coverage from  Fortune Looking to stay up-to-date regarding the latest energy developments? Check out our recent coverage: The IEA wants to empty its oil reserves faster ‘Ukraine’s Yuriy Ryzhenkov: Steelmaking on brink of collapse as Russian bombing intensifies Oil theft is on the rise in the heart of U.S. shale country Frequently asked questions How is the current price of oil per barrel actually determined? The current price of oil per barrel depends largely on supply and demand, including news about potential future supply and demand (geopolitics, decisions made by OPEC+, etc.). In the U.S., prices also move based on how friendly an administration is to drilling, as it can affect future supply. For example, 2025 saw the Trump administration move to reopen more than 1.5 million acres in the Coastal Plain of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge for oil and gas leasing, reversing the Biden administration’s policy of limiting oil drilling in the Arctic. How often does the price of oil change during the day? The price of oil updates constantly when the “futures” markets are open. A futures market is effectively an auction where people agree to buy or sell oil in the future. As long as people and companies are trading contracts, the oil price is changing. How does U.S. shale oil production affect the current price of oil? In short, shale is rock that contains oil and natural gas. Think of shale as energy yet to be tapped. The more shale the U.S. accesses, the more energy we’ll have—and the more easily oil prices can keep from spiking as much thanks to a greater supply. How does the current price of oil impact inflation and the broader economy? When oil is expensive, it tends to make everyday items cost more. This can be related to energy (your heating, gas utilities, etc.), but it’s also due to the logistics involved with making those items accessible to you. Shipping, for example, can affect the price of things at the grocery store, as it’s more expensive to get those products from warehouses and farms onto the shelf. events.title: A ‘Mathpocalypse’ is freaking out cyber and finance experts. Should you be worried?
events.summary: The world has seen plenty of scary cybersecurity threats in recent years, but nothing quite like what emerged last week. The new threat came in the form of a document drop from OpenAI that The Economist proclaimed to be “judgment day for mathematics” and others simply dubbed “The Mathpocalypse.” This isn’t just idle media chatter. In the view of a prominent cybersecurity expert at Johns Hopkins, “We might lose public key cryptography.” Hoo boy. So what exactly is going on? It’s helpful to know that the OpenAI documents in question don’t describe a scary new way to hack global computers. Instead, they reveal the solution to hundreds of math problems that top mathematicians have struggled for decades to solve. And contrary to some reports, the OpenAI math dump isn’t going to accelerate the arrival of so-called “Q-day” when quantum computing cracks popular encryption algorithms. The real reason the OpenAI documents have sparked an uproar is that they signify the arrival of a new species of mathematical super-genius—one that may be capable of finding flaws in the algorithms we use to encrypt banking passwords, email accounts, and the rest of our digital lives. These algorithms have been part of daily life for years, and have long been regarded as sound by top cryptographers. They may hold up for years to come. But if there are flaws in these algorithms, it’s a matter of time before someone uses powerful new AI math tools to find them—and potentially wreak havoc with the world’s financial system. Predictably, it is the crypto community—who are paranoid at the best of times—who have been at the forefront of the debate over how to respond to the “Mathpocalypse.” Citing the possibility that the so-called ECDSA (Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm) protocol could soon be cracked, one Bitcoin researcher suggested crypto holders “calmly begin planning for ‘bunker mode'” by moving their funds to secret new addresses. Other crypto experts have replied that such a move is too drastic for now, but the impulse to freak out is understandable. While the “Mathpocalypse” threatens banks and financial institutions of all sorts, most of those companies would be in position to reverse transactions carried out by an AI-powered hacker. That’s not the case, though, in the crypto world, where blockchain transactions are deemed irreversible—which is likely to make popular currencies like Bitcoin and Ethereum prime targets. It’s also notable that, if an AI supervillain does discover a flaw in the algorithms that secure blockchains, we’re unlikely to find out right away. As TBPN noted , there is a game theory element at play: If a bad guy possesses a killer hack, they would be foolish to carry out a massive heist since doing so would likely destroy the value of the crypto. The right play would be not to steal all the Bitcoin, but to conduct a series of smaller and more subtle robberies to avoid showing their hand. So what happens now? For starters, it’s encouraging that news of the Mathpocalypse created barely a ripple in the market—a signal that crypto and financial leaders have at least some time to figure out what to do next. One of the more intriguing ideas so far—aside from hiding your Bitcoin and heading to a bunker—comes via Dragonfly’s Haseeb Qureshi, who published a blog post titled “Against Cryptographic Doomerism.” In it, Qureshi posits that there is a 95% chance that “everything is totally fine” but says it’s imperative that blockchains up their governance game and, for now, prioritize speed over decentralized purity. He goes on to call for blockchains to introduce updates mandating a signature system that will leave a clunky copy of everyone’s transactions, ensuring a chain can survive a wipeout at the hands of some AI dark lord. I have no idea if this would work—or even if it’s a good idea. But I do like the spur to action and the lively debate taking place about how to harden our encryption systems against powerful AI-driven attacks. This is crypto at its best: Smart people operating at the cutting edge of technology looking to solve hard problems. Don’t be surprised if the broader financial world, once it comes to recognize the threat, looks to the blockchain sector for ideas to handle it. Jeff John Roberts jeff.roberts@fortune.com @jeffjohnroberts This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: US says Hormuz oil flows recover to 14 million bpd despite Saudi attacks
events.summary: Up to 14 million barrels of oil a day are moving through the Strait of Hormuz , with Gulf crude flows recovering to between 80 and 90 per cent of prewar levels, US Energy Secretary Chris Wright has said. Additional supplies from the Gulf are also being transported through pipelines bypassing Hormuz, Mr Wright said on Monday, addressing the 25th WPC Energy Congress in Riyadh remotely. "The crude problem we talked a lot about – it's still there but it's mostly handled," he said, offering a more optimistic assessment than ship-tracking data suggests. Figures from analytics firm Kpler show oil exports through Hormuz averaged slightly under nine million bpd in September, the highest monthly level since the war began, but only about 44 per cent of the 20.6 million bpd recorded in February. About 22 vessels crossed the strait daily in the 30 days to October 12, about two thirds of them tankers, according to Kpler. The data is provisional and subject to revision as tracking information is updated, reflecting movements registered by 2pm UAE time on October 12. Laden crude tankers leaving the Gulf carried about 8.9 million bpd over the past month, mostly from Saudi Arabia and Iraq. The figures are not directly comparable with Mr Wright's broader recovery estimate, which includes supplies transported through bypass pipelines. Kpler's September data nevertheless suggests lower volumes through Hormuz than those cited by the US official. Mr Wright's comments came after an attack on Riyadh airport on Saturday killed 13 people and injured about 300, underscoring the security risks facing the world's biggest oil-exporting region. "I want to start out by strongly condemning the cowardly attacks by the Houthis on the people of Saudi Arabia, on civilian infrastructure," Mr Wright said in addressing the energy congress on Monday. He reaffirmed Washington's commitment to the kingdom as energy ministers and industry executives gathered in Riyadh despite heightened security concerns. "We are here as your partners," he said, reiterating the US's "unwavering support for Saudi Arabia". Mr Wright warned the recovery in crude supplies had yet to ease pressure on fuel markets, with diesel prices remaining "very high", and jet fuel and petrol prices also elevated. "The challenge is still here and the challenge is still ahead of us," he said.

events.title: UAE wealth set to hit $6 trillion in 2030 despite short-term war volatility
events.summary: Net wealth in the UAE is set to jump to $6 trillion by the end of this decade despite the short-term volatility caused by conflict in the Middle East , a new report has found. In the five years to the end of 2030, net wealth in the Emirates is set to increase by more than $2.3 trillion, at annual growth of 10.6 per cent, the report by global advisory firm Boston Consulting Group said. The sharp projected increase, driven by a rise in real assets and financial wealth, “points to the UAE's long-term wealth creation potential”, BCG said in its Global Wealth Report 2026: The Great Reordering report on Monday. Last year alone, net wealth in the Arab world’s second-largest economy grew by almost 13 per cent on an annual basis to reach $3.6 trillion. Real, or physical, assets with intrinsic value such as property portfolios reached $2.4 trillion in 2025, jumping from $2.2 trillion at the end of the previous year. Financial wealth grew to $1.4 trillion in 2025, rising from $1.2 trillion a year earlier, while liabilities for the same period rose from $210 billion to $220 billion. The report estimates liabilities to rise to $340 billion by 2030. The Iran war has introduced “short-term volatility across Middle Eastern markets, with investor sentiment shaped by geopolitical uncertainty and oil-price movements”, said Lukasz Rey, managing director and partner at BCG. “While we anticipate slightly lower growth over the next one to two years, a rebound is expected towards the latter part of the decade.” Sovereign wealth strength, economic diversification agendas, family-business liquidity events and private capital activity will all help drive wealth creation in the country, Mr Rey said. Caution to prevail BCG, he said, expects wealth managers to remain cautious in the near term. However, “the region's wealth development story remains structurally resilient over the five-year projection horizon”, Mr Rey added. The Iran war, which began on February 28, has led to increased economic uncertainty across the Middle East. Despite a halt in all-out hostilities since early April, several attempts to reach a permanent deal to end the conflict have failed. The World Bank last week said Gulf economies would contract by an average of 4.3 per cent this year, a downwards revision of 5.7 percentage points from its forecast in April. The International Monetary Fund also expects economies in the region to contract this year but anticipates a sharp expansion next year once the conflict settles, managing director Kristalina Georgieva said. Despite the geopolitical uncertainty and economic headwinds, wealth generation and flow of new money to the UAE continues. The country remains a magnet for the ultra-wealthy , as well as global wealth managers and trillion-dollar asset managers. A base in the country offers global investors and money managers opportunities to expand regional operations and work with some of the world's largest sovereign wealth funds, as well as family offices and institutional partners. Concentration of wealth The UAE’s financial wealth remains concentrated among high-net-worth individuals, with “the composition of wealth expected to evolve by 2030 as more wealth accumulates within the lower high-net-worth segment”, the BCG report said. The country had about 500 ultra-high-net-worth individuals – those with assets in excess of $100 million – in 2025. That number is expected to jump to about 800 by the end of the decade, while their share of total financial wealth will rise marginally from 26.3 per cent to 26.5 per cent. The upper high-net-worth segment, featuring people with assets of $20 million to $100 million, is forecast to grow from about 2,700 to 4,200 individuals, with their share of wealth broadly stable, rising from 7.4 per cent in 2025 to 7.6 per cent in 2030. Meanwhile, the group of 200,000 lower high-net-worth individuals, with an asset range of $1 million to $20 million, are estimated to increase their share of financial wealth from 29.3 per cent in 2025 to 31.5 per cent in 2030. The affluent segment with assets worth $1 million is expected to expand from about 500,000 to 600,000 individuals in 2030. However, its share of wealth will decline from 15.5 per cent to 14.6 per cent, BCG data found. Centre of choice The UAE also continues to strengthen its position as a global wealth booking centre, with cross-border wealth belonging to international clients and booked in the country jumping more than 11 per cent to $721 billion last year. Currency and deposits, valued at $471.8 billion in 2025, are projected to rise more than 10 per cent annually to $778.9 billion by 2030. Bonds are estimated to grow almost 12 per cent on an annual basis to $27.8 billion, while equities are expected to reach jump to $591.9 billion by 2030, from $419.4 billion last year, BCG found.

events.title: India’s retail inflation jumps to 5.54% in September, above estimates
events.summary: India’s consumer price inflation increased to 5.54% in September from 4.82% in August. India's central bank expects core inflation to be at 4.4% for the financial year ending March 2027 and headline inflation at 5.2%, higher than its medium-term target of 4%. India's headline inflation rose to 5.54% in September from 4.82% in August , adding pressure on the country's central bank to further tighten monetary policy. The consumer price index print was slightly above economists' expectations of 5.40%, according to a Reuters poll. Inflation has been on the rise for 11 straight months in the world's fastest-growing economy and has touched a 22-month high in September. India's food inflation climbed 7.74% in September from 5.97% the month prior, with prices rising faster in rural areas than cities, India's Ministry of Statistics and Program Implementation said in a Monday release. Transport services for goods inflation rose 14.73% while that for personal transport jumped 7.46%, as per the release. Earlier this month, the Reserve Bank of India raised its interest rates for the first time since 2023 , joining several major central banks in tightening monetary policy in a bid to arrest accelerating inflation. India's central bank also said that in the "current conditions" further rate cuts were "off the table in the near term" and policy action could either be a rate hike or a pause. India is among the countries most vulnerable to the supply disruptions caused by the Iran war. It imports nearly 85% of its fuel needs, and before the Iran war it heavily relied on energy supplies through the Strait of Hormuz . Oil prices have been elevated due to the tensions in the Middle East. Experts, however, predict that prices will remain volatile in the near term amid concerns over the Middle East conflict and the impact of Hurricane Isaias. India's central bank expects core inflation to be at 4.4% for the financial year ending March 2027 and headline inflation at 5.2%, which is higher than the RBI's medium-term target of 4%. The RBI raised India's economic growth estimate by 40 basis points to 7.1% but cautioned that protracted geopolitical tensions, trade frictions, tightening of financial conditions and elevated international commodity prices would likely weigh on economic activity. Food prices in particular and India's rural economy also face an added risk from the Super El Nino , with the country receiving its lowest rainfall in over a decade during June to September, a key season for its largely rain-fed farms and reservoirs. The rainfall was the fourth lowest since 2001, and the 13th driest since 1901, according to the India Meteorological Department. Several parts of key farm states such as Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, Punjab, and Haryana are facing extreme drought conditions. HSBC said in a report on Oct. 7 that it expects another rate hike in December, a day after the RBI policy action. "This may not be a deep tightening cycle, but a tightening cycle it is," the analysts said, adding that the September retail inflation data is likely to show a "sizeable headline pop."

events.title: American professors Hall and Woodford win Nobel economics prize
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Americans Robert E Hall and Michael Woodford win Nobel memorial prize in economics Robert E Hall (left) and Michael Woodford shared the economics award. ( Reuters: Anders Wiklund ) American professors Robert E Hall and Michael Woodford have won the Nobel memorial prize in economics. They were honoured for their groundbreaking work on the micro-economic foundations of macro-economic stabilisation. The will receive around $900,000 each for winning an award that began in 1968. American-born economists Robert E Hall and Michael Woodford have won the Nobel memorial prize in economics for their work on the micro-economic foundations of macro-economic stabilisation. Hall, 83, is a professor with Stanford University in California, and 71-year-old Woodford is a professor at Columbia University in New York. The award was announced by the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in Stockholm. "The laureates' work has provided us with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world," John Hassler, chair of the Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences, said. "With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume." Last year, three researchers who study business innovation won for explaining how new products and inventions promote economic growth and human welfare, even as they leave older companies in the dust. The Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences was first awarded in 1968. ( Reuters: Tom Little ) The economics prize is formally known as the Bank of Sweden Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel. The central bank established it in 1968 as a memorial to Nobel, the 19th-century Swedish businessman and chemist who invented dynamite and established the five Nobel prizes. Nobel purists stress that the economics prize is technically not a Nobel prize, but it is always presented together with the others on December 10, the anniversary of Nobel's death in 1896. The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.8 million), whether for an individual, small group of laureates or organisation, so they will receive around $900,000 each. Journalists in Stockholm were able to interview co-winner Michael Woodford on the telephone from the US. ( AFP: Jonathan Nackstrand ) "It's a surprise, but I'm feeling very good about it," Woodford told reporters via phone during the announcement of the prize, saying he felt "elated" over receiving "a tremendous honour". The US imposes sanctions on the International Criminal Court hours after one of its former judges is given the Nobel Peace Prize. A concrete example of his work implemented in practice was when the 2008 financial crisis created a situation where "traditional tools of monetary policy were not really adequate to deal with the problem of restoring economic activity," he said, noting that interest rates were already lowered to zero in many countries. One of the new approaches employed by central banks was to start making "more explicit statements" on where they believed guiding interest rates were headed in the future, which continues to this day. The majority of previous economics laureates have been from the US. Only three women have ever won, most recently Claudia Goldin in 2023 for work on how gender has affected pay and employment over time in the United States. Nobel prizes for the categories of medicine, physics, chemistry, literature and ​peace were announced last week.

events.title: Recruiters could soon interview a candidate’s AI twin before meeting a real person
events.summary: Good morning! Your next recruiter screening interview might not require a candidate to show up. Ashutosh Garg, CEO of AI talent management platform Eightfold AI, predicts job seekers will soon be able to send their digital twin instead. Garg recently launched TwinCafe, a platform where job seekers can upload their résumé, LinkedIn profile, work samples, and other relevant documents to create a digital version of themselves. The platform generates a shareable link that Garg envisions candidates placing at the top of their résumé or LinkedIn profile. The idea isn’t simply to save candidates time. Garg believes digital twins could change the way companies screen talent. Rather than spending the first 20 minutes of an interview walking through a résumé, a recruiter could question the candidate’s twin beforehand, digging into previous roles, skills, or gaps in their work history. The recruiter could then reserve time with the actual candidate for questions that require human judgment and interaction. “My main motivation was that a résumé is so limiting,” Garg says. A digital twin, he argues, can “fill in the blanks” on parts of a candidate’s background that might otherwise raise questions, such as career breaks or moves between industries. Recruiters today spend much of an initial screening interview verifying information on a candidate’s résumé, Garg says. If they can do some of that with a digital twin beforehand, the actual interview “could be a lot more focused on the human aspect versus the fact-check aspect,” he says. “The quality of the interview dramatically improves.” Garg envisions a future in which a recruiter may not even need to be present for the first screen at all: They can simply send their own agent to talk to the job seeker’s digital twin. This would allow them to surface people the standard résumé would have rejected—and interview way more people. “Why limit a screening to five candidates?” Garg says. “Why not interview everyone?” Kristin Stoller Editorial Director, Fortune Live Media kristin.stoller@fortune.com This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: HMV to close Oxford Street store after three years
events.summary: HMV says it is looking for a new site in London's West End HMV has said it will shut its flagship Oxford Street store three years after it reopened the site, blaming a proposed doubling of the rent for the closure. The entertainment chain said it would leave the shop in March 2027, in a move affecting more than 50 staff. It said it was looking for a new site in London's West End district for its flagship shop and said it planned to maintain a "significant presence" in the capital. Phil Halliday, managing director of HMV, said it was "frustrating" that the Oxford Street shop was "commercially unviable". He said: "This is a special store, it's where we began 100 years ago and bringing it back to life in 2023 was a big moment in our recent history. "We are looking ahead, and our focus is now on what we do to make exciting steps for HMV in 2027." HMV shut its Oxford Street store in 2019 after it went into administration The group said its landlords had proposed doubling the rent on the site at 363 Oxford Street, and it was also facing a bill for "substantial" renovation works at the store, which together would make the shop "commercially unsustainable". HMV said it would look to transfer affected workers to its two other London stores and head office while it looked for a new site. The chain reopened its historic Oxford Street store in November 2023 after a four-year absence following a deal secured with landlords. It first opened the Oxford Street site in 1921. HMV has 113 stores across the UK, including six sites under the Fopp brand, as well as another eight in Europe. The group said it remained committed to high street stores. events.title: Ukraine’s Zelenskyy accuses Russia of violating Trump’s ‘energy ceasefire’
events.summary: The EU also announced that it officially added almost 1,600 new sanctions on Russia’s military industrial complex. Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused Russia of violating the “energy ceasefire” that United States President Donald Trump unilaterally announced at the weekend and promised to respond if the attacks continue. Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum via videolink on Monday, the Ukrainian president urged the US to step in to ensure ⁠that Moscow abided by the truce, noting that there have already been “Russian violations of the energy ceasefire announced by ‌President Trump.” list 1 of 4 Trump calls on Ukraine to replace Zelenskyy amid tensions over Russia deal list 2 of 4 Russia’s Yandex says data centre shut down after drone attack list 3 of 4 Oval Office spat to public rebukes: A timeline of Trump-Zelenskyy ties list 4 of 4 Zelenskyy says Russia violated energy truce announced by Trump “We are waiting for the details of the conditions between the Americans and Russians, ⁠and we are waiting ⁠to see what specific steps the Americans are ready to take,” said Zelenskyy, who expressed surprise at the ceasefire deal. “This ⁠energy ceasefire, it can work, and it can become a major step toward ending ‌the war if the Americans truly step in now and make ‌sure ‌Russians respect it … If Russia does not agree to an energy ceasefire, we will respond,” Zelenskyy told the Warsaw Security Forum. Trump’s announcement on Sunday that the two countries had agreed to an “energy ceasefire” caused confusion. It came two days after Trump declared a temporary easing of US sanctions on Russian diesel, prompting outrage from European allies and Kyiv, who said it would only embolden Russian President Vladimir Putin. Both Ukraine and Russia have been launching mutual attacks on each other’s energy infrastructure for months, adding to upward pressure on global energy prices that have risen amid the US-Israeli war on Iran. Zelenskyy initially denied any knowledge of the agreement and said it was “news to him,” according to Axios. Trump has previously taken to his Truth Social account to announce truces or other arrangements before either Kyiv or Moscow confirmed them. “An energy ceasefire and other steps to reduce escalation and guarantee security are truly needed here in reality, not just on Truth Social,” Zelenskyy added. European leaders expressed encouragement at the proposed ceasefire, but agreed with Zelenskyy that it had not taken effect. “I have not noted, over‌ the last 48 hours, any energy ceasefire coming from the ‌Russian ‌side,” French President Emmanuel Macron told reporters at a Paris autoshow. At the Warsaw Security Forum, ⁠Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that “Russia is not interested in ‌a ceasefire, de-escalation, or peace … that is why I will go to Brussels to urge all European partners ⁠to consider increasing ⁠sanctions.” In Brussels, the European Union announced that it has officially added almost 1,600 new sanctions on Russia’s military industrial complex, including individuals and entities involved in its four-and-a-half-year war , in a bid to maintain pressure on Moscow. “This is the single largest expansion of our sanctions list since Russia started its war,” EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas wrote online. “Europe is again showing a united front … We are making it significantly harder, slower and more expensive for Russia to produce the weapons it uses to kill Ukrainians,” she added. Meanwhile, Russia ⁠attacked Ukrainian gas production facilities belonging to its state ⁠oil and gas ⁠company Naftogaz in the Kharkiv region overnight, which caused a fire, the ‌company said on Monday. “The attack damaged critical equipment. Our employees are doing everything possible ⁠to repair the ⁠damage as quickly as possible and ⁠prevent risks to ⁠the stable ⁠operation of the energy system,” Naftogaz acting CEO ‌Sergii Fedorenko wrote on Telegram. A day earlier, Zelenskyy had said that Ukraine was ready to halt attacks on Russian oil refineries if Moscow ceased its own attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.

events.title: Tanzania seeks investment to tackle youth job pressure
events.summary: The News Tanzania is counting on increased investment to accelerate industrialization and create jobs for its young population, the prime minister said. The government has targeted $15 billion in annual foreign direct investment, roughly triple last year’s figure, as part of its long-term economic plans . Mwigulu Nchemba, speaking on the sidelines of an investment forum in London, said the government had put money into rail and port infrastructure, as well as expanding power generation to create an industrial base. This was on top of cutting the cost of doing business, and strengthening supply chains. Nchemba said increased industrialization would boost local processing of natural resources leading to more employment opportunities. Tanzania, like many African countries, has a rapidly expanding population. The UN estimates 42% of people are aged 14 or under . The prime minister said the path to creating work for all the country’s school leavers rests on developing the private sector through investment. “There is no way you can absorb all those graduates,” the prime minister told reporters. “The only way you can solve the issue of job creation is by empowering the private sector to create those vacancies for our youth.” Know More Tanzania has large offshore gas resources and deposits of minerals needed for the energy transition and digital infrastructure — such as copper, lithium, and cobalt — as well as precious metals and stones, including gold and diamonds. In August, the country commissioned a 2,115 MW hydropower plant that more than doubled its electricity generation capacity and ​created a surplus that officials said could support power exports and industrial growth. Tanzania, like governments across the continent, is looking for ways to add value locally instead of raw minerals exports. In neighboring Kenya, President William Ruto has focused on job creation through industrialization as a key plank in his campaign to secure a second term in next year’s election. Notable Liquefied natural gas development offers Tanzania its most obvious means of monetizing its giant gas reserves after the wars in Ukraine and Iran upended global energy markets, wrote Neil Ford in African Business.

events.title: Sheng Siong, OCBC, SGX receive analysts’ downgrades
events.summary: New challenges are emerging for Sheng Siong, while its previous competitive advantage might be fading, says an analyst. SINGAPORE – A few Singapore stocks received downgrades by analysts recently, including OCBC, Sheng Siong and the Singapore Exchange (SGX). Maybank analyst Hussaini Saifee downgraded the supermarket’s stock to “hold”, leading to the stock sliding more than 2% on Oct 12. Hussaini said Sheng Siong remains a high-quality operator, but its “strong share price re-rating now prices in much of it”. He added that Sheng Siong has benefited from resilient consumption, market share gains and targeted vouchers that channelled spending directly to supermarkets, but that support is weakening as assistance is shifting to GST vouchers and cash payments. “Supermarket growth has already eased to low single digits,” he said, adding that growth will track underlying income and population trends, instead of repeating the “unusually favourable” conditions of recent years. He added that new challenges are emerging for the supermarket brand, while its previous competitive advantage might be fading. Previously, Sheng Siong captured displaced demand when Giant and Cold Storage shut some stores. Hussaini also noted that people may be crossing the border into Malaysia to shop, given the upcoming Johor Bahru-Singapore Rapid Transit System Link, or going online to get groceries, which might pose challenges to Sheng Siong. “While neither appears disruptive enough to reshape the industry in the near term, both point to a less favourable backdrop than in recent years,” he added. He downgraded the target price to $3.12, from the $3.22 he previously aimed for. Meanwhile, Citi analyst Tan Yong Hong downgraded OCBC to “sell” and reiterated his call to sell UOB. However, he kept DBS at a “buy” call. He said analysts see downside earnings risks to the third-quarter forecasted results, based on “market misplaced optimism on Singapore dollar rates and after an exceptional first-half wealth-related income”. This is particularly the case with OCBC, which he said is trading at the tightest dividend yield spread over bond yield, followed by UOB and DBS. This means that the market is pricing in most aggressive growth, he noted. “Singapore banks have enjoyed a three-year re-rating cycle from 2024, starting from capital management hopes from 2024, wealth management growth from 2025, and recently crowding positionings amid the Equity Market Development Programme and ‘anti-AI’ trade,” Tan said. The programme refers to a $6.5 billion initiative launched by the Monetary Authority of Singapore to boost the liquidity and vibrancy of the local equities market. Tan also said there are risks that forecasters have been mispricing net interest income upside by assuming higher rates because of the resurgence in loans growth. Higher Singapore dollar funding costs is a key risk to that, alongside fixed-rate loans repricing lower, he noted. However, JP Morgan analysts recommended trimming OCBC and DBS, while relatively preferring UOB. They noted that banks in the region may be impacted by the ongoing sharp increase in long bond yields. All three banks saw share price gains on Oct 12 despite the downgrades. DBS rose 0.8% to hit $73.94 on Oct 12, while OCBC rose 0.2% to $29.06. UOB gained 1.4% to close at $40.50. Separately, SGX was also downgraded by Macquarie analysts a week ago. It was labelled as “underperform”, down from “neutral”, as analysts noted its monthly statistics were starting to wane. Citi analysts noted that the SGX acts as a proxy to the Singapore market. If there is an improved economic outlook, SGX will see upsides. But if there is news of a slowdown, it could imply downside risks for the exchange. The analysts also noted that turnover of securities and derivatives on the local bourse has been volatile, among other factors. SGX closed 3% higher at $21.35 on Oct 12. Sue-Ann Tan is a business correspondent at The Straits Times, covering capital markets and sustainable finance.

events.title: Dangote's Kenya refinery triggers political battle
events.summary: The News The $16 billion project to build Aliko Dangote’s refinery on the Kenyan coast is at the center of a high-stakes political battle ahead of elections in 10 months. President William Ruto is hinging his second-term bid on a series of major infrastructure developments. He has argued that the refinery could raise Kenya’s annual gross domestic product by 12%. Additional expected benefits include 500MW added to the national grid and thousands of new jobs. But mounting litigation, some initiated by his political rivals, is threatening to delay its construction, scheduled to be completed by 2030. Groups behind the legal action allege that the project is only the latest in a series of “secretive deals” signed by Ruto and his administration. The government’s refusal to make public key agreements related to the refinery has been criticized by opposition leaders, including one of Ruto’s main challengers, Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna. He has launched a bid in parliament for the documents, including the refinery contract, to be released. Unanswered questions remain over the impact on the environment, the community living near the refinery, and taxpayers. The president and his allies have warned that legal hurdles and uncertainty affecting key projects could dampen investor confidence. Ruto’s government is no stranger to court challenges to its financial deals. Its plan to privatize the country’s fuel pipeline company was eventually approved after various cases were dismissed. Last month, the $1.6 billion sale of a government stake in telecoms company Safaricom to UK’s Vodafone was declared illegal by the courts — the administration has launched an appeal. Both deals are meant to fund Ruto’s infrastructure push, according to government documents. Know More Ekuru Aukot, leader of the opposition Thirdway Alliance,told Semafor he would “definitely file a suit” if the government failed to meet an Oct. 23 deadline in his access to information request seeking more details about the refinery including the names of those who stand to benefit. “We are not opposed to investment. What we are saying is follow the law, follow the constitution,” he said. “The era of secretive deals negotiated in the dark will end when we kick this current regime out and return our country back to the rule of law,” Sifuna said on social media , adding that Ruto was frustrating his parliamentary push for more details. He insisted that the disclosure was “a constitutional imperative.” The threat of protracted litigation also looms over a suit launched by more than 100 Lamu residents arguing that the site of the refinery is part of their ancestral lands, with a court halting construction until the matter is heard. In addition, campaign groups have raised the alarm over the government’s failure to publish the environmental impact report, with Greenpeace threatening legal action . Last year, its five-year effort to block the construction of a $2 billion coal plant in Lamu ended in success for the activists. Despite the legal cases, Dangote and Ruto, who broke ground on the refinery project on Sept. 30, have expressed confidence that the project will overcome the legal hurdles. Step Back Seen as the candidate for the young and downtrodden in the last election, Ruto’s popularity has waned especially among the youth after the deadly 2024 Gen Z-led protests in which dozens of demonstrators were killed by police. Instead, Ruto is now leaning heavily on his infrastructure plans and the promised opportunities to shore up support for his re-election campaign. He has promised to move Kenya “from third world to first world” within 10 years, and unveiled a $38 billion infrastructure fund meant to finance various projects. The View From Nigeria Dangote is taking the objections in his stride. Speaking to investors in Nairobi ahead of the groundbreaking ceremony, Dangote said legal challenges were “normal for us in Africa. In fact, this is small.” He drew parallels with concerns over his cement plant in Senegal , which faced delays over land-related legal disputes. “They stopped our factory for one year. We went up to the Supreme Court to get a judgment,” he said. Notable Kenya’s Capital Markets Authority approved the Dangote IPO , enabling local investors to participate on the Nairobi Securities Exchange.

events.title: AI FOMO driving some family offices into tech investments, survey suggests
events.summary: Investment firms of ultra-wealthy families are feeling FOMO (Fear of Missing Out) about artificial intelligence, a new study suggests. While 85% of family offices cited AI as their top investment theme, three-quarters of respondents said they expected an AI bubble burst in the next five years, according to a poll by RBC Wealth Management and Campden Wealth. The survey results also indicate cautious optimism and concerns about the technology. A version of this article appeared in CNBC's Inside Wealth newsletter, a weekly guide to the high-net-worth investor and consumer. Sign up to receive future editions, straight to your inbox. Eighty-five percent of family offices rank artificial intelligence as their top investment theme, despite 75% expecting an AI bubble to burst within the next five years, according to a new survey. The poll of 155 North American family offices was conducted by RBC Wealth Management and Campden Wealth. RBC's Bill Ringham said these mixed feelings about AI can be traced to several potential factors, including cautious optimism about the technology and concerns about sitting on the sidelines of an investment boom. "Even patient capital can be caught up in the fear of missing out," said the director of private wealth strategies. A combined 85% of respondents ranked AI an asset class or investment theme likely to reward investors over the next 12 months, the next two to five years, or both. The next most popular picks were U.S. equities and direct investments, selected by 76% and 72% of respondents, respectively. However, while AI was the top investment theme of 2026 at 59%, family offices said they were more bullish on U.S. equities in the long run. When asked about returns over the next two to five years, 69% of respondents chose U.S. equities compared to 64% for AI. Direct investments closely followed at 62%. And while only 26% of family offices said real estate was likely to reward shareholders over the next 12 months, nearly twice as many (51%) picked it as a rewarding investment in the two- to five-year horizon. Ringham said the results may reflect how AI enthusiasm is influencing investors' short-term focus more than their long-term strategy. "Fear of missing out is a short-term view," he said. "You're seeing AI over the next 12 months as being that top priority. Their long-term look swings back." Ringham said family offices were cautiously optimistic about AI, especially in the startup space. "Those optimists are also not afraid to say that there might be a bubble down the road," he said. "You're investing in what you think is going to be incredibly successful in the longer term. But at this stage, there are so many new companies that you really have to go into these things with your eyes wide open." Get Inside Wealth directly to your inbox The Inside Wealth newsletter by Robert Frank is your weekly guide to high-net-worth investors and the industries that serve them. The survey found that 76% of respondents ranked "excessive government borrowing" as the top market risk likely to crystallize over the next five years. That was followed by "AI investment bubble burst" (75%) and "AI advancements impact employment" (66%). While the survey did not ask how family offices planned to change their allocations around AI, Ringham said that many asset classes are touched by the technology. 31% of family offices planned to make more direct investments in private equity and just over a fifth said the same of real estate and venture capital, respectively. "I'm sure AI is embedded in a lot of those underlying categories," he said.
