events.title: Why Trump’s Russia-Ukraine energy ceasefire may offer oil markets little relief
events.summary: US President Donald Trump's declaration of an " energy ceasefire " between Russia and Ukraine has raised questions over its validity, after Moscow offered no confirmation about the truce and Russian strikes hit Ukrainian power plants within hours of the announcement. The move sent oil and diesel prices into decline early on Monday, but analysts cautioned that even a sustained halt to attacks on energy infrastructure would offer limited relief to global fuel markets, with much of Russia's refining capacity offline after months of Ukrainian drone strikes. Brent fell 1.3 per cent to $103.35 a barrel in early trading, while West Texas Intermediate declined 1.4 per cent to $90.55 a barrel. ICE gas oil futures, a benchmark for diesel, dropped about 3 per cent. The oil benchmarks pared losses by midday, with Brent trading 1.10 per cent higher at $105.87 a barrel by 1.55pm UAE time, while WTI was up 1.13 per cent at $92.89 a barrel. “Effective immediately, there is an energy ceasefire in the war between Russia and Ukraine,” Mr Trump wrote on Truth Social on Sunday. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Kyiv supported a ceasefire but was awaiting details from Washington. A similar announcement by Mr Trump in September failed to produce a lasting halt to strikes. “Only time will tell how durable it proves to be,” said Giovanni Staunovo, commodity analyst at Swiss bank UBS. “We have seen similar commitments in the past that ultimately failed to hold.” Diesel squeeze The announcement follows a US Treasury decision on October 9 to temporarily ease sanctions on Russian diesel transactions until April 7, 2027, after Mr Trump said Russian President Vladimir Putin had agreed to release additional fuel into global markets. But the volumes are modest relative to the scale of the disruption. The proposed 300,000 tonnes for the rest of this month equates to about 100,000 barrels a day, Mr Staunovo said. That “would only partially offset the decline in seaborne diesel exports, which in September were around 1.3 million barrels per day below the levels seen at the start of the year”, he said. Francesco Sassi, assistant professor of energy geopolitics at the University of Oslo, said Washington's decision to suspend sanctions on Russian diesel for six months marked a significant shift in energy geopolitics that threatened to undermine western unity against Moscow. He described the move as the clearest failure yet of efforts to isolate Russia through energy sanctions. “What remains unsaid regarding the guarantees that Russia had from the US for supplying diesel is far more important than the few details we know so far about the energy ceasefire,” Mr Sassi said. Ukraine's response would also be a test of its relationship with Washington, potentially increasing pressure on the European Union to sustain support for Kyiv without US backing, he added. Russia's capacity to deliver the additional fuel is also in doubt. Its diesel exports fell from about 706,000 bpd in January to 47,000 bpd in August and almost nothing last month, according to Kpler data, as Ukrainian drone attacks damaged refineries and curtailed fuel production. Total Russian oil exports declined to about 6.8 million bpd in September from 8 million bpd in May. Shipments to India , Russia's biggest buyer, have more than halved since June to 1.2 million bpd, the data showed. The drop highlights the difficulty of restoring Russian fuel supplies without first repairing damaged infrastructure, a process that could take months even if attacks cease. S&P Global Commodity Insights said the announcement could weigh on diesel refining margins but only if Russian exports increase. “We see the immediate market impact as limited,” analysts James Bambino and Richard Joswick said. Additional Russian shipments would cover only about 10 per cent of the global shortfall in diesel exports, assuming they represent new supply rather than cargoes diverted from existing buyers, S&P Global said. About half of Russia's refining capacity is offline and repairs could take months, limiting the scope for a rapid recovery. Any additional cargoes are likely to remain in the Atlantic Basin, potentially reaching the US East Coast or Brazil and freeing up US Gulf Coast supplies for Europe. That could put downwards pressure on diesel margins in north-west Europe and the US but only “as long as a ceasefire holds”, the analysts said. Middle East risks persist Even if Russian fuel exports recover, the broader oil market remains exposed to disruption in the Middle East, where the Iran war has restricted supplies and forced major changes to established shipping routes. Crude has largely remained above $100 a barrel in recent weeks as attacks on infrastructure and shipping continue to threaten supplies from the Gulf. Goldman Sachs raised its December Brent forecast to $90 a barrel from $85, saying Gulf supply disruption was likely to ease more slowly than previously expected. The bank estimates geopolitical tension is adding slightly more than $20 a barrel to prices and does not assume a quick resolution to the US-Iran conflict. “Potential renewed escalation still poses significant net upside risk,” the bank's analysts said.

events.title: What we learned from ‘guilty’ Man City’s win over Liverpool at Anfield
events.summary: City beat Reds despite a hostile Anfield reception, but Premier League season still hangs in the balance. Despite the hostile atmosphere created by Liverpool at Anfield for Sunday’s fiery clash, it was leaders Manchester City who had the last laugh with a superb 3-0 victory to maintain their perfect start to the Premier League season. The noise centred on off-pitch matters as City returned to action after a bombshell ruling by an independent commission found them guilty of breaking more than 100 Premier League financial rules . list 1 of 3 Pep Guardiola backs Man City after guilty verdict on financial charges list 2 of 3 Man City will win appeal against financial charges, Maresca says list 3 of 3 What are the top five clashes between Liverpool and Manchester City? Enzo Maresca’s side could not have chosen a worse venue to restart their campaign after the guilty verdict. Anfield for years has dished out an angry welcome to City. On Sunday, the vitriol was at its highest with flags reading “cheats” and “114 charges”, a common sight in the merchandise on sale. But even as the red smoke engulfed Merseyside and chants of “Cheating bastards” rang around the stadium, none of it could derail the defiant Manchester team, who turned the game around in six second-half minutes. Ryan Gravenberch was sent off in the 62nd minute, reducing Liverpool to 10 men. City capitalised on the one-player advantage as Erling Haaland and Jeremy Doku scored in quick succession before Rayan Cherki added another, silencing the noisy Kop end of Anfield. “It was not easy for the players after the last two or three weeks, but they dealt with the situation very well,” Maresca said after the match. “I said during the week we need to learn how to deal with the outside noise but make our own noise, which is to win games. Our fans were singing at the end, so the noise was from us.” Haaland, this season’s leading Premier League scorer with six goals, looked close to tears after the victory, which he described as a “lovely moment” and one that he said would stay with troubled City for a long time. “It’s time to stay strong and stick together and do what you can do something about – stick together,” he added. City win, but Premier League stuck in limbo While City emerged unscathed from Sunday’s hostile face-off, the victory highlighted the uncertainty that now surrounds the remainder of the Premier League season. Maresca’s side are at the top of the table with 18 points and a 100 percent record. Yet those results could count for nothing unless City, who deny any financial wrongdoing, are successful in their appeal against the guilty verdict. No sanctions have been decided yet, but if City’s appeal fails, potential punishments include a significant point deduction and expulsion from the Premier League. There is even the prospect of three Premier League titles being stripped from City, who won them from 2009 to 2018, the period to which the charges relate. This guilty verdict on widespread financial impropriety thus leaves a question mark over every City result and what it means for other clubs. “This is really bad for the Premier League, and it’s going to continue for a few months,” former Manchester United captain-turned-pundit Gary Neville told Sky Sports. Earlier, Liverpool manager Andoni Iraola stressed that “ the uncertainty is not good for anyone ” while ex-Liverpool defender Jamie Carragher said he hoped the appeal process does not drag on for months. “There’s no way this can carry on to the end of the season because we’re all getting kidded,” Carragher said. Then there is also the debate about City’s past successes. Former Manchester United captain Roy Keane argued that any title City won while engaging in financial wrongdoing would be difficult to celebrate. “Some people might think it’s a bit stronger, but I wouldn’t feel I have earned a league title if I thought there was something dodgy going on in the background. Absolutely not,” he said. “We talk about lads going out, giving their all and picking up injuries, … but that is your job. But you hope everyone is on the same page, being honest and doing things the proper way.” What’s next for City and the Premier League? Moments after City’s players broke into celebrations at the final whistle, Anfield’s DJ played the Fleetwood Mac song Little Lies over the loudspeakers. Many would argue that was Liverpool’s, and by extension, their fans’ final act of defiance, but it certainly won’t be the last hostile reception City face at stadiums across England and beyond this season. From now on, every time a team loses to City, their players and fans may be left feeling robbed. Such is the state of the Premier League right now when its best-performing team is also its most controversial team. Much of this stems from the uncertainty that City and 19 other clubs in the top flight are facing. What’s next? What sanctions, if any, await City? Will they be stripped of their titles?

events.title: AI set to continue growing, but how it unlocks value is the question: TikTok, Broadcom, Intel CEOs
events.summary: TikTok chief executive officer Chew Shou Zi speaking at the DBS Asia Future Forward Conference at Suntec Convention and Exhibition Centre on Oct 12. AI will keep growing and may beat some human skills, but leaders said its real value depends on human judgement, creativity and safe use. TikTok’s Chew Shou Zi warned about alignment and cybersecurity risks, and said people still value authenticity as AI-made content remains low. Broadcom and Intel CEOs said AI demand for compute will stay strong for three to five years, but growth depends on supply, ROI, costs and talent. SINGAPORE – Artificial intelligence is set to continue its growth and may even surpass some human capabilities, but what matters is how it can unlock value for businesses and society, said the chief executives of three major tech companies. TikTok CEO Chew Shou Zi said there is a “non-zero chance” that AI could surpass humans in certain ways in the future, but he also noted the importance of human judgment and creativity even as AI becomes more widely used . Meanwhile, in response to a question by DBS CEO Tan Su Shan on whether the world is “overbuilding” AI infrastructure , Broadcom CEO Hock Tan and Intel CEO Tan Lip-Bu said the demand for AI infrastructure will continue to grow in the next three to five years, limited mainly by supply constraints. They were speaking on panels at the inaugural DBS Asia Future Forward Conference held at Suntec Singapore Convention and Exhibition Centre on Oct 12. Organised by DBS, the new flagship event brings together global leaders across technology, business and investment to examine the forces shaping the region’s future. Chew said AI models might currently be unable to do certain things that humans can, such as rapid visual learning or long-term memory retrieval. But he added: “The technology is evolving, (and) you can see a world where silicon is just superior to carbon. “You can see a world where it will last longer. It’s more scalable. It finds it easier to connect information together than us human beings.” But Chew also said there is a place for human judgment in AI usage. He noted that there are some extreme examples of how machines can behave without human alignment, such as the “paper clip analogy”, where a machine is asked to produce paperclips and goes completely overweight on paperclip production at the expense of everything else. “My view is that in the next two to three years, we’re going to have a real scientific breakthrough: physics, biotech, chemistry, material science, because of AI. It’s very, very, very possible,” he said. “And if that happens, then you know the question will be: How do you align the models? How do you align the machines to be doing things that are obvious to us as human beings?” These include moral and ethical boundaries that humans recognise, but AI models may not. “I don’t think we have an answer, to be honest, at this moment in time. I think it really is a very complex issue, but it will matter in the age of AI,” Chew said. Human creativity is also a very relevant question, especially for TikTok, he added. He noted that AI -generated content has not totally taken off yet, with views in the low single-digit percentages. “I think people still value authenticity when they see a video and it’s very obviously... artificially generated. I think there’s still a little bit of pushback in terms of consumption. So I agree that human creativity will continue to be important,” he said. Chew added that in the long term, AI agents might be able to do more things autonomously, especially as the trust and guard rails are built. But in the short term, referring to the next two to three years, Chew said that what matters is developing skills to be able to use AI effectively. “I think that’s probably the most important thing for us internally. We are encouraging not just our engineers, but also our lawyers and people working in corporate functions to have more first-hand experience,” he said. “If you don’t use these products yourself, you cannot figure out exactly what it can or cannot do just by reading about it.” He added that users should be curious and hands-on while understanding the boundaries of this technology. Education is also important, Chew said, especially as AI also poses cybersecurity risks . This is particularly the case when users give agents permission to do things for them, like making purchases using credit cards , without fully understanding what the technology does. Intel CEO Tan Lip-Bu (right) and Broadcom president and CEO Hock Tan (left) participating in a panel discussion moderated by DBS Bank CEO Tan Su Shan during the DBS Asia Future Forward Conference at Suntec Convention and Exhibition Centre on Oct 12. At a separate panel, the Broadcom and Intel CEOs were grilled by DBS’ Tan on whether AI will end. Broadcom’s Hock Tan said: “My presumption is this might continue. events.title: I drove Honda's new Prelude. It may matter more to Honda than to buyers.
events.summary: The 2026 Honda Prelude. Ain't she pretty in blue? Ben Shimkus/Business Insider Honda revived the Prelude as a roughly $44,000 hybrid coupe after 25 years. I drove the car for a week. It's fun and spunky — but who is going to buy this? Limited supply suggests Honda may see it more as a halo car than a volume seller. It's been a quarter century since Honda had a new Prelude arriving at dealerships. The coupe — which was popular in the 1990s with enthusiasts who liked to tinker with tuner cars — was discontinued in 2001. So, I wouldn't blame you if you don't recognize the nameplate. I also wouldn't blame you if you do remember it and find Honda's new approach to the beloved car a little surprising. Unlike the Prelude of yesteryear, the new one is certainly not cheap. My Boost Blue tester has a sticker price of $43,650, including destination. Optional summer tires pushed the suggested price to $44,850. On paper, this car makes almost no sense. Who exactly is the buyer? Prelude purists may bristle at the hybrid powertrain and price. Young shoppers looking for an affordable coupe have cheaper options. Drivers chasing outright performance can get substantially more power elsewhere. After 400 miles, I started to think the Prelude makes more sense for Honda than it does for any one obvious customer. The Prelude is fun — just not in the obvious way The Honda Prelude is a looker from the front. Ben Shimkus/Business Insider Honda calls the new version a sporty grand tourer. It's aiming for a niche part of the US market: It's comfortable and efficient enough for long drives, while maintaining a visual appeal that's very different from the vehicular blobs filling today's grocery store parking lot. I say it nails the aesthetics. My Boost Blue tester was almost aggressively photogenic, with bulging wheel arches and a sloping roofline that gave it a poor man's Porsche vibe. As I drove slowly past a construction site in Brooklyn, a worker asked me to lower my window. "Sweet car!" he said. As I drove away, I heard him yell to a coworker: "Damn, that's a Honda?" Underneath its curvy coupe body sits Honda's deeply engineered two-motor hybrid system, good for 200 horsepower and an EPA-estimated 44 mpg combined. It also borrows suspension, steering, and Brembo brake hardware from the Civic Type R and luxury interior elements from its high-end luxury brand, Acura. Looks like an Acura with some Honda badges! Ben Shimkus/Business Insider It's not particularly fast. That trade-off became obvious pretty quickly. The Prelude's getup is plenty for merging onto the highway, and it actually felt sprightlier once moving at speed. But its immediate shove is nowhere near what I've felt in similarly priced performance cars — or some EVs, like the Tesla Model 3. What it lacks in outright speed, though, it makes up for elsewhere. The car stays impressively flat through bends, the steering feels direct, and the Brembos are grabby enough to remind you that Honda raided the fun-loving Type R's parts bin. Good news, too, for drivers mourning the death of manuals: Honda's new S+ Shift system does a surprisingly convincing impersonation of a traditional transmission. There aren't actually eight gears, but steering-wheel-mounted paddle shifters, simulated rev-matched downshifts, and surprisingly natural engine sounds add some fun driving nostalgia theater. More useful was the fuel economy. I averaged 43.5 mpg on my mostly highway drive, almost exactly matching Honda's 44-mpg combined estimate. Its backseat, however, is nearly useless. Okay, Honda, what is this? Ben Shimkus/Business Insider The second row is difficult to get into because of the sloping roofline, has virtually no headroom, and will only fit riders with calves as thick as a sheet of paper. Honda may not need many people to buy one "Damn, that's a Honda?" - a construction worker. Ben Shimkus/Business Insider Is this car a fit for most American buyers? Not really. It's effectively an expensive two-seater with a Honda badge and a luxury interior. On paper, it doesn't really stack up against its competition: the Ford Mustang is more powerful, the Mazda MX-5 Miata is sportier, and the Toyota GR-86 is nearly $10,000 cheaper. That's a particularly small cubbyhole of a market for the Prelude. Honda may not need the Prelude to become a volume seller. Dealers I've spoken with said supply is limited, and one told me there's already a waitlist to get one onto the lot. Another dealer said the Prelude could draw curious shoppers into the showroom — even if many ultimately leave in something like the ever-popular CR-V. So maybe there's a better question surrounding this car: Is the Honda Prelude attention-grabbing? The construction worker clearly thought so. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: The era of the 400-mile range EV is upon us
events.summary: The next generation of EVs is rolling out. Their biggest improvement: more range. Sjoerd van der Wal/Getty Images There's a fresh batch of EVs heading to the US. They're getting 400 miles of range. That type of range in the US has been reserved for shoppers splashing out on six-figure vehicles. The new batch still has luxury prices — but could quickly filter into mass-market vehicles. Range anxiety? That's so 2026. The auto industry is slowly flipping its calendars into the 2027 model year , and the transition is bringing a new crop of EVs with 400-plus miles of range. That was once a rare bragging point reserved for ultra-luxury sedans and gargantuan electric trucks. It's an important development, especially for the US market. While the rest of the world has started to embrace fully electric driving amid sky-high fuel costs , American drivers have lagged China and Europe in adopting EVs , held back by range anxiety, high vehicle prices, and limited public charging access. Automakers' response: Make EVs go farther in the US market. European manufacturers are leading that charge. BMW's next-generation EVs, called Neue Klasse, are the clearest example. The coming i3 sedan is expected to travel up to 468 miles on a charge, while BMW says its new iX4 SUV coupe can go as far as 428 miles. Those are preliminary estimates based on EPA testing procedures. Its iX3 crossover SUV, meanwhile, has an official EPA rating of up to 434 miles. Strikingly vibrant. Introducing THE NEW BMW iX4. #BMWiX4 #BMW #BMWNewEra #NeueKlasse #BMWGroup https://t.co/4kqvYE1E9s — BMW (@BMW) October 7, 2026 Fellow German luxury automaker Mercedes-Benz is also joining the race. The coming electric C-Class has a range of up to 474 miles, under Europe's more generous range testing system. Swedish automaker Volvo is also releasing the EX60 next year, including a trim with 400 miles of range. The cars are largely priced in the mid-$60,000 range. America has seen some 400-mile electric vehicles before, but so far, they've remained in a small corner of the consumer market. The Lucid Air, priced between $70,000 and $250,500, boasts a 400-plus-mile range for consumers willing to make mortgage-like payments on a vehicle. GM's electric trucks and Cadillac Escalade IQ can also clear 400 miles, but their longest-range versions rely on enormous 205-kilowatt-hour battery packs. The fresh EVs coming from luxury European carmakers feature smaller, more energy-dense battery cells that use their power more efficiently. The iX3, for example, has a 109-kWh battery, almost half the size of GM's highest-range EVs. That won't entirely solve America's EV woes. A $60,000 car is still out of reach for many buyers, and public charging can be scarce or unreliable, particularly in rural areas. Still, luxury automakers often preview where the rest of the industry is going. If this new generation of battery technology filters downmarket, 400 miles of range could eventually become less of a luxury flex — and more of a baseline. events.title: Melbourne man ‘strongly rejects’ links to flydubai attack suspect
events.summary: Samir Mohtadi “strongly rejects” any attempt to associate him or Islamic centre in Melbourne with the alleged attacker. A Melbourne man whose Islamic community centre has been linked by prosecutors in the United Arab Emirates to the co-pilot who allegedly attacked the captain of a flydubai jet has hit out at “false accusations”. The Omani co-pilot, now in custody in the UAE, had drawn inspiration from Al-Qaeda’s September 11, 2001 attacks, and carried out his attempt “with the aim of causing the greatest possible loss of life”, according to the Emirati prosecutor’s findings published by state media last week. list 1 of 4 What are the five questions being asked regarding the Flydubai attack? list 2 of 4 How was Flydubai co-pilot cleared despite being deemed a security risk? list 3 of 4 Police investigating Flydubai co-pilot’s Australia ties list 4 of 4 Flydubai co-pilot plotted ‘suicide’ attack on Israel, UAE says The prosecutor said the co-pilot, who has been identified in multiple media reports as Hamam al-Hammami, first became radicalised while studying in Australia “through reading extremist literature and following online content glorifying terrorist organisations and suicide attacks”. The prosecutor alleged he was acquainted there with an organisation known as “MyCentre” managed by a Lebanese man called Abu Hamza. Neither “MyCentre” nor Abu Hamza are accused of any criminal wrongdoing. In a video posted on social media on Sunday, Abu Hamza – also named by local media as Samir Mohtadi – rejected what he called “false accusations”. “Right through the ages, those who’re righteous, they’ve always been attacked, abused, accused, killed, imprisoned — and this is the way it is”, he said in a four-minute video shared on MyCentre’s Facebook page. He did not directly comment on the UAE prosecutor’s claims in the video, but in a separate statement cited by Australia’s ABC news outlet, Mohtadi was quoted as saying that he “strongly rejects” any attempt to associate him or the centre with the alleged attacker. “The relevant authorities should have verified these claims with me before releasing or publishing such information,” the statement said. “Throughout my life, I have consistently preached peace,” he said. “Both in my work and the work of the centre have always focused on promoting peace, harmony, mutual respect and community wellbeing. We unequivocally reject violence in all its forms,” Mohtadi said. “I strongly reject any attempt to associate me or [the] Multicultural Youth Centre with Al-Hammami. Such claims are unfounded, misleading and risk unfairly damaging the reputation of an organisation that has served the wider Australian community for decades.” During the September 30 flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv, the suspect used an emergency axe to attack the plane’s Indian captain, Smit Machchhar, who fought back and tried to call for help. Another pilot assigned to the return flight who was also on board “noticed the cockpit door opening and closing repeatedly in an unusual manner”, according to the findings. After gaining entry, he “intervened with the assistance of a cabin crew member and several passengers, and together they rescued the injured captain and restrained the suspect”. Police and intelligence services in Australia and New Zealand are still investigating the alleged attacker’s links to both countries , where he allegedly spent time as a student and where he completed some of his flight training, according to national broadcaster Radio New Zealand (RNZ).

events.title: Obama cuts ad in Mississippi Senate race
events.summary: Former President Barack Obama has cut an ad for Mississippi Senate candidate Scott Colom, the latest sign of Democrats putting real effort behind boosting their candidate in the deep red state as they eye a potential upset next month. The Colom campaign will run the 30-second spot on digital and radio statewide in Mississippi as part of a seven-figure media buy in Mississippi, according to details shared first with Semafor. In the ad, Obama tells voters: “Mississippi, it’s time for a change.” “You need to send Scott Colom to the US Senate,” Obama continues in the ad . “Scott made his community safer, prosecuting violent crimes as a district attorney and fighting corruption.” Colom is running against Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, a conservative GOP senator who blocked Colom’s nomination to a federal judgeship under then-President Joe Biden. Colom currently serves as a district attorney in Mississippi. The race to defeat Hyde-Smith is not a must-win for Democrats to retake the Senate and Colom remains an underdog in deep red Mississippi. But national Democrats have been eying the race for months due to the state’s large Black population, and Obama’s ad is a clear effort to juice turnout. Sen. Raphael Warnock, D-Ga., will appear with Colom on Wednesday in Jackson and Democratic Sens. Cory Booker of New Jersey, Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland, and Lisa Blunt Rochester of Delaware have also previously campaigned with the Democratic candidate.Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer has also listed Mississippi as a target for Democrats. Democrats tried to beat Hyde-Smith in the past and failed. She defeated former Democratic Rep. Mike Espy by 7 points in 2018 and a wider margin in a 2020 rematch. But most Senate Democrats think Colom, a young father, is a stronger candidate in a tough environment for Republicans.

The maker of Africa’s bestselling phones closed its bookbuilding on Monday, with preliminary figures showing the offering attracted about 14,000 applications and was oversubscribed roughly 3.5 times, according to people familiar with the matter. Retail participation in Hong Kong initial public offerings (IPOs) has dropped sharply since September. Out of 12 listings last month, only two – Camsense Technologies and Mech-Mind Robotics Technologies – drew more than 100,000 retail applicants, while Red Avenue New Materials Group recorded the lowest demand with just 12,645, according to the companies’ allotment results. In contrast, 11 out of 19 listings across July and August topped 100,000 applicants, with Momenta and Basic Semiconductor each surpassing 200,000.

events.title: Learning to Play Like a Pro: Adaptive Motion Planning and Tracking for Humanoid Robots
events.summary: This White Paper provides roboticists and control engineers with a comprehensive overview of how motion planning and motion tracking can be decoupled to preserve professional athletic style in humanoid robots, and why adaptive, speed-aware control is essential for closing the gap between simulation and real-world deployment. What you will learn about: Why combining a professional athlete’s motion style with reliable task performance remains an open challenge in humanoid ball-sports robotics, and how separating a high-level planner from a low-level tracker addresses this trade-off. How motion data extracted from broadcast video and motion-capture recordings can be reconstructed, retargeted, and physically corrected into reference motions a humanoid robot can safely track. Why the sim-to-real transition introduces compounding tracking errors, and how training a tracker on randomized execution speeds, paired with a learned motion-speed adapter in the planner, improves robustness on physical hardware. How this adaptive framework was validated across two humanoid platforms, including full-size, in-the-wild serving performed without any motion-capture system. Download this free whitepaper now!

events.title: UAE approves 2027-2029 budget with Dh292.5bn in spending
events.summary: The UAE Cabinet has approved its federal budget for 2027 to 2029 with spending of Dh292.5 billion ($79.64 billion). The allocation marks an increase of 28.3 per cent compared to the previous three years, Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid, Vice President and Ruler of Dubai said on Monday. The Cabinet also approved the 2027 budget with expenditure of Dh90.1 billion. Main sectors covered by the new federal budget include community protection and safety, the economy of the future, future-orientated education, employment and empowerment, health and quality of life, leadership, government affairs and international relations, the UAE Government Media Office said in a statement. The budget will also focus on industry, technology, energy, infrastructure, culture, media and sports. “Our priorities remain fixed and unchanged … Education, health, housing, social services, and the quality of life and stability of the citizen,” Sheikh Mohammed said in a post on X. The UAE last year launched its 2027-2029 budget cycle , focusing on sustainability, artificial intelligence and efficiency. It followed four consecutive cycles during which the total federal budget reached about Dh900 billion ($245 billion), officials said in July last year, adding that the cycle focuses on sectors such as education, health care, social welfare and core government services. Mohammed bin Rashid: Today, we approved the UAE Federal Government’s general budget for 2027 to 2029, with total expenditure of AED 292.5 billion, up 28.3% compared with the previous 3 years. We also approved the 2027 budget, with total expenditure of AED 90.1 billion. Our… pic.twitter.com/0vkaH0AljA — Dubai Media Office (@DXBMediaOffice) October 12, 2026 The UAE's economy grew 0.4 per cent annually to Dh961.9 billion in the first half of 2026, driven by non-oil business activity, despite the impact of the Iran war . The non-oil sector's contribution to the country's gross domestic product during the six-month period increased by 1.8 per cent to 79.2 per cent, the Federal Competitiveness and Statistics Centre said last week. The Iran war has tipped the Middle East into one of its worst geopolitical crises in decades. The conflict, which began on February 28, led to Iranian strikes on its Arab neighbours and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. The UAE, the Arab world's second-largest economy, continues to grow despite the conflict. Ratings agency Fitch said on Monday that the UAE non-oil growth model is broadly resilient to the war baseline. The non-oil growth model of the UAE has leveraged a role as a hub between Asia and Europe “backed by a favourable operating environment, supportive government policy, and the ability to attract and retain foreign labour and visitors”, it said in a report. It added that it expects further measures to “improve the operating environment along with a smoothing of administrative procedures” for corporates and residents, backed by higher spending and other sources of financial support at the sovereign and government-related entity level. “Fitch sees structural strengths that will support the resilience of the non-oil economy. However, a persistent period of regional insecurity will call into question logistical advantages and perceptions of the country as a commercial and financial centre and tourism destination,” said Paul Gamble, senior director at Fitch Ratings. The approval of the budget confirms the UAE government’s “keenness to achieve a balance between current development requirements and investment in future opportunities, and to establish a government financial system characterised by flexibility, efficiency and sustainability”, the media office said on Monday. It enhances the UAE’s position among the most advanced and prosperous countries in the world, it added. Budget breakdown for 2027: Dh34.6 billion (38.4 per cent) – Social development and social benefits Dh29.1 billion (32.3 per cent) – Government affairs Dh17.8 billion (19.7 per cent) – Federal expenses Dh5.6 billion (6.2 per cent) – Financial assets and investments Dh3 billion (3.4 per cent) – Infrastructure and economic resources

events.title: Mars may be a hellhole, but the moon is not far behind
events.summary: Welcome to the second space race. You can be forgiven for experiencing déjà vu. Last time, it was the Soviet Union and the United States vying to be the first to plant some flags. Now it’s a sprint to the lunar surface between America and China—alongside a host of varyingly friendly and rival nations—plus a cornucopia of private spaceflight companies. And this time it looks like they’re getting ready to set up camp. There will be, the contenders say, bases on the moon, permanently inhabited castles under the stars. The notion of a moon base, fanciful as it might sound, isn’t new. But this year, under the leadership of Administrator Jared Isaacman, NASA has been flooding the zone with bold announcements . If all goes according to plan—a plan that will likely cost tens of billions of dollars to start—there will be drones , robotic landers, communication satellites , and a nuclear power plant ; there will be plant terrariums and moonquake sensors; there will be mechanized scouts exploring craters for water. Initial astronaut missions to the lunar surface, which the US is currently planning to start in 2028, will be focused on exploration and technological experimentation. But the idea is that we will—some time in the 2030s—get to a point where there will be habitation quarters for long-term stays, surrounded by a network of scientific research stations, resource mining and processing plants, and landing pads for spaceships. “It’s going to be an expanse,” says Carlos García-Galán, NASA’s moon base program manager—one that will add up to “hundreds of square miles.” The effort is undoubtedly being fueled by nationalistic competition. China has near-identical plans to build its own base on the moon. And being first matters, because the “victor” gets to define the terms. What is the moon, exactly? Is it a militarized outpost? Is it a manufacturing hub? Is it a wilderness to be studied and preserved? But there are also other reasons to go. Earth’s companion contains primeval rocks that hold clues to the formation of the entire solar system. The lunar surface, with virtually no atmosphere in the way, is an ideal place to put telescopes that could examine the most ancient epochs of the cosmos. The far side of the moon would be “a fantastic place to explore the further universe,” says Josef Aschbacher, the European Space Agency’s director general. And it’s way more energy efficient to launch rockets from the low-gravity lunar surface than it is from Earth, meaning sending astronauts—or robotic spacecraft—farther into the solar system will become much less difficult. “The moon is critical. It will be a stepping stone for going further—that means to Mars and beyond,” says Aschbacher. SELMAN DESIGN But if these bold visions are to become reality, there’s a daunting amount of work to be done. A sprawling moon base must be safe for its astronaut inhabitants—protected from falling asteroids, endless cosmic radiation, razor-sharp lunar dust, and torturous temperature swings. It also must be somewhat self-sustaining, so that it can weather changing political fortunes and not cost ruinous amounts of money to maintain. For that, we’ll need to find a way to use the moon’s resources to keep the base operating—and ideally generating revenue. And we’ll need autonomous robots that can build, maintain, and expand the base even when their human masters aren’t present. “It’s almost like starting civilization from scratch,” says Simon Middleburgh, co-director of the Nuclear Futures Institute at Bangor University in Wales. Assuming we can overcome these starting challenges, decades from now—let’s say, by the year 2100—our initial moon bases could grow from barely visible structures into luminous cities, perhaps not too dissimilar from those dreamed up by authors and screenwriters the world over. “It’s like science fiction today that we really want to turn into a reality,” says García-Galán. Will anyone succeed? The moon is a tremendously hostile place to set up camp. In general, daytime temperatures can reach more than 250 °F; at night, they can plummet to less than –200 °F. Exposed to the vacuum of space, the surface is constantly showered in carcinogenic radiation and frequently hit by meteoroids. And its volcanic dust is sticky and corrosive, a destroyer of equipment and choker of lungs.  Sadly, the lunar south pole—the area NASA is targeting—is even harsher. NASA wants to build a base there because its permanently shadowed craters are thought to harbor caches of water ice, which would be more precious than gold. Purify it, and you can water crops and hydrate astronauts; split it into oxygen and hydrogen, and you have breathable air and rocket propellant. But the temperature in those craters can be lower than –410 °F, making them some of the coldest places in the known universe. On the surface outside those pits, astronauts would be bathed in the scorching sun for 14 days before experiencing an equally long frigid night. But there is only so much money we can spend on safety. “What it comes down to is acceptable risk of death,” Philip Metzger , a spaceflight engineering researcher at the Florida Space Institute, said while pondering some of the dangers. “What can we reasonably survive without breaking the bank?” Temperature is one of the easiest problems to handle. Materials science has come a long way, and there are myriad metals, ceramics, plastics, compounds, and alloys that can resist wild temperature swings. Radiators keep things cool; heaters keep batteries from dying prematurely. Astronauts survive just fine too, with their fancy spacesuits—but that technology has proved itself only during brief excursions. It’s not yet clear how long this equipment could operate under such tempestuous conditions. The temperature in the moon’s south pole craters can be lower than –410 °F, making them some of the coldest places in the known universe. Outside those pits, astronauts would be bathed in the scorching sun for 14 days before experiencing an equally long frigid night. Space radiation, which can wreak havoc on electronics and trigger a cancerous division of cells, is far more pernicious. And as Stuart George, a physicist at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston, explains, it comes in two unpleasant forms.  The first is galactic cosmic rays , which rain down on the moon almost constantly. “They’re made by supernovas and neutron star mergers—all these kinds of things,” says George. And because the atomic nuclei, protons, and electrons that make them up are moving at significant fractions of the speed of light, these cosmic rays have oodles of kinetic energy, meaning they can punch through thin shielding (say, a metal wall) with ease. “They also have this habit where the heavier ions are fragmenting in that shielding and making secondary particles,” says George. That means if your shield is too thin, the astronauts behind it will be blasted with a surprisingly large dose of radiation.

events.title: Passengers ranked the top 10 airlines with the best in-flight WiFi. Elon Musk's Starlink is all over the list.
events.summary: Airlines are upgrading their in-flight WiFi offerings. eastwest photo/Getty Images Skytrax's World Airline Awards introduced a new award in 2026: World's Best Onboard WiFi. Qatar Airways won first place, followed by Delta Air Lines and United Airlines. Seven out of the top 10 airlines are partnered with Elon Musk's Starlink. Move aside priority boarding and extra legroom — airlines are investing in high-speed in-flight WiFi as a key amenity to attract customers. This year, Skytrax's World Airline Awards added a World's Best Onboard WiFi category "to reflect the importance to today's customer experience of fast and free onboard connectivity," Skytrax wrote in a press release. The ranking was determined by surveying passengers from over 100 nationalities between September 2025 and August 2026 in the world's largest airline passenger satisfaction survey. One WiFi provider popped up again and again in Skytrax's ranking of winning airlines: Starlink. Of the top 10 airlines recognized for having the best in-flight WiFi offerings, seven have partnerships with Elon Musk's high-speed internet company — an indication of how Starlink is cornering the market. Over 40 carriers worldwide have partnered with Starlink, which provides streaming-quality WiFi on flights via its network of over 11,000 satellites. Here are the top 10 airlines with the best onboard WiFi, ranked by passengers. 10. Emirates A Boeing 777-300ER aircraft operated by Emirates, registration A6-ENM, takes off from Warsaw Chopin Airport in Warsaw, Poland, on May 3, 2026. The airplane is operating flight EK180 to Dubai, United Arab Emirates. (Photo by Mateusz Wlodarczyk/NurPhoto via Getty Images) Mateusz Wlodarczyk/NurPhoto via Getty Images Emirates was one of the first airlines to offer Starlink WiFi on its A380 aircraft, and plans to add Starlink to its fleet by mid-2027. 9. EVA Air This picture taken in Tangerang on February 15, 2012 shows an Eva air airplane is flying over the Sukarno-Hatta airport in Tangerang. Eva air is the second largest Taiwanese airline founded in 1989. More than 200 U.K. travel and hospitality executives, including the head of Londons iconic Ritz hotel, joined a chorus of airlines and airports calling for the government to introduce air bridges to boost tourism and scrap contentious plans to quarantine visitors. Photographer: Anthony Devlin/Bloomberg via Getty Images Bloomberg/Getty Images As the first UK airline to partner with Starlink, Virgin Atlantic began offering flights equipped with streaming-quality WiFi in May. 7. Bastian told CNBC on Friday that he pays little heed to the feud. "I'm a big fan of Starlink," Bastian said. "I'm a fan of what Elon does. I drive a Tesla. OK? So there's nothing. events.title: Trump turns to Russian diesel ahead of midterms, but analysts see little price relief
events.summary: Oil prices eased on Monday after Donald Trump declared an "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine on Truth Social. It comes after he struck a deal for Russia to supply diesel, as energy costs weigh on voter sentiment ahead of the midterm elections. But analysts question Russia's capacity to release the agreed volume and doubt it could ease prices if it could. U.S. President Donald Trump 's latest geopolitical dealmaking effort to ease a diesel supply crunch ahead of November's midterm elections is unlikely to make a dent in prices, according to analysts. Trump's declaration of an " energy ceasefire " between Russia and Ukraine on Sunday surprised policymakers across the world — not least in Kyiv — and prompted oil prices to fall on Monday, despite Russia striking a power plant shortly after the announcement. Oil later rose. The president's declaration comes after he announced a deal for Russia to release 300,000 metric tons to the U.S. and global markets immediately, followed by another 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons after that. Moscow will then deliver another 3 million tons of diesel based on the condition of Russia's refineries, Trump said. Trump has sought to tame inflation ahead of the congressional midterms in November, when his Republican Party is at risk of losing both houses. According to the Pew Research Center , 84% of registered voters say the economy is "very important" to their vote. Diesel prices hit a record high average of $6.5276 a gallon in late September, according to AAA , as the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East took their toll on supply. "Trump is exploring all avenues to bring down diesel prices before the mid-terms," Mohit Kumar, chief European economist at Jefferies, said in a note on Monday. "The deal with Russia has drawn opposition both from within the US and from European leaders, as it would be bypassing the Russian sanctions in place," he added. "While more supply of diesel would ... ease some pressure on diesel prices, the volumes agreed are unlikely to make a substantial difference." The U.S. Treasury has issued a temporary license easing sanctions on Russian diesel to facilitate the deal Trump announced Friday. Lombard Odier analysts said in a Monday note that the agreement, in addition to Chinese plans to resume refined-fuel exports, are "potentially significant because diesel shortages have amplified the inflationary consequences of disrupted energy supply, particularly through transportation, agriculture and industrial production." But they cautioned that "announced shipments are not equivalent to delivered supply," and "neither agreement immediately restores damaged infrastructure or normalizes maritime transportation." Neil Atkinson, former head of the Oil Division at the International Energy Agency, was less optimistic, telling CNBC in a note: "Where the volumes to supply the Trump deal come from is a mystery, unless it comes from domestic supply, which will cripple the Russian economy." Atkinson noted that the G7 recently authorized the release of 50 million barrels of oil products , mainly diesel, but "it has made almost zero difference to the underlying diesel market tightness" due to lack of clarity over how much will be released, or when and where. "The same will be true of the new US/Russian deal to allow exports from Russia," he said. "Even if the initial 300 kt (about 70 kb/d over a month) were available tomorrow it would have little impact. "The lack of impact is because the US uses 3.7 million barrels a day of diesel. The world uses 29 million barrels a day of diesel. The US is sitting on 105 million barrels of commercial diesel stocks," Atkinson added. "Pre-war, the Middle East Gulf exported nearly 1 million barrels a day of diesel. This is still largely lost due to damage to refineries and the difficulty of exporting products by ship." Deal to 'fail economically' — and embolden Putin In a Monday note to clients, analysts at Singapore's Quantum Strategy outlined a particularly pessimistic outcome. "We expect this deal to fail economically. We remain long distillates and crude. We remain short US assets," they wrote. "We expect Putin to read the deal as an open invitation to escalate his gray-zone warfare in Europe to a much higher level. The effects would be negative for the Euro and for EU sovereign debt, as European powers scramble to ensure their defense."

events.title: The creepiest urban legend from every US state
events.summary: Bigfoot is the star of one of the most well-known urban legends in the US. Christy Rowe/Getty Images There are famous urban legends, including Bigfoot and the Loch Ness monster. However, there are also plenty of local myths that have not made it into mainstream pop culture. Keep reading to find out the creepiest urban legend that takes place in your state. Have you ever felt a chill as you walk down your street, or drive along a dark highway in your home state? You might want to check this list to see if your state's creepiest urban legend unfolded near you. Every country, state, and town has its own urban legends known to residents and fans of the paranormal. Some are attempts to explain mysterious phenomena or tragedies, while others are passed down due to our fascination with the dark and macabre. Some areas have capitalized on local urban legends to attract tourists and boost local economies. In the West Virginia city of Point Pleasant, for example, the legend of Mothman is integral to the community. The Mothman Festival is held every September and includes guest speakers, a street fair, bus tours, live music, food trucks, and more. There's even a Mothman museum. It's not for nothing. The Main Street Point Pleasant organization told The River Cities Tribune & Register in 2024 that it estimates the festival brings about $2 million to the city's economy every year. But not every urban legend is that well known. We chose the creepiest urban legend we could find in every state, from the little-known to the mainstays like Bigfoot and the Jersey Devil. ALABAMA: Hell's Gate Bridge The bridge. Google Maps The generally accepted story of Hell's Gate Bridge starts in the 1950s, according to the Oxford Paranormal Society ; a young couple driving over the bridge somehow drove their car off the bridge one night, and they both drowned. There are two legends associated with Hell's Gate Bridge: one is that if you drive your car out to the middle of the bridge and turn off the lights, the couple will magically appear in your car and leave a wet spot on the seat. The other, which is how the bridge got its name, is the belief that if you drive over the bridge and look over your shoulder halfway through, the scenery behind you turns into a portal to hell engulfed in flames. Potentially to curb ghost hunters and bored teenagers, Hell's Gate Bridge is closed to cars, according to The Anniston Star , and it is in such disrepair that walking across is strongly discouraged. ALASKA: The Kushtaka of the Alaskan Triangle David McNew/Getty Images Everyone knows the story of the Bermuda Triangle, but you might not know about the Alaskan Triangle. On average, five out of every 1,000 people go missing in Alaska, the Los Angeles Times reported in 2005, so even if there's nothing supernatural going on, it's easy to get lost in the Alaskan wilderness. The Tlingit tribe, who lives in Juneau, has their own explanation for the high number of missing people: evil spirits called the Kushtaka. According to books such as "In Search of the Kushtaka: Alaska's Other Bigfoot," the Kushtaka are shape-shifters (half-man, half-otter) who lure women and children to the water with fake cries in order to steal their human spirits and drown them. ARIZONA: The ghosts of Slaughterhouse Canyon The Chapel of the Holy Cross in Oak Creek Canyon, near Sedona, Arizona, April 1967 Slim Aarons/Hulton Archive/Getty Images The story of Slaughterhouse Canyon (not pictured), also called the less-frightening Luana's Canyon, takes place during the Gold Rush, according to The Miner. During the 1800s, there was a family who lived in the canyon. They were very poor, so the father would venture out for food for his family. One day, the father did not return, so his family slowly starved and descended into madness. The mother, unable to bear listening to her children's cries anymore, put on her wedding dress, murdered her children, and then threw them into a nearby river. The next day, she succumbed to starvation herself. The legend states that if you go down to Slaughterhouse Canyon at night, even now, you will hear the loud, anguished cries of the mother who lost her mind. ARKANSAS: The Boggy Creek Monster Caution. CineBlade/Shutterstock According to Atlas Obscura , the Boggy Creek Monster of Fouke is Arkansas' version of Sasquatch. He's commonly accepted to be around 7 or 8 feet tall and covered in hair. Legend says that he roams the creeks of rural Arkansas. He was first spotted in 1834 when people reported seeing a "wild man." These days, after people claim to spot the Boggy Creek Monster, the sightings are documented on the official Boggy Creek Monster's website . He has been the subject of at least five feature-length films, including 1972's "The Legend of Boggy Creek." CALIFORNIA: The Char-Man The Char-Man calls Ojai his home. David McNew/Getty Images The Char-Man's origin story, told in the journal "Western Folklore," is gruesome: A father and son were both caught in a house fire and horribly burned in 1948. After the fire, the son became so mentally unstable that he killed his father. When the police found the son, he was so unrecognizably burned that they didn't realize he was alive, so he ran away before they were able to arrest him for the murder of his father. The story goes that, ever since then, the Char-Man can be spotted wandering the woods surrounding Ojai, occasionally approaching tents of innocent campers or pretending to be a hitchhiker and attempting to attack them. COLORADO: The many legends of Riverdale Road A portion of Riverdale Road. Google Maps Riverdale Road is the site of not one, but  eight  creepy stories. Ranging from a "Hell Gate" to ghosts of slaves hanging from the trees, the stretch of road is decidedly spooky, as reported by local news affiliate Fox31. The creepiest story, though, is that of the phantom jogger. One day, there was a driver who hit a jogger and left him for dead. Now, it's said that if you park at the site of the crash, you'll hear disembodied footsteps getting closer and closer to your car. People have reported handprints on their windows and banging noises as if someone was kicking the outside. CONNECTICUT: Hannah Cranna You can visit Hannah Cranna's real grave. Hulton Archive/Getty Images Known as the "Wicked Witch of Monroe," per CT Insider , Hannah Cranna gained a reputation as a witch in the 19th century when her husband died by mysteriously falling off a cliff — and locals reportedly believed that she had bewitched him. People also believed that she would cast spells on people she didn't like. Hannah lived to the age of 77, but right before she died, she asked to be carried down to the cemetery in her coffin on foot, not by wagon. events.title: Maps show how Israel’s ‘Yellow Line’ keeps squeezing Palestinians in Gaza
events.summary: Shackled, bleeding, raped: Abuse in Israeli prisons Does Trump have real leverage over Netanyahu? A year into a ‘ceasefire’, Israel restricts access to 65 percent of Gaza and crams 2.1 million people into the rest. Israel has expanded its military occupation in the Gaza Strip in violation of a United States-brokered ‘ceasefire’ , forcing Palestinians into an ever-smaller share of the besieged territory, devastated by Israel’s ongoing genocidal war. Nearly two-thirds of Gaza is now under Israeli military control or subject to access restrictions. The original ‘Yellow Line’, established under US President Donald Trump’s 20-point plan to end the war, marked the area to which Israeli forces initially withdrew. They were expected to make further withdrawals gradually, but instead, they have seized more territory. On Sunday, Israeli forces moved yellow concrete blocks dozens of metres west in Shujayea, a neighbourhood in southeastern Gaza City, forcing Palestinian families to flee and bringing more of the neighbourhood under Israeli military control. “It’s not simply about where the ‘Yellow Line’ is today but where it can move next,” Al Jazeera’s Ibrahim al-Khalili said, reporting from Gaza City. “For families who have been repeatedly displaced in the past three years, the situation remains dire, and they have to make the impossible decision of where they can go.” More than 90 percent of Gaza’s 2.1 million population has been forcibly displaced by Israel’s war, launched on October 7, 2023, after Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel. Using maps, Al Jazeera shows how much of Gaza Israel has grabbed since the ‘ceasefire’. Before the war, Palestinians were spread across the Gaza Strip, a 365sq km (141sq-mile) territory roughly 41km (25 miles) long and from 6km to 12km (4 to 7 miles) wide. That made it one of the most densely populated places on Earth with about 6,000 people per square kilometre, similar to Nairobi or London. Each person had, on average, about 160sq metres (1,722sq ft) of land. Even then, not all of Gaza’s land was accessible. Israel enforced a buffer zone along the fence with Israel, and Palestinians who approached it risked being shot. In 2010, the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) estimated that the restricted area covered 17 percent of Gaza’s land and 35 percent of its farmland. Gaza has been under an Israeli land, air and sea blockade since 2007. Under the first phase of the “ceasefire”, Israeli forces were to withdraw to the “Yellow Line” within 24 hours, after which a 72-hour period began for the handover of Israeli captives held in Gaza. Trump first published a map of the line on his Truth Social platform. The line left Israel in control of 53 percent of the Strip, mostly farmland and border areas in the east, and confined Palestinians to the remaining 47 percent, about 172sq km (66sq miles). By October 2025, two years of war had killed more than 67,000 Palestinians, and tens of thousands more had left the territory, reducing Gaza’s population to about 2.1 million. Pushed into less than half of Gaza’s territory under the “ceasefire”, its density doubled to about 12,000 people per square kilometre, comparable to New York City. Each person was left with about 82sq metres (883sq ft). Since the “ceasefire”, Israeli forces have repeatedly moved the yellow concrete blocks marking the “Yellow Line” farther west, sometimes overnight, expanding the areas under their control. Satellite imagery has also documented continued demolitions in areas held by Israeli forces. The research group Forensic Architecture estimated that Israel controlled 58 percent of Gaza by December. In March, the Israeli military sent aid agencies maps of a new “orange line”, a restricted zone beyond the “Yellow Line” where humanitarian movements must be coordinated with the army. According to OCHA, restrictions now cover 65 percent of Gaza. Israel itself said it controls about 70 percent of the territory, a UN official told the Security Council in June. That leaves 2.1 million people in about 35 percent of the Strip, roughly 128sq km (49sq miles). The population density has nearly tripled since before the war to about 16,000 people per square kilometre, close to central Tokyo. Each person now has about 61sq metres (657sq ft) of land for everything: shelter, roads, schools, hospitals and farmland. Unlike Tokyo, Gaza has little space left to house its people. The UN Satellite Centre, UNOSAT, found 82 percent of structures in the Strip are damaged or destroyed. The UN Food and Agriculture Organization says only 3 percent of Gaza’s cropland is both undamaged and accessible. OCHA says the remaining 35 percent of Gaza is “already overcrowded” and access restrictions are a key obstacle as aid groups try to relocate families before the rainy season.

events.title: Business is booming in a small Louisiana town as a huge Meta AI data center project brings in thousands of workers
events.summary: Holy Tacos and other businesses are opening in Richland Parish as Meta builds its data center. Tim Allen Meta is building its largest data center to date in northeast Louisiana. Over 7,500 workers are expected to be on the construction site at the project's peak. Residents are launching businesses to capitalize on the opportunity. The construction workers building Meta's largest-ever data center are arriving in a tiny Louisiana town with more than specialized skills and manpower. They've also got cash to spend. It's a fact that local entrepreneurs are leveraging to build new businesses. "It's been a good opportunity for everybody," David Rodgers, the cofounder of Ice Queen, a local business, told Business Insider. "I tell people, you can't stop it unless you have $50 billion. You might as well get on board and go with the flow." Meta is building its largest data center to date, Hyperion, in Louisiana's Richland Parish. USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect Meta said the data center , dubbed Hyperion, will span nearly 10 million square feet in rural Holly Ridge and will support more than 7,500 jobs at peak construction. That's a workforce larger than the population of Aspen, Colorado. While the influx of workers is straining the local housing market and disrupting aspects of daily life, their presence has also boosted the region's economy. Spinning straw into gold Holly Ridge is a very small sliver of the nearly 19,600 residents in Richland Parish , where agriculture has been the main industry for decades. Before Meta arrived, the smattering of towns, villages, and unincorporated areas that make up Richland Parish hadn't seen significant economic growth in years. Tim Allen, a Richland Parish restaurant owner, lived through that stagnation in the nearby town of Rayville. "Rayville has been a small community my whole life, and it's been in decline over the last several years. We have a lot of people whose children are moving out, and they usually don't come back," Allen said. "Growing up, downtown Rayville had multiple businesses, hardware stores, and clothing stores. One by one, they shut down until only a couple of stores were left." When Meta announced its project in 2024, Allen and his family were among those who saw an opportunity to turn things around. Holy Tacos in Rayville, Louisiana, opened its doors in April 2025. Tim Allen "Since Meta's announcement, we've seen old businesses revitalize and new ones open, including ours," Allen said. Holy Tacos opened in April 2025. TJ and Kaycie Weed, also based in Rayville, said the new demographic created by Meta's project has boosted their sales. They first opened their café, HeBrews Coffee & Eats, near the end of 2021. "When we first started, we thought 30 tickets was a good day," TJ said. "Now, we're hitting 30 tickets before the first hour and a half through the drive-thru alone. We're probably hitting 130 tickets now." The café in Rayville is a brick-and-mortar, but the couple has two franchise locations, including a food truck that opened in 2025 directly across the street from the construction site in Holly Ridge. They said the Holly Ridge location opened specifically because of Meta. "Holly Ridge does most of the catering. If it's any of the businesses under the umbrella of Meta, I send it to Holly Ridge," TJ said. TJ and Kaycie Weed of Rayville, Louisiana, opened HeBrews Coffee & Eats in 2021. TJ and Kaycie Weed The wave of construction workers inspired Rodgers and his former business partner, Linda Edwards, to cofound Ice Queen in 2025. The business sells $3 bags of ice to subcontractors and companies working on the Meta project. The parish has weathered several heat waves this summer, making ice a necessity for outdoor trade workers. Since July, residents have seen temperatures reach 100 degrees Fahrenheit more than two dozen times. The pair keeps the ice bags in a large tractor-trailer parked near the construction site and has a separate ice truck available to make deliveries. Ice was only the beginning, though, and soon Ice Queen transformed into a one-stop shop of sorts for the work crews. Coffee machines. Cups. Sugar packets. Fridges. Microwaves. Straws. You name it, Ice Queen tries to supply it. Robert Cleveland, president and CEO of the local economic development authority, Grow NELA, said the economic growth happening in Richland Parish is undeniable. Data collected by Grow NELA shows that Richland Parish's annual sales tax revenue jumped from $21 million in 2024 to $39 million in 2025. At the end of 2026, Grow NELA expects the parish will see $92 million in annual sales tax revenue. Richland Parish has gained more annual sales tax revenue in 2025 alone than in the last 20 years combined, Grow NELA says. "We have a number of small businesses that have propped up and have grown significantly because of the project," Cleveland said. Supply and demand Part of the business growth in Richland Parish is supplying construction workers with what they need while they are away from home: lodging, food, and basic necessities. Angel and Bryan Crawford, for example, chose to address the housing market gap with their rental company, Parish Line Properties . The couple owns a mobile home park called Antley Pines that opened in 2025. Angel and Bryan Crawford built the Antley Pines mobile home park in Delhi, Louisiana. Angel Crawford "We added two homes last December, four this May, and our last four in July. All the homes were secured by deposits from Meta workers before we even got them into the park," Angel said. A fully-furnished four-bedroom, two-bathroom mobile home that's eight miles from the construction site costs an average of $3,000. The couple previously worked in the nursing field, but decided to dive into real estate and property management after becoming empty nesters. "In 2024, we started buying older houses that had been on the market for a long time or needed a lot of work. We had a vision to create a mobile home park and already purchased some land when we heard about Meta's data center," Angel said. The Crawfords own Antley Pines through their rental company, Parish Line Properties. Business Insider The company now owns 18 rental properties, 14 of which the owners have set aside as workforce housing. "Location is very important to Meta's workers because they work six to seven days a week and 12-plus hours a day. They leave around 4:30 in the morning, and they don't come home until 7 at night," she said. Those long days can be taxing, making places like HeBrews Coffee & Eats popular with workers. Shelbie Stephenson, owner of the Holly Ridge location, said they deliver 450 lunch plates to the Meta work site twice a month. Stephenson said they also do breakfast and coffee catering several times a month. This HeBrews Coffee & Eats location sits across the street from Meta's construction site. events.title: Starbucks Korea regains coffee chain lead five months after ‘Tank Day’ controversy
events.summary: Starbucks regained the top spot in South Korean sales after four months in second place. Starbucks Korea regained the No. 1 sales spot in September, with estimated card payments of 121 billion won, overtaking A Twosome Place after four months. Its sales recovery followed backlash over the “Tank Day” promotion, which caused public anger, a CEO dismissal, an apology, and history education for staff. Other chains fell in September, but the data only covers card spending, so it does not prove full revenue or a full recovery in customer trust. SEOUL – Starbucks Korea regained the top spot in sales among South Korean coffee chains in September, overtaking A Twosome Place after four months in second place following a public backlash over its controversial “Tank Day” promotion . According to estimated credit and debit card spending data released on Oct 11 by Mobile Index, a market intelligence platform operated by IGAWorks, Starbucks recorded an estimated 121 billion won (S$116 million) in card payments in September, up 4.3% from August. Monthly card spending fell to 100.39 billion won in June before rising for three consecutive months. Meanwhile, A Twosome Place recorded 110.5 billion won in September, down 6.4% from 117.99 billion won a month earlier. The gap between the two chains narrowed from approximately 7 billion won in July to 1.9 billion won in August. Starbucks then pulled ahead by 10.58 billion won in September. The figures indicate a weakening of negative sentiment against Starbucks, which came under fire for using phrases such as “Tank Day” to promote its tumbler discount on May 18, the anniversary of the 1980 Gwangju Democratic Uprising. The campaign drew public criticism for evoking the military crackdown on pro-democracy protestors, prompting Shinsegae Group to dismiss Starbucks Korea’s chief executive, issue an apology and introduce history education for employees. The coffee chain also suspended product launches and promotions before gradually resuming them in July. Other major coffee chains recorded declines. Mega MGC Coffee’s estimated card payments fell 3.2% to 94.75 billion won, while Paik’s Coffee posted a 6.4% decrease to 22.94 billion won. The figures exclude prepaid cards, mobile gift vouchers and other payment methods, meaning they do not represent total revenue or establish whether consumer confidence has recovered. events.title: How to avoid getting stung if you miss credit card payments
events.summary: Published 12 October 2026, 00:19 BST An increasing number of people are missing credit card repayments as finances are stretched by rising bills, according to the Bank of England. Lenders also told the Bank they expected the number of unpaid credit card debts to keep going up this autumn. This could lead to more demand for advice on how to deal with debts – but, if you are struggling and need help, there are some traps to avoid. And it is worth remembering that impartial advice is available free of charge from debt charities. So here's what to think about. If you find yourself with money troubles, it can be tempting to seize any opportunity to get things back on track. Social media and internet search pages are full of supposed quick-fix debt solutions. Cold calls and WhatsApp messages also promise debt help. But they may well come with upfront fees, unrealistic claims about writing off debt, and pressure to make a quick decision. Suggestions on the best way to find help include: Impartial, authorised debt advice comes free. You can find a provider on the government-backed Moneyhelper website , external Check whether a firm offering debt help is authorised by the regulator, the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA). You should cross-check the authorisation details they give with the FCA's Firm Checker , external Anyone unhappy with the service from an authorised firm can complain and, if you are still not happy, go to the independent Financial Ombudsman Service. Alison Walters, director of consumer finance at the FCA, said: "Anyone struggling with debt deserves advice that puts their interests first. "Free, impartial debt advice is available to everyone, and no one should be pressured or misled into paying for a debt solution that may not be right for them." The FCA says that some unregulated firms collect people's details, through cold calling or online adverts, sometimes impersonating debt advice charities or debt collectors, and pass this information on to firms offering debt solutions that you pay for. A quick search online will throw up lots of businesses offering ways to clear your debt, not all of which are trustworthy, according to charities. Warning signs of unscrupulous firms include pressure tactics, such as repeated contact, often in messages and on the phone, pushing people to agree to a debt solution, the FCA says. Some people have been encouraged to change financial details on lenders' paperwork, or are "coached" in ways to respond. Sometimes people are steered towards a fee-charging debt solution, such as Individual Voluntary Arrangements (IVAs) or some debt management plans, without alternative options being properly explained or offered first. And, do you know who you are talking to? Ask them who they work for, and check if their details match the firm's official details. "Before making any decisions around how to deal with your debts, it's always worth getting full, free and impartial debt advice first, exploring all options to clear your debt in the safest and most sustainable way," said Vikki Brownridge, chief executive at debt charity StepChange. events.title: A tech CEO who cut his staff from over 1,000 to 120 says AI is boosting the value of 'high-agency' generalists
events.summary: Bird's CEO Robert Vis says AI is making high-agency generalists more valuable at work. Jose Sarmento Matos/Bloomberg via Getty Images Bird CEO Robert Vis said AI gives an edge to 'high agency' generalists who can work across roles. Bird's head count has dropped from more than 1,000 to 120 as AI automates more tasks. "If you had very high performance but you were not multidisciplinary, you would not stay," he said. Being a specialist may be getting harder at some AI-powered companies. "The profile that we were very focused on was people with high agency," Robert Vis, the CEO of communications infrastructure company Bird, told Business Insider. "If you're high agency and you're full stack, then AI leverages you to basically be your best self." Vis made the comments in late September after Bird announced that it had completed $450 million in debt financing led by JPMorgan, Capital One, and Citi. The company also said its head count fell from more than 1,000 people to 120 over roughly three years as it automated more of its operations and favored employees with high agency and multidisciplinary skills. Vis said AI is helping employees work across tasks that companies have historically treated as distinct roles. In engineering, for example, he said the technology favors people who understand not just how to write code but also how a product should work. "If you're an engineer and you're extremely good at just code but you have no product sense, that wouldn't work at Bird," he said. A new kind of generalist Vis isn't the first executive to argue that AI could give an edge to workers with range and initiative. Figma CEO Dylan Field has said the technology is empowering " generalist behavior " as the once-distinct worlds of product, design, development, and research start to blur. Ravi Kumar, CEO of Cognizant, has similarly said workers who combine subject expertise with technological skills may become more relevant than people with narrow expertise alone. The trend is not universal, however. Business Insider previously reported that consulting firms are increasingly prioritizing specialists with deep industry or technical expertise as AI erodes the value of broad strategy work. At Bird, however, Vis said AI is widening the work employees can take on beyond engineering. The tools can help workers operate within design systems or automate routine parts of support, sales, and accounting. "It's not like you need zero designers, but you need less, and it enables entire teams to be able to output good design within a framework that a design team sets," Vis said. That does not mean every specialist role disappears, Vis said, noting that Bird still employs specialists like a revenue accountant and security engineers. The company's layoffs involved a qualitative assessment of whether workers were multidisciplinary, performing strongly, and wanted to work in a more autonomous environment. "If you had very high performance but you were not multidisciplinary, you would not stay," Vis said. The Amsterdam-founded company said it generated $165 million in EBITDA — earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization, a common measure of operating performance — in 2025 after extensively automating its operations. Still, Vis said companies should not use AI simply as a pretext to cut workers. Instead, he said, leaders should identify repetitive tasks that no longer need to be done and assess whether AI can remove them without overburdening the people who remain. "I don't think people should be looking to reduce their employee base," Vis said. "The moment you are struggling to have certain employees perform well within your environment or have a certain amount of output, then I think AI is a good tool to automate more of this."
