events.title: I spent years trying to be a supermom. Getting sick taught me that my son needed to see me rest, too.
events.summary: The author, pictured with her son, said she is glad she is modeling healthy self-care. Courtesy of Ashley Archambault. Health struggles have forced me to be a less-present mom than I've been in the past. I felt a lot of guilt about this until I realized that my son needs to see me take care of myself. Now I'm showing him that rest is allowed and needed, and that's important, too. I've been dealing with health struggles for years and often feel a ton of mom guilt about not being there for my son as much as I used to be when he was younger. I was a single mom for the first seven years of his life, and he watched me do it all. He saw me work and then do everything around the house, all while still spending a lot of time with him. But I sometimes wonder if the pressure I put on myself to do it all on my own is part of why I burned out. About five years ago, it seemed like I got sick suddenly, but my symptoms had likely been mounting for years. It's also possible that being so busy kept me from noticing and dealing with my symptoms. I used to be able to do so much with my son outside, like playing basketball or going on a family hike nearly every weekend. Those are the things I miss doing with him the most, but what he misses most is me getting down on the floor to build Lego creations with him. My current orthopedic struggles make that impossible right now. I seriously hurt my back and hips about two years ago. After years of repeated injuries in the area, my back locked up out of nowhere, and I couldn't walk the next morning. I lost so much function overnight that just sitting and standing became major challenges. While I can't quite build Legos on the floor yet, I have come a long way in my physical recovery. At first, I didn't handle missing out on things well When I first started getting sick a lot, I cried often about missing out on things with my son. For instance, if I got a terrible migraine , I'd miss entire weekends with him or important events. It felt like I was missing major moments. Instead of giving myself any grace, I just put more pressure on myself to get better for my son. But of course, that's not how getting better works. I was finally diagnosed with endometriosis last year and have seen improvements with various treatments. That has given me a lot of hope. But getting to this point took me accepting that I have a health condition that isn't going away and requires a lot of management. That takes time, time that will take me away from parenting how I have for the last 13 years. Accepting my new reality helped me start moving forward I've had to learn how to ask family members for help , which is something I used to avoid to my own detriment. But I'm getting better at it because I've realized that asking for a little help is a lot better than hurting myself and backsliding in my rehabilitation process. The author said she had trouble taking a step back and accepting help when her health issues began. Courtesy of Ashley Archambault. When it comes to my son, I've had to find new ways to spend time with him. We were always so active together, often going for bike rides or playing catch, but I'm still working up to walking long distances again. I am extremely grateful that my son is OK with just walking by my side. In fact, he asks if he can tag along on my nightly strolls around the neighborhood. There are other things that I never had to stop doing, such as watching a movie with him or cooking something together in the kitchen. When I realized I was fixating on what I couldn't do with him anymore, I worked to reframe my thinking to focus more on everything I can still do with him. It turns out, it's a lot. I'm now modeling the benefits of slow living I realized that the way I t ake care of myself will also likely be the way my son cares for himself one day. When I started thinking of my healthcare as a model for him, it made me want to be nicer to myself. And when I started being more gentle with myself, the guilt I felt for being unwell started to slip away. I want him to see me doing my best to get better, but I also want him to see me resting or asking for help when I really need it. I want him to see that there is no award for doing everything on your own or pushing yourself too hard. Alternatively, a lot of good comes from pacing yourself and taking a beat when you need one. I know that now, and I want him to know it, too. When I'm feeling frustrated for not being able to do more, because I still do have those days, I remind myself that I need to rest in order to show up as the best parent I can be. No one in my family benefits from me overdoing it and then burning out for the rest of the day or several days afterward. I want my son to listen to his body and recognize his needs Once I reshaped the way I saw my health affecting my son, I stopped feeling like I was letting him down all of the time. I'm still showing up for him in every way I can, and when I have to pause and care for myself, I'm also showing him that rest is allowed. I have hope that all the work I'm putting in to get better and the self-care that I now prioritize is influencing him in a positive way. A few weeks ago, I found him watching basketball clips in his room, a face mask on, while foam-rolling his sore muscles. It made me so much more proud of him to see him stop and rest, instead of pushing himself in spite of being tired. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: I retired in my early 50s to care for my husband with dementia. We've exhausted his 401(k) and had to sell our house.
events.summary: Wendy Rowland cared for her husband with early-onset dementia before he went into a care facility. Wendy Rowland Wendy Rowland returned to work in her 50s to support her husband with early-onset dementia. Her husband, once a printing worker, now resides in a costly memory care facility in Tennessee. Rowland navigated financial challenges like selling the home and managing expenses with limited aid. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Wendy Rowland, 53, who lives in Mississippi. Rowland, who was a stay-at-home mom , returned to work in her 50s to help pay for her husband's long-term care , as he suffers from early-onset dementia. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. My husband has early-onset Lewy body dementia . He is 59 and has been in a memory care facility for over two years now. We have already used his 401(k), and I sold the house we had for over 20 years. Once the money from that is gone, I'm not sure what will happen. We met at the same printing company in Memphis. My husband had been printing since he was 18. We had a strong suspicion that his job may have had something to do with his condition because of all the chemicals. He worked in brand labels. I worked until our first son was born. I had another son from a previous relationship. We started to notice things that were going on in his early 50s. He would try to do things he had done a million times over the course of his life, and they would come out a little backward. The rest of the family would say, "Oh, that's just him." I would reply, "No, it's not really." We noticed this most clearly when he was driving. He would make turns in front of others, and the accidents started happening. He would also fix a water line incorrectly. All of his wires were getting crossed. Are you paying for your own or your loved one's long-term care? Do you have thoughts to share about long-term care in the US? To share your story with a reporter, please fill out this quick form . There were vacations we would go on a little before his diagnosis, when he would wander off or get agitated because he thought he had left something somewhere. He was let go from his job, and that's when we went for his official diagnosis. His mother was diagnosed around the same time as him. He had two kids, a wife of 20-something years, the house in the country that he always wanted, and the boat he always wanted. He did everything that he was supposed to do, and then life happened. His specific dementia is not as planned out as Alzheimer's. There aren't specific stages. You can see him one day, and he's one person, and you meet him later in the day, and he's another. With Lewy body dementia, they don't necessarily forget who someone is, and if you talk to him enough about someone, he can answer things about them. His physical health has gone down for a while. He was in hospice and was losing weight. They took him out of hospice, and he's a little more stable than he was. We believe his condition might be progressing more now, but there isn't a way to actually know what stage he's at. Things can change from one minute to another. Right before all of this, we pretty much decided to separate, and the paperwork had already been filled out. It was in his best interest that I stay and make sure he was taken care of. I wasn't going to leave that to our son or his sister, who was already dealing with their mother. I had put cameras in the house to make sure he wasn't wandering out. Still, he had hallucinations that made it hard for me to leave him. I would come home some days, and my furniture would be outside. There were knives and a pivot cutter on the table one night when I got home, and at that point, when it became dangerous, that's when I started searching for a new research facility and got a neurologist involved. I pay $6,750 a month for his facility. We got him in when there was a price lock, so we know that won't go up for us. I pay for his medicine and doctors visits , essentially whatever Medicare doesn't cover. I bring toiletries and pay for his visits to have his nails cut, which cost $60. He does get disability, but that doesn't even cover half of his facility, as he gets $2,700 a month after Medicare gets taken out. There hasn't been a whole lot of information out there unless you go to an elder law attorney. I've navigated this mostly on my own. It's more than a lot of people can take, and it was almost more than I could take. It was a really dark time when everything first started, but I knew I had to keep it together at least a little to take care of everything. I had to go back to work , which was fine, but I hadn't worked in 20-something years because I was taking care of the kids and the house. A friend knew of an opening and got me an interview, which I was grateful for because it would've been very difficult for me to find something where I would make enough to keep the house as long as I did. You don't think about these things when you're taking care of your family because that's what you're supposed to be doing. As his condition progressed, we had to sell our house. We had it built back in 2004, and the area we were in had grown a lot, so I was able to make a substantial amount off the house. I was able to put a nice chunk down on a new townhouse in Mississippi just south of the Tennessee border, which made my house note about $800 a month. I live about three and a half hours away from him. My granddaughter still lives near him, and I'll often make trips to see him and do what he needs. There's no joy, and it's hard for me to say that because you would hope there would be some moment here and there, given the nature of our relationship. It's a lot of frustration. I'm not angry at him for getting sick, but you're angry that you're in this situation at an age where you're not even thinking that could remotely happen. I feel bad about this resentment, but I don't think it's going to change. He was putting money in his 401(k), but you don't often think about long-term care insurance because you don't know if and when you'll get dementia. We've valued having financial advisors to talk about what to do with his 401(k) when looking for facilities. But I had no clue at first who anyone was to talk to, so I could get all this information. It would've been easier to learn some of this before the process started. I hope nothing like that happens with me, and if it does, I don't know if I would want anybody else to go through the same thing of having to figure out what to do with me. This has made me a little more cautious about my money in case I need a nest egg. At this point, though, when life is more than halfway over, there are only so many things that I can do to be prepared. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: The ecologist revealing the invisible networks that revive rainforests
events.summary: In a research station in central Panama, you can walk through a century of forest time, watching scrubby plots of adolescent trees give way to cathedral-­like canopies of mature growth. Forest ecologist Daisy Dent, a senior scientist at ETH Zurich, oversees this sequence of plots across the Barro Colorado Nature Monument, some of which date as far back as the 19th century. Not one of the trees she surveys was planted by human hands. She maps, measures, and tracks each trunk that emerges, revealing how waves of tree life rise from bare earth.  Tropical forests like these are our planet’s biggest terrestrial carbon sink, accounting for around 40% of carbon stored on land . As part of an international network of researchers, Dent is deciphering the networks of animal and plant interactions that enable some forests to recover after destruction. The goal is a low-cost, high-impact alternative to typical carbon-­crediting schemes, which plant huge areas with a single species of tree. For over a decade, her research has built a body of evidence that such large “monocrop” programs could be expensive mistakes—and that more resilient forests can rebound naturally in just a few decades, re-creating ecosystems that suck up vast quantities of carbon dioxide. Few places are better to demonstrate this than Barro Colorado, a reserve covering the forested peninsulas and islands that formed when construction of the Panama Canal flooded the area in 1914. Under the management of the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute, generations of ecologists have amassed more than a century of records.  That means Dent can trace why some plots rebound after clear-cutting for farming and forestry while others falter. Fruit-eating animals—including spider monkeys, bats, and parrots—are responsible for planting more than 70% of trees in tropical forests, and Dent’s dataset can tell which built each patch of trees by depositing seeds in their nutrient-rich droppings. Many of these creatures worked together to plant a diverse 70-year-old patch whose canopy is approaching the stunning structure and richness of an ancient jungle. In contrast, a patch of similar age populated by narrow trunks of a single long-lived species, Gustavia superba , hints that tropical rodents called agoutis are more or less the sole animal architects behind this more homogeneous forest.  The data she collects helps write a playbook for when to let ecosystems regenerate and when to give them a helping hand. One 2024 estimate in Nature found that some 215 million hectares of forest worldwide (an area larger than Mexico) could regenerate naturally. “Tropical forests are underpinned by this massive network of interactions,” Dent says—interactions between life-forms like the fungi that help trees take up nutrients, as well as pollinators and seed-distributors. Supporting those relationships is key to growing forests that lock up carbon and help sustain local communities and wildlife.  Filling in the gaps Just over a decade ago, as the landmark Paris Agreement was being codified in 2015, forest recovery seized global attention as a solution to the climate crisis. Global leaders rallied behind plans to regrow a trillion trees , after the ecologist Thomas Crowther highlighted their potential to capture a decade’s worth of global carbon emissions. But the biggest question has lingered: How, exactly, do you regrow two trees for every star in the Milky Way? While startups have proposed seed-spraying drones and nutrient-coated seed bombs , Dent has spent two decades studying what happens when we let forests rebuild themselves. As a PhD student around the turn of the millennium, she researched old-growth forests in northern Borneo but felt hopeless watching entire landscapes felled for palm oil plantations. Rather than despair, she turned to restoration. Then, as a postdoc in 2005, she joined Panama’s Prorena, a joint initiative between the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute and the Yale School of Forestry and Environmental Studies, which aimed at determining how best to establish diverse native forests on clear-cut land. Back then, secondary forests—ones that grow naturally after the original forest was lost—had been “a bit of a niche research area,” Dent says. But as farming and human infrastructure have driven deforestation, resurgent forests now account for some 70% of all tropical canopies. Prorena initially followed the usual playbook of transplanting nursery trees to rangelands, but Dent began to question whether planting was necessary. In 2009, she published an encouraging paper showing that animal populations rebound quickly as forests naturally regrow. In 2010, she began working in Barro Colorado on the plots established by the pioneering American ecologist Julie Denslow. In 1994, Denslow identified plots that had been regenerating naturally for 20 to 100 years, and Dent would add younger ones to continue the sequence.  The site provides not just general data on forest regrowth but in-depth demographic information over time, says Robin Chazdon, a professor emeritus of ecology and evolutionary biology at the University of Connecticut who collaborated with Denslow when she established the plots. “It tells you more about the actual processes that are happening in the site,” she says.  For example, previous research had shown that fast-growing “pioneer trees,” the first to thrive in the damaged land, are eventually overtaken by larger carbon-storing trees. Dent’s research helped fill in gaps about the mechanics of how this happens—or doesn’t happen—in individual cases. In the Gustavia -dominated patch, for instance, stubborn grasses planted by cattle ranchers smothered most other trees before they could take root. These trees can hang around, crowding out the light, for 150 years, blocking the second wave of large-trunked trees.  To plant or not to plant Dent found herself well placed for the massive influx of interest in reforestation that began in 2015. She’d already become a principal investigator for 2ndFor, an international research network aiming to learn how best to manage secondary forests. Using data gathered from the Barro Colorado plots, the team authored a 2016 paper in Nature showing that a hectare of naturally regenerated secondary forest can capture 11 times as much carbon each year as an old-growth one, with young trees absorbing it quickly as they compete to grow toward the sun. Then, in a 2022 study published by the Royal Society, Dent and colleagues showed that locations such as Barro Colorado are among the best-case scenarios for what can be achieved without planting a single seed. Clearings are often surrounded by lush environments filled with birds, bats, and other animals, all of which help tree cover regain old-growth levels of richness and abundance within a few decades. events.title: World Bank jobs council urges 'crisis-era' employment support measures as IMF warns of AI ‘tsunami’
events.summary: IMF’s Georgieva warned AI is hitting labor markets like a “slow-moving tsunami,” with about 40% of jobs worldwide eventually affected and young graduates most exposed. Singapore President Tharman urged governments to make "crisis-era" support measures permanent and incentivize firms to hire young graduates. World Bank’s Banga backed “small AI” tools and called on governments to unlock private capital to create jobs for 1.2 billion young people. BANGKOK — Policymakers are moving from debating whether artificial intelligence will hit jobs to issuing stark warnings about AI-led disruption and recommending measures on cushioning the fallout. International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva warned on Monday that artificial intelligence was hitting the global labor market like a "slow-moving tsunami," with young graduates first in line to be knocked down. "People to worry about, first and foremost, [are] young people that are coming into the labor market," Georgieva said at a panels on Monday. "Normally, they would get into these routine, repetitive jobs and then grow up the ranks. But if they're gone, I don't think any young person wants to be a barista in a coffee shop as ... professional future." Speaking on the same panel, Singapore President Tharman Shanmugaratnam, who co-chairs the World Bank's Jobs Council, called for governments to make "crisis-era" support measures a permanent tool for getting young people into work. What governments did during the Covid-19 pandemic and, in some cases, the global financial crisis "now has to be thought of not as a crisis measure, but as part of the structural, the menu of structural policies," he said. That means working with the private sector, and incentivizing firms to hire fresh graduates, because "the first rung in employment, your first job upon graduation, is now seeing less demand," Shanmugaratnam said. The remarks show that policymakers are moving from debating whether AI will disrupt jobs to deciding how to cushion the fallout, at a time when rapidly aging populations, particularly in Asia, already threaten to shrink workforces. World Bank President Ajay Banga, estimates 1.2 billion young people will turn 18 over the next 15 years, and the private sector, which already generates 75% to 85% of jobs in any country, will have to absorb most of them. Governments' role is to make that possible, he said, by building infrastructure, setting policy and "de-risking" private capital, or lowering the risks that deter investors from putting in money at scale. "It is private capital that creates jobs," he said. The IMF estimates that about 40% of jobs worldwide will eventually be "augmented, downgraded or eliminated." Exposure is about 60% in advanced economies and 23% in low-income countries, she said, but poorer nations are not better off: that is "just because AI is further away." The squeeze is clearest in tech, Shanmugaratnam said, adding that in the U.S. "for the first time in a century, demand for graduates has gone down," with the wage premium for a college degree also shrinking. Without action, a cohort of graduates loses more than a year of skills: "you lose trust in the future," he said. AI has also been the major driver propping up growth this year. AI-related investments and trade have lifted output in a handful of economies, helping keep global expansion near 3% despite an energy supply shock, Georgieva said. "Love it, hate it, or fear it. It [AI] is here, and we are already seeing the first wave of impact," Georgieva said, estimating AI adoption could lift growth by 0.5 percentage point to 1 percentage point in advanced Asia, and 0.2 percentage point to 0.8 percentage point in emerging Asia. At the high end, that "would more than offset the loss that comes from aging population," said Georgieva. Shanmugaratnam cautioned that growth alone may not necessarily deliver job creation. China, India and developing Southeast Asia are "growing quite well, but job creation is weak," he said, and AI "is going to widen that divergence if we are too passive about it." AI-induced job displacement, however, will come "task by task," he said, "and that gives us time" — provided workers can learn on the job and universities shift toward applied training.

events.title: TikTok's CEO says people are going all in on AI agents without understanding how they work
events.summary: TikTok CEO Shou Chew said users should review the permissions and controls they grant to their AI agents. Taylor Hill/FilmMagic TikTok CEO Shou Zi Chew said people are using AI agents without understanding how they operate. He said users need to be more mindful about what permissions they give their agents. The personal AI agent horror stories have been rolling in as more companies launch these tools. TikTok CEO Shou Zi Chew has a reminder for AI agent fans: take a beat to understand them before diving in. "A lot of users may be giving permissions to the agents to do a lot of things for them, without really understanding what kind of permissions you have actually given," Chew said, speaking at a conference organized by DBS Bank in Singapore on Monday. For example, he said that agents who have been given credit card information to purchase items for users may be "overly eager to deliver," and end up buying much more than they were asked to. The executive added that TikTok is training its staff on what information they should not include in public chats with AI agents, such as trade secrets or privileged legal information. "So people, you know, sometimes are over enthusiastic about how they use it," he said. "So I think understanding, you know, where the boundaries of what is reasonable and acceptable use, is important." Chew made these comments at the DBS Asia Future Forward Conference, whose theme centered on how AI could be implemented in Asia to create real value. During his fireside chat, he also talked about how he uses AI as a diet coach and to answer medical questions. Personal AI agents have seen a boom in the past few months, with the introduction of tools like Meta's Muse assistant, SpaceXAI's Grok Bot, OpenAI's Dots, and the startup Instinct's AI agents. They've been hailed as productivity boosters, handling mundane tasks for users, such as bookings, audits, and repetitive purchases. But users have also shared some nightmare stories of their agents going rogue and taking actions they hadn't anticipated. Software company founder Shane Mac told Business Insider that his AI agent, tasked with sending him a month-end audit of his bank account, accidentally posted it to his company's Slack chat . Others have talked about their agents hallucinating information and misunderstanding instructions. Austin Welch, who works in finance in Houston, told Business Insider that his Instinct agent accidentally ordered 20 pounds of chicken for his meal with his partner. events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Thousands of properties in Central Australia without power after sudden storm lashes Alice Springs A damaging storm cell has caused a blackout in Alice Springs after it raged through Central Australia this afternoon. ( ABC News: Xavier Martin ) The Bureau of Meteorology says "severe thunderstorms" have brought heavy rains and damaging winds to Alice Springs. The Hilton DoubleTree is among the properties damaged, with parts of its roof collapsing in during the storm. The weather bureau says more storms are possible through the week and emergency services are urging locals to remain vigilant. Thousands of homes are without power after a surprise storm brought wind speeds of almost 100km/h to Central Australia, pulling down trees and damaging properties. According to the Bureau of Meteorology (BOM), heavy rain and hail fell on Alice Springs at 3:30pm this afternoon and wind gusts of 96km/h were recorded locally at 3:44pm. It's the second storm to rock Alice Springs in just a few short days. ( Supplied: Damien Ryan ) "A surface trough coincides with a warm and unstable air mass in southern parts of the Territory, which has resulted in the development of severe thunderstorms," the weather bureau said. The short-lived storm cell pushed trees onto roads, powerlines and roofs. The Alice Springs Hilton DoubleTree was among the properties to suffer significant damage. The Alice Springs Hilton DoubleTree sustained damage to its ceiling. ( ABC News: Xavier Martin ) In a statement released on Monday afternoon, Power and Water Corporation said "approximately 9,000 properties" had lost power "due to damage caused by a sudden storm cell". "Our crews are assessing the damage and will work to restore services as quickly as is safely possible," the statement said. "The communities of Arumbera, Burt Plain, Ilparpa, Simpson, Hermannsburg, Hugh, Namatjira and Wallace Rockhole have also been affected. Territorians can check power outages via Power and Water's online tracker . Cars parked outside the hospital in Alice Springs were damaged in the storm. ( ABC News: Xavier Martin ) The BOM's Robert Urbaniak said Centralians were "not out of the woods yet", warning another similar storm cell was predicted for Tuesday afternoon and evening. "Unfortunately another day of it, but after that should settle down somewhat." NT Emergency Services (NTES) said it had received 47 calls for assistance since the storm hit. Adam White from NTES said Alice Springs residents would need to remain vigilant in the coming few days and urged people to keep an eye on SecureNT for updates . "I've got some reports of multiple trees down, some damage from the hail and the winds," he said. It was the second storm to hit Alice Springs in less than a week. Two cells are moving east over parts of Central Australia and the Barkly region, according to the BOM, which are likely to persist through this evening. events.title: Healey faces £35bn Budget challenge to meet spending pledges, says think tank
events.summary: Published 12 October 2026, 00:04 BST Chancellor John Healey faces having to find £35bn to avoid cuts to public spending while meeting defence promises in his first Budget, an influential think tank has warned. The Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said that if the government wants to raise defence spending to 3% of national income by 2030 and lift health spending without squeezing other departments, it will need a "top-up" of billions of pounds. Higher inflation, caused by the Iran war, could eat into what the government hoped to spend on public services, meaning Healey will have to choose between spending cuts, tax rises, or a mixture of both, the IFS said. The government is under growing pressure to show financial markets that it has a tight grip on finances as the cost of borrowing rises. The IFS said that Healey must set out "credible" spending plans in the Budget, which will take place on 28 October. "A 'steady-as-she-goes' Budget is not an option available to the chancellor," said IFS director Helen Miller. "Choosing to stay the course with the inherited tax and spending plans would mean allowing inflation to blow departments' spending plans off course. "Simply pencilling in implicit cuts that he has no intention of delivering would make the Budget a work of fiction," she added. Speaking ahead of the annual International Monetary Fund meeting this week, Healey said: "The consequences of conflict in the Middle East and Europe are hitting countries worldwide, leading to higher prices at the pumps and more expensive mortgages at home. "But Britain and our allies can face up to these challenges together." He said his Budget "will build on this approach with fiscal discipline helping to deliver economic resilience" and give people "breathing space". Miller told the BBC's Today programme that Healey had inherited spending plans for government departments where spending growth would slow in the coming years. "[It] already looked likely that he would have to make spending cuts just to live within those," she said. "Now, along comes the Middle East war, inflation goes up and those spending plans look very tight indeed." Added to that, the chancellor has said he wants to get defence spending up to 3% of national income. Under Keir Starmer's leadership, Healey resigned as defence secretary in June in a battle with the Treasury over military spending. Miller said: "You put all that together, if he wanted to do all of that within current spending plans he's looking at having to cut some other services by something like £35bn." She said the government would have a "tough time" if it wanted to raise taxes to stop cuts to departments and fund defence spending. Former chancellor Rachel Reeves announced billions of pounds in tax rises. Meanwhile, Labour pledged in its manifesto "not increase taxes on working people", ruling out rises to National Insurance, income tax or VAT. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he will stick to that promise. Miller said: "You'd really have to be scaping around and doing lots of small things to get up to big sums." The chancellor does not have to address spending totals in this Budget, and may choose to leave such decisions until future events - for example, next year's Spring Statement or Spending Review - by which time the outlook for the economy could look very different. But the IFS warned not addressing it would cast doubt on the credibility of the government's plans. Previous chancellors have relied on a similar strategy of pencilling in unrealistic future spending plans to ensure that they meet the fiscal rules on the day - only to change the plans further down the line. Miller said Healey's focus on fiscal discipline was a "good first start but what he needs to do is not just say he's going to cut borrowing in coming years but actually deliver on those plans." The US-Israel war against Iran and Russia's invasion of Ukraine have together helped drive up energy prices around the world. These higher costs have been passed to customers via higher prices on shelves and at the pumps. The wars have also contributed to a rise in the cost of UK government debt interest payments, adding to the pressure on Healey. Although higher inflation will boost tax revenues, it will also eat into the value of departments' cash budgets, the IFS said. Like other analysts, the IFS thinks recent turbulence on bond markets and higher inflation will add around £10bn to forecasts for the government's borrowing costs in 2029-30. However, it still expects the government to meet its self-imposed fiscal rules - that it will only borrow for investment projects by the financial year 2029-30 and also be reducing debt as a percentage of GDP - not least as inflation pushes up tax revenues. But it expects those rules to be met by a smaller buffer - known as "headroom" - of around £20bn.

events.title: Saudi Arabia says oil supply to continue to flow despite Riyadh attacks
events.summary: Saudi Arabia sought to reassure the world’s energy industry that escalating attacks on the kingdom would not disrupt its role as a major oil supplier. “The word ‘fear’ in the Saudi dictionary does not exist,” Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman said on Monday at the opening of the WPC Energy Congress . “We, as Saudis, are fearless, combatant and determined people.” The remarks came after King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh was struck four times in five days, emphasising the growing security risks facing the world’s biggest crude exporter amid the Iran war. A missile attack on the airport on Saturday killed 12 people and injured 309, Saudi authorities said. Another projectile struck the airport on Sunday evening, killing one person and injuring 11. The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen blamed the Iran-backed Houthi rebels for Saturday’s attack. But Riyadh is to press ahead with a week of high-level energy meetings, including Sunday’s International Energy Forum ministerial talks and the WPC congress, which the kingdom is hosting for the first time. “Riyadh is the capital of energy security and your presence here today proves that,” Prince Abdulaziz told delegates. “Our gathering today does not mean that risks have disappeared.” The attacks have sharpened focus on Saudi Arabia’s ability to keep oil flowing during periods of conflict, particularly as threats mount around the Strait of Hormuz and Bab Al Mandeb strait, two of the world’s most important energy chokepoints. Prince Abdulaziz said Saudi Arabia’s ability to withstand disruption was the result of decades of investment in storage, redundancy and alternative export routes. “Resilience is built before a crisis begins,” he added. He referred to the kingdom’s East-West pipeline , which carries crude from eastern oilfields to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, allowing exports to bypass the Strait of Hormuz. The flow was halted after Houthi attacks in September, before recovering to about 5.8 million barrels per day by October 6, compared with capacity of about seven million bpd. The disruption showed the importance of restoring operations quickly, Prince Abdulaziz said. Resilience depends not only on infrastructure but also on domestic expertise, he added. “Pipelines do not repair themselves. Our systems do not restore themselves. Facilities do not restart themselves. People do,” he said. At Sunday’s IEF meeting, he pledged that Saudi Arabia would continue to supply domestic and international customers “regardless of circumstances”. The gathering took place against an increasingly volatile market backdrop. Brent crude hovered at about $104 a barrel on Monday as the Riyadh attacks and strikes on two tankers near the Strait of Hormuz and Oman added to geopolitical risks. “The events of recent weeks are serious,” Prince Abdulaziz said. “Our response must be equally serious.”

events.title: Stellantis CEO urges incentives for carmakers who build in Europe as Chinese rivals gain ground
events.summary: Stellantis CEO told CNBC that Europe needs to incentivize carmakers who build in the region. It comes as Chinese carmakers are quickly accelerating their share of the European car market. Stellantis' CEO has called on European regulators to create stronger incentives for carmakers to manufacture vehicles in the region, as it faces intensifying competition from Chinese rivals that are dominating the market. Antonio Filosa, who has served at the helm of the automotive giant since 2025, spoke with "CNBC Conversation" ahead of the Paris Motor Show on Monday about the company's declining sales amid China's "impressive" acceleration in the European market. "What we are supporting a lot in Europe is to establish for everybody a level playing field," Filosa said in an interview with CNBC's Charlotte Reed . "In concrete terms, it means to work on true regulation... starting from "Made in Europe," that should be regulation that incentivizes, rewards, and protects the ones that are able to demonstrate that they design cars, engineer cars," Filosa added. Made in Europe refers to proposed legislation drawn up by the EU Commission which would require carmakers to meet minimum local content requirements to sell within the regional market. The global carmaker, which is known for its key car brands such as Jeep and Ram, has been in the midst of a $70 billion turnaround strategy as it struggles with declining demand. The company's shares are down almost 60% so far since the beginning of the year. Chinese car brands are dominating the global market , with their global auto-sales share jumping by nearly 70% from 2020 to 2025, according to market research and consulting firm GlobalData. Meanwhile, the market share of European car sales was close to zero in 2020, but is up to 12% in August this year, according to data from Germany-based Dataforce. "I believe that Chinese automakers, the ones that we know, can really offer many consumers in many segments, good technology, and competitive prices," Filosa said. European trade commissioner Maroš Sefčovič said Friday that China has agreed to halve its exports of hybrid cars to the bloc, after Beijing had repeatedly rejected requests. European carmakers moved higher Monday morning after news of the agreement. Stellantis added 2.7% and French carmaker Renault were up around 3%. French automotive parts suppliers Valeo and Forvia also rose in early trading. A spokesperson for China's Ministry of Commerce responded on Monday to the request, saying that China and the European Union have maintained a dialogue on trade and investment and reached "several consensuses and achievements that are conducive to maintaining a stable and balanced key trade partnership," according to CNBC's translation from Chinese to English. As part of the agreement, one principle laid out was "non-discrimination," which says that no measures will specifically target or discriminate against Chinese companies. "China's quota will not be lower than that of any other import source for the EU." — CNBC's Michael Wayland helped contribute to this report.

events.title: The giant cavity in America's dental care industry
events.summary: Getty Images; Alyssa Powell/BI When Elysse Morris decided to become a dental hygienist , it seemed like a natural fit. She was a fairly "sciencey" student in high school and generally liked going to the dentist. Plus, she'd always been a talker. Eleven years into her career, Morris, now 34, knows she could probably be making more money. Her home state of Virginia has a severe shortage of dental hygienists, and temporary workers can command high hourly rates by hopping between practices. But Morris has spent four years at the same privately owned office because she's happy there. Her boss gives her decent equipment, benefits, a bonus, and — most importantly — respect. The dentist treats her like a clinician rather than a pair of hands. "We're not workers to her," Morris says. Her setup is what those in the business call a "unicorn" office, and the short supply of these quality workplaces is helping cause a short supply of dental hygienists across the country. I'm not kidding when I say I love my dental hygienist. I was going to quit my dentist , who I feel like often tries to push questionable treatments on me, but then Andrea started, and she's amazing. Last time I was in the office, I mentioned my union was bargaining a new contract, and she said she wished hygienists had a union of their own. It makes sense that they don't — the United States doesn't do sectoral bargaining , and most hygienists have traditionally worked in small, private offices where organizing would be difficult — but it got me thinking. I have no idea whether hygienists, in general, are having a good time. Turns out, they're not. According to the American Dental Association's Health Policy Institute, only 60% of dentists report having an adequate number of dental hygienists on staff. States such as Virginia, Missouri, Texas, and California say they need hundreds more clinicians. The problem isn't a lack of demand — the Bureau of Labor Statistics expects employment for hygienists to grow much faster than average over the next decade. The real struggle is that the field is having a hard time getting new hygienists in the door, as experienced hygienists are heading for the exits. Dental hygiene programs at community colleges and universities aren't agile enough to increase their flow of new graduates, all while veteran clinicians are deciding the physical toll, heavy workload, and lack of benefits aren't worth it. "Burnout is so high," Morris says. You're basically "trying to be a perfectionist all day long." The result: long wait times for patients and proposed solutions that some hygienists worry could lead to worse care. Prior to 2020, dental hygienists weren't exactly skipping gleefully into work — there were already issues around workplace culture, compensation, and opportunities for growth. But the pandemic exacerbated many of these problems. Many offices temporarily closed , hitting staff's bottom lines. When they reopened, hygienists suddenly found themselves on the front lines, exposed to the virus in their close-contact, aerosol-generating work and managing new safety and equipment protocols — all while juggling their disrupted daily lives. On a typical day, hygienists see eight to 10 patients, each with different anxieties, histories, and baggage. One person comes in ranting about how COVID isn't real , the next talks about their grandfather dying of it. In both cases, the hygienist must manage the emotional climate while scraping tartar from tooth enamel with microscopic precision. After months of this, many decided they'd had enough. Those who were close to retirement pulled the trigger, and others went shopping around for new careers. An estimated 3,300 hygienists left the field. The acute issues of the pandemic exacerbated long-standing problems in the industry. Dental hygiene is a physically demanding job . Professionals find themselves hunched over for large parts of the day, and injuries to the neck, shoulders, wrists, and lower back are common. Many dental practices — especially the smaller ones — don't provide benefits such as health insurance to their workers. That may propel hygienists to pursue jobs in more corporate environments, such as dental service organizations or private equity-backed groups. These entities often have a reputation for pushing higher-cost treatments and compressing appointment times to generate higher profits. While hygienists may initially be enticed by the benefits and pay at these operations, the pace can be exhausting, resulting in a revolving door. "They're not retaining people any better than other practice models are," says Dr. Kathryn Rothas, a New York-based dentist and spokesperson for the American Dental Association. Rothas is the dental director of Whitney Young Health, a federally funded community clinic in Albany. As we're speaking, she says they're trying to fill an open dental hygienist position. While they offer solid benefits, they don't pay as much as bigger corporate dental groups. Graduating more hygienists while failing to address why existing hygienists leave the workforce is like filling a bucket without addressing the leak. Brandon Patel manages the front desk at his wife's two Connecticut dental practices. He tells me they're in a similar situation. "I've had a job post up for almost six months, and we have had basically no applicants," he says. "The applicants we've had are full-time employees just looking for a better offer." His clinic is offering $55 to $60 an hour, but no health insurance, which Patel says is "very difficult to provide as a small-business owner ." Dental office dynamics are complicated. People are often working in tight quarters, and personalities can clash. Some dentists may have a way they like doing things that simply doesn't jibe with certain employees. Morris once worked for a lovely older dentist who did beautiful work — but he insisted on using old instruments, and after her paychecks started to bounce, she quit. The pay and flexibility of temping or part-time work appeal to many hygienists, but it increases the chance they end up in offices where they're not comfortable. Dental hygiene is also a female-dominated field, and some clinicians scale back their hours or stop working once they start having families. The obvious answer to workplace shortages is to train more people, especially since dental hygiene seems pretty AI-proof , and the prospect of a high salary should make it an enticing career. That's easier said than done. Unlike nursing programs, where universities send students to partner hospitals for clinical rotations, dental hygiene programs must build, equip, and operate their own dental clinics. A single chair alone can cost upward of $8,000, not to mention X-ray machines, simulation labs, and other equipment. events.title: Oman aims to launch new international financial centre by 2027
events.summary: Oman plans to launch full licensing at its new international financial centre by 2027 and is to begin registering companies later this year. IFC Oman, the plans for which were first revealed in January, is currently working on its legal framework, rule book and registry system, it said in a statement on Monday. A package of laws for business registration and licensing, financial services regulation and an independent dispute resolution framework are to be issued shortly, the financial centre said. They will provide the legal basis for IFC Oman’s authorities to adopt an initial package of regulations and rules. A registry system, which will enable businesses to submit their applications online, is to move into the testing phase soon, the statement added. “IFC Oman is accelerating towards opening its doors, with its legal, regulatory and digital infrastructure moving into place," said Mahmood Al Aweini, chairman of the IFC Oman Authority Board. "The centre will offer global businesses and investors a stable and competitive place to do business." IFC Oman will join other existing financial centres in the Gulf, including Abu Dhabi's international financial centre ADGM, the Dubai International Financial Centre and the King Abdullah Financial District in Riyadh, as well as the Qatar Financial Centre. The financial centre has started boosting its international outreach to engage prospective businesses, investors and professional services firms around the world, the statement said. Oman has been taking steps to diversify its economy away from oil , with investments in sectors such as logistics, manufacturing and property helping to expand its non-oil economic base. Under its economic and social reforms programme, Oman aims to reduce its dependence on oil income from about 30 per cent to 16 per cent by 2030 and 8.4 per cent by 2040. The sultanate has also announced the introduction of personal income tax starting in 2028, with a 5 per cent rate of tax on annual income exceeding 42,000 Omani rials ($109,134). Muscat also unveiled a golden visa programme in August to attract more foreign investment into the country. It also has plans to build a new economic area centred on developing its artificial intelligence capabilities, as it aims to accelerate its technology sector to strengthen its economy. Last month, S&P Global Ratings boosted the economic growth forecast for Oman to 3.5 per cent on the back of favourable trade logistics amid the Iran war. The outlook is more than double the previous 1.6 per cent real GDP growth estimate for the sultanate. It is also higher than the 2.3 per cent growth posted by Oman last year.

events.title: Campaigners claim minister attempting to undermine 'Holiday Hunger Bill'
events.summary: Paul Givan has now proposed amendments which would give him discretion to decide when the payments would take effect Published 12 October 2026, 06:23 BST Campaigners have accused the education minister of attempting to undermine a proposed Stormont law which would help poorer families with the cost of food. The Democratic Unionist Party's (DUP) Paul Givan has been consistently critical of the legislation which is being brought forward by Sinn Féin assembly member Danny Baker. Givan has warned it would immediately cost his department £20m a year at a time when it is already struggling to balance its budget. The Holiday Meals Payment Bill , external would create a new payment for families whose children receive free school meals which would be made during school holidays to help with the cost of food. The matter is due to be discussed in the assembly on Monday. Givan has now proposed amendments which would give him the power to delay implementation. He will need support from other parties for the amendments to be accepted. It is not clear if he will get that support, although the Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) has expressed reservations about the proposal. The payment would be made during school holidays to help with the cost of food As it is based on school meals, the cost of the scheme would be on the Department of Education. It is modelled on the School Holiday Food Grant scheme introduced during the pandemic, which paid qualifying families £27 per child every fortnight. In April, Givan warned MLAs that his department did not have funding for the scheme, so they would be voting to cut education spending if they supported it. He has now proposed amendments which would give him discretion to decide when the payments would take effect. A coalition of campaign groups, including the National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children (NSPCC) and Save the Children, say the amendments would mean "no guarantees about when, if ever, payments might begin". They added: "We are calling on all political parties and all MLAs to reject the amendments tabled by the education minister and support the bill as it currently stands." Baker has said the education minister is attempting to "obstruct" the implementation of the bill. "His proposals would give him control over when, if ever, holiday hunger payments begin. "This is an attempt to delay and undermine legislation that has the support of the majority of parties in the assembly." A Department of Education spokesperson said the minister's amendments "do not seek to delay or block the Bill". "They reflect the Department's duty to manage its budget responsibly, taking account of financial pressures, competing priorities and the impact of new spending on existing services, particularly at a time when education faces significant financial challenges across the system," they added. "The amendments fulfil that duty while preserving the Bill's intended purpose. The Bill's key provisions remain unchanged, including eligibility, payment levels, holiday coverage and the Education Authority's responsibilities." events.title: MAS introduces enhanced safeguards around public events by financial institutions
events.summary: Under the enhanced safeguards, financial institutions are expected to conduct public prospecting activities only within designated areas at commercial premises. SINGAPORE – The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) on Oct 12 announced more safeguards around public prospecting activities by financial institutions. This comes as these activities, including roadshows, allow financial institutions and their representatives to engage consumers and market financial products and services in public places, and may cause “concerns” when conducted inappropriately. Such inappropriate conduct includes instances when consumers are subjected to unsolicited or “persistent solicitation”, said the authority. Under the enhanced safeguards, financial institutions are expected to conduct public prospecting activities only within designated areas at commercial premises, and appoint “suitably qualified individuals” to oversee their representatives’ conduct at such events. Representatives must clearly inform consumers at the outset that they intend to market financial products or services, and obtain consumers’ consent before proceeding with the engagement. Street canvassing and door-to-door prospecting will also remain prohibited. The enhanced safeguards follow a public consultation by the authority on proposals to strengthen standards of conduct in this area. Lim Tuang Lee, assistant managing director for capital markets at MAS, said consumers should not feel “pressured or caught off guard” when approached about financial products and services. He added that the enhanced safeguards assist in ensuring that consumers are treated “fairly and professionally”, while allowing financial institutions to continue engaging consumers through appropriate channels. MAS will issue the updated guidelines in 2027, and financial institutions will be given a nine-month transition period to implement the enhanced safeguards thereafter. THE BUSINESS TIMES

events.title: 'I just live on noodles': Report reveals scale of NT cost-of-living crisis
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Territorians 'in crisis' as report shines light on skyrocketing cost of living over past decade Four generations of Shirley Napurrula Miller's family in Central Australia are supporting each other to try to make ends meet. ( ABC News: Xavier Martin ) New data has revealed the rising cost of essentials is making it harder for people to meet their basic needs in the Northern Territory compared to a decade ago. The report by the NT Council of Social Service examines the changes in the cost of living between 2016 and 2026 across key spending areas of housing, utilities, transport and food. The community sector peak body is recommending federal government welfare payments be increased along with the remote area allowance for people in isolated areas. For an Alice Springs grandmother who receives a disability pension, the struggle to afford groceries between pay cheques is constant, with the cost of food "too high". Shirley Napurrula Miller is among the nearly 50 per cent of the Northern Territory's population who experienced food insecurity because of rising prices in 2025, according to a new report. "Sometimes I can't buy groceries, or meat, or anything," she said. Shirley Napurrula Miller says she struggles to afford the basics for herself and her family. ( ABC News: Xavier Martin ) The report by the NT Council of Social Service (NTCOSS), released today, examines changes in the cost of living between 2016 and 2026 across key spending areas of housing, utilities, transport and food. It shows every day, across all spending areas, many Territorians are having to make impossible money decisions and weigh up what they must prioritise to live. Hunger relief charity Foodbank Australia estimates that 46 per cent of NT households experienced food insecurity in 2025, above the national average of 33 per cent, according to the NTCOSS report. The report found that while incomes have increased in real terms in the past 10 years, the cost of essentials has too. ( ABC News: Xavier Martin ) In remote areas, the cost of food is even more prohibitive than in urban centres such as Darwin and Alice Springs, where prices have also risen substantially. "In 2023, the average cost of a healthy food basket was 40 per cent more in remote stores than in a supermarket," the report states. The 10-year comparison report found that while incomes have increased in real terms, the cost of essentials has too, making it harder for everyone — especially those on low incomes — to meet basic needs. Power costs have risen 18 per cent and those on prepaid plans, predominantly First Nations people in urban and remote public housing, are having their electricity cut off more frequently, with 2,284 more disconnections per month on average last year than in 2019-2020. The report found there were 103,648 involuntary self-disconnections in major centres in the NT last year. ( ABC News: Xavier Martin ) Further compounding cost pressures for those already on the poverty line, the report states the prepaid electricity price is higher than for standard postpaid billing to account for customers not paying a fixed daily charge. According to the report, there were 103,648 involuntary self-disconnections in major centres in the NT last year. "Affordability challenges are a key driver of such disconnections," the report states. Ms Miller said she had faced disconnection many times and Aboriginal families often lent on each other to share their limited incomes and keep the power on, particularly in the heat over summer. Linda Lechleitner says her electricity bill alone is more than her Centrelink payment. ( ABC News: Xavier Martin ) Her daughter, Linda Lechleitner, who lives between Alice Springs and a remote Aboriginal homeland near the community of Papunya, about a 3-hour drive away, said she worried about electricity costs amid a heating climate. "It's more than the government payment that they give you, the Centrelink payment doesn't carry people through fortnightly," she said. "Every little dollar counts … it's not carrying through to the next fortnight or the next week, they're having to borrow money from family and then pay that back. The report reveals rents have skyrocketed 55 per cent over the past decade. Meanwhile, the NT's social housing stock only increased by 4 per cent between 2017 and 2025, while social housing applications increased by 37 per cent over the same period. The report shows transport costs have also shot up, with an 80-litre tank of diesel now costing $28 more in Darwin and an extra $88 in Alice Springs.

events.title: AI less regulated than milk, Microsoft president says in warning over safety
events.summary: Brad Smith adds to calls for tougher rules for AI, including ‘kill switches’ and legal obligation to victims of rogue agents Artificial intelligence is less regulated than milk and washing machines, the president of Microsoft has said, as the tech industry warns over the safety of AI. Brad Smith said there should be more safety rules to govern the technology including a legal obligation to a “victim” if their system was breached by rogue AI agents. He told the BBC: “Right now, your washing machine is subject to more safety rules than AI. Every carton of milk that you see in the grocery store is subject to safety rules and inspection.” There are growing calls from experts, politicians and regulators for tougher rules to control AI, as well as warnings from Anthropic, Google DeepMind and OpenAI that the pace of the technology’s development should slow. Smith said AI could be a “tool and a weapon” that should be regulated urgently. Companies needed “emergency brakes”, also known as “kill switches”, to pause or slow down AI if it grew out of control, he told the BBC. Microsoft, which operates AI infrastructure and is a shareholder in the ChatGPT owner, OpenAI, is led by chief executive Satya Nadella. On Saturday, Nadella also called for AI models to have an “emergency brake”. He wrote: “We can’t treat super intelligence as a set of nested black boxes and simply accept or reject its recommendations, answers, and actions. “We must build contained systems whose behaviour we can observe, limits we can test, and actions we can always contain.” His and Smith’s comments came as Britain’s AI minister, Kanishka Narayan, prepared to call on firms developing frontier AI to do more to make sure it is safe. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning In a speech on Monday, Narayan is expected to say companies building AI models should do more to deal with risk and build better safeguards. He will also say the UK government is preparing to legislate to increase oversight of AI, according to reports. Experts have said enemy states could also steal unreleased, powerful AI models. Geoffrey Irving, a former chief scientist at the UK’s AI Security Institute, said that AI companies did “not have security that would prevent an adversarial country from stealing the models”. Meanwhile, cases of rogue AI behaviour continue to come to light. Last week, Anthropic revealed that when it was testing a version of its Claude model, the AI contacted police and falsely claimed it could help solve a murder .

events.title: AI is less regulated than milk, says Microsoft president
events.summary: Microsoft boss: 'If a company builds AI agents and they break loose, there should be a legal obligation to tell the victim' Published 12 October 2026, 00:07 BST Milk and washing machines are currently more regulated than AI, the president of Microsoft has said. Brad Smith said there needed to be global safety rules in place, including a legal obligation to tell a "victim" if their system is breached by a rogue AI agent as well as deciding when outside evaluators should sign off on an AI product before it is released. His comments put him at odds with President Donald Trump, who said the sector should regulate itself so US firms don't lose out to Chinese rivals. But Smith said: "Right now, your washing machine is subject to more safety rules than AI. Every carton of milk that you see in the grocery store is subject to safety rules and inspection." Demands for laws and rules to control AI have grown after experts in the sector said they believed the technology is a threat to humanity. The bosses of the US-based AI giants such as Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind have all backed the idea of an AI development slowdown , but Trump has pushed against this. Speaking to the BBC's Big Boss Interview podcast, Smith called AI both a "tool and a weapon" that urgently needed to be regulated. "Let's get started today," he said. He said firms need "emergency brakes" – often known in the industry as 'kill switches' – to pause or slowdown AI if it got out of control in some way. He also said there should be a legal requirement for firms to write "incident reports" and tell victims if the technology goes rogue. He also suggested that independent government evaluators should vet new AI technology. "We know how to do this for other products," Smith said. "We should build on that knowledge and think about how to apply it to AI." Smith said the UK was best placed to drive forward these global rules for AI because of its AI Security Institute , external , launched during former prime minister Rishi Sunak's government as the AI Safety Institute. "In the world of technology, in the tech sector, most people that I know would say, if you ask them, name the country that is the leader in having this technical capability, they would say, it's very simple. It's the United Kingdom. They are the best." Smith's views are very different to those of his president, who believes the US should be going full-steam ahead on AI. Trump has repeatedly said that "whoever wins AI, wins". However, Smith does not believe the US government would be as opposed to UK-led AI regulations as Trump's comments make it seem, suggesting the US would be more accepting of the UK making standards than the EU. "In Washington DC, people don't look at the UK and they don't look at London the way they look at Brussels – that's a strength," he said. "When you look at AI agents that have escaped human control, when you look at models that are so powerful that they're putting the world's cybersecurity at risk. I would say: The moment has arrived. "Let's speak calmly, maybe even softly, but firmly, and start to bring people together. I hope that's the role we can play as a company. I hope that's the role the UK can play as a country." Big Boss Interview: Microsoft's Brad Smith The president of the tech giant calls for global rules on AI, and says the UK is in the "best position" to lead the charge. At the end of last month, Trump hosted the leaders of US tech giants OpenAI, Anthropic, Nvidia, SpaceX, Meta, and Google at the White House where the executives signed a "morally binding" document . The companies agreed to work with "independent auditors" to assess whether their AI systems are working as intended and make sure they do not "hack or access technical systems in unintended ways". Smith said he applauds the statement and Microsoft is "happy to sign it". "It's a good step, it's a necessary step... But I don't think it's sufficient any longer." He added that the challenge for any "self-regulatory regime" is that "the good companies will do what you want". "It's the companies that are not as responsible that you need to worry about." events.title: AI investment boom offsets energy shock to keep global growth at 3%, IMF chief says
events.summary: Strong investment ⁠in AI infrastructure is keeping global growth at about 3 per cent, yielding major ​benefits for many Asian economies that supply the hardware, such as Thailand, International Monetary Fund managing director Kristalina Georgieva said on Monday. The artificial ⁠intelligence investment boom was already delivering a “demand shock, an investment shock” that could boost growth in advanced Asian economies by a half to one full percentage point, and emerging Asian economies by 0.2 to 0.8 percentage point, she said. “AI, love it, hate it. It's already here,” Ms Georgieva said. “That ⁠shift into higher gear is what is keeping the world economy growing at around 3 per cent, despite the fact we are ​being dragged down ⁠by the energy supply shock,” she told ‌hundreds of participants on the first day of a week-long series of meetings of the IMF and World Bank in the ​Thai capital. The IMF in July forecast global growth at 3 per cent in 2026. It will release an updated outlook on Tuesday. About 18,000 people are expected to attend the meetings this week, including finance officials from the IMF's 191 members. Several ministers will skip the meeting to focus on domestic priorities, including US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Spanish Finance Minister Arcadi Espana, sources said. Profound consequences Ms Georgieva said AI amounted to a “slow-moving tsunami” that would have profound consequences for jobs, growth, education and even how governments generate revenue through taxation, given the expected shift from labour to capital. The IMF estimates that AI could lead to 40 per cent of jobs being augmented, downgraded or eliminated, over time, she said. An initial study showed that 10 per cent of jobs in the US already required AI skills. While routine, repetitive jobs were shrinking, low-paying jobs were increasing in two lower-paying sectors, construction and data centres. “It is a transformative technology . It so completely changes how we work, how we live,” she said, noting that an AI assistant now gave her a ​30-second message about her schedule each day. The US, China and India are the most important ‌producers in the AI supply chain, but many of ⁠the firms building the needed infrastructure are in Asia , Ms Georgieva ​said, referring to Thailand, host of this year's annual meetings. Impact on entry-level jobs World Bank President Ajay Banga, who ​has made jobs ‌a central focus of his presidency, said the development bank was focused on leveraging “small AI”, which is not dependent on large language models, to generate ⁠enormous productivity gains for farmers, healthcare systems, educators and others in emerging markets. Singapore's President Tharman Shanmugaratnam, speaking at the same event, ⁠said governments should address how AI was reducing job opportunities for graduates. “There is a particular problem that we have to address very soon … and that is that, the first rung in employment, your first job upon graduation, is now seeing less demand,” he said. Mr Shanmugaratnam said the world should also guard against AI resulting in a “new divergence” in growth and job creation between ​developing and advanced economies. “AI is going to widen the divergence if we are too passive about it,” he said. “So we've got to do everything we can to first use AI to create good jobs and to create jobs that can be done well by human beings, can allow them to ride up a career ladder despite AI.”

events.title: Human judgment and intentional outcomes are vital in AI use: DBS CEO
events.summary: DBS Bank CEO Tan Su Shan during the DBS Asia Future Forward Conference at Suntec Convention and Exhibition Centre on Oct 12. DBS CEO Tan Su Shan said AI must be used for clear business and work goals, not just added on. She called this “AI lipstick” and urged firms to redesign workflows. DBS’s new AI report said advantage now depends on solving real problems, building trust, and linking intelligence to real outcomes. It also said businesses should start with the intended result. Tan said Asia must stay connected through trade and cooperation to avoid AI supply chain blockages. She stressed that human judgment, wisdom and creativity are vital to guide AI well. SINGAPORE – Applying artificial intelligence is not enough – it has to be harnessed for intentional business and work outcomes, said DBS chief executive Tan Su Shan on Oct 12. She was speaking at the inaugural DBS Asia Future Forward Conference at Suntec Singapore Convention and Exhibition Centre. Organised by DBS, the new flagship event brings together global leaders in technology, business and investment to examine the forces shaping the region’s future. In this first edition, the focus was on AI and how such technology is transforming industries, business models and the nature of work. Tan spoke about Asia’s emergence as a region and how it has proved that AI can be brought to everyday use cases, from enterprises to solving health issues to supporting finance. “I think Asia’s proven and shown that we are able to use AI for good business outcomes and good human outcomes – whether it’s to help the elderly at home, whether it’s to redesign workflows,” she said during her opening address. She added that simply applying AI is not good enough. “We call that AI lipstick. That’s not going to work,” she said. “What we have to do is we really have to rethink our workflows and our work processes so that we can truly unlock our potential. So just adding AI in it might help marginally, but it’s not going to change the way we work.” Tan made these remarks in conjunction with the release of a DBS report on AI outcomes. The report noted that as AI capability becomes more widely available, technical advantage becomes harder to sustain. “Competitive advantage increasingly depends on identifying important problems, earning the trust required for adoption and connecting intelligence to real-world outcomes,” it said. The report said that businesses can start with the intended outcome. “Redesign workflows, partnerships and operating systems around that outcome, then demonstrate that it improves organisational performance and delivers measurable value for customers,” it said. It added that for Asia, the challenge is to turn regional strengths into shared advantage. Tan also said in her speech that countries need to be better connected with one another, and mentioned agreements such as the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership, signed by 15 Asia-Pacific countries, and the Future of Investment and Trade Partnership, which was co-convened by New Zealand, Singapore, Switzerland and the United Arab Emirates. Better connections have to be made, even while countries become increasingly protectionist, Tan said. She noted that AI depends on everyone trading with one another, because each country has its own niche area. For instance, Taiwan has the semiconductor foundries, South Korea has the memory components, and the raw materials come from China and South-east Asia. “So if we don’t cooperate, we will continue to have blockages in our AI supply chain. Even if we want sovereignty, you need to have some trade cooperation,” Tan added. “So stay connected, but keep your sovereignty with your models or data. We have sovereignty, but we also stay connected.” She added that AI has created both visions of a dystopian future where technology takes over or a utopia where AI helps to solve many issues. “What we need now is for humans to exercise good judgment, good wisdom, good creativity to ensure that this AI journey that we take together as a human race will take us up the right path,” Tan said. Sue-Ann Tan is a business correspondent at The Straits Times, covering capital markets and sustainable finance.

events.title: China’s domestic car sales downturn continues, exports retain momentum
events.summary: Chery and Leapmotor vehicles at a Chinese auto show in Buenos Aires, Argentina, on Oct 2. BEIJING – China’s domestic car sales extended their decline for a 12th successive month, while exports remained a key growth driver as automakers looked overseas to cushion the impact of a sluggish home market. Passenger vehicle sales fell 28.1% from a year earlier to 1.63 million units in September, worsening from a 23.7% decline in August, data from the China Passenger Car Association (CPCA) showed on Monday. Annual car exports jumped 73.2% to 923,000 vehicles last month, versus a 77.5% rise in August. Sales of battery electric vehicles and plug-in hybrids at home slid 16.7% from the year before to 1.08 million units, compared with a 10.1% fall in August. The segment’s export growth quickened to 163.5% from August’s 154.7%. Any curbs on plug-in hybrid exports are unlikely to significantly affect overall new energy vehicle exports, given the dominant role of pure EVs, said CPCA secretary-general Cui Dongshu. China and the EU have reached a deal that could halve Chinese hybrid vehicle exports to the bloc over four years, EU trade chief Maros Sefcovic said on Oct 9, though volume limits and terms for shipments above those quotas remain unclear. Shrinking domestic sales reflect broader economic weakness, with subdued consumer spending and a prolonged property downturn weighing on demand. Regulators have shifted focus from growth to safety and value, proposing rules that would curb rushed vehicle launches lacking sufficient validation. REUTERS

Some are building on commodity DRAM or holding models in on-chip SRAM, while others stack memory directly onto compute. Data movement at all levels of the stack remains a critical bottleneck, too. Interconnect technologies, networking chips, and photonics were the most active areas of the quarter, with startups tackling the problem with diverse approaches ranging from manufacturing-ready co-packaged optics, millimeter-wave RF signals over plastic waveguides, and ferroelectric glass modulators to optical couplers printed directly onto chips and coherent DSPs designed specifically for AI optics. Nearly $7.5 billion of the quarter’s total was directed to just 22 startups that raised $100 million or more, including eight that saw investors return within roughly a year, some more than doubling the previous round.
