events.title: Model blitz at Paris motor show as Europe-China rivalry heats up
events.summary: The DS F3VER concept car, by DS Automobiles, at a Stellantis NV presentation ahead of the Paris Motor Show in Meudon, France on Oct 11. Europe’s carmakers used the Paris motor show to fight back against Chinese rivals, with new launches and EU support as Brussels moved to cap Chinese hybrid imports at 350,000 a year. Chinese brands, including BYD, Chery and Changan, expanded their Europe push, as sales and exports rose fast and some firms explored local production in France and elsewhere. Volkswagen, Stellantis and Renault also unveiled new plans to defend market share, boost EV output and speed up development, while EU “Made in Europe” rules may tighten pressure on Chinese imports. PARIS – Europe’s car industry fought back against rising Chinese competition at the Paris car show on Oct 12 with a wave of new model launches and fresh support from Brussels, even as Chinese automakers expanded their push into the region. The show opened days after the European Union announced a deal with China to curb imports of Chinese hybrid vehicles into the bloc, with a cap of 350,000 a year, according to a European Commission official. While details of the arrangement have yet to be finalised, it was welcomed by European manufacturers. The flood of hybrid imports into the EU is “not sustainable” for Europe, said Renault chief executive officer Francois Provost, with the current deal “better than a trade war”. China’s Leapmotor International said it needed to understand how the cap would work in practice, but that it was an “interesting alternative to tariffs”. Around 20 Chinese brands, including BYD and Chery, are attending the show, double their presence in 2024 as they seek growth overseas amid intense competition and weaker demand at home. Chinese brands have gained share rapidly in Europe in the last three years, while total Chinese exports of hybrids to the EU’s 27-member states tripled to US$7.5 billion (S$9.6 billion) in the first half of 2026, according to Chinese customs . The EU-China deal could hit BYD, Chery and state-owned SAIC’s MG brand hardest as between them they accounted for 90% of Chinese brand hybrid sales in the EU in the first eight months of 2026, said analysts at Jefferies on Oct 11. Volkswagen CEO Oliver Blume welcomed progress in EU-China trade talks, saying on Oct 11 that companies selling cars in Europe should compete under comparable conditions and create jobs and value in the region. The German carmaker’s deliveries fell 14.3% in the third quarter, the steepest quarterly drop in four years, dragged down by a further decline in demand in its top market, China, it said on Oct 12. Deliveries also fell in North America and Western Europe. As part of its bid to regain lost market share in Europe, world No. 4 automaker Stellantis is launching six new models across its European brands at the show and unveiling nine concept cars, marking a significant expansion of its presence at the show. On Oct 11, Stellantis chief executive officer Antonio Filosa hailed “the reinvention of a European icon” as he unveiled an affordable retro electric version of Citroen’s 2CV. The company is also adopting faster Chinese-style development cycles, chief technology officer Ned Curic said, outlining plans to build small EVs in Italy using a platform being developed with Leapmotor. Renault’s head of growth, Fabrice Cambolive, said the carmaker could increase EV production in France by at least 50% over the next 12 months. Like other Western car shows, Paris had been in decline until Chinese automakers started showing up in Europe in force four years ago. Alongside BYD and Chery, this year’s show will feature new Chinese brands like Aito, while state-owned automaker Changan is launching its Nevo and Avatr brands in Europe. Chinese automakers also used the event to outline further European expansion plans. Changan president Zhao Fei said the company was in talks with manufacturers about producing vehicles in Europe and hoped to build its first European-made car in early 2027. BYD is studying the possibility of building a factory in France, executive vice-president Stella Li told broadcaster BFM TV on Oct 12. The EU imposed tariffs on Chinese-made fully electric vehicles in October 2024. The European Commission is also working on legislation that would include “Made in Europe” provisions mandating minimum local content in EVs to gain access to large parts of the EU’s car market. Agreement between France and Germany on the provisions is “imminent”, French President Emmanuel Macron said at the show. “Preserving this European sovereignty and our capacity to manufacture within Europe is crucial for us,” he said, adding that despite a “difficult” European market, companies on the continent were “innovating, advancing and accelerating”. Chinese automakers have sought European production bases ahead of the proposed rules, often in partnership with established manufacturers.

events.title: McKinsey strips partner of leadership role over LinkedIn posts
events.summary: The decision came after an internal review sparked by Chris Bradley’s LinkedIn comments on a book that discusses the “glass cliff” for women. McKinsey & Co removed a senior partner from his leadership role at the firm’s research arm after he posted online comments questioning the uphill battle female executives face in the workplace. Chris Bradley, one of a handful of directors at the McKinsey Global Institute, its high-profile business and economic research unit, was removed from that role, the consulting firm said in a statement on Oct 11. He remains a senior partner at the firm and is based in Australia. The unusual decision came after an internal review sparked by Bradley’s LinkedIn back-and-forth in September with one of the authors of a new book discussing the workplace “glass cliff” for women. The comments were deleted, and McKinsey previously distanced itself from Bradley’s remarks. “Following our conduct review process, we have removed the partner from his leadership roles, including at the McKinsey Global Institute. His public comments fell well short of the standards we expect at our firm,” McKinsey spokesman Taylor Burns said in an e-mailed statement. Bradley also served as a leader on some internal committees, Burns said. Bradley could not be reached immediately for comment outside of normal business hours. The term “glass cliff” was coined by academics to describe the phenomenon in which female leaders are more likely to be offered CEO jobs at struggling companies. Proponents of the theory say research shows that women are more likely to get an opportunity to be CEO when a company is in crisis or turnaround mode. Bradley called the glass cliff “a very convenient way to always be a victim in the rain” in the deleted posts and generally questioned whether the concept even exists. McKinsey has long sought to advance the conversation about challenges women face in the workplace. The company has published a Women in the Workplace study, compiled with Sheryl Sandberg’s LeanIn advocacy group, for more than a decade. It surveys about 9,500 employees from 124 organisations; participants consistently report that women leaders face stronger resistance than men and are more likely to have their judgment questioned. A 2020 report from McKinsey about women working in healthcare even references the term “glass cliff” when outlining hurdles cited by women of colour. Over the past decade, women CEOs of Russell 3000 companies left after an average tenure of 6.2 years versus 8.9 years for men, according to Exechange, a researcher that tracks corporate leadership changes and scores them on the likelihood that the exit was forced or voluntary. In examining the reasons for CEO departures over the same period, the research firm found that women were more likely than men to be forced out. Just one in 10 S&P 500 companies is led by a female CEO. BLOOMBERG

events.title: AI may change the price of your Big Mac and groceries — what this means for shoppers
events.summary: Supermarkets and fast food giants are increasingly using artificial intelligence to digitize their operations. Some have been accused of using so-called "dynamic pricing" to set rapid real-time changes in prices that could dramatically affect shoppers' experiences. Experts told CNBC that this could raise the risk of shoppers facing more individualized prices. Fast-food giants and supermarkets are rolling out a range of AI tools that could affect the prices shoppers pay, but experts warn the spread of data-driven tools could make personalized pricing easier to deploy. Just this week, a federal antitrust lawsuit filed against McDonald's alleged the fast food giant uses an AI-powered "pricing engine" to set menu prices across U.S. locations and overcharge customers for Big Macs and fries. McDonald's has denied that it's using AI to determine what individual customers are willing to pay and said it provides its franchisees with "tools, resources, research and recommendations to help them make informed decisions." Even so, food businesses globally are increasingly digitizing operations with AI. Earlier this year, American grocery chain Kroger said it's using an AI platform called FlashFood to mark down perishables nearing the end of their shelf life and marketing them to shoppers via an app. Meanwhile, electronic shelf labels (ESLs), which display prices on digital screens, are becoming increasingly popular at supermarkets like Kroger, Walmart , and Amazon Fresh. Whole Foods Market spokesperson Rachel Malish said the supermarket chain "does not use dynamic pricing" in a statement to CNBC. Malish said that digital shelf labels "simplify the price tag change process for our employees [and] reduce paper waste from traditional tags." The technology is also gaining traction among U.K. supermarkets such as Tesco , Morrisons, and Asda. Morrisons declined to comment to CNBC on its ESLs . The British Retail Consortium's director of food & sustainability, Andrew Opie, has said that supermarkets have "no intention to use dynamic or surge pricing in their stores," and that digital pricing is instead a way of updating and checking prices quickly. More recently, global financial platform Revolut trialed facial recognition checkout in select coffee shops, allowing customers to pay with just a picture at checkout. The technology relies on a pre-existing selfie ID that Revolut customers submit as part of standard security checks for comparison, but no additional information is collected. CNBC reached out to Tesco and Asda for comment on the use of AI tools but did not receive a response. As AI use becomes normalized among retailers, experts warn that this could lead to more dynamic pricing, which refers to frequent, rapid real-time changes in prices that could dramatically affect shoppers' experiences. "Dynamic pricing means changing prices in response to changing market conditions, such as demand, timing, capacity or competitors' prices," Miroslava Marinova, a senior lecturer of commercial law at the University of East London, told CNBC. "It is not new. Airlines, hotels, and ride-hailing services have used it for years." Bank of England economists Clare Lombardelli and Rupal Patel said in April that more sophisticated technology is leading to prices changing more frequently and also becoming more individualized, which could see more firms charging "as close to the maximum price a consumer is willing to pay for a good or service," which they defined as "perfect price discrimination." These conditions could make it harder for statisticians to "measure and interpret" month-to-month inflation data, as the consumer price index is based on a representative sample of prices for shoppers. "That works well when prices mostly move slowly and uniformly. But when prices shift continually – and differently for each shopper – the idea of a 'representative' price becomes strained," the BOE economists added. While dynamic pricing has been in play for a long time, the BOE economists and Marinova noted that AI tools such as ESLs and facial recognition checkout are changing the amount of information that companies can collect on consumers, from transaction histories to browsing behavior, location, and purchasing patterns. On Wednesday, U.K. supermarket chain Sainsbury's released "SmartLists," an AI feature that helps customers create shopping lists and find products just by uploading pictures of what they need or by typing out meal ideas. CNBC reached out to Sainsbury's for comment but did not hear back immediately. "This is also why the traditional distinction between dynamic and personalised pricing is becoming less clear in practice," Marinova explained. "Dynamic pricing responds primarily to market conditions, whereas personalised pricing uses information about the consumer to estimate willingness to pay.

events.title: UK van drivers face extra £2.5bn in diesel costs this year, figures show
events.summary: Calls for planned fuel duty rise to be scrapped as analysis finds average fuel bill could hit £1,965, up from £1,294 Millions of British van drivers face a combined £2.5bn cost to cover the rising price of diesel this year, according to figures, fuelling calls for the government to scrap its planned fuel duty rise. The owners of diesel vans and pickups can expect to collectively spend almost £8.5bn at the pump this year, according to analysis for the Guardian, after diesel prices climbed to record highs due to a global fuel shortage caused by disruption to refineries in the Middle East and Russia. The estimated fuel costs, calculated by analysts at Moneysupermarket, is significantly above the £5.95bn spent last year, raising concerns that the price of food and goods transported by road could rise sharply as retailers pass on increased logistics costs. The comparison site warned last week that the average fuel bill for a van driver could reach £1,965 this year, up from £1,294 for the average van in 2025 based on typical mileage and fuel consumption. The number of vans on British roads has grown significantly in recent years fuelled by the boom in online shopping, home deliveries and the rising number of self-employed people working in trades . Although the adoption of electric vans has begun to increase, about 95% of light commercial vehicles are still powered by diesel. The average pump price climbed to a above £2 a litre for the first time this month, up over 40% since late February, when the US-Israel war on Iran began disrupting supplies of crude and refined oil products from the Gulf, leading to cost increases across the economy. The rising cost burden has led to calls for government help in the upcoming budget, including abandoning plans to raise fuel duty from next year. The planned increase – postponed from September – will add 3p a litre in duty from 1 January, and another 2p from 1 March, in “a hammer blow” for costs, according to the Road Haulage Association (RHA). Richard Smith, the RHA’s managing director, said: “Many of our members run on margins of around 2%. Surging diesel prices are impacting firms across the country, with some spending many thousands extra every week on fuel. “Adding [fuel duty rises] on top of today’s fuel prices would be a hammer blow for many firms that move goods and the households that buy them. A fuel duty hike is a food price hike.” Data from the motoring group RAC showed that, despite a recent dip in the cost of diesel, the price remains about 57p a litre higher than before the US-Iran conflict while petrol remains 42p higher. This means households are paying £31 and £23 more respectively every time they fill up a family sized car, according to the group. The fuel duty rise “will only make prices at the pump even more expensive,” according to Simon Williams, the head of policy at the RAC. “As things stand, this year is still set to be the second most expensive year on record for drivers,” Williams said. “The government has the power to take some of the sting out of higher fuel costs, either by extending and increasing the fuel duty cut or reducing VAT as they’ve done with domestic electricity.” Smith added that the RHA was calling on the chancellor to bring in a 15p a litre rebate for British van, coach and haulage operators after Spain, France and Italy offered similar help for commercial vehicle businesses. “It’s time we caught up,” he said. On Friday, the US president, Donald Trump, attempted to ease pressure at the pump for US drivers by announcing a deal for Russian deal, in a move which infuriated the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy . The government was contact for comment.

events.title: The Gulf has entered a new era of instability. If its leaders think they can rely on old alliances, they are wrong | Nesrine Malik
events.summary: The Gulf has entered a new era of instability. If its leaders think they can rely on old alliances, they are wrong The latest attack by Houthi rebels on Saudi Arabia may prove to be more calamitous for the region than the world imagines O n Saturday, Houthi rebels launched a shocking and deadly attack on Saudi Arabia’s capital city, Riyadh. At the time of writing, the missile strike on King Khalid international airport has killed at least 13 people and left 300 injured, marking a significant turn in a regional conflagration that is only getting more intense. It was the single most deadly attack on any Gulf country since the US and Israel launched their war on Iran in February. In Saudi Arabia, a country that is unaccustomed to such fatalities, the death toll is bewilderingly high and likely to prompt a bloody response. Over the past year, the Gulf has entered a new era of instability that is not temporary and cannot be reversed. This may feel like an overstatement – casualties have been relatively low, after all, compared with Gaza and Iran – but the gradual erosion of peace and security in places such as Saudi Arabia , Qatar and the UAE has changed the region more dramatically than its leaders would like to acknowledge. The first audacious and unthinkable thing happened just over a year ago, when Iran fired missiles at an airbase in Qatar that hosts American troops, in retaliation for US strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities. Lighting up Doha’s skies and scattering shrapnel, it was a dismaying moment for the Qataris, who have tried to maintain good relations with Iran. But even then there was a degree of warning and coordination that signalled this was a face-saving measure on the part of the Iranians. Yet later in 2025, with no similar warning or choreography, Israel struck Doha , targeting Hamas members and killing five Palestinians and one Qatari. That was the beginning of the end of a longstanding norm and expectation – that there was a sanctity to Gulf lives and sovereignty, one secured by the management of the relationship with Iran and alliances with the US. Then came Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu’s war on Iran , which drew the Gulf once and for all into the fray. In retaliation for what Iran perceives to be political, military and logistical support for the offensive against it, Tehran struck Saudi Arabia, Qatar, the UAE, Bahrain, Kuwait and Oman. Iran targeted military sites, energy facilities, desalination plants – an entire infrastructure that underpins the economies of these countries. Much damage was inflicted by the suspension of normal life, the shuttering of schools for months, the closure of airports and airspace. The most disastrous consequence of all, from the perspective of Gulf rulers, has been the way the attacks have disrupted the integration of these countries into the cosmopolitan international community as places for tourism, entrepreneurs, sports and entertainment. They spent billions in securing Formula One , golf and boxing franchises and tournaments, only for a flurry of cheap drones to put it all at risk. The result is a fractious unravelling that has reactivated hostilities that had laid dormant. Yemen’s civil war began in 2014 when Iran-backed Houthi rebels, in aspiration to greater autonomy in the minority Shia homelands, took over the capital city, Sana’a . In 2015, a coalition of countries led by Saudi Arabia led a brutal campaign to dislodge the Houthis from territories they had gained, intensifying a grinding civil war that killed hundreds of thousands and triggered a humanitarian catastrophe . The war deescalated in 2022 with a de facto but unformalised division of the country between the Houthis and an internationally recognised, Saudi-backed government; the ceasefire was followed by rapprochement between Saudi Arabia and Iran. But the 2026 war against Iran opened up strategic opportunities and stirred political loyalties, triggering a surge of Houthi advancement in Yemen. The closure of the strait of Hormuz, for example, shifted more commercial traffic along Yemen’s coastline, prompting the Houthis to make advances and seize territory in order to gain control of the now crucial Bab al-Mandab strait in the Red Sea. Tensions came to a head five months after the start of the war, with Saudi Arabia escalating strikes against the Houthis, and the Saudi-backed government bombing its own airport in Sana’a to prevent an Iranian plane from landing. These developments are not just the result of a mischievous group seizing the moment, acting as spoiler in a bigger contest between Iran and the west. The Houthis are backed by Iran, but they are not empty proxies for Iran; they have domestic ambitions and sharp regional animosities, particularly against the House of Saud, which they see an imperious and arrogant master to whom they shall never submit.

events.title: Drivers forced to use parking apps can pay up to 40% more
events.summary: Council car parks have switched away from ticket machines to cut costs, leading to extra fees for users Drivers are unwittingly paying up to 40% more to park as more councils switch to app-only payments and force customers to pick up the tab. Many councils across England have removed pay and display machines and replaced them with app payments, including a number in London. Most local authorities encourage drivers to pay by app to beat queues, while apps are often the only way to pay when ticket machines are out of order. However, many car park signs fail to mention that app payments may incur an additional service fee. Parking apps save councils money by removing the cost of installing and maintaining ticket machines, but while a few pay the app providers directly for their services, many leave drivers to foot some or all of the bill through “convenience fees” or “service fees”. These typically range from 10p to 30p, but they are not included in the advertised parking tariffs in car parks, even when an app is the only payment option, and they are often not strongly flagged within the apps. Of the parking apps tested by the Guardian, none clearly displayed the service fee until the payment stage, and even then, some required customers to click on an information symbol to find out why the price had increased. These surcharges can push up the cost of an hour’s parking slot dramatically. In Harrogate, North Yorkshire, drivers who park in the town centre and pay by app are hit with a mandatory 30p service charge – a 38% rise on an 80p tariff. Meanwhile, the price of two hours at the council’s Christleton Road car park in Chester soars by 40% when the 20p convenience fee is added to the 50p tariff. Extra fees are added if drivers agree to receive booking confirmation and expiry alerts. They are typically between 10 and 30p per text. According to the Advertising Standards Authority, quoted prices must include all mandatory fees for a contract to be valid. Drivers enter a contract with a council as soon as they accept the car park’s terms and conditions and park their vehicle. However, few realise that they enter a separate contract with the app provider if they choose to pay online. App fees, therefore, may not legally have to be displayed on parking council signs. Because service fees are agreed between local authorities and individual app providers, and since they can vary depending on location, drivers have no way of predicting what they will be charged. The Guardian tested the apps by booking an hour’s parking at car parks around the country. RingGo’s convenience fee added an extra 20p to the £2 tariff at Kings Yard in Lancaster. Drivers have to click on a small “see prices” link above the prominent “Next” button when they have chosen their location to see the charge. It is mentioned again on the payment page, but only when the “i” symbol beside the final price is clicked. PayByPhone charged a 15p service fee on top of the £5.10 parking tariff at Dudley Street car park in Birmingham. The existence of the charge was not explained until the payment page and was hidden behind the Apple Pay button. Customers have to scroll down to the end of the page to see it. Customers using JustPark have to click on a tiny pale grey “i” symbol beside the final price at the end of the booking process to discover its transaction fee. This added 12p to a £3.50 parking charge at Charmouth Road car park in Lyme Regis, Dorset. MiPermit listed its 10p convenience fee above the final price at the end of the booking. This was levied on top of the £1.90 parking charge in Littlehampton, West Sussex. RingGo said the fee funded the service it provided and that it was up to the councils it worked with whether or not to display it on car park signs. “In line with existing regulations, wherever pricing information is shown in the RingGo app, we also display any additional fees,” said Adam Dolphin at its parent company Arrive. JustPark said mandatory fees were included in the price quoted during payment. “Nothing is added at the payment stage,” said a spokesperson. “The ‘i’ icon simply shows how that all-in price is made up, for drivers who want the detail.” PayByPhone said its pricing was transparent. “The pricing elements related to parking, SMS options and service fees are presented before payment confirmation,” said a spokesperson. “Applicable pricing information – whether fees, parking rates or options – is available on the website and in the app.” MiPermit was contacted for a comment. The Local Government Association, which represents councils, said it was up to app providers to ensure their fees were clear and upfront. The Department for Transport said parking tariffs and surcharges were a matter for councils. “Drivers should be able to see clearly what they will be charged before they pay for parking,” a spokesperson said.

events.title: Father was asked for DNA test to get a passport for his daughter
events.summary: New post-Brexit rules mean that dual nationals cannot enter the UK unless they have a British passport My teenage daughter is unable to see her grandparents because of the UK’s new requirement for dual nationals to hold a UK passport. I’m a UK citizen, married to a French national, and we live in France. Our two older children have both French and UK passports. Our third child was born while we were living in Zimbabwe and only has a French passport. I began her application for a British passport in February. I had to submit photos of my wife when pregnant, family photos from the birth to the present day, hospital records and official translations of French marriage and birth certificates. During an official interview I was asked about my job, commute and the layout of my house, but very little about my relationship with my daughter. I was then told that there was insufficient evidence to prove my paternity and was invited to consider a DNA test, which will cost £600 and take yet more time. We need to visit my elderly father who is unwell in the UK but cannot risk it in case our daughter is denied boarding. Your daughter is a victim of new rules that came into force in February and effectively deny entry to the UK to dual national Britons who do not have a British passport. Foreign nationals can enter freely on passports issued by their country of residence, but expats cannot unless they stump up £589 for a certificate of entitlement. The law has caused chaos, with children being stranded abroad or arbitrarily denied a passport granted to their siblings. Since the UK government is not accepting that your daughter is a UK national, you asked if she could travel on her French passport. No one could answer the question. As a result, you face Christmas apart from your parents. Home Office rules state that officials must consider a passport application on the “balance of probability” if an applicant refuses a DNA test. They must also explain why an application is refused. You have never been told why your copious proofs of paternity have been deemed inadequate. The Home Office will not comment on individual cases, but it did tell me that additional evidence, such as the layout of a home, may be requested to add “credible authenticity”. Soon afterwards, you were informed that the application had been accepted after all, despite no new paperwork having been sought since April. I can only assume that press scrutiny prompted the realisation that your domestic floorplan is credibly authentic. We welcome letters but cannot answer individually. Email us at consumer.champions@theguardian.com or write to Consumer Champions, Money, the Guardian, 90 York Way, London N1 9GU. Please include a daytime phone number. events.title: The small business drama involving Kelly Clarkson, a Brooklyn toy store, and an animatronic bird
events.summary: Kelly Clarkson said she was treated like Julia Roberts' character in the '90s rom-com "Pretty Woman" when she visited a Brooklyn toy shop. Weiss Eubanks/NBCUniversal via Getty Images Kelly Clarkson said a Brooklyn toy shop gave her the "Pretty Woman" treatment. Here's how the dispute between Clarkson and the store unfolded. A publicist said a celebrity pile-on can hurt a small business before people know the full story. A Brooklyn toy shop has found itself at the center of a celebrity internet drama after Kelly Clarkson said she received the " Pretty Woman " treatment when she inquired about a $15,000 item in the store. In an X post on Saturday, the singer said she had a negative experience at Art of Play, a toy store in New York City . "Just drove all the way to Brooklyn to check out this store I thought looked really rad and had a few things in mind to buy and literally was looked at as if I couldn't afford it and was told he could find something comparable for me," Clarkson wrote in her post, adding that the store "just lost a huge sale." Just drove all the way to Brooklyn to check out this store I thought looked really rad and had a few things in mind to buy and literally was looked at as if I couldn’t afford it and was told he could find something comparable for me. Wow, dude. You’re an idiot and just lost a huge sale. But y’all should go check out Art of Play in Brooklyn if you enjoy being treated like Julia Roberts character in Pretty Woman. For sure, check it out 👎 — Kelly Clarkson (@kellyclarkson) October 10, 2026 She then compared her experience to the treatment Julia Roberts' character receives in the '90s rom-com "Pretty Woman," telling people to visit the store if they enjoyed being treated that way. Clarkson's post on X had received more than 39.4 million views and over 261,000 likes as of Sunday evening. As her post gained traction, Art of Play responded on Instagram the next day with its own account of the interaction, saying the toy Clarkson had inquired about was a bird automaton that's "permanently attached to the wall and isn't for sale." The store said it understood why Clarkson's account "would resonate with anyone who has ever felt judged in a shop," but said that it welcomed visitors equally, whether they came to browse or buy. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Art of Play (@artofplay) "Imagine our surprise when our small local business was suddenly attacked by 8 million people who have never visited our store. It's been a surreal experience to be the focus of such widespread outrage after just one mention by a celebrity," the store said in a statement on Instagram. The store then thanked its supporters and said it planned to keep a low profile, while hoping to "clear things up" with Clarkson one day. The public exchange did not end there. On Instagram Stories and on X, Clarkson countered Art of Play's account, sharing a photo she said showed the bird's $15,000 price tag, along with additional details about her conversation with a staff member. "Cool, cool. Sure, it wasn't for sale. That's the narrative Art of Play is gonna go with," Clarkson wrote on Sunday. She said the staff member "elevator eyed her" and told her "in a condescending tone" that the item was for sale but cost $15,000, before offering to find her a "comparable" alternative. Cool, cool. Sure, it wasn’t for sale. That’s the narrative Art of Play is gonna go with 👍 so the whole conversation we had when I asked you if it was for sale whilst pointing to the price tag hanging on the wall with the title Singing Bird didn’t happen as you elevator eyed me saying in a condescending tone “yes, it’s for sale but it costs 15,000 dollars so if you’d like me to find something comparable for you I can.” That all never happened and now it’s not for sale. Okay, cool. So you’re not only rude, you’re also a liar. Got it ✅ And by the way, I obviously support small businesses because I was literally at a small business trying to purchase things. I love small businesses and know they are important and I always support them, but you don’t get a free pass to treat people less than in your store just because you are a small business. It’s not that hard to be kind. I never blast people but you my friend were an exception. Your store is really cool. Unfortunately, you aren’t. — Kelly Clarkson (@kellyclarkson) October 11, 2026 "That all never happened and now it's not for sale. Okay, cool. So you're not only rude, you're also a liar. Got it," Clarkson said in her post. On Sunday night, Art of Play issued another Instagram statement saying that although the toy Clarkson inquired about was permanently attached to its wall, the creator of the automaton owned a nearly identical bird and was willing to sell it for $15,000. The store said it had explained this distinction to Clarkson and had also offered to show her a different, German-made singing-bird automaton priced at about $2,000, although she "did not stick around long enough to see it." It said it had contacted Clarkson directly in an effort to "clear the air." View this post on Instagram A post shared by Art of Play (@artofplay) Clarkson and Art of Play did not immediately respond to Business Insider's requests for comment, which were made outside regular business hours. The internet weighed in The public back-and-forth also appeared to prompt a bout of review bombing on Art of Play's review pages. When Business Insider first checked the store's Google Reviews at around 9 p.m. ET on Sunday, it had a 4.7-star rating based on 273 reviews, including several recent one-star complaints that appeared to be connected to the store's ongoing public dispute with Clarkson. About three hours later, the store's Google Reviews showed a 5-star rating based on 253 reviews. The recent negative reviews Business Insider had viewed earlier were no longer visible. Google did not immediately respond to questions about whether it had removed reviews connected to the incident or taken other action on the listing. On Yelp, Art of Play had a 2.4-star rating based on 154 reviews when Business Insider checked the page at 12:17 a.m. ET on Monday, with recent posts reflecting a polarized response to the dispute. Some criticized the store, referencing Clarkson and "Pretty Woman," while others defended it, citing their own positive experiences. Several reviewers also acknowledged that people were weighing in despite not having visited Art of Play, with one calling on the public to stop attacking a small shop over a celebrity's complaint. Yelp did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Business Insider. Business Insider could not independently verify whether the recent reviewers had visited the store. The risks of taking a dispute online Danny Deraney, founder of LA-based Deraney Public Relations, said he doesn't believe there will be a winning side in the dispute. events.title: IFS: budget will be ‘work of fiction’ without clear plan to cover UK’s £35bn spending pressures
events.summary: Thinktank’s influential pre-budget report urges key decisions to be made now and not put off until next year John Healey has been warned by Britain’s leading tax and spending experts that his budget risks being a “work of fiction” unless he sets out plans to cover £35bn in spending pressures. As the war in the Middle East rattles the public finances, the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said the damage from higher inflation meant the chancellor would need to either top up funds for his current government spending plans or impose deep real-terms cuts by the end of the decade. Against a febrile backdrop in the bond market, the thinktank warned Healey that failure to address the issue at his 28 October budget risked leaving the impression that Labour was setting unrealistic spending plans. Helen Miller, the director of the IFS, said: “Simply pencilling in implicit cuts that he has no intention of delivering would make the budget a work of fiction.” Her comment echoes a criticism levelled at Jeremy Hunt , the former Conservative chancellor, who before the 2024 general election was accused by the then head of the Office for Budget Responsibility of setting unrealistic spending plans. Publishing its influential “green budget” report, which analyses the public finances before Healey’s speech to the Commons, it called on the chancellor to avoid announcing a “steady as she goes” budget that delayed decisions until next year’s spending review. “If John Healey sets out spending envelopes for public services that he would not be willing to live within, his plan for meeting the fiscal rules will not be credible,” it said. Last week, the governor of the Bank of England, Andrew Bailey, said fiscal policy “must be credible and be seen as such by financial markets”. The following day, the Times quoted a government source as saying: “Andrew Bailey needs to focus on doing his job.” Miller said the Treasury adopting an assumption that “everything can be kicked forward” to next year’s spending review risked undermining the chancellor’s credibility. “We would be better served by a chancellor who hopes for the best, but plans for the worst, rather than sets out plans that either say, ‘I hope it’ll be fine and some money will come in’, or ‘I’ll get a plan in a year’s time’.” Attention before the budget has largely focused on the hit to the chancellor’s headroom against Labour’s main fiscal rule to balance day-to-day public spending with revenues in 2029-30. With the war in the Middle East fuelling a dramatic sell-off in the market for government debt, higher borrowing costs are expected to erase a significant chunk of the £24bn buffer left by the former chancellor Rachel Reeves at the spring statement. Leading economists have predicted the market moves since the start of the war in February could wipe out about half of the headroom, adding to nerves in the Treasury over the risk of a market backlash. The IFS said that although the surge in debt interest costs could add £10bn to borrowing in 2029-30, the exchequer would benefit from higher inflation boosting tax revenue – meaning Healey could see headroom cut by only £4bn. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning However, it warned against focusing on this buffer because the inflation shock rippling from the Middle East would also dramatically hit the government’s plan for funding public services. Higher inflation squeezes public spending power, forcing the government to choose between accepting real-term cuts and finding efficiency savings or topping up departmental budgets either by raising taxes or allowing an increase in borrowing. The IFS said a choice to leave spending totals unchanged at the budget would implicitly mean allowing the quality or quantity of public services to fall. However, it said compensating for the inflation shock, and funding Healey’s pledge to raise defence spending to 3% of GDP by 2030, would require tax rises or benefit cuts of about £35bn. “Choosing to stay the course with the inherited tax and spending plans would mean allowing inflation to blow departments’ spending plans off course,” Miller said. “It would be a choice to tolerate chunky cuts to the quantity or quality of some public services – cuts that would be larger if defence spending was increased within existing totals.” She said Healey would not need to make detailed plans for the next spending review period at the budget but merely set out overall spending envelopes that he would be prepared to live within. A spokesperson for the Treasury said: “The chancellor is fully focused on his priorities to boost business, help with the cost of living and support people in every postcode, underpinned by fiscal discipline and a commitment to meet the fiscal rules with a buffer against uncertainty.

events.title: Why some have no choice but to pay costly oil prices
events.summary: Many heating oil customers are having to buy early in preparation for the colder months As the temperature drops, some of us will start putting the heating on but for the one-and-a-half million people across the UK that are not on the mains gas network - and who are relying instead on heating oil - that decision may give them pause. The vast majority of those people live in rural locations. The heating oil market is unregulated, unlike gas and electricity, so any changes in the global price quickly gets passed on to customers . Tensions in the Middle East and the ongoing war in Ukraine are two issues currently both affecting supply which is causing prices to rise. Author shares how books have 'magical way' of reaching you when struggling Published 1 day ago Accessible playground to 'allow all children to play' Published 23 hours ago 'What terminal cancer has taught me about life' Published 2 days ago Until March this year, the price was quite stable at about 60p per litre (ppl) but when the war in Iran started in March, it jumped to a high of 134ppl . After a dip in the past few months, it is rising once again and it currently stands at 111ppl, according to price comparison site Boiler Juice. The BBC has spoken to a number of business and homeowners across the West about how that rise is affecting them. Peter Mason lives in Minety, in north Wiltshire, where most homes rely on heating oil. "I'm getting toward the end of the tank and need to top up for winter... it will be over £550," he said. Mason said that last year "it was about £300 to fill up - it is horrendous". He said: "The price goes up and down. It can vary plus or minus £50 but it has never been as high as it is today. "It means I'll have to eek out what I spent my money on. I'm retired, its not like I can change jobs. "I have to be really careful and pull money out of savings." Most tanks hold 500 litres of oil and would cost about £550 to fill currently Dylan Williams owns van-driving business Van & I of Monmouth, Wales and regularly operates in the Forest of Dean, Stroud and South Gloucestershire. events.title: Documents falsified to evade tax on Abramovich's wealth, BBC finds
events.summary: Watch: The documents that were falsified to allow Roman Abramovich to evade tax The world's biggest accountancy firm helped in falsifying documents to hide Roman Abramovich's wealth and evade tax, BBC Panorama has found. Accounts signed off by Deloitte in Cyprus meant assets such as superyachts, mansions and private jets worth $672m (£508m) vanished from Abramovich's company accounts. Deloitte also appears to have advised on a scheme to evade a huge tax bill on the oligarch's wealth through the falsification of documents. Barrister Andrew Mitchell KC, an expert in financial services law, said Panorama's evidence showed the scheme was "straightforward" tax evasion and "it couldn't be more blatant". Roman Abramovich's lawyers said he denies that he evaded tax or concealed his fortune. They said Panorama provided no evidence he knew about, authorised or directed the falsification of any document and said it was legitimate to rely on advice from professionals. Deloitte Cyprus said it "acts in compliance with applicable laws". The findings are being revealed following a joint investigation between BBC Panorama and the Bureau of Investigative Journalism. For nearly two decades, Roman Abramovich was the most famous Russian oligarch in the UK, welcomed in London where he bought Chelsea Football Club in 2003 and bankrolled the club's most successful period. But after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, he was sanctioned by the UK government as an associate of President Vladimir Putin and forced to sell the club. Abramovich has been reported to be living in Turkey, a safe haven for him because it did not apply sanctions. In the Channel Island of Jersey, £5.4bn of his assets remain frozen and a criminal investigation has been going on for four years. The oligarch's lawyers told the BBC he denies the allegations in the Jersey investigation and says it was "undertaken for political purposes". Our investigation has uncovered new evidence about the way Abramovich's business empire has been run. It also raises serious questions about the integrity of some of his professional advisers. Chateau de la Croe (top left) in the south of France, Fyning Hill in Sussex and two superyachts vanished from company accounts The evidence is contained in a leak that includes thousands of documents about the oligarch's finances and the operations of a network of offshore companies administered from Cyprus - which used to be a tax haven popular with Russians - between 1995 and 2022. The BBC and media partners including the Guardian, Paper Trail Media, the Organised Crime and Corruption Reporting Project, and the Cyprus Investigative Reporting Network - as well as the Bureau of Investigative Journalism , external - have been reporting on the leaked files since 2023 as part of the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists' Cyprus Confidential , external investigation. In 2022, Panorama also reported on how Abramovich had made his fortune from a corrupt deal to buy a Russian state-owned oil company in the 1990s, selling it back to the government a decade later for billions in profit. He has previously said allegations of corruption in the deal are false. The profits from Abramovich's oil deals in Russia were funnelled into a web of offshore companies. They were administered from Cyprus by a corporate services firm called MeritServus, in Limassol, the island's second-largest city. Until 2005, Deloitte - now the biggest of the "big four" firms which dominate the accounting industry - owned MeritServus. After they split, the two companies worked closely together with Abramovich's associates to manage his global fortune. The leaked documents from MeritServus reveal some of their practices. Panorama - Roman Abramovich: How He Hid His Fortune He was the Russian oligarch who brought his wealth to the UK. But what’s the truth about Roman Abramovich’s fortune? Panorama investigates the documents that were falsified to hide his wealth and evade tax. Watch now on BBC iPlayer or on BBC One at 20:00 BST on Monday 12 October. Our first example of backdated paperwork comes in 2006, after a new law in Cyprus meant that company accounts had to be made public. The new transparency law threatened to expose the secrets of Abramovich's vast wealth. Deloitte Cyprus had prepared draft accounts for 2003 - but had not yet finalised them - for his Cypriot company Amiscan Investments. The accounts detailed $672m of luxury property. A mansion in West Sussex, a luxury flat in London and an estate in the south of France were all included - plus helicopters, private jets and a small fleet of boats the oligarch owned at the time, including the $147.5m Pelorus. Deloitte in Cyprus appears to have advised Abramovich's company on a scheme to evade tax To keep them secret, Abramovich's associates and Meritservus decided to rewrite history.

events.title: Roman Abramovich aides falsified paperwork to disguise assets and dodge tax, records suggest
events.summary: Accountancy firm Deloitte Cyprus among those that appear to have backdated records outlining the Russian billionaire’s assets A ides of Roman Abramovich – including staff at the global accountancy firm Deloitte – falsified paperwork mapping the oligarch’s sprawling offshore business empire, records suggest, helping his businesses dodge tax and disguise assets. New analysis of leaked corporate records uncovers what appears to have been a long-running and carefully orchestrated strategy of backdating documents. The Russian billionaire’s closest aide, London-based Eugene Tenenbaum, appears to have been involved in the backdating and may also have given false evidence to the UK high court during a potentially costly lawsuit, the papers indicate. Abramovich’s personal and financial affairs are now restricted, owing to sanctions imposed by the UK and EU in response to Russia’s war on Ukraine. But the documents raise questions about how Abramovich was able to shield his financial affairs from the authorities for more than a decade, with the apparent assistance of apparatchiks and blue-chip advisers. The findings are based on the Cyprus Confidential leak , more than 500,000 documents, first released to the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists (ICIJ) and analysed by organisations including the Guardian, the Bureau of Investigative Journalism and the BBC. The digital paper trail charts the reorganisation of billions of pounds that the former Chelsea FC owner obtained via the controversial acquisition of oilfields in the frozen wastes of Siberia, amid the break-up of the Soviet Union. From 1999 until at least 2013, a cadre of aides and accountants tasked with shifting the funds between offshore jurisdictions deployed tactics that experts say may have constituted fraud and tax evasion. This, it seems, involved backdating documents to create a convenient paper trail showing that agreements and transactions had taken place years earlier. Lawyers for Abramovich denied any wrongdoing and said he relied on the advice of his advisers and Deloitte Cyprus. Tenenbaum denied any wrongdoing and said he also relied on the specialist advice given by Deloitte Cyprus. Deloitte Cyprus said that it “acts in compliance with all applicable laws” and that it could no longer access the relevant material because of the time that has elapsed. A crown jewel in Russia’s rich seam of natural resources, Sibneft’s oilfields fell into Abramovich’s hands during the chaotic post-Soviet privatisation era. The famously shrewd entrepreneur obtained the business for roughly $250m, reportedly spending as little as $19m of his own money. By the time he sold the last of his shares to Gazprom in 2005, Abramovich had raised $16bn, money he ploughed into investments, mansions, superyachts and Chelsea FC. One Cyprus-based company, Kravin Investments, was among several early vehicles through which that cash flowed. Kravin received a $3bn windfall in May 2003, of which it retained about $2bn. The money sat in Kravin’s bank account or was loaned to other companies, accruing interest that was, in theory, taxable in Cyprus. But Abramovich’s aides soon began devising plans to “eliminate” a tax liability that one financial adviser warned could be “very large”, records suggest. The gatekeeper to Abramovich’s fortune was Demetris Ioannides, who was the chair of Deloitte Cyprus before spinning out his own business Meritservus. That firm became Abramovich’s go-to financial advisory, serving him for nearly 20 years, before it was sanctioned by the UK in 2023 , along with Ioannides, for its role helping Russian oligarch hide their wealth. “It will be necessary to change the [Kravin’s] financial statements and the accounting records accordingly for 2003 and 2004,” Ioannides wrote in an August 2005 email, citing discussions with Deloitte Cyprus partners and erstwhile colleagues Antonis Taliotis and Nicos Charalambous. The following month, in an email copying in staff at Meritservus and Abramovich’s investment vehicle, Millhouse, Taliotis appeared to agree. “Certain changes will have to be made to the accounts […]” he wrote. Millhouse and Meritservus duly began producing paperwork showing that Kravin was simply holding and investing the Sibneft billions as a trustee for another business, the British Virgin Islands-based Kelvedon Worldwide. Documents detailing this supposed fact, including correspondence and trust agreements, were given dates between March and December 2003, despite being created at least two years later. The result was simple: although the billions had sat in Kravin’s accounts for years, it now appeared that the money had never really been Kravin’s at all. Deloitte Cyprus, apparently aware of the deception, duly signed off the accounts. History had effectively been rewritten, analysis of the documents suggests, disappearing $2bn from Kravin’s balance sheet – and with it any tax liability.

events.title: Job losses likely at remote island mine as costs nearly double due to flooding
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Redundancies likely at South 32's Groote Eylandt mine The Groote Eylandt Mining Company mine has begun redundancy consultations with staff. ( ABC News: Jano Gibson ) South 32 is likely to make redundancies at its manganese mine on Groote Eylandt in the Northern Territory. The company is looking to cut $129 million from the business and spend about $100 million on new water infrastructure. The company says it will make changes to strengthen its long-term viability. Job losses are likely at South 32's manganese mine on Groote Eylandt in the Northern Territory as the operation battles years of flooding impacts and skyrocketing production costs. The Groote Eylandt Mining Company (GEMCO) mine has begun consultations with staff. The ABC understands it needs to cut $129 million from the business in response to costs increasing by more than 80 per cent in recent years. The island and mine site were hit hard by Tropical Cyclone Megan in March 2024, but it is understood multiple wet seasons and persistent seepage of groundwater into the pits are also responsible. Mining pits on Groote Eylandt filled with water after Cyclone Megan in 2024. ( Supplied ) A South32 spokesperson said in a statement the company would make changes to strengthen its long-term viability and was speaking to workers. "GEMCO has completed an internal review in response to a more challenging operating environment and increased cost pressures, and has begun implementing changes designed to strengthen the long-term sustainability of the business," the spokesperson said. "The review forms part of a program focused on improving structures, systems and processes and ensuring GEMCO is well positioned to operate successfully into the future. As part of this work, GEMCO has reviewed its workforce requirements and commenced consultation with employees and contractors who will potentially be impacted. Officials from two separate unions representing workers at GEMCO told the ABC they believed office staff would likely be the target of redundancies . A spokesperson for the NT branch of the Construction, Forestry and Maritime Employees Union said it was closely monitoring the situation to see if blue-collar workers were affected. Union officials were told South 32 management would provide staff with more information about the redundancies by the end of the week. According to GEMCO's enterprise bargaining agreement, the company must consult with workers before making any significant organisational changes. The bargaining agreement is due to expire at the end of 2027. The MV Anikitos was loaded with 41,000 tonnes of manganese ore when it crashed into a loading wharf on Groote Eylandt. ( Supplied ) The island's wharf was destroyed in 2024 when Tropical Cyclone Megan pushed a loaded bulk carrier into the structure during high tides . Heavy rainfall damaged the mine's pits, a critical bridge and several roads. Exports from the island did not restart until 2025. Mining is expected to conclude on the island within the next 10 years, according to the local Aboriginal land council. events.title: Sheng Siong shares fall 3% after Maybank downgrade, target price cut
events.summary: The research house also lowered its forecast for new Sheng Siong stores in 2028 from five to four. Maybank downgraded Sheng Siong to “hold” and cut its target price to $3.12, sending the shares down as much as 3% on Oct 12. The broker said Sheng Siong is now one of the region’s “most expensive food retailers” after a strong rerating, even with 8% NPAT CAGR to 2028 and a 2.5% dividend yield. Maybank also trimmed profit forecasts and warned that vouchers, competition, RTS-linked shopping and online grocery growth could weaken Sheng Siong’s future growth. SINGAPORE – Shares of Sheng Siong fell as much as 3% on Oct 12 after Maybank downgraded the supermarket chain to “hold” from “buy” and cut its target price. The counter fell as low as $2.83 in early trade on Oct 12, but pared some losses to be 1.7% down at $2.87 as at 10.10am. On Oct 9, it was the biggest decliner on the Singapore Exchange, having fallen 5.5%. The decline followed Maybank cutting Sheng Siong’s target price from $3.22 to $3.12 on Oct 9. This was due to a narrower upside that makes the supermarket chain one of the region’s “most expensive food retailers” at a forward price-to-earnings ratio of 28.4 times. This is despite a net profit after tax (NPAT) compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 8% through 2028 and a 2.5% dividend yield. Maybank analyst Hussaini Saifee said: “Within the consumer space, we prefer Food Empire, supported by its strong NPAT growth (31% CAGR), moderate valuations and 5% dividend yield.” The research house also lowered its forecast for new Sheng Siong stores in 2028 from five to four and reduced financial year 2026-2028 net profit after tax by a range of 1% to 3%. “Sheng Siong remains a high-quality operator, but its strong share price re-rating now prices in much of it,” said Saifee. “With growth normalising and slight headwinds emerging, we see limited scope for further re-rating.” While Sheng Siong has benefited from “resilient consumption”, market share gains and targeted vouchers that channelled spending directly to supermarkets, such tailwinds are weakening. Maybank said that more assistance is being provided through unrestricted goods and services tax vouchers and cash payments. The $500 tranche of CDC vouchers, originally scheduled for January 2027, was brought forward to June 2026, boosting financial year 2026 demand but raising the comparison base for FY2027. With supermarket growth already easing to low single digits, the research house expects Sheng Siong’s growth to track underlying income and population trends, rather than benefit from a repeat of the unusually favourable conditions of recent years. Sheng Siong’s capture of displaced demand from store closures at Giant and Cold Storage has also petered out, as the two competing chains have closed only one store between them. Cold Storage’s new owner, Macrovalue, which bought both chains from DFI Retail Group in 2025, has “resumed expansion” through its On The Go convenience stores. It will be rolled out progressively to all 58 Esso petrol stations across Singapore through 2026 and targets more than 100 outlets over time. Saifee said: “Although the convenience-led format does not directly replicate Sheng Siong’s full-basket proposition, it adds competition for top-up grocery purchases, convenience items and ready-to-eat meals.” Separately, Johor Bahru-Singapore Rapid Transit System (RTS)-linked cross-border shopping and the gradual evolution of online grocery fulfilment could also pose headwinds for Sheng Siong. The supermarket chain appears more exposed to northern Singapore catchments than its larger competitors. About 10% of its network – nine stores – is within 5km of the RTS station, while about 27.5% – 25 stores – is within 15km. “While neither appears disruptive enough to reshape the industry in the near term, both point to a less favourable backdrop than in recent years,” said the analyst. events.title: TikTok CEO sees major scientific breakthroughs from AI within three years
events.summary: TikTok CEO Shou Zi Chew expects artificial intelligence to drive major scientific breakthroughs within the next three years. Chew said rapid advances in AI were opening up possibilities far beyond the technology's current applications. SINGAPORE — TikTok CEO Shou Zi Chew expects artificial intelligence to drive major scientific breakthroughs within the next three years, transforming a broad range of sectors. "In the next two to three years, we're going to have a real scientific breakthrough: physics, biotech, chemistry, material science, because of AI. It's very, very, very possible," Chew said at the DBS Asia Future Forward Conference in Singapore on Monday. Chew's remarks come as ByteDance, TikTok's Chinese parent, expands its artificial intelligence research beyond consumer applications. In April, the company's Seed research team unveiled Protenix-v2 , an AI model focused on biomolecular structure prediction and design, with potential applications in drug discovery. Chew said rapid advances in AI were opening up possibilities far beyond the technology's current applications, even as questions remain over how to ensure increasingly powerful systems operate within human ethical boundaries. "If that happens, then you know the question would be: how do you align the models? How do you align the machines to be doing things that are obvious to us as human beings?" he said. Chew highlighted the accelerating pace of technological development, particularly in scientific research, arguing that the longer-term implications of AI could be far greater than currently anticipated. "The trend is very very clear. It's that we are only at the beginning of what artificial intelligence can probably do," he said. "And if you look at where the trend is, [where] the progress is, particularly in areas of science, it's really trending on a very steep curve at this moment in time." Chew explained that while the technology's immediate impact could be overstated, its longer-term potential remained underappreciated. "I think in the short term we are probably overestimating it, but in the long term we are probably underestimating it," he said. His optimism comes at a time when technology giants have been pouring billions of dollars into AI-powered scientific research. Last week, the U.S. government, Meta and Google announced their participation in a $1.8 billion initiative to develop AI models capable of predicting how cells behave, in an effort to accelerate biological research and drug discovery. TikTok's parent company, ByteDance, is also developing its own AI models and exploring opportunities to collaborate with scientists on research. "There's an effort to see how we can collaborate with a lot of scientists to make some progress in science as well," Chew added. "There's been some work that we've done in this area, and it is very exciting." He described scientific discovery as one of the most promising applications of AI, even as the technology increasingly reshapes TikTok's operations, from content creation and recommendations to search and moderation. Chew cautioned that AI's growing capabilities would require stronger safeguards, particularly as autonomous systems become more widely adopted. "I think the cybersecurity risks are quite big," he said, warning that users may grant AI agents extensive permissions without fully understanding the potential consequences. He pointed to the risks of allowing AI agents to make purchases autonomously, saying the systems could end up buying more than users intended in their eagerness to complete a task. Chew also highlighted the growing cybersecurity challenges facing companies, as increasingly sophisticated AI models make it significantly cheaper for malicious actors to carry out fraudulent activities. "So you need the right tools to now you know defend against the fast falling cost of creating problems for platforms like us, security problems for us," he emphasized.

events.title: Kaniva wants to be known as an EV charging hub
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Tesla applies to nearly double the number of chargers in Kaniva Kaniva could soon become one of the biggest EV charging sites in Australia. ( Supplied: Bale Farming ) Tesla hopes to nearly double the number of fast chargers it has in the country town of Kaniva from 10 to 18. Experts say more investment is required to ensure EV charging infrastructure keeps up with vehicle sales. Residents have until next Monday to object to the company's plans. On a long stretch of highway roughly halfway between Melbourne and Adelaide is a farming town hoping to cement its reputation as an electric vehicle (EV) charging must-see. The western Victorian farming town of Kaniva, with a population of roughly 800 people, already has 10 Tesla Superchargers behind its quaint country pub. The global tech giant has submitted plans to the local council to install another eight, and publican Bob Cane couldn't be happier. Kaniva is home to 10 EV charging sites, with plans to install another eight. ( ABC News: Nethma Dandeniya ) "It's about bringing people to Kaniva, connecting them with a classic, quintessential Australian classic town," Mr Cane said. Painted sheep have adorned the streets of Kaniva since 2012. ( ABC News: Martin Boulton ) Kaniva currently markets itself as the first and last highway town in Victoria, the gateway to the Wimmera Mallee Silo Art Trail and the "home of Sheep Art". Mr Cane said the chargers were invigorating the town and adding another string to its economy. "When they plug in their car, what are they going to do? [They will] go for a walk into town, get a coffee, grab a hamburger," he said. Bob Cane is hoping the new Supercharger stations will be up and running before Christmas. ( ABC News: Nethma Dandeniya ) The Windmill Cafe owner Jemma Hill said the chargers had been a boon for the town. "They [travellers] stop, they come over, they grab their lunch and their coffee, they come into town," she said. "It's creating extra foot traffic within the town, which is fantastic, makes it feel very alive." Jemma Hill says the current EV chargers have helped her business. ( ABC News: Nethma Dandeniya ) The existing chargers are a lifesaver for some travellers already tackling the trek between Melbourne and Adelaide. "We do this trip a few times a year … If we didn't have this, we couldn't get [to Melbourne]," Tom Beresford said. Kaniva is home to about 800 people. ( ABC News: Nethma Dandeniya ) West Wimmera Shire Council deputy mayor Helen Hobbs said the site, which has been open for about nine months, had already made a difference in the town. "That has actually given people like the bakery confidence to invest," Cr Hobbs said. "To have a brand new bakery with seating for 100 people, it's beyond anything I could have imagined." Helen Hobbs says the EV chargers have brought outside investment into the town. ( ABC News: Nethma Dandeniya ) EV sales doubled in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period last year, according to the Electric Vehicle Council of Australia. The council's Aman Gaur attributed the jump to cheaper EVs, rising fuel costs and improved charging networks. "We're now up to 4,200 charging locations across Australia and over 11,000 connectors," Mr Gaur said. "Charging stations have definitely been increasing in Victoria and the number of connectors has also been following suit." Ampol this month paid $225 million to buy Evie, one of the country's largest charging networks. Milad Haghani says if EV demand continues to grow at the same pace, charging infrastructure will have to catch up. ( ABC News: Patrick Stone ) University of Melbourne associate professor of urban resilience and mobility Milad Haghani said charging infrastructure would have a serious job keeping up if the EV sales boom continued. "It's hard to predict whether or not the spike in demand that we have observed this year is going to be sustainable," he said. "But if even a fraction of this demand continues into the future, that means that the infrastructure has some catching up to do." Public chargers have rarely had queues, he said, but that could change as more people buy EVs. The West Wimmera Shire Council has published Tesla's planning application online while it assesses the proposal. The application says the upgrade would cost $250,000 and that the existing 10-stall site, open for about nine months, has exceeded the company's expectations. A traffic report filed with the application says 10 to 20 EVs charge at the site each day, with holidays a natural peak period. Residents have until next Monday to lodge an objection to Tesla's plans.

events.title: NutryFarm shareholders seek CEO’s removal as company pivots from durians to data centres
events.summary: The dispute comes as NutryFarm seeks to rebuild its business and resume trading on the SGX mainboard after more than four years of suspension since April 2022. The dispute adds pressure to NutryFarm as it tries to restart trading on the SGX mainboard after years of suspension. The company says it is reviewing the allegations and seeking legal advice. NutryFarm is shifting from durians to data centres and AI services. Its restructuring could turn creditors into major shareholders, but it may also dilute existing holders and deepen the control fight. SINGAPORE – Shareholders seeking to remove NutryFarm International chief executive Niu Liming have challenged his right to vote on behalf of a major shareholder, complicating matters at the former durian distributor as it tries to rebuild its business around data centres and artificial intelligence services. NutryFarm said on Oct 11 that it had received a letter the previous day objecting to the validity of proxy votes granted by shareholder Jia Lijie to Niu, including any conflict of interest arising from the arrangement. The letter concerns votes that Niu allegedly intends to exercise at a special general meeting. The announcement did not identify the specific meeting. This follows an Oct 9 request from shareholders identifying themselves as Tianci International, Cheng Meng, Lee Bee Li, Lim Hean Nerng, Gao Huazhu, Ang Poh Guan and Wu Jiansheng, who claim to hold at least 10% of NutryFarm’s paid-up capital, to convene a special general meeting. At the meeting, the shareholders want to remove Niu as a director and from his other appointments within the group, elect shareholder Charlie In to the board, and ask directors to consider appointing In as CEO. In, identified as In Nanny (sic) Sing Charlie in the Oct 9 filing, is chairman of corporate advisory firm Raffles Financial Group. His biography lists experience in investments, restructuring, capital raising and helping Chinese companies list overseas. According to media reports, his connection to NutryFarm dates back to March 2021, when Raffles Financial invested $5 million in exchange for 10 million NutryFarm shares through a married deal with a substantial shareholder. Charlie In is chairman of corporate advisory firm Raffles Financial Group. PHOTO: RAFFLES FINANCIAL GROUP LIMITED In a separate demand letter on Oct 9, the same shareholders demanded Niu’s immediate removal from all executive positions and his exclusion from board discussions and voting on the matter. NutryFarm said it was reviewing the allegations in the demand letter, and seeking legal advice on the other two letters. However, its announcement did not detail the allegations or explain the reasons for the removal demand. The dispute comes as NutryFarm seeks to rebuild its business and resume trading on the Singapore Exchange mainboard after trading was suspended more than four years ago in April 2022 . NutryFarm was placed under judicial management in June 2022 and discharged from the arrangement in February 2026, returning control of the company to its board. Its restructuring involves creditors who could become major shareholders by exchanging loans for shares, and lenders with security over its new AI business. According to NutryFarm’s 2024 annual report, Jia held 21.7 million NutryFarm shares, or 15.78%, making her the largest shareholder of the company. Niu directly owned just 360,000 shares, or 0.26%. However, the report lists him as having a deemed interest in Jia’s shares and a further 13.3 million shares belonging to Cheng through a share pledge arrangement. Together with his own shares, these amounted to a 25.72% direct and deemed interest in NutryFarm. Niu’s involvement in NutryFarm began before he became its executive director and CEO. He has an ownership interest in Corpbond IV, the creditor that applied to the High Court to place the company under judicial management in June 2022 . Judicial management puts a distressed company under an appointed manager to try to rescue the business or achieve a better outcome for creditors. According to NutryFarm’s 2022 annual report, Niu was appointed executive director and CEO on Dec 19, 2022, when the company was under judicial management. Niu Liming’s involvement in NutryFarm began before he became its executive director and CEO. At its annual general meeting on Dec 5, 2025, In asked Niu about the difficulties the company faced during judicial management, the prospects of the new AI business and his suitability to continue as executive director. Niu said he had been NutryFarm’s largest creditor when he initiated judicial management over a company with no cash and with difficulties retaining control of overseas subsidiaries. He said he lent the company another $1 million in December 2022 to support operations and cover the judicial manager’s fees. NutryFarm previously operated nutrition and health food businesses and expanded into durian distribution.
