events.title: My cofounder and I were rivals at hackathons. At 21, I've put college on hold to build a startup with him.
events.summary: Raymond Loong Ng put his college plans on hold to build a startup in San Francisco. Provided by Raymond Loong Ng. At 21, Raymond Loong Ng put college on hold after his startup raised $250,000 from VC firm Afore Capital. He and his cofounder spent two months in a program in San Francisco, working on their startup. A subsequent investment brought their total funding to $1 million, and they're now back in Singapore awaiting O-1 visas. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Raymond Loong Ng, 21, the cofounder of Makeable, a San Francisco-based startup. It's been edited for length and clarity. I was born in Vietnam and moved to Singapore when I was 9. As a kid, I always had some kind of side hustle . In school, I sold toys, snacks, in-game currency, and sneakers to my classmates — anything that might earn me a little extra pocket money. When I was 16, I did an internship at an auditing firm, where I had the chance to speak with a lot of business owners. I began to see technology as a tool that could help me advance in the business world. I ended up getting a diploma in applied AI and analytics at a polytechnic after finishing secondary school. I was never the best at math or coding, but it offered me a way to turn my ideas into actual projects. Have you relocated abroad for career opportunities, retirement, or lower living costs? We want to hear from you. Fill out this short form to share your story. I always saw myself as the connector: I could spot a problem, form a vision, attract resources, then bring in my smartest classmates to make things happen. That was how I began building projects of my own. I built an AI tool that helps ex-offenders build résumés and find jobs. I also started a community of young AI builders that runs workshops for students across Singapore. From rivals to cofounders In school, the projects we built often felt theoretical. Participating in hackathons gave me the chance to build solutions under real-world market constraints. Although we had crossed paths earlier through a separate scholarship program, hackathons were also how I got to know the person who would later become my cofounder better. Ng and his cofounder started out on rival hackathon teams before deciding to work together. Provided by Raymond Loong Ng. We competed as rivals on different teams, but would often find ourselves among the only people still working at 2 or 3 a.m. Eventually, we decided we wanted to be on the same team. We started entering competitions together in late 2023 and went on a winning streak. We soon realized that full software solutions were becoming harder to differentiate in hackathons as AI tools and models advanced. We ventured into hardware because it gave AI a way to be deployed in the real world. At a medical technology hackathon in 2025, we built a device to help paralyzed patients communicate through brainwaves and eye blinks. That became our startup, Neural Drive. The product caught the attention of a local hospital and is set to undergo a clinical trial there. At the same time, I was trying to find my way to the US. I grew up fascinated by the people and stories of Silicon Valley . My favorite films were "Jobs" and "The Social Network," and they made me feel that if I wanted to build something that could change the world, I had to be there. While serving my two years of mandatory military service, I applied to several US colleges but was rejected by all. I ended up being accepted into the computer science program at the National University of Singapore, but I still wanted to go to the States. I kept reaching out to venture capital firms in the US, and Neural Drive eventually caught the attention of Afore Capital in June. In June, Afore Capital made a $250,000 pre-seed investment in Neural Drive. My cofounder and I then joined its two-month Founders-in-Residence program in San Francisco . Ng and his cofounder spent two months in San Francisco as part of Afore Capital's founders-in-residence program. Provided by Raymond Loong Ng. The timing was tricky. College was due to begin in August, so I had to defer my enrollment before classes started. My cofounder had to request a leave of absence from school, too. It wasn't an easy decision, but we took a bet on ourselves. I found a city that moved as fast as I did I had visited Shenzhen in China before and expected Silicon Valley to look even more futuristic. Instead, I was surprised by how ordinary it looked. Because we were scrimping on rent, we moved into a hacker house in San Francisco's Tenderloin neighborhood. Those two months in San Francisco were intense, but incredibly rewarding. We were often working until 4 a.m., but we made as much progress as we would have in two years in Singapore. The sheer density of talent inspired us: "What are you working on?" felt like the way people said hello. It was a city full of workaholics. I thought: This is my kind of place. Ng said he enjoyed the fast-paced lifestyle in Silicon Valley. Provided by Raymond Loong Ng. We went through several pivots before landing on Makeable, our startup that lets people build a physical product from an idea. All they have to do is describe their idea in a prompt. Makeable can generate everything from the 3D model to the electronics and code, then sends users a kit they can put together themselves, like Lego. In our final week of the program, Afore Capital made a follow-on investment, bringing our total funding to date to $1 million. We flew back to Singapore to apply for our O-1 visas . While we're home, we're still working. The plan is to return to San Francisco for the next few years and keep building our company. I probably have to extend my leave of absence. If it doesn't work out, I'll go back to school. I want to keep that option open. But honestly, I hope I don't have to. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: UAE Property: 'Can my tenant legally list my apartment as a holiday rental without my consent?'
events.summary: Question: I own an apartment in Dubai Marina, which I've rented to the same tenant for two years. A neighbour recently contacted me because different people appear to be entering the apartment every few days with suitcases. I checked one of the holiday rental websites and, to my surprise, found what appears to be my apartment being advertised for short-term stays . I never agreed to this and my tenancy contract says the property is for residential use by the tenant. The tenant is paying the rent on time, so financially, I haven't lost anything, but I'm uncomfortable with strangers continually using a property I'm responsible for. Can a tenant legally do this without my permission, and could I as the owner face problems if something happens? Ahmed, Abu Dhabi Answer: I wouldn't ignore this simply because the rent continues to arrive on time. There's an important distinction between a tenant occasionally having friends or family stay and somebody commercially offering another person's property as short-term accommodation. Dubai's holiday-home sector is regulated, and properties being used for this purpose need to comply with the relevant licensing and registration requirements. Separately, your tenancy agreement determines what your tenant is permitted to do with the apartment. Subletting in Dubai is not illegal; however, the landlord must be informed and agree to the subleasing. Since you were not informed, his actions are illegal and he cannot simply decide to turn your property into his own short-term rental business. Before taking any action I suggest you document what you've discovered. Save screenshots of the advertisement, including photographs that clearly identify your apartment and keep any messages from neighbours or building management. I would then write to the tenant and ask for an explanation rather than immediately making accusations. I'd also establish whether the apartment has actually been registered as a holiday home and, if so, how this was done without your knowledge. There's another practical concern: short-term occupation can mean considerably more wear and tear than a conventional tenancy, as well as possible issues with access cards, building security and insurance. For landlords, this is a useful reminder that receiving the rent doesn't necessarily mean everything is fine with the property. Sensible asset management means knowing how your investment is actually being used. Q: My former partner and I bought a villa in Dubai several years ago in both our names. We have now separated. I want to sell the property so we can both move on financially, but my ex refuses. He says that because he owns half of the villa I cannot force him to sell his share. Neither of us can realistically afford to buy the other person out, and there is still a mortgage on the property. What happens when two people jointly own a Dubai property but one wants to sell and the other simply refuses? Are we effectively stuck owning it together indefinitely? Emma, Dubai A: This is unfortunately one of the complications of joint property ownership that people rarely think about when they're happily buying together. You cannot ordinarily sell your former partner's ownership interest simply because you want the whole property sold. Equally, however, joint ownership doesn't necessarily mean two people must remain financially tied together indefinitely. The first thing I'd establish is exactly how ownership is recorded on the title deed and the respective ownership percentages. Then have the property independently valued. Once you know the realistic selling price, deduct the outstanding mortgage and likely selling costs so both parties can see what equity would actually be available. Sometimes having a real number on the table makes negotiations considerably easier. Possible solutions include one party refinancing and purchasing the other's interest, an agreed sale on the open market or another mutually acceptable transfer arrangement, subject of course to the lender and Dubai Land Department requirements. I'd also check who has been paying the mortgage , service charges and other property expenses since the separation because those contributions may need to be considered when the financial position is ultimately resolved. If agreement genuinely cannot be reached, this moves beyond estate agency advice. You should speak to a Dubai lawyer experienced in property and co-ownership disputes about the legal mechanisms available to bring the joint ownership to an end. The wider lesson for unmarried couples, friends and relatives buying together is simple: discuss the break-up before the purchase. A written co-ownership agreement setting out what happens if one person wants to sell can prevent an enormous amount of difficulty later. events.title: The extra stripe that's landed Australian retailer White Fox in court
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Adidas sues White Fox Boutique over its trademark three-stripe design A pair of Adidas shorts with its trademark three-stripe design next to White Fox Boutique shorts with four stripes. ( Supplied ) German sportswear brand Adidas has accused Australian fashion retailer White Fox Boutique of infringing its trademark three-stripe design with garments featuring four stripes. Legal experts say the case could test the trademark registration. The matter is set down for hearing in early 2027. When is a stripe not a stripe? According to sportswear brand Adidas, when it is part of its trademark. The global sportswear giant is suing Australian online fashion retailer White Fox Boutique for selling items allegedly "deceptively similar" to its three-stripe logo, in a case experts say could test the trademark's registration. The German-based brand has filed a trademark infringement claim against the Sydney-based company, popular with teenagers, in the Federal Court of Australia. According to court documents, Adidas accuses White Fox of replicating its trademark across multiple clothing items and advertising content that feature four parallel stripes of equal width in a colour contrasting with the colour of the clothing. Adidas claims this design is "deceptively similar" to its three-stripe trademark, which it has used in Australia for more than 65 years and globally for more than 75 years. White Fox is defending the case, which will play out in court hearings next year. A White Fox Boutique advertisement seen on the back of a bus. ( Supplied ) According to the documents, White Fox Boutique has promoted and supplied clothing with four parallel stripes on it since March this year, including advertisements on buses, bus stops and on social media. Adidas said it asked White Fox to remove the garments from sale in March and to stop using the four-stripe design, which White Fox declined to do. Adidas further claimed White Fox used genuine Adidas shoes, in the same colours as its clothing, in some promotional material, which it said took advantage of the brand's reputation and may lead consumers to draw an association between the two companies. An Instagram post advertising a White Fox Boutique outfit paired with genuine Adidas shoes. ( Supplied ) It alleges White Fox's actions are likely to cause damage to its reputation. In court on Friday, White Fox's barrister Ed Heerey KC said the online fashion retailer would argue the four stripes emblazoned on the label's clothing were simply decorative rather than a trademark. He highlighted similar items bearing the four stripes from other brands, including fast-fashion labels Princess Polly, Glassons and Shein. Intellectual property law expert Muhammad Abbas said this case was not just about a fourth stripe. "Adding a stripe is neither a complete answer to a trademark claim nor automatically an infringement," Dr Abbas, a Queensland University of Technology lecturer, said. He explained a 2023 High Court decision considered the impression a notional buyer, "allowing for imperfect recollection", would have of the registered trademark, compared to the impression created by the sign used. The three-stripe design dates back to the brand's foundation in 1949, but was not trademarked until 1952 after Adidas discovered a Finnish brand Karhu had trademarked the same logo. Founder Adolf Dassler struck a deal and traded two bottles of whiskey and the equivalent of 1,600 euros ($AUD2,500) for the logo, which it has extensively protected ever since. In 2013, it successfully sued Pacific Brands over its use of a four-stripe design on some of its Dunlop and Grosby shoe designs, with the court ruling that three of the 12 designs in question were "deceptively similar". However, University of Technology Sydney School of Law senior lecturer Sarah Hook said challenges overseas had led to Adidas losing its trademark registration in some jurisdictions. In the US, Adidas unsuccessfully took high-end designer Thom Browne to court over a four-stripe design. Thom Browne wore socks with the four-stripe design to court in New York. ( Reuters: Eduardo Munoz ) Thom Browne then challenged the trademark registration in the UK, and the High Court ultimately ruled the trademark was invalid. Fashion designer Thom Browne emerges from a New York courthouse victorious over sportswear giant Adidas. University of Melbourne intellectual property law studies director Benjamin Hopper said distinctiveness was a core doctrine of trademark law, meaning it had to be distinguishable from other goods or services from other traders in the same marketplace.

events.title: Judge halts Trump administration's taxpayer-funded ads
events.summary: A federal judge on Sunday ordered the Trump administration to immediately halt taxpayer-funded ads featuring President Trump. Why it matters: The ruling temporarily blocks the ads weeks before November's midterm elections as multiple lawsuits challenging the Trump administration's use of taxpayer money play out in court. Sunday's ruling stems from a suit filed in the Southern District of New York by Washington, D.C.-based watchdog Common Cause, non-profit Democracy Forward and other plaintiffs. A similar lawsuit , filed by the Democratic National Committee, was filed in D.C. federal court earlier this month. The big picture: The Trump administration maintains that the ads are public service announcements and that previous Republican and Democratic administrations have used taxpayer-funded advertising to promote government policies. Trump pledged to pay for the ads himself after both lawsuits were filed, though the White House told Axios there were no plans to reimburse the government for millions already spent on the ads. Driving the news: The plaintiffs in the New York lawsuit allege that the Trump administration exceeded congressional authorization and violated restrictions on publicity and propaganda. In a brief order , U.S. District Judge Jennifer Rochon found that a motion filed by the coalition was "not moot." She found they had "demonstrated that they are likely to succeed on the merits, will suffer irreparable harm in the absence of an injunction, the balance of the equities tips in their favor, and an injunction serves the public interest," according to the order. The suit names the Department of Homeland Security, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought, and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles as defendants. What they're saying: The coalition said in a statement emailed by Democracy Forward it was "pleased the court acted swiftly to prevent more taxpayer dollars from being used for such blatantly unlawful political propaganda." The statement added, "There is no legal justification — and no precedent — for the president to use the machinery of the government and funds set aside by Congress for other uses to influence electoral outcomes that further his own agenda." Representatives for the White House and DHS did not immediately respond to Axios' Sunday evening request for comment. What's next: A hearing is scheduled for Oct. 13 to discuss next steps in the case. Editor's note: This story was updated with a statement from the plaintiffs.

events.title: Beyond AI: How HKICC 2026 Develops Judgement, Resilience and Global Leadership
events.summary: As technology transforms how business problems are analysed and solved, the HKUST International Case Competition 2026 challenges students to develop the human capabilities that remain essential to leadership. [The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.] AI can generate an answer in seconds. Knowing which answer to trust—and how to act on it—still requires human judgement. The HKUST International Case Competition (HKICC) 2026 put that distinction to the test, bringing together twelve elite undergraduate teams from leading business schools around the world to navigate ambiguity, defend complex decisions and work across cultures under pressure. The University of British Columbia Sauder School of Business emerged as champion after a week of competition focused on the innovation and application of artificial intelligence. As businesses navigate technological disruption and growing complexity, future leaders must look beyond fast answers. They must use technology to strengthen analysis while retaining responsibility for context, trade-offs and long-term value. Supported by HSBC for the fourth consecutive year, HKICC brings together high-performing teams from universities across Australia, Canada, Hong Kong SAR, Hungary, the Netherlands, Singapore, South Korea, Spain, Thailand, and the United States. Participants tackle real-world business challenges while collaborating across cultures and perspectives. “At HSBC, we are committed to nurturing the next generation of business leaders,” said Mr. David GRIMME, Chief Operating Officer, Asia and Middle East, HSBC. “HKICC is an exceptional platform for talented students to tackle real-world business challenges while sharpening strategic judgement, strengthening creative problem-solving, and building collaboration skills.” Turning AI-Enabled Analysis into Decisions Business challenges rarely have a single correct answer. Leaders must still evaluate assumptions, weigh risks and make decisions under uncertainty. Leaders must decide which assumptions to test, which risks to accept and where limited resources can have the greatest impact. At HKICC, participants developed practical strategies related to the innovation and application of artificial intelligence. Working within tight timelines, teams adjusted their strategies as new information emerged and defended their reasoning before experienced industry judges. Liron SAEDI of the University of Southern California Marshall School of Business, who received the Best Presenter Award, said: "AI can help with the research behind a case, but at the end of the day, we are the ones recommending and implementing the solutions.” While participants spent much of the week analysing cases, their learning also extended beyond the competition room. A highlight of this year's programme was the HSBC Student Engagement Event, where participants engaged directly with senior leaders and gained insights into leadership and career development. After a week of intense competition, the University of British Columbia Sauder School of Business emerged as Champion of HKICC 2026. The University of Southern California Marshall School of Business and the National University of Singapore secured the first and second Runner-up titles respectively. UBC Sauder also received the Outstanding Business Concept Award for its innovative and compelling solution. Beyond the case analyses and final presentations, participants practised the behaviours that effective teamwork requires: managing time, testing assumptions and ensuring different perspectives were heard. Anjana SRINIVASAN, Chief Administrative Officer Asia & Middle East and COO Asia International Markets at HSBC, who served as one of the final judges, said: "Great teamwork is more than simply sharing the work. It means listening as much as contributing, challenging ideas respectfully, and ensuring every voice is heard and valued. The ability to collaborate across different perspectives while working under pressure is a skill that will serve these students well throughout their studies and careers.” For participants, those principles were tested in practice. Boin KANG from the National University of Singapore said: "It's really about time management, working under pressure, stress-testing our knowledge and rationale, and explaining our thinking to one another." Together, these experiences required teams to move beyond dividing tasks. They had to challenge ideas constructively, reconcile different viewpoints and maintain a coherent recommendation under pressure. The Capabilities Future Leaders Will Need Through HKICC, HKUST Business School and HSBC share a commitment to developing leaders who can navigate uncertainty, adapt to change and work across cultures and markets.

events.title: Fox stays positive on data centers even as public backlash grows
events.summary: The News Despite increasingly critical media coverage of AI and the spread of data centers across the US, one news network has been painting a more positive picture. More than half of the references to data centers on Fox News over the last two years would have left viewers with a favorable impression, compared to less than 10% on CNN and 5% on MS NOW, according to a new Semafor analysis of mentions of data centers on each network. The mentions were pulled from closed captions preserved by the Internet Archive, which keeps a digital, searchable library of recorded TV news. A pair of AI models from Anthropic and OpenAI scored each reference on its content, with the network’s name removed. Mentions of data centers have, predictably, shot up across all three networks in recent months as political backlash against AI swells and the data centers themselves have become a salient issue ahead of the midterms. But Fox’s opinion and morning shows, including, , and leaned on the promise of AI, economic investment and the race with China, skewing Fox’s coverage more favorably, the analysis showed. The network’s news shows were more measured. In an Aug. 23 monologue that at one point featured a chyron reading “The case for data centers,” Fox host Brian Kilmeade acknowledged “real concerns,” but argued that “saying no to data centers nationwide also means saying no to the tax dollars that can flow into a community. … If Americans don’t build the infrastructure to meet the demand, somebody else will.” On CNN and MS NOW, the criticism focused as much on the facilities’ political toxicity as on harms like power bills or water use, casting them as unpopular with voters and a liability for politicians who back them heading into the midterms. Data centers “are driving up energy costs, sucking up water supplies, wiping out rather than creating jobs,” MS NOW’s Katy Tur said in May. “Politicians beware.” Polling shows that across demographic groups, Americans hold increasingly negative views of data centers: More than half of Americans say data centers are mostly bad for the environment , Pew Research Center found last month, compared with 39% in January. Fox News did not comment for this story. Max’s view The pro-data center programming on Fox News comes as the right tries to define its positions in an AI-fueled, post-Donald Trump future. Fox’s favorable data center coverage mirrors Trump’s position on their growth and the need for AI companies to help fuel the US economy. “The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor,” Trump wrote on Truth Social in August. “If we kill the Golden Goose, you will only have yourselves to blame.” But anger about data centers and the rapid advancement of AI represents a faultline within the MAGA coalition that swept Trump back into office. Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis and Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., have questioned some data centers in their states, while Texas Gov. Greg Abbott seems to have flipped from supporting data centers to looking to slow their growth in his state amid a tougher-than-expected reelection campaign. Some on the right I have talked to in the last several months worry that Fox News, which Trump watches religiously, and other pro-data center voices are encouraging the president to take positions that are broadly unpopular with his rural and suburban base. “The Big Tech oligarchs, the guys driving AI, did a terrible job,” Steve Bannon, a staunchly anti-AI Trump ally, told the Daily Signal in September. “They came in to try to muscle local communities, and particularly since President Trump’s strongest base is in exurban and rural communities, that’s where they were really the ugliest, and they haven’t made their case, and they particularly haven’t made their case at the local level about the economics of this, and the energy of this, and the water of this, and the manifestation of what these things are going to be used for.” Room for Disagreement Not all of Fox’s data center coverage has been rosy; its tenor grew slightly less favorable in 2026 compared to last year. “It’s taxing our system way too much on water, agriculture land, or electricity. We’re gonna implode,” the Texas agriculture commissioner said in an interview on a weekend Fox show in August. “We just can’t do it. There’s not enough.

events.title: Hack reveals Netanyahu campaign's media ties
events.summary: The News Hacked messages from an adviser to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu are providing a glimpse of his aides’ close ties to the media. The incumbent prime minister’s reelection campaign has been repeatedly rocked by hacked and leaked documents, part of broad attempts to destabilize a wildly divisive leader both inside and outside his country ahead of Oct. 27 elections. The latest breach comes from the WhatsApp account of Netanyahu aide Jonatan Urich, who appears to have exposed sensitive information through a vibe-coded media-monitoring app. Haaretz reported Sunday that it had “verified” the leak. The messages include conversations between Urich and Amit Segal, a central media figure who is chief political analyst for Channel 12 News, the country’s leading broadcaster, and host of the program , an analogue of the US show of that name. In the exchanges, Segal offers advice about the campaign’s videos and its messaging: Netanyahu’s management of the aftermath of the October 7 attack is his core political advantage, he suggests. Segal mentions he offered the same advice to Netanyahu’s campaign spokeswoman. In another message, Urich shares a speech Netanyahu is planning to give. Segal declined to discuss the messages on the record. Urich, who is also enmeshed in a scandal over payments from Qatar, didn’t respond to an inquiry, but in a lawyers’ statement posted to X confirmed that he had been hacked and threatened legal consequences against anyone who published the content of the leaks. Israel’s Privacy Protection Law prohibits republishing content obtained through illegal means. Ben’s view Hacks and leaks are challenging to cover. The most important story in most hacks — including this one — is the hack itself; this is part of the broad internationalization of the Israeli political campaign, in which actors across the region and in the US line up for and, mostly against, the leader who led his country’s response to the October 7 attacks. But Israeli commentators also professed shock, if not surprise, Sunday at how closely aligned the journalist and spin doctor appeared to be. Segal is a center-right figure broadly aligned with Netanyahu — but he’s also a top journalist who appears on international platforms, like the American political figure Dan Senor’s widely-followed podcast, as an independent analyst. One Israeli journalist compared Segal’s role in Israel to that of Fox News host Bret Baier, who maintains journalistic independence despite working for a right-wing platform. The messages put a dent in Segal’s version of that image, and offer a glimpse at parts of an Israeli media that has grown very close to its prime minister. Room for Disagreement Segal addressed the controversy on News 12, describing the messages as part of a “very delicate tango between the journalist and the subject of their coverage.” He added that “any people I’ve covered over the years gave me drafts of speeches, saying, ‘This will be our campaign, what are your thoughts?’” Notable The region’s politics have been buffeted — and illuminated — repeatedly by aggressive cyber campaigns for years. Semafor reported in 2023 on extensive, leaked Iranian government communications that revealed Iranian attempts to influence US politics.

events.title: ABC News offers contradictory explanation for vanishing Anduril story
events.summary: The News When ABC News removed a story about Donald Trump’s sons from its website without explanation on Thursday, an unnamed company source told media reporters the article had been published “prematurely.” Nathan Lee, the investigative reporter who wrote the original piece , used the same language in emails to Powerus and Anduril, two of the companies at the center of the piece. But emails between ABC News and its subjects, provided to Semafor, show the network seeking to downplay its errors by misrepresenting its own processes. On Oct. 7, ABC News published an investigation into a new $6.6 billion deal between defense contractor Anduril and the US Navy to build a new high-tech submarine shipyard in Maryland. The piece largely focused on the financial ties between President Donald Trump’s son and defense companies, noting that Donald Trump Jr. is a partner at investment firm 1789 Capital, which “claimed a major stake in Anduril in June 2025 from a $2.5 billion investment into the company.” After the piece was published, a spokesperson for Anduril reached out to Lee with several urgent requests for correction. The company — which had not responded to ABC News’ inquiries prior to its publication, according to an Anduril source — wanted the network to clarify connections between Anduril and 1789, noting that the firm had invested $50 million in Anduril’s latest round, a small percentage of the $2.5 billion total. “Today, 1789 owns approximately 0.13% of Anduril and has no major investor rights. Any suggestion that 1789 financed the round or holds significant ownership, governance position or ‘major stake’ in Anduril is inaccurate,” Anduril’s spokesperson wrote to Lee, according to emails obtained by Semafor. After the story was published on Wednesday, Lee told Anduril that the network was slightly tweaking the language in its piece, but it was otherwise standing by its story. “I have spoken to my editors and we have updated the story for accuracy,” Lee said in a note. “We had pulled the ‘major stake’ language from previous reporting. 1789 Capital did claim a stake from the $2.5 billion investment your company received, so we are standing by our language to that extent.” Anduril’s PR team was not satisfied, and continued to press the network to clarify its story, saying that the piece misstated 1789 Capital’s investment in Anduril’s fundraising round. “It’s still not clear. I read your text and it reads as if they invested the full $2.5b. Would be much more accurate to list their actual investment of $50m and even more accurate to share that they own less than a percentage point in Anduril,” a spokesperson wrote. In another email later Wednesday afternoon, Lee said ABC News’ editors had reviewed the language and were standing by the piece. “Apologies, but my editors said we are standing by the language. I’ll make sure to reach out to both of you directly for any future stories,” Lee said. But by Thursday, the network had changed its mind. The network removed the piece without explanation, and Peter Charalambous, an ABC News producer in New York, reached out to Anduril and Powerus, a drone contractor mentioned in the story, saying the story had been “published prematurely and removed from our website.” On Friday evening, ABC News republished a new version of the story re-reported by Charalambous, now without a byline . An editor’s note did not include language that the initial piece was published early. “Editor’s Note: CORRECTION: A version of this story published on Oct. 7 contained errors in the description of certain company investments, government contracts and event chronologies. After subsequent reporting, this version contains corrected information and additional context regarding some of those investments, contracts and events.” A network source told Semafor: “We always review every situation in a thorough and thoughtful manner and will not be providing further comment at this time.” The source also noted that it was extremely rare for ABC News to remove a story. Status reported Sunday that the article was mentioned during the network’s regular 9 am editorial call the day it was published, “suggesting at least some staffers were aware of its publication,” and it “circulated it through its usual email distribution without raising any immediate alarms.” Max’s view ABC News’ suggestion that its initial story was published prematurely is familiar spin to anyone who has dealt with crisis PR. It minimized the company’s mistakes and made the situation seem like an accident. But at a time when distrust in the news media continues to rise, deflections like this can damage the credibility of mainstream, nonpartisan American journalism. Tellingly, the network seemed to know the difference in its official response, acknowledging that the original piece contained errors. Brett Velicovich, co-founder of Powerus, another company mentioned in ABC News’ initial piece, complained that the network’s handling of the story reinforced his frustration with much of the media coverage of his company and the president’s administration. “It’s destroying the integrity of what reporting is all about,” Velicovich said. “The damage is already done.” The Trump family’s mix of business and governing, unprecedented in recent history, is an important reporting target, as journalists attempt to understand how companies and countries are attempting to influence policy by investing in Trump businesses or bringing the Trumps on as partners themselves. But ABC News’ decision to remove its story without explanation while misleadingly telegraphing that it was simply published on accident gave the president’s son and many on the right another opening to criticize mainstream news outlets. If more and more people continue to believe that news organizations are willing to mislead or fail to take full accountability for mistakes, will they listen when outlets have legitimate stories? Room for Disagreement Remove the numbers, and the most basic version of the story — the Pentagon is paying very large sums to a defense contractor in which the president’s sons have invested, and whose co-founder, Palmer Luckey, is a high-dollar Trump donor — is correct . It also follows a pattern congressional Democrats have promised to investigate should they retake power after the midterms.

events.title: Amazon in talks to buy AI start-up Decart for around US$7 billion: Report
events.summary: Decart was valued at nearly US$4 billion (S$5 billion) in May, the Wall Street Journal report said. Amazon is in talks to buy AI startup Decart for about US$7 billion, the Wall Street Journal reported, citing people familiar with the matter. Decart makes the Lucy model for live video editing and Oasis for robotics and self-driving tests. It was valued at nearly US$4 billion in May. A deal could happen soon, but it is not certain. Reuters could not verify the report, and Amazon and Decart did not comment. Amazon is in talks to acquire artificial intelligence start-up Decart in a deal that could be valued at around US$7 billion (S$8.96 billion), the Wall Street Journal reported on Oct 11, citing sources familiar with the matter. Decart’s Lucy model, backed by Nvidia, can edit live video in real time, according to the company’s website. Decart has also developed Oasis, a model that generates simulated environments to train and test robotics and autonomous driving systems. The Journal reported that Decart was valued at nearly US$4 billion in May, the Journal report said, citing PitchBook data. Amazon declined to comment outside regular business hours, while Decart did not respond to requests for comment. A deal could happen soon if talks do not fall apart or another suitor does not emerge, the report said. In September, Anthropic decided not to pursue an acquisition of Decart after conducting due diligence, Bloomberg News reported. It had explored the deal in August for potentially US$6 billion, Bloomberg reported. Decart raised US$300 million in May in a funding round led by Radical Ventures, with Nvidia joining as a new investor. REUTERS

events.title: Oil dips after Trump announcements on Russian diesel, Ukraine energy ceasefire
events.summary: The attacks threaten to inject fresh volatility into a pivotal week for markets. Oil prices fell as hopes grew for a Russia-Ukraine energy ceasefire and more Russian diesel supplies after Donald Trump’s announcements. Brent and WTI dropped, while ICE gasoil fell 3%, but analysts said doubts over the ceasefire may limit further price falls. Middle East conflict and tanker attacks kept Brent above US$100, while Goldman Sachs raised its Brent forecast and warned of ongoing supply risks. LONDON – Oil prices slipped on Oct 12 on expectations of more Russian supplies after US President Donald Trump said Ukraine and Russia had agreed to halt attacks on each other’s energy facilities following a US diesel-supply deal with Moscow. Brent crude futures fell 22 cents, or 0.2%, to US$104.50 a barrel by 0821 GMT (4.21pm Singapore time), while US West Texas Intermediate crude was at US$91.45 a barrel, down 40 cents, or 0.4%. Both benchmarks were down more than 1% earlier in the session. Intercontinental Exchange gas oil futures fell 4.6% to $1,415 per tonne after Trump said on Oct 9 that Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tonnes (2.25 million barrels) of diesel to US and global markets, with more to come later. “The immediate impact of the deal is questionable, as Russia’s refining capacity has been severely reduced,” PVM analyst Tamas Varga said. “However, Moscow has partially lifted its ban on diesel exports, allowing 500,000 tonnes (around 3.7 million barrels) to be released onto the international market – equivalent to roughly one day of US consumption and around 13% of global demand.” Trump also unexpectedly announced on Oct 11 that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to an energy ceasefire, but Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelensky said he was still waiting to see details of the energy ceasefire, while Russia did not comment. The International Energy Agency’s Fatih Birol said all members should assess whether additional diesel releases are necessary and that countries which have not yet fully delivered pledged volumes should accelerate their remaining releases, prioritising diesel. Crude supported by Middle East conflict However, the Middle East conflict continued to support Brent crude at above US$100 a barrel. The Iran-aligned Houthis claimed responsibility for an Oct 10 strike on Riyadh’s international airport that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300. In addition, more attacks on tankers sailing through the Strait of Hormuz have been reported in October , threatening to dampen a recovery in Middle East crude exports seen in September. Trump said on Oct 10 that the US was considering joining Saudi strikes on the Houthis in the conflict, a spillover from the wider war with Iran that the US and Israel launched in February. A tanker was struck by a drone in the vicinity of Sohar anchorage in Oman, while another was damaged by an unknown projectile while transiting the Strait of Hormuz, the ​United ​Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations reported over the weekend. Goldman Sachs raised its Brent crude price forecast for December to US$90 a barrel, up from US$85 previously, its analysts led by Daan Struyven said in a note. “We maintain our base case that continued adaptation of Middle East supply will eventually reduce crude oil prices, while potential renewed escalation still poses significant net upside risk,” the analysts said, estimating a risk premium of just over US$20 a barrel. “We forecast WTI (West Texas Intermediate) prices, which are unusually low versus Brent because of high US-Europe shipping costs, to average US$81 in December 2026 and US$73 in 2027,” they added. In the Gulf of Mexico, energy majors Shell, Chevron and BP were seeking to redeploy personnel and restore production at their platforms after Hurricane Isaias made landfall early on Oct 10. REUTERS

events.title: Roofing scammers con homeowners out of thousands of pounds
events.summary: Published 12 October 2026, 00:19 BST Scammers pretending to be legitimate workmen are charging homeowners thousands of pounds for roofing work that is not completed, done badly or not necessary, according to Citizens Advice. The consumer advice charity says one in 10 of all the scams it recorded over the past year were related to roofing, making it the most common type of scam brought to them. It can leave victims like Crystal, from the Midlands, thousands of pounds out of pocket. The 68-year-old was frightened and found it hard to sleep after a rogue builder left her roof with dislodged bricks and blocked gutters. She said she felt pressured into agreeing to having her roof re-done and paid a total of £5,500, only for the original contractor to send his son instead, who left work in the eaves incomplete. "We had heavy rain a couple of weeks after he did the job, and it ended up like a waterfall coming down the wall," she said. Her neighbour's house was also damaged. "They took the lead off my neighbour's side of the chimney, which caused bricks to fall into his attic and the rain to go into his house," she told the BBC. The experience still haunts her: "I can't sleep. I don't eat properly." In the year to August the Citizens Advice Consumer Service received 9,000 complaints about roofing work, including problems with construction, repairs and weatherproofing. Of those 2,205, or about one in four complaints, were suspected scams, up from 2,098 the year before. Dame Clare Moriarty, chief executive of Citizens Advice, urged consumers to carry out thorough checks on traders before agreeing to hire them. "Scammers exploit the fact that roofs are out of sight and reach, knowing most people can't easily inspect the work themselves," she said. Victims also reported aggressive and intimidating behaviour, with three quarters of fraudsters using "doorstep" sales tactics. Citizens Advice cited the case of Charlotte, 65, who lives alone in north eastern England. Tradesmen she found online initially offered to fix her leaking gutter for £250. The two men then said there was further work that needed to be done, that would cost £2,500. "An hour later they said it was sorted, but they'd found another problem," she said. It was dark and Charlotte felt afraid. "They knew I was alone, I didn't feel like I could deal with anything that might happen after, so I paid £3,500," she said. But the next day she could see no sign of any work having been done, she said. To avoid falling victim to roofing scams, Citizens Advice suggests: Be alert: Always ask for references and for everything to be in writing. Be wary of unsolicited doorknockers and callers Gather evidence: If a trader causes problems, be sure to take photos and gather the necessary paperwork and receipts Know your rights: Traders must give you the information about your right to cancel in writing. If the job is not done with "reasonable care and skill," the Consumer Rights Act 2015 also entitles you to ask for the problem to be fixed or a refund Lord Bichard, chair of National Trading Standards, said rogue traders were "criminals deliberately preying on people in their own homes". He described roofing fraud as "particularly cruel", and said Trading Standards would pursue fraudsters through legal routes. "Victims can lose life savings in a matter of hours and be left with damaged homes, financial hardship and a profound sense of vulnerability long after the criminals have gone," he said. events.title: Trump faces growing backlash over plans to import diesel from Russia
events.summary: Global fuel prices have soared since the US-Israel war with Iran began at the end of February Published 12 October 2026, 00:18 BST US President Donald Trump is facing a growing backlash over plans to import diesel from Russia as the Iran war continues to impact global energy prices. Trump on Friday announced that Russian President Vladimir Putin had agreed to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel immediately "to the American and global marketplace" followed by several other shipments. That is despite signing legislation to authorise fresh US sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas just weeks ago. The move has been criticised by some Republican and Democratic lawmakers, who believe the deal violates US laws. As well as the initial release of 300,000 tonnes of diesel, Trump said Russia would then supply 500,000 tonnes in November and one million more after that. This would be followed by a further three million tonnes, which would be delivered "within a short period" dependent on the condition of its refineries, which have been attacked by Ukraine during the ongoing war between the two countries. "Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority," Trump wrote in a Truth Social post. Russia's Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak confirmed these numbers to Tass, the country's state-owned news agency, saying the export volume could reach three million tonnes per month in future. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has called the deal a gift to Putin that amounts to "an investment in a war that must be ended". It is understood the US Treasury is suspending sanctions on Russian diesel exports until 7 April as part of the deal, but other assets like those in American banks are still frozen. A group of seven senators - four Republicans and three Democrats – on Sunday said the deal violated US laws, urging Trump to "reverse course". "The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians," the lawmakers said. They added that Congress had "explicitly banned Russian energy imports in 2022 to prevent American dollars from financing Putin's brutal war against Ukraine". The statement was signed by Republicans Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski, Thom Tillis and John Curtis, as well as Democrats Jeanne Shaheen, Richard Blumenthal and Ron Wyden. Trump's 'energy ceasefire' claim welcomed by Zelensky but Russia silent Published 16 hours ago Trump wants to reduce the cost of fuel as the midterms loom - will it work? Published 2 days ago Analysis: Trump's shock Russia deal highlights mounting pressure to curb fuel prices Published 2 days ago Not everyone is opposed to the deal. Republican Thomas Massie, who has sparred with Trump a number of issues, said the US should lift sanctions on all petroleum products. Trump's Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News the agreement would work through existing legal channels the US has to help bring prices down and that anyone in Congress who said it would not was wrong. Global fuel prices have soared since the US-Israel war with Iran began at the end of February, with the fighting severely disrupting supplies of crude oil - a key ingredient in petrol and diesel. The rising prices have become a key issue for Americans ahead of next month's midterms elections, which will determine if Trump's Republican Party maintains control of Congress. Polls show a majority of Americans disapprove of his handling of the economy and the war in Iran and he has been searching for ways to ease his party's political pain. The toll the war is taking has been acutely felt by US agricultural states, which rely heavily on diesel to operate farming machinery and to transport their products to market. The average diesel price in the US is currently $6.28 (£4.74) a gallon, according to the AAA, down from the record high of $6.53 recorded at the end of September. Analysts have questioned whether Russia is capable of providing that quantity of diesel and the extent to which doing so will ease prices for American consumers. The US uses approximately 3.6 million barrels of diesel a day, so even if Russia delivers its promised 300,000 tonnes this month, it amounts to approximately half of the US daily consumption. It is not only at home that Trump is facing opposition to his diesel deal with Russia. A number of international leaders have criticised it, including Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, who said the US and other allies of Ukraine should focus on ramping up pressure on Russia to end the war. Meanwhile, Trump announced in Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had reached an "energy ceasefire" but did not give more details. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky welcomed this but there was no response from Moscow.

events.title: AI scale-up PhysicsX comes to Singapore with ambition to accelerate industrial innovation
events.summary: PhysicsX CEO and co-founder Jacomo Corbo at the launch of the PhysicsX Singapore Hub at Temasek Shophouse on Oct 8. PhysicsX, led by former F1 strategist Jacomo Corbo, is using AI to replace slow engineering simulations and speed up industrial innovation. The London-based scale-up has set up its Asia-Pacific hub in Singapore, where high-value manufacturing, engineering and chip production make it a strong regional base. PhysicsX has raised about US$500 million, works with major firms like NVIDIA and Siemens, and plans to grow its Singapore team to 100 in three years. SINGAPORE – As a race strategist, Jacomo Corbo helped the Renault F1 team win back-to-back double world championships with driver Fernando Alonso in 2005 and 2006. Now he is chief executive of a scale-up that offers a winning formula to accelerate industrial innovation. Before a product is physically built – whether it is jet engine parts or a machine that makes semiconductors – engineers in manufacturing firms run computer simulations to replicate, predict and optimise the behaviour of materials, mechanical systems and factory workflows. PhysicsX develops AI models that replace these slow, traditional numerical computer simulations with high-speed AI inference, where a trained AI model applies learnt patterns to new, unseen data to generate real-world predictions, decisions or outputs. After winning customers across the Atlantic, Corbo’s London-headquartered PhysicsX is now in Singapore, establishing its Asia-Pacific hub and promising to overhaul what engineering and manufacturing look like today. Corbo co-founded PhysicsX with his former F1 colleague, Robin Tuluie, a theoretical physicist. PhysicsX’s customers span advanced manufacturing sectors that involve very complex engineering design and processes, including automotive, materials science and energy. “Aerospace and defence are our largest sectors, followed by semiconductors, where we are working mostly on the equipment manufacturing side,” Corbo said, adding that the firm is increasingly deploying into chip fabrication plants. Since its official launch in 2020, the firm has established partnerships to deploy industrial AI and advance its platform and large physics models with companies such as Leonardo Aerospace, carmaker Audi, miner Rio Tinto, tech giant NVIDIA and industrial automation firm Siemens. With many of its customers and partners already in Singapore, it made perfect sense for PhysicsX to choose the Republic as the company’s regional hub, Corbo told The Straits Times in an interview last week. For years, multinational firms have gravitated to Singapore for its strategic location and a clear-eyed policy focus. But for manufacturing firms, it has been a bit more than just that. Corbo said: “The physical constraints on the city-state have meant that Singapore’s strategy has orientated itself towards high-value manufacturing. But it’s also where high-value manufacturing is co-located with high-value engineering.” The Republic recognised early on that for supply chains to be efficient, engineering and manufacturing must co-locate. “And now it plays a linchpin role in a number of really important supply chains.” Singapore today accounts for one in 10 chips and one-fifth of global semiconductor equipment produced annually. It is also one of the world’s top 10 exporters of chemical products. It contributes 10 per cent of global aerospace maintenance, repair and overhaul output, and is home to eight of the top 10 biopharmaceutical companies conducting manufacturing or R&D activities here. And bridging the gap between research and industrial application are 14 of the world’s top 20 international engineering design firms and 10 of the top 20 engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) services providers that operate in Singapore. Hence, engineering teams in companies here can design a high-value tool or component and instantly test it on a nearby production line, closing the feedback loop between blueprint and physical asset. However, much of industrial engineering, manufacturing and goods production worldwide is run on software that has remained largely unchanged for decades. Also, even very innovative firms in advanced manufacturing have proprietary software and workflows that are fragmented across different departments and engineering teams. PhysicsX AI platform integrates with a company’s existing systems, such as computer-aided design tools, numerical solvers that solve complex engineering equations, and product lifecycle management systems which are the repositories of all their designs. “We absolutely tell our customers that, look, you don’t have to move off the tools that you use and rely on at scale. You can stay on these systems of record... and we can bring optimisation enablement and put AI at the heart of these workflows,” Corbo said.

events.title: Environmental watchdog to review new Kimberley gas project
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Buru Energy sends gas project for EPA approval, saying it could power northern WA by 2029 Buru Energy's proposed Rafael conventional gas project in the Canning Basin. ( Suplied: Buru Energy ) Buru Energy has referred its Rafael conventional gas project to WA's Environmental Protection Authority for assessment. Environmentalists claim it could be a "Trojan horse for fracking" — something the company rejects. Buru expects a decision from the EPA by the end of the year. The company behind a proposed gas project in Western Australia's Kimberley says it could meet the region's power demands with locally produced energy for the first time. Buru Energy referred its Rafael conventional gas project to WA's Environmental Protection Authority (EPA) for review in early October. The proposal involves developing a facility at the project site, located in the Kimberley's Canning Basin about 85 kilometres south of Derby, to process conventional gas from two co-located production wells. Conventional gas is natural gas extracted using simple drilling and pumping methods, as opposed to unconventional extraction methods like hydraulic fracturing, or fracking. Well testing underway at Buru Energy's Rafael conventional gas project. ( Supplied: Buru Energy ) Buru executive chairman David Maxwell said the Rafael project was the only proven conventional gas and liquids resource in the greater Kimberley region. "At the moment, the Kimberley relies on imported energy … from Karratha, Perth, Darwin, and Asia," he said. He said the Rafael project would improve energy security and be cost-effective, with reduced road traffic another potential benefit. Up to 300 tonnes of Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) would be produced at the Rafael plant per day — the equivalent of about 16 or 17 terajoules of energy — alongside LPG and condensate. Mr Maxwell said the Kimberley used between six and 13 terajoules per day for power generation, with the amount varying based on the time of year. "We'll also supply beyond the Kimberley into, for example, the northern Pilbara. "In the case of LPG, we would be supplying in the order of a quarter to a third of the Kimberley's LPG demand." The West Australian government has banned fracking in over 98 per cent of the state, but this does not include parts of the Kimberley including the Canning Basin. Earlier this year, WA's EPA recommended a fracking proposal by Black Mountain Energy subsidiary Bennett Resources go ahead subject to conditions. The Valhalla Gas Exploration and Appraisal Program would see up to 20 exploration and appraisal wells drilled in the basin. A record 8,000 appeals were lodged against the project. Community members gather in Broome to protest the Valhalla fracking proposal. ( ABC Kimberley: Dunja Karagic ) When asked about the fracking proposal in Broome this month, WA Mines Minister Daniel Pastorelli said the method had drawn varied perspectives. "I understand everyone has differing views on these types of things and I respect that completely," he said. "Obviously our policy and our approach is based on science, and that is what we're doing when it comes to hydraulic fracturing." Daniel Pastorelli acknowledges fracking is a controversial topic. ( ABC News: Keane Bourke ) Environmentalists have expressed concern Buru's Rafael project, although a conventional gas project, could pave the way for fracking to occur in the future. Environs Kimberley executive director Martin Pritchard said Rafael "could be a Trojan horse for fracking". "They (Buru) might be saying right now that they're not intending on fracking, but their statements to the ASX clearly say that they want to undertake fracking in the future," he said. Buru's David Maxwell rejected the accusation. "It's got nothing to do with fracking at all," he said. "And if there was any fracking involved — and I stress there is not — that would be a separate [EPA] referral, a separate application and a separate approval process and we're not in that process at all." Buru Energy's Yulleroo 2 wellhead 60 kilometres east of Broome was fracked in 2010. ( ABC Kimberley: Ben Collins ) The company previously used the hydraulic fracturing technique at its Yulleroo gas field also in the Canning Basin, but Mr Maxwell said it no longer did so. "We do not currently practice hydraulic fracturing," he said. "In the past Buru has, but Buru has put that on the shelf, and at the moment we have no plans for fracture stimulation." Mr Pritchard said solar and batteries, rather than gas fields, were the way forward for cheaper and cleaner electricity in the Kimberley.

events.title: Six senators call for Trump administration to 'immediately reverse course' on Russian diesel plan
events.summary: A bipartisan group of six senators are calling on President Donald Trump’s administration to “immediately reverse course” on a plan to purchase diesel from Russia as part of an effort to lower high fuel prices WASHINGTON -- A bipartisan group of six senators on Sunday called for President Donald Trump's administration to “immediately reverse course” on a plan to purchase diesel from Russia as part of an effort to lower high fuel prices. Trump shocked lawmakers when he announced on social media Friday that he struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin in a phone call. He said Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to the American and global market, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons “immediately thereafter.” Russia will deliver an additional 3 million tons “within a short period of time” after that, he wrote. Four Republican senators and two Democratic senators signed onto the statement released Sunday in protesting the deal. They said the administration failed to consult with Congress or submit any explanation to justify its decision as required by statute. “The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians. The Administration must immediately reverse course,” they wrote. The Republican senators who signed onto the statement are Sens. Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, Thom Tillis of North Carolina and John Curtis of Utah. The Democratic senators are Sens. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire and Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut. Tillis, in an interview that aired Sunday on NBC’s “Meet the Press,” said there's a legitimate case for saying the president is not following the law if the administration goes through with its diesel purchase plan. “We were very clear that Russia is the aggressor. Russia is the one who can end this war by backing out of territory that they occupied,” Tillis said. Trump's announcement came just a few weeks after Congress passed legislation that directed Trump to impose substantial tariffs on the top importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia’s natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports. The congressional effort was aimed at cutting the flow of money Russia receives from oil and gas sales to finance its war against Ukraine. The lawmakers also noted that Congress explicitly banned Russia energy imports in 2022 to prevent the United States from financing the war. “Congress was clear: the U.S. should not import oil from Russia until it ends its aggression against Ukraine and ceases threats against our NATO Allies,” the six lawmakers wrote in their statement. “President Trump’s decision to allow Russian diesel imports to the U.S. runs directly counter to that law.” Sen. John Barrasso, R-Wyo., said Trump is focused on reducing the cost of energy when asked whether the president's action would be in violation of U.S. law. Hurricane Isaias: At least 4 dead as Isaias downgraded Fort Hood survivors speak out on Pentagon's decision to livestream Hasan's execution Christa Pike asked 'Where am I?' after waking up following botched execution: Lawyer “The president is balancing and has to make tough decisions,” Barrasso said on CBS's “Face the Nation.” He also encouraged Trump to enforce the sanctions law that Congress passed last month. “This is just another point of leverage for the president to use against Putin in an effort to get a long-term solution in that part of the world,” Barrasso said. Energy experts say the Russia deal is unlikely to make a dent in high prices at the pump. Richard Nephew, a senior research scholar at Columbia University’s Center on Global Energy Policy, noted that the total amount of diesel appears to be less than what the U.S. uses in a day. Nephew argued that Iran and Russia might benefit more than the U.S. “The Iranians are probably very excited because it shows that there’s a lot of pressure still on the U.S. And the Russians are excited because it puts a big hole in the sanctions regime,” he said. Trump has recently sought to blame record U.S. diesel prices on Ukraine rather than the U.S.-led war in Iran , which has elevated world energy prices. events.title: Buttigieg gambles on a different path for 2028
events.summary: Pete Buttigieg has been able to campaign for Democrats across the country more than many of his potential 2028 rivals this past year. One reason: He doesn't have a job. That's by choice. Buttigieg said no when top Democrats urged him to run for governor or the U.S. Senate in Michigan this year. Why it matters: That decision is a gamble for Buttigieg's presidential ambitions. He's been able to build a national network over the last two years but hasn't added to his relatively thin resume as a former mayor of South Bend, Ind., and Joe Biden's transportation secretary. Buttigieg, 44, became a national political figure without following the typical path. He ran for president in 2020 as a small-town mayor and won the Iowa caucus by offering an optimistic vision and impressing voters with his communication skills — including in hostile environments. Driving the news: In early 2025, Democratic lawmakers and strategists including New York Sen. Chuck Schumer and former Michigan Sen. Debbie Stabenow urged Buttigieg — who had moved to Michigan — to run for office in his new state. Winning such an office, they argued, would help Buttigieg build his resume for a future White House run and give him a chance to distance himself from the unpopular Biden administration. Buttigieg passed, citing both a desire to stay home more with his husband and young twins, and figuring that he could still get his message out without being in the Senate. Instead, he set about building a larger national network among Democrats — particularly with Black voters in the South, where he had struggled in the 2020 Democratic primary. Buttigieg has traveled to 37 states since he left the Biden administration, Politico reported last week. Democratic candidates in vital swing districts and states have welcomed him to campaign for them this year while resisting offers from other potential presidential candidates such as former Vice President Kamala Harris , New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and California Gov. Gavin Newsom. In Buttigieg, many Democrats see a surrogate who can draw attention and crowds without the degree of negative attention that other prominent Democrats attract. Buttigieg also will campaign in key races in the final weeks before the Nov. 3 election. He's scheduled to be in Michigan and Virginia — which happen to hold early contests in the 2028 presidential primary. Between the lines: Buttigieg has tried to position himself as a candidate of the next generation who also has enough experience in the executive branch to be able to deliver. He's betting that the traditional ladder of running for president — becoming a senator, governor, or vice president first — no longer applies, especially after the Trump era. What they're saying: Buttigieg "knows what no one else on the Democratic side does, which is what it's actually like to run for this office — the pacing, the pressures and imperatives," David Axelrod, a former senior aide to President Obama and an outside adviser to Buttigieg in the past, told Axios. "At a time when the party and country will be searching for youth and forward-looking vision, he has the capacity to articulate one in a powerful way," Axelrod added. Axelrod said that if Buttigieg runs, "it will be because he feels the timing is right for someone like him, and the big mission is more compelling than the statewide races on which he took a pass." A Buttigieg spokesperson said that "when Pete decided not to run for office in Michigan, he promised he would still get to work to help candidates everywhere. He's been doing just that."

events.title: Turning AI Ambition into Real-World Advantage
events.summary: As enterprises race to adopt AI, Amitabh Sarkar, argues that AI’s real test is on infrastructure, and durable transformation will depend on converging networks, cloud, security, governance and trust. When executives talk about artificial intelligence today, they often talk in absolutes: an existential threat, a historic opportunity, the next great productivity leap. For Amitabh Sarkar, Tata Communications’ Vice-President, Asia Pacific and Japan, the more important story lies beneath the rhetoric and inside the data centres, networks and operating models trying to empower corporate ambition to meet their targets. “In the last 20 to 30 years, technology has moved from supporting the business, to enabling the business, to increasingly becoming the business,” he says. That shift has transformed corporate technology leadership. Once, CIOs were judged largely on uptime, efficiency and cost control. Today, the question is whether an enterprise has the infrastructure to launch new digital services across markets in weeks rather than months. For Tata Communications, the evolution has also been internal. Long associated with global connectivity, the company is positioning itself as a digital infrastructure and intelligence partner. The story is no longer only about pipes and bandwidth, but about platforms, AI readiness, cybersecurity and measurable business outcomes. A decade ago, customers came to Tata Communications with a simple request: connect one location to another. “Ten or fifteen years back, the prime reason clients talked to us was: can you connect country A to country B, data centre A to data centre B?” Sarkar recalls. “Transactional connectivity and interconnected data centres are all still important, but it’s now just one part of the story.” Enterprises today operate across multiple clouds, legacy and modern applications, overlapping cybersecurity tools and fragmented data. What they need is not another layer of complexity, but a partner who can simplify and orchestrate it. Tata Communications has built its business around that shift. Today, it positions itself as a digital infrastructure and intelligence partner. Its network fabric still underpins global connectivity, but it now sits alongside cloud and edge capabilities, security services, digital platforms and customer experience tools. The aim is to help enterprises connect, secure and control complex environments end to end. The story is no longer only about pipes and bandwidth, but about platforms, AI readiness, cybersecurity and measurable business outcomes. That evolution has changed not just what the company offers, but whom it serves. “Yesterday it was just the chief network officer,” Sarkar says. “Today the buying centre has expanded to several functions - the CMO, CDO, CTO, CIO and line-of-business leaders. Decisions on customer experience don’t always sit with IT any more.” As a result, Tata Communications’ teams have moved from selling technology to selling outcomes: revenue growth, cost efficiency, customer experience, resilience and security. The question is no longer whether a network is fast, but whether the architecture can support the business model the organisation wants to build. Sarkar’s view of the future begins with a contradiction at the heart of the AI boom. Boardrooms are moving quickly, but enterprise infrastructure is often the least regarded vector in the equation. “There is a widening gap between AI ambition and AI readiness,” he says. “Boardroom ambitions have perhaps moved faster than the infrastructure required to support these ambitions.” The mistake, he argues, is treating transformation as a purchase, and buying the latest model, tool or cloud service to automatically deliver transformation. “Technology is the easy part to buy,” he says. “The harder questions are those that technology alone cannot answer. What business outcome are you actually trying to change? Can your operating model support it? Can your data move across the organisation? Will your people adopt it? And can your infrastructure scale it securely?” Many companies can build impressive AI demonstrations quickly. The challenge is turning pilots into production systems connected to real workflows, governed data and secure infrastructure. Without that foundation, AI risks becoming a boardroom showcase rather than an operating advantage. The rise of AI agents will make those questions more urgent. Sarkar believes organisations may soon manage more digital agents than human employees. “You and I walk into an office with an ID card. Agents don’t,” he says. “How do you identify, govern and securely manage them? What are they allowed to access? What actions can they take? Can we trace why they made a decision and pivot quickly if it’s not the right move?” His conclusion is clear: the real AI story is increasingly an infrastructure story, not simply one about models and GPUs. Hybrid cloud is where many of the stress fractures are already visible.

events.title: askST Jobs: I keep having to pick up a colleague’s work. How should I raise it with my boss?
events.summary: An employee’s role is to highlight the issue and its impact, while managing the colleague’s performance is ultimately the manager’s responsibility. - Workers should raise workload concerns calmly, with clear examples of extra tasks, missed deadlines and work they covered for a colleague. - Experts say to avoid blame, scorekeeping and phrases like ‘pulling their weight’; focus on the impact on the team and ask for solutions. - Managers should be asked to clarify duties, rebalance work or reset priorities, while performance issues remain the boss’s responsibility. In this series, business correspondent Timothy Goh offers practical answers to candid questions on navigating workplace challenges and getting ahead in your career. Get more tips by signing up to The Straits Times’ Headstart newsletter . How can employees raise concerns about an uneven workload without blaming a colleague? Raising a genuine workload concern is not the same as complaining, but the difference lies in how employees present it, said Michelle Koh, managing director at executive search firm The Edge Partnership. “Raise the issue when you are calm rather than in a moment of frustration... If you approach your manager when emotions are running high, it can easily come across as a complaint about a person rather than a genuine concern about the work,” she said. Before speaking to their manager, employees should have specific examples ready, including the tasks they have taken over, deadlines they have stepped in to meet and instances where responsibilities have fallen back on them. “Avoid sweeping statements such as ‘I’m always doing their work’ unless you can back them up,” said Koh. “Keep the conversation focused on the impact on the work and the team – once it sounds like an attack on your colleague, it becomes personal and your point gets lost.” Koh noted that it also helps to remember that employees may not know the full circumstances behind a colleague’s performance. Their role is to highlight the issue and its impact, while managing the colleague’s performance is ultimately the manager’s responsibility. “Above all, go into the conversation looking for a solution... Ask whether responsibilities can be clarified, workloads redistributed or priorities reset,” she said. Tan Weixi, managing partner at Workplace Asia, said the biggest mistake employees can make when raising concerns about a colleague is framing the issue around whether the person is “pulling their weight”. “That is a judgment, and it puts the boss in the uncomfortable position of having to referee between two employees,” he said. Employees should also avoid keeping a running scorecard of every mistake and instead focus on patterns that genuinely affect the delivery of work, Tan said. Where appropriate, they could speak to the colleague first, as there may be circumstances that they are unaware of. “Don’t make your boss the judge of your colleague. Make your boss aware of the work problem – and be clear about what you need them to help resolve,” he said. Timothy Goh is a business correspondent at The Straits Times. He covers commodities and currencies, with occasional forays into listed companies.
