events.title: Aaron Sorkin’s ‘The Social Reckoning’ is off to a weak start
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. “The Social Reckoning,” Aaron Sorkin’s follow-up to “The Social Network,” is on track to make only $5.5 million at the domestic box office this weekend, according to Sunday estimates. That’s below the already underwhelming $7 million to $8 million the studio had projected, and it means Sorkin’s new movie is unlikely to become a “Social Network”-sized hit. The earlier film had a $22 million opening weekend and made a total of $97 million domestically (and that’s at 2010 ticket prices). It also won Sorkin an Oscar and became one of most influential on-screen depictions of Silicon Valley and startup culture. Beyond the fate of a single film, the weekend box office could also offer hints about audience excitement, or lack thereof, as we kick off a fall full of movies starring villainous, real-world tech CEOs . There’s Alex Gibney’s four-hour documentary “Musk” (which also opened this weekend), Nathan Fielder’s apparently uncategorizable Elizabeth Holmes documentary “You Can See Everything” (coming next weekend!), and the OpenAI boardroom drama “Artificial” (which has a new distributor after being dropped by Amazon). Outside of theaters, Netflix also has a series called “The Altruists” coming in November , telling the story of Sam Bankman-Fried and the collapse of FTX. As for “The Social Reckoning,” while “The Social Network” was a notable success, the theatrical landscape has changed significantly in the last 16 years. And where the first film focused on the excitement and drama of Facebook’s early days, the sequel is darker and heavier — it’s all about whistleblower Frances Haugen’s decision to leak what became known as the Facebook files. So maybe a movie about Senate hearings and algorithm changes was never going to be a big hit. Or maybe the real audience is among older moviegoers who have only returned sporadically to theaters . And I wonder if critiquing Facebook feels a bit less urgent to audiences who are more likely to be losing sleep over AI. Maybe just as importantly, the new movie’s reviews just aren’t very good . (For what it’s worth, I enjoyed “The Social Reckoning” but will fully admit that it’s overloaded with Sorkin’s trademark speechifying. And I couldn’t help dreaming about a version directed — like the original — by David Fincher, with a score by Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross.) “Musk,” meanwhile, made $69,000 during its opening weekend in four theaters. It will roll out more broadly in the coming weeks, but given its length and subject matter, the documentary will probably reach many more viewers once it starts streaming on HBO Max. events.title: Mildura and South Australia connected by bus service after six-year hiatus
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts New bus service re-establishes link between Mildura and South Australia The Monty Express can drop Mildura residents off in South Australia, and SA residents off in Mildura. ( ABC News: Wade Stephens ) The Monty Express coach will re-establish a direct road transport link between Mildura, Renmark and Adelaide. The route has not been serviced in almost six years. The service will make its first interstate journey on October 12. A new bus service has launched connecting Mildura in Victoria's north-west to South Australia. From this week, a bus named The Monty Express will be travelling the Sturt Highway between Sunraysia and Adelaide via Renmark. It has been nearly six years since the route was serviced, with Greyhound Australia canning its Mildura to Adelaide coaches in 2016 , and another bus company ceasing its operations in 2020, in the early stages of the COVID-19 pandemic. The lone direct flight between Mildura and Adelaide also no longer exists, with Rex Airlines terminating the service in May 2023. Ever since, getting into the festival state from Mildura involved detours via Ouyen, Horsham or Broken Hill, or at greater cost, flying to Adelaide via Melbourne or Sydney. The Monty Express will start taking passengers from October 12. ( ABC News: Wade Stephens ) Former Sunraysia resident Stuart Saunders ran a survey six months ago to gauge interest in restoring a Mildura to Adelaide bus service. He said support was overwhelming, and he soon prepared to pivot from his information technology career to become a bus driver. He purchased a 36-seat bus, which he named The Monty Express after the family's pet Cavoodle, Monty. "There's very much a sense of community in the coach industry," he said. Stuart Saunders and his family in front of their new business venture. ( ABC News: Wade Stephens ) The Mildura–Renmark–Adelaide service begins today. It will initially run twice a week, departing Adelaide on Mondays and Thursdays and returning on Tuesdays and Fridays. It will run as an express service with pick-ups at Mildura, Renmark, Adelaide Airport and the Adelaide Central Bus Station. Under a service agreement with the SA government, The Monty Express cannot pick up South Australian residents unless they go to Mildura. Stuart Saunders with his children, Matilda and Gabriel, wife, Melody and dog, Monty. ( ABC News: Wade Stephens ) The agreement exists to avoid impacting passenger numbers on the existing Stateliner coach service route between the Riverland and Adelaide. Mildura man Steven Haby describes himself as a transport enthusiast. The former Melburnian is a member of the Bus and Coach Society of Victoria and the Australian Timetable Association. He will be travelling from Mildura to Adelaide to experience the first service of The Monty Express on Monday. Steven Haby has booked his ticket on The Monty Express. ( Supplied: Steven Haby ) "I'm very much an advocate and supporter of public transport," Mr Haby says. "I thought this was a really good opportunity to support the service going forward and be one of the first passengers on the run. "You can have a sustainable public transport network in a city like Mildura … making it frequent, reliable, cheap, and to places where people want to go." Mr Saunders hopes The Monty Express will not only benefit Mildura residents, but will connect people in the Riverland with Sunraysia's V/Line bus services and flights. "Not only are we trying to give an express service into Adelaide from Mildura, but the challenges for the Riverland people trying to get into Mildura, I'm hoping we can solve some of their problems as well," he said. Tamille Hunter is a resident of Cobdogla, a South Australian town less than two hours from Mildura by car. Ms Hunter is unable to drive and has occasionally used existing transport options to get to Mildura. The journey she took involved catching a bus to Adelaide, a flight to Melbourne, a train to Swan Hill and a bus to Mildura. The Monty Express can seat as many as 36 passengers. ( ABC News: Wade Stephens ) "At the moment, for us to go to Mildura it takes us 24 hours and over $600," Ms Hunter said. She said getting The Monty Express to Mildura would open up lots of opportunities for her. "From there, I could visit my family and friends in Melbourne on the V/Line," she said.

events.title: Ongoing Birdsville Track closure hits outback businesses
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Birdsville Track's long-term closure hurting outback businesses Cooper Creek over the Birdsville Track, in June 2025. ( Supplied: Marree Roadhouse ) The Birdsville Track has been closed for 400 days of the past two years. The road is a major freight and tourism route cutting through outback South Australia and Queensland. Part of the track is expected to reopen next week, while northern sections could remain closed for many months. One of Australia's most iconic outback roads has been closed for 400 days out of the past two years due to rain damage, with remote businesses feeling the pinch. Stretching more than 500 kilometres, the Birdsville Track connects Birdsville in south-west Queensland, to Marree in far-north South Australia. It provides access to local pastoral properties to move cattle, allows stock to flow to the South Australian market and has become increasingly popular with outback tourists. The track is largely unsealed, meaning flooding and heavy rain have periodically closed the track over the years — but never for this long. Despite the challenges, Lyall Oldfield is "very happy" living in the outback. ( Supplied: Marree Roadhouse ) Marree Roadhouse owner Lyall Oldfield said his business was "probably one third of what it normally is". "It's just dreadful what's happening with the roads. It's not even a joke." Business at the Marree Roadhouse is one third of what it normally is. ( Supplied: Marree Roadhouse ) About 230km north of Marree is the Mungerannie Hotel, which was taken over by new owners in 2023. Three years later, the business has not opened all year, with road closures stopping the daily water deliveries it relies on. Cattle coming off Clifton Hills Station on the Birdsville Track in South Australia after flooding. ( Supplied: Pete Nunn ) Co-owner Andrew Norman said it was a similar tale in 2025, when there was "no sort of season whatsoever". Mr Norman said the closure north of Mungeranie is having the biggest impact, deterring tourists from making the trip. The Birdsville Track has sustained significant damage from rain events. ( Supplied: Department for Infrastructure and Transport ) Mungerannie Hotel secures water source The owners of the Mungerannie Hotel on the Birdsville Track will now truck 13,000 litres of water to the pub each day, after being told they can no longer use a nearby bore. "Nobody's really coming up to Mungeranie to turn around and go back," Mr Norman said. "If they can get that road open just north of us and get the Birdsville Track open, next year should be fine. "If the track is open, we'll be open. But without a track, we're not open." The SA Department for Infrastructure and Transport hoped to reopen the 200km section between Marree and Mungeranie "next week", but the route north of Mungeranie is expected to remain closed for some time. Large parts of the Birdsville Track remain underwater. ( Supplied: Department of Infrastructure and Transport ) Regional north and outback road maintenance manager Juanita Chester said with some northern parts of the Birdsville Track still underwater, it would be "several more months before [the department] can even consider reopening". While the construction of a single-lane access route has been considered, Ms Chester said the local pits where materials are sourced have flooded too. The track has sustained damage from several significant rain events in the past 24 months. ( Supplied: Department for Infrastructure and Transport ) "They're like a dam when it rains, they fill with water," she said. "If we can't get in there to get material, there's very little we can do short of carting material from a long, long way away, which then impacts the roads." The department is assessing the scope and price of the remaining work, which will then require approval before it can begin, and Ms Chester said this would be unlikely in the next two months.

events.title: From crane rental to marine transport: How this third-gen leader is steering his family business up the value chain
events.summary: Led by Michael Ang, Tiong Woon Corporation, multiple award winners at the Singapore Corporate Awards 2026, is investing in talent and engineering expertise to take on haulage and large-scale projects Tiong Woon Corporation chief executive officer Michael Ang is steering the third-generation family business beyond its crane-rental roots. It is past midnight in Pasir Ris. With sections of the road closed to traffic, massive precast girders are lifted, manoeuvred into position and lowered onto their supports for a new flyover. Beam-launching work like this is usually done overnight, when there is enough space to move heavy equipment safely with minimal disruption to other road users. Behind the operation is Tiong Woon Corporation, whose role in projects like this reflects how far the business has moved beyond its beginnings in crane rental and transport. In recent years, the 48-year-old family business has expanded into engineering and marine services, allowing it to take on bigger and more complex projects. Its fleet has grown with that ambition: The company now operates several hundred cranes, with the single largest rated at 2,200 tonnes. “A lot of people still perceive Tiong Woon as purely a crane rental company,” says chief executive officer Michael Ang. “Crane rental is still our core business, but we also offer marine, transport and engineering services. We want to show our clients and stakeholders that we can provide a more integrated solution.” For Ang, who joined the company 23 years ago, the transformation is also part of his role as the third-generation leader of his family business. Tiong Woon’s first 300-tonne crane, acquired from Soon Douglas in 1987. His grandfather, the late Ang Choo Kim, founded Tiong Woon in 1978 with a single 20-tonne crane. Two years later, the business was incorporated as Tiong Woon Crane & Transport by the next generation of the family. Today, Ang represents the third generation of leadership, while his father, Ang Kah Hong, serves as executive chairman and his uncle, Ang Kha King, remains on the board as an executive director. His family’s involvement across several generations has deepened his understanding of how far the company has evolved from its beginnings as a crane and transport operator. Over the past five years, Tiong Woon has worked towards an integrated model that combines its heavy lift equipment with its haulage and marine fleet and engineering expertise. Instead of supplying a crane or vehicle, it aims to take on more parts of a project and provide customers with a more complete heavy lift solution. For contractors and project owners, that can mean dealing with one company rather than coordinating several across different stages of a job. The Tiong Woon team dismantling a 200-tonne gantry crane at PSA Singapore, an example of the more integrated heavy-lift work the company now undertakes. The company is also expanding into new sectors. Oil and gas, petrochemical and construction firms have traditionally made up the bulk of its customer base. Data centres, semiconductors and biopharmaceuticals are newer targets. In February 2026, the company announced more than $40 million worth of projects across the semiconductor, public infrastructure and biopharmaceutical sectors, ranging from crane deployment to lifting engineering and project support. But taking on more complex work requires more than a larger fleet and workforce. Today, the company has about 1,300 employees across Singapore and markets including Malaysia, Thailand, India and Saudi Arabia, and is looking to hire more crane operators, engineers and technicians as the business expands. As the company tries to move up the value chain, its next stage of growth will depend not only on adding physical assets, but on building the human expertise needed to take on bigger projects and new revenue streams. A 4,500-tonne module being loaded out at Laem Chabang, Thailand, where Tiong Woon is expanding its heavy-lift capabilities. In the last financial year ended June 2026 (FY2026), the wage bill reached $65 million, about a third of revenue. “Our single largest investment is actually our human capital,” says group chief financial officer William Tan. The challenge is particularly apparent in Singapore, where Tiong Woon has more cranes than operators, Tan says, reflecting the shortage of skilled trades workers in the built environment sector. Knowing when to move, and when to wait In December 2023, Tiong Woon formed a strategic alliance in Thailand with Netherlands-headquartered heavy lift specialist Mammoet and acquired heavy lift, haulage and transportation equipment to strengthen its capabilities and position in the market. The move reflects the broader direction of the business: using the heavy lift expertise it has built in Singapore over decades as a base to take on a larger and more complex role in overseas projects.

events.title: This intelligence building is top secret. Here's what we know about it
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts This National Security Office Precinct will cost more than $1 billion. What do we know about it? Some details about the National Security Office Precinct were revealed to Senate estimates in May. ( ABC News: Callum Flinn ) A stone's throw from Parliament House, six giant cranes have been working on the biggest Commonwealth construction project in Canberra in almost 40 years. The development of a National Security Office Precinct has been heralded by the federal government as a solution to "critical accommodation and capability requirements" of several agencies. Despite the huge scale of the project, many of the details have been kept secret. We know the precinct in Barton will be utilised by a range of Commonwealth entities. That includes the Office of National Intelligence and the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT). In Senate estimates in May, we heard some details and there may be more to come. Construction of the National Security Office Precinct in Canberra continues. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) "We are engaging with other agencies as part of the development for the precinct going forward," said Nick McClintock of the Department of Finance, which is leading the development. Next to the main buildings, there will also be hospitality and retail venues, servicing both the wider public and workers in the precinct. Up to 5,000 workers are expected to be based at the precinct. At the sod turning for the project, Finance Minister and ACT senator Katy Gallagher said a "purpose built" and "specifically designed" building was needed to allow the national intelligence community "to do the work they need to do in a changing world". "[It's] clearly needed in terms of our national security agencies being able to work in a facility that actually allows them to do their job properly." Katy Gallagher says the new building will be more secure. ( ABC News: Pete Garnish ) She said the precinct would be "more appropriate" and "more secure" than existing buildings, with several government agencies reaching, or at, capacity. The project's price tag has not been revealed because of "commercial-in-confidence and national security sensitivities". But, we know it will cost at least $1 billion. "It is the most significant investment we've seen in the territory in a long time," Senator Gallagher said in 2023. The total cost of the precinct is expected to be revealed publicly once it's completed. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) She also told Senate estimates "it is a very significant infrastructure spend" and she has also described it as a "multi-year billion-dollar investment". The final cost is expected to be revealed publicly, but only after construction is completed. The precinct is the biggest Commonwealth construction project in Canberra since the development of the new Parliament House, which opened in 1988. Senator Gallagher has previously rejected claims Canberra had missed out on its fair share in recent federal budgets, pointing to the precinct as an example of spending in the territory. Construction is expected to be completed by the end of 2028, with the precinct starting to be occupied from 2029. The federal government has said the project will support more than 10,000 jobs over the construction period, which commenced in late 2024. The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade is consolidating its presence in the ACT into two new buildings. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) Due to the "security requirements" of the project, it was exempt from needing the green light of the public works committee, which scrutinises major public capital expenditure projects. We also haven't seen any artist impressions or plans for the precinct, which means we won't know exactly what it will look like for a while yet. The precinct is being built on the site of a former car park. What happens to the buildings after agencies move out? A Department of Finance spokesperson said as existing buildings were "privately owned commercial properties", their future use was a commercial decision for the landlords. We know DFAT is consolidating its presence in the ACT into two new buildings — the precinct and another new building also being built in Barton. The head office of the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade will be vacated. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) It means its current head office, the RG Casey building, will be vacated. The lease is due to run out in 2031, and as noted by the department, its future after that will be up to the private landlord. events.title: Trump bears down on Zelensky as Russia keeps up attacks on Ukraine
events.summary: President Trump's announcement Sunday about an "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine referred to a potential deal that includes each side stopping attacks on oil refineries — and he expects Volodymyr Zelensky to abide by it, a White House official said. The official said if attacks on oil refineries cease, a deal to stop hitting power plants and energy grids could come next. Why it matters: Trump appears to be singlehandedly trying to will a partial ceasefire into existence. But for now Russia hasn't accepted any kind of ceasefire — and Ukraine wants one that forbids attacks on power plants. Reality check: The "refinery for refinery" proposal, as the official dubbed it, is lopsided. A Ukrainian official told Axios that the country has a single oil refinery which the Russians have attacked multiple times and isn't fully functional. Russia, by contrast, has a vast network of refineries. "We import diesel and gas. What we need is for the Russians to stop attacking our electricity grid," the Ukrainian official said. "The Russians are thinking about" it, the White House official said. "We will know soon if they are ready." Case in point: Hours after Trump's announcement, Russia conducted strikes on power plants in Ukraine, according to Ukrainian media. What he said: Trump's Truth Social post sounded at first like a major breakthrough. "Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!" he wrote. It appears much more tenuous than that. Zelensky said the announced ceasefire "was news for me." State of play: After reaching a deal with Russia Friday to lift diesel sanctions, Trump remains focused on stopping Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries. He believes the strikes are driving up U.S. gas prices. White House officials warn that Ukraine's attacks on Russian refineries are hurting Zelensky's relationship with Trump more than they're damaging Russia. "Trump is really mad. He feels Zelensky is taking the U.S. for granted," the White House official said. Zoom in: Amid the crisis with Ukraine, presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have put their planned trip to Moscow on hold, at least until they get clarity on whether Ukraine and the Europeans are ready to agree to a new unified proposal for Putin. A Ukrainian official told Axios on Friday that during a meeting with U.S. negotiators in Miami on Friday, Witkoff and Kushner threatened that Trump could stop sharing U.S. intelligence if it continued to ignore his requests. A U.S. official denied that, saying Witkoff and Kushner told the Ukrainians that the U.S. was a strong partner, providing munitions and intelligence. Ukraine therefore shouldn't take actions that hurt American consumers, the two said. On Sunday, the Financial Times reported that the U.S. told European countries it might stop selling weapons to Ukraine through NATO if Ukraine continues to strike Russian refineries.

events.title: Insurer underpaid hundreds of NSW accident victims in 'mind-blowing' error
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts NRMA Insurance underpaid hundreds of injured motorists in NSW since 2019 NRMA Insurance initially estimated that about 700 people had been underpaid, a number later revised down to 400. ( Facebook: NRMA Insurance ) Hundreds of people injured in car accidents have been repaid by NRMA Insurance after the company miscalculated some compulsory third party benefits since 2019. The company said 700 people were affected but the number was later revised down to 400. Neither the insurer nor the State Insurance Regulatory Authority noticed the error. NRMA Insurance has been forced to repay hundreds of people who were injured in motor vehicle accidents, after failing to correctly calculate some compulsory third party (CTP) benefits since 2019. The original error was not detected by the insurer, nor was it noticed by NSW's State Insurance Regulatory Authority (SIRA), despite it having previously launched an audit of the company's practices. Instead, the mistake was spotted by a lawyer who realised their client's weekly payments did not add up. Neither the insurer nor the State Insurance Regulatory Authority picked up on the original error. ( Supplied ) Initially, NRMA Insurance estimated about 700 people who had been injured in motor vehicle accidents had been underpaid, before revising the number down to 400. However, the company told the ABC it had also identified a "further cohort" of people it believed were owed interest, after previously receiving lump sum payments. Greens MP Abigail Boyd said NRMA Insurance, a trading name of Insurance Australia Limited, should have been capable of indexing payments correctly. "It actually blows my mind," she said. Abigail Boyd says it was "extraordinary" that NRMA had not discovered the issue itself. ( Four Corners: Rob Hill ) She said it was "particularly extraordinary" that NRMA had not discovered the issue itself. "You have this massive power differential between these insurers and these injured people who are going through some of the worst times of their lives. "[Yet] it's somehow expected that [the victims] are the ones, or their lawyers … that will pick up these errors." Under the state's CTP scheme, people injured in motor vehicle accidents are entitled to income support payments if they are unable to work as a result. It starts at 95 per cent of their pre-accident weekly earnings, before dropping to a maximum of 85 per cent from 14 weeks onwards, depending on their capacity to work. The payments, made by CTP insurers like NRMA Insurance, are supposed to be adjusted twice a year, in line with average weekly earnings. The insurer markets itself as a "help company". ( Supplied: NRMA ) However, NRMA Insurance, which markets itself as "a help company", acknowledged it had incorrectly applied this principle, costing the average affected claimant $940. "We became aware in late April this year, through a customer's legal representative, that the statutory indexation may not have been correctly applied to weekly benefit payments for customers who continued receiving payments more than 78 weeks after their accident," a spokesperson said. "Our investigation confirmed an error in the application of indexation in our system, which has been corrected. We apologised to the customer, paid the amount outstanding (and interest) and notified the regulator." NRMA Insurance, which is a separate entity to the NRMA, said it had recently completed the process of repaying customers, along with the interest they were owed. "We sincerely apologised to all affected customers," the spokesperson said. This is not the first time NRMA Insurance has failed to properly pay the required weekly benefits to people who have been injured in motor vehicle accidents. In February 2023, SIRA issued a letter of censure to the company, after finding it had contravened NSW legislation and its licence conditions by underpaying more than 2,000 customers. NRMA Insurance repaid more than $735,000 to those affected, but it was not fined. In March the same year, another censure letter was issued over the late processing of weekly benefits. No fine was issued. And in June 2023, SIRA sent another censure letter to NRMA Insurance over delays in commencing weekly payments. No financial penalty was imposed. In 2023, NRMA Insurance had to repay more than $735,000 to people injured in car accidents. ( ABC News: Adriane Reardon ) Ms Boyd said SIRA's enforcement actions to date had given NRMA Insurance little incentive to raise its standards.

events.title: Gas shortage culprit to slip through reservation 'loopholes', say critics
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Critics say 'Santos-sized loopholes' will make gas reservation a joke Liquefied natural gas ships from Curtis Island in Queensland. ( Supplied: Photopia Studio ) Gas market players say the federal government's draft gas reservation scheme has been weakened by loopholes. They argue that changes to the policy favour the Santos-led GLNG venture, which has been blamed for rising prices on the east coast. The government is expected to release legislation for the scheme in the coming weeks. A giant LNG plant blamed by critics for driving up east coast gas prices could largely or totally escape a federal scheme designed to protect local buyers, observers have warned. The Albanese government last month released a draft plan to force gas exporters to set aside up to 20 per cent of their production for the domestic market in a bid to force prices lower. But analysts and industry players say the draft is full of loopholes that will allow some exporters to reduce or even eliminate their exposure. They point to the Gladstone LNG project, a plant on Curtis Island in Queensland that is operated by Adelaide-based Santos, as the exporter most likely to benefit. An ABC investigation revealed GLNG had sucked up and exported the equivalent of 20 per cent of eastern Australia's domestic gas demand over the past 10 years. This was because the venture built an LNG plant with a capacity of 7.8 million tonnes a year despite not having nearly enough gas of its own to fill it. By contrast, the other two LNG projects in Queensland — run by global super-major Shell and Australian company Origin along with US firm ConocoPhillips — had overwhelmingly been supplying the local market in net terms. Paul Farrow is unsympathetic to Santos. ( ABC News: Kit Mochan ) Australian Workers' Union (AWU) national secretary Paul Farrow said "Santos-sized loopholes" threatened to turn the government's reservation plans into a joke. Mr Farrow said that, compared with earlier iterations of the plan, the draft had been watered down in significant ways that appeared to favour GLNG above all others. "Australian industry and Australian consumers deserve to derive an advantage from Australia's gas because it's our sovereign wealth," Mr Farrow said. "The government is so close to getting it right. "But the exposure draft, as it stands, contains a bunch of Santos-sized loopholes. Curtis Island in Gladstone is home to three gas plants that export Australian gas. ( Supplied: Nearmap ) Under the draft policy, the Australian Energy Regulator would be able to reduce an exporter's supply obligation below 20 per cent, while the minister could cut it to zero. But critics say a raft of other provisions in the bill could enable Santos and its GLNG partners to slip the net themselves. They say the draft, unlike earlier iterations, effectively allows GLNG to count contract extensions as "existing contracts" that are exempt from consideration. Crucially, this would allow GLNG to extend a supply agreement with South Korea's KOGAS for five years from 2030. The current deal is for 3.5 million tonnes of LNG a year, an amount equivalent to about 40 per cent of annual east coast gas demand. Observers also say the draft will give rise to "take-or-pay" deals that allow Santos to generate paper sales to the domestic market without actually supplying any gas. And they argue the government has given too much ground to Santos over questions about whether the company can "reasonably" find enough gas without breaking export contracts. Mr Farrow said the provision should require Santos to explore all practical options, such as buying gas from other providers in the local market, substituting LNG cargoes from its international operations or using flexibility in its contracts to reduce overseas sales. Instead, he said the draft appeared to allow Santos itself to set those terms, which he argued the company would do so however it liked. "If a massive project like GLNG wants to claim that it simply doesn't have enough gas to share with the Australian market, it should have to prove it's actually explored all practical options to get hold of that gas," Mr Farrow said. "These options might incur a small cost for Santos' shareholders. The government hopes its reservation plans can encourage more gas wells. ( ABC News: Hamish Harty ) As well as these provisions, Mr Farrow said the draft contained other clauses that would allow GLNG off the hook. Among them was a so-called "additional gas" test. While Mr Farrow said the test was theoretically supposed to encourage new production and increase supplies, in reality he said it was likely to be gamed.

events.title: Citroen revives the 2CV for an electric age
events.summary: French carmaker Citroen has brought back its 2CV brand in a bid to boost sales of electric cars in a difficult market. The new model, unveiled at the Paris Motor Show, is a small city runabout with retro styling which harks back to one of the company's most famous designs. As a "concept car" intended to show Citroen's direction of travel, it is not yet ready to go on sale but the plan is to have a version in showrooms by 2028. As they face mounting competition from Chinese manufacturers, Citroen and other European brands are exploiting their heritage as a means of selling modern motors. Citroen chief executive Xavier Chardon described the new car as "a modern, ingenious and refreshing response to the mobility challenges of tomorrow". The original Citroen 2CV was launched in 1948, as Europe was recovering from the ravages of World War Two. It was designed as a cheap, robust way for French farmers and country folk to get around. The car had high wheel arches and soft suspension, letting it travel across a ploughed field or rough roads - as legend would have it, without breaking a tray of duck eggs. Its high roof let drivers wear a hat at the wheel. It was easy to drive and simple to repair. The car was so popular, it remained in production for more than 40 years. Over time, it went from being a utilitarian tool for the countryside to a cult classic, and a favourite of hippies and counter-culturalists. Fans of Citroën's 2CV hold annual meet-ups such as this muddy gathering in Switzerland Now, Citroen wants to draw on that heritage to sell an electric, small city car that is expected to sell for about £13,000. The look of the new 2CV may well evolve as Citroen develops its design. But as it stands, it shares plenty of styling features with its famous predecessor. The high, flared wheel arches, the tall, curved roof and the eye-like headlights are all reminders of the original "deux chevaux" or "two horses". By using memories of an old car to sell a new one, Citroen is following a well-travelled road. VW notoriously brought back the Beetle in the late 1990s, with limited success. BMW's Minis have always carried styling designed to hark back to the very British original. Fiat has been selling a retro-styled Fiat 500 for the past two decades. But the retro-nostalgia trend has accelerated recently, as carmakers have looked for ways to sell electric cars to sceptical consumers. Citroen's French rival, Renault, has led the charge. It started with the Renault 5 E-Tech, which visually echoed the distinctive boxy styling of the original Renault 5, once an ever-present sight on French streets. It has since revived the Renault 4 and Twingo brands as well. VW has the distinctive ID-Buzz minivan, a throwback to the classic T2 Transporter, while Ford is working on a new EV which is widely expected to be called the Fiesta. Rachel Burgess, senior editor of Autocar magazine, thinks it is a strategy that makes perfect sense. "It's a brilliant differentiator from all-new car brands", she says. "An older audience might remember the originals and feel warmly towards them, and a younger audience might find an appeal in the retro aspect." Finding new ways to make cars appealing has become more important than ever, at a time when European manufacturers are facing growing competition from Chinese brands. "Many in the industry believe the big automotive players in Europe…face a very serious existential threat from aggressive Chinese manufacturers," says David Leggett, automotive editor at Global Data. Back to the future: VW looked to the past when designing its ID-Buzz minivan In this hostile business environment, heritage and nostalgia could prove to be powerful weapons for more established brands, thinks automotive researcher and author Dr Paul Nieuwenhuis. "In a world where a wave of credible decent quality Chinese EVs are hitting Europe, linking European designs back to their history while using the latest powertrain technology is something the Chinese cannot do," he says. "The Chinese can establish new design trends, but there is limited history there." But Leggett thinks Citroen will need more than a heady whiff of nostalgia to turn its new car into a best-seller. "A reimagined Citroën 2CV should give a big nod to its ancestor - especially on price and design simplicity as well as visual cues," he says. "But it also needs to be a credible modern electric car in terms of functionality and features, with widespread appeal." On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast , Sean O’Kane, Rebecca Bellan, and I discussed Amazon’s announcement, which came in the middle of a longer blog post making the case that data centers are actually good for communities. Rebecca was a bit skeptical that the recent spate of data center moratoriums will have a lasting effect, especially since the moratoriums only last for a year or two and “these data centers aren’t coming online for the next two, three, four, five years,” though I countered that data center backers definitely seem worried. Sean, meanwhile, suggested that a big reason for the backlash is the industry’s poor communication. “We’ve seen, through a lot of the controversy and backlash to AI and data centers, that the industry just does a really poor job explaining itself, and that they are obviously and constantly frustrated with the fact that most people can’t envision a world in which this stuff is useful for them,” he said. Keep reading for a preview of our conversation , edited for length and clarity. Sean: It’s an interesting thing that it was sort of buried in the blog post and part of a larger story that Amazon’s clearly trying to tell. I guess I understand why they weren’t putting it in the foreground, but to me, this is at the root of so many of the problems that the tech industry currently faces when it comes to AI broadly, but data centers in particular. There are so many things that could be said about whether or not people should be worried about the effect that data centers have on their property values, on their electricity bills, on their water usage in the area, and whether or not those things are real problems, inflated problems, etc. I think so much of that just really goes back to the fact that a lot of these projects are being negotiated essentially in secret. Sometimes they’re being negotiated [with the public knowing] that it’s a data center, but just not knowing who’s actually going to use it or occupy it at any point. This is a long-standing issue with the tech industry. I always go back to the mid-2010s when Uber was expanding really fast. Uber was one of the companies that really used this tactic a ton when it came to working with local governments. In particular, I remember I was working at The Verge at the time and we had a freelancer write a story about a city outside of Orlando where Uber was trying to negotiate tax subsidies to subsidize rides for people to use public transit after the Uber trip. The whole thing was negotiated in secret. And not only that, which was frustrating on its face, but also, because of the secrecy, you could just see Uber getting really comfortable with asking for a lot of other stuff, too. So there needs to be more of this. I’m glad Amazon’s doing this. We’ll see if it actually does have any positive effect, but people are pretty entrenched right now. Rebecca: Yeah, I’m curious about what effect this will have and whether it will lead to communities successfully delaying or or killing any infrastructure that the companies need to build. What I’ve heard from some people I’ve spoken to, who deal with data centers every day, a lot of these moratoriums that are getting passed — and there are a significant number of them, including one recently in San Francisco , which is pretty ironic — but they’re only for like a year or two years. But these data centers aren’t coming online for the next two, three, four, five years. All of the buildouts are going to be massively delayed for a number of reasons from zoning to funding. Of course, if the pushback keeps going, then it might have an effect, but I often wonder just how much of an effect this political pushback is having on this. Anthony: The moratorium I’m most familiar with is the one in New York . I believe it’s a one-year moratorium, and that’s on permits for large projects. [Technically, it’s until the state finalizes an environmental review process, which is expected to take a year.] So already, there’s some wiggle room within that. And often, they’re framed as: “It’s not like we think [data centers are] bad, let’s not do this. It’s [that] we need to take the time to study this.” Which gives them a lot of room to say later on, “Actually, we’ve decided this is great. We love it.” But you can tell that the people trying to build these data centers are worried, which is why you have these unhinged tweets from people like Trump or David Sacks. Only time will tell in terms of how long and how deep that [community] resistance is, but I do think they are worried.

events.title: Trump sticks with tariffs even as US voters turn against them before the midterms
events.summary: President Donald Trump shows no signs of budging from a trade policy that many Americans don't like as the midterm elections loom NEW YORK -- Maybe President Donald Trump really does believe that “tariff” is the most beautiful word in the dictionary . Despite higher prices, criticism from trade experts and displeasure among voters, Trump holds fast to his belief that imposing the highest import duties on U.S. trading partners since the Great Depression is a winner . A recent poll suggests that is a big gamble with less than a month before the Nov. 3 midterms. Most U.S. adults disapprove of his trade policies, with more than 64% saying he has gone too far with his latest tariffs, compared with 58% in January. A look at the political, legal and economic challenges to the Republican president's approach to trade. The United States has set taxes on imports from most countries in the low double digits, although the rates have gone up and down because of legal setbacks as well as Trump's habit of changing them seemingly on a whim . In the biggest round last year, Trump levied what he called “reciprocal” tariffs and other duties on dozens of countries. He cited a 1977 law that he said allowed him to act without congressional approval in an economic emergency. After the Supreme Court struck that down in February, Trump turned to an array of other trade laws to accomplish his goals. The primary one he is using now, Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 , allows him to impose tariffs on countries that he believes are engaging in unfair trade practices, such as not adequately enforcing a ban on forced labor. The new duties range from 10% to 12.5% on imports from 60 economies, including big U.S. trading partners such as the European Union, India, Japan, Canada and Mexico. Trump is taking a sledgehammer to a relatively open global trading system that many mainstream economists think has benefited the U.S. enormously. It has helped boost growth, keep prices low and make U.S. businesses more competitive and often dominant in global industries. The U.S. is the second-largest exporter in the world, after China. It exported $3.4 trillion in goods and services last year, far ahead of third place Germany’s $2.3 trillion. Although Trump claims foreign exporters are paying tariffs, it is mostly Americans who are footing the bill. Studies, including ones from New York Fed and Harvard , have shown that overseas companies have largely not lowered their prices to offset the tariffs that U.S. businesses pay at the border. Those businesses are absorbing the added costs or passing them along to consumers through higher prices. Hurricane Isaias: At least 4 dead as Isaias downgraded Fort Hood survivors speak out on Pentagon's decision to livestream Hasan's execution Christa Pike asked 'Where am I?' after waking up following botched execution: Lawyer The White House responds that the factory boom is already underway and points to statistics showing that manufacturing jobs, after falling last year, are on the upswing and work in certain nonresidential construction trades is rising, too. “Factory construction jobs of today mean more manufacturing jobs down the road once those factories come online,” said White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers. In the four years after China joined the World Trade Organization in 2001, nearly 3 million U.S. manufacturing jobs were lost, accelerating a shift away from factory work. Even global trade enthusiasts recognize the damage. Many U.S. companies struggled to compete with an influx of discounted products from China, which has suppressed consumption to encourage exports It also is true that some countries have higher tariffs than the U.S., manipulate their currencies lower to ensure to make their exports to the U.S. cheaper and help industries with subsidies. But tariffs among U.S. major trading partners are low, often comparable to U.S. rates and sometimes lower. Before the trade war, the U.S. rate averaged 1.47% for goods from the European Union, slightly above the average 1.35% imposed by the EU on American products , according to the Brussels think tank Bruegel. Europeans are big buyers of what America wants to sell. About 30% of European imports are from U.S.-owned companies, according to the European Central Bank. The relationship with Canada, America's big trading partner to the north, was also similar before trade talks broke down this summer. Canada's effective tariff rate on U.S. imports was about 2.4%, less than half the 5% that the U.S. had on Canadian imports, according to calculations by Oxford Economics. I’m back from a sojourn through New Hampshire’s White Mountains — a few days of respite before Disrupt 2026 , TechCrunch’s annual tech conference in San Francisco. Now, after a few days immersed in fall colors, I am ready for the action. And there is gonna be a lot of it. Self-driving truck companies Aurora Innovation and Kodiak AI received a federal exemption this week that removes a massive barrier to commercialization. Under federal regulations, if a traditional big rig runs into trouble, the human driver must pull over, activate the hazard lights, and then physically place reflective warning triangles on the road within 10 minutes to alert other road users. But if a mechanical problem forces a self-driving truck to pull over, there’s no human driver to deploy those warning devices. It was a big enough hurdle that Aurora took federal safety regulators to court over the requirement. After the court denied its request for an exemption, the company escalated the fight to the District of Columbia Court of Appeals. (Companies did have a temporary waiver as it awaited a decision.) Now Aurora and other self-driving truck developers have been given the green light from the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration . The agency has granted a five-year exemption allowing companies to replace roadside warning devices, such as reflective warning triangles, with cab-mounted warning beacons. Check out Aurora’s first responders page to see how it works. Daniel Goff , vice president of external affairs at Kodiak AI, said the exemption will help the industry “usher in an autonomous era of freight movement on U.S. roads, one that can save lives and improve the efficiency of goods delivery.” Gerardo Interiano , Aurora’s head of government relations and public affairs, echoed that sentiment, saying the decision underscores the government’s recognition of the economic and community benefits of autonomous trucking. He described the high-visibility, cab-mounted warning beacons as a “critical, 21st-century solution that enhances roadside safety by immediately alerting other road users without ever needing to put a person in harm’s way.” One question I’m left with: Could these cab-mounted warning beacons eventually become standard equipment across the entire trucking industry? events.title: Trump’s deal with Putin will have little impact on US diesel prices, experts say
events.summary: Analysts say fuel will take weeks to ship and quantity is too small to affect prices, while full deal is unlikely to be met given damage to Russian refineries Trump announces partial ceasefire but Zelenskyy says deal is ‘news to me’ Donald Trump’s deal with Vladimir Putin to temporarily lift sanctions on US imports of Russian diesel will have little “meaningful” effect on motorists and businesses in the US and overseas, energy and foreign policy analysts have predicted. The US president infuriated Volodymyr Zelenskyy when he announced the deal on Friday, writing on Truth Social that the agreement with his Russia counterpart to supply millions of tonnes of diesel was essential to reduce fuel prices in the US, which have soared after his decision to go to war against Iran. The package announced by Trump involves 300,000 tonnes of diesel released immediately “to the American and global marketplace” followed by 500,000 tonnes in November and a further 1m tonnes after that. The 300,000 figure equates to about three-quarters of what the US would use in a day, according to calculations using figures from the US Energy Information Administration . “Diesel prices for Americans and, indeed, the world, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST! Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my greatest priority,” Trump posted. However, experts suggested that the quantities involved – and the time it will take for the supplies to arrive in the US – is “too little, too late” to affect current high diesel prices, which observers have linked to challenging Republican party polling numbers before next month’s midterm elections. US prices have surged by almost 70% since the start of the Iran war, to about $6.30 a gallon , according to American Automobile Association. In the UK, the average price of diesel climbed to a record £2 a litre earlier in October, and sat just below that mark on Friday. Ashley Kelty, an energy analyst with the investment bank Panmure Liberum, said: “It is not going to have any impact on prices. The first amount [due to be shipped to the US] is so small. “They are going to have to charter vessels, load them and transport the cargo to the US. That will take about three weeks – so we are pretty much at the end of the month and about a week before the midterms.” The US Treasury secretary, Scott ⁠Bessent, said on Sunday: “This is ​good ‌for the ​American ​people … bringing these diesel prices down.” However, Kelty said the diesel shipments would also cause complications in a global supply chain, including multinational companies having to work out which of its supplies originated from Russia and therefore might breach sanctions in other jurisdictions, including Europe . The US Treasury suspended sanctions on Russian diesel exports until 7 April as part of the deal, while keeping in place other sanctions on Russian products. Zelenskyy described Trump’s deal as a “weak decision”, saying it would encourage Russia to keep attacking Ukraine, but Trump then blamed Kyiv’s strikes on Russian energy infrastructure for rising fuel prices. Trump said Ukraine neeeded “a new leader” . On Sunday, Zelenskyy said he would be ready to stop hitting Russian oil refineries if Russia curbed its attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure. Trump later posted on Truth Social: “Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine . Both parties have agreed. Do not break it! Thank you for your attention to this matter.” Maximilian Hess, the founder of the political risk consultancy Enmetena Advisory and a fellow at the Foreign Policy Research Institute, said: “It will not have any meaningful domestic US effect or international effect given its full terms are highly unlikely to be met as a result of the impact of Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian refining which have limited its diesel output. “The whole point of the deal for Putin is that it fails, which he can blame on Ukraine and thus stoke tensions between Trump and Zelenskyy. Indeed, it’s already working.”

events.title: Trump claims Russia and Ukraine agree to energy ceasefire
events.summary: President Trump claimed Sunday that Russia and Ukraine agreed to an " energy ceasefire " and will halt attacks on each other's energy facilities. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky tells Axios the announcement "was news for me. But if Russians agree to an energy ceasefire, Ukraine will agree." Why it matters: An "energy ceasefire" would be a dramatic diplomatic breakthrough ahead of the winter. It remains unclear if Russia indeed agreed to stop the strikes. Trump made a similar announcement last month, but neither party confirmed that there was a deal. Both Russia and Ukraine continued attacking energy infrastructure. What they're saying: "Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!" Trump wrote on Truth Social. In a short interview after Trump's announcement, Zelensky told Axios, "If President Trump negotiated it with Putin, please tell us when the ceasefire begins. We are ready, and we will accept it." Catch up quick: The announcement follows days of escalating tensions between Trump and Zelensky over Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries. On Friday, Trump announced a deal to ease sanctions on Russian diesel exports in an effort to lower soaring fuel prices, infuriating Ukraine. On Saturday, Trump called for Ukraine to replace Zelensky , accusing him of refusing opportunities to end the war. Zelensky responded Sunday on ABC's "This Week," saying Ukraine would hold elections if Russia agreed to a 60-day ceasefire. He also said Ukraine was prepared to stop attacking Russian refineries if Moscow halted strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure. The big picture: The war with Iran has driven up global fuel prices, intensifying pressure on Trump to deliver relief for American consumers. "It's more difficult to stop Putin than to pressure others," Zelensky told ABC on Sunday. Editor's note: This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

Sepsis, an acute inflammation triggered by infection, is a leading cause of childhood mortality, claiming roughly 3 million children under the age of five annually. Efferon , a startup selected as one of TechCrunch Disrupt 2026’s Startup Battlefield 200 , is on a mission to drastically lower that number. The company has developed a medical device that it says lowers organ failure rates and significantly accelerates recovery in children. When standard treatments like antibiotics cannot stop the immune system’s overreaction, a patient’s blood must be filtered to remove deadly toxins. That is where Efferon’s devices, of absorbers of dangerous cytokines and toxins, step in to make a critical difference. Dima Romashin, Efferon’s co-founder and CEO, compares what happens in the body during sepsis to a fire, where an immune response overwhelms the body rapidly. “In a fire, there are two things: the flame itself and smoke that it produces,” he told TechCrunch. In sepsis, endotoxins are the flames and cytokines are the smoke. Efferon, unlike other devices on the market, has developed a mechanism that can absorb both at once, according to Romashin. Although Efferon makes absorbers for adults, Efferon NEO, its pediatric device developed specifically for young kids, is proving especially effective. Since children have a significantly lower circulating blood volume, they require medical devices engineered specifically for their physiology, according to Romashin. In April, Efferon NEO received a CE mark , Europe’s equivalent to FDA approval, making it the first multimodal blood purification device specifically engineered for pediatric sepsis. Efferon NEO is used in intensive care units across 30 countries, including European hospitals, Saudi Arabia, and Thailand. The company is now preparing to file for FDA approval and is on track to hit $2 million in annualized revenue by the end of 2026. The startup’s technology was originally developed by scientists at Moscow State University, including co-founder Ivan Bessonov. Recognizing its potential, Romashin, a serial entrepreneur, stepped in earlier this year as CEO to help commercialize it. Although Romashin admits that Efferon isn’t growing at the breakneck pace of today’s AI startups, true success for the company is measured by something else entirely: every child who gets to go home. events.title: Ukraine strikes Yandex data centre in third attack on Russian tech giant
events.summary: Yandex's data centres have been targeted three times this week - like this one in Sasovo on Thursday Yandex has been forced to pause its operations at a data centre near Moscow after the facility was damaged in a Ukrainian drone strike - the third attack on the Russian tech giant's sites this week. The company - dubbed "Russia's Google" - said no one was injured at the centre in Vladimir, east of the capital, but some of its services were unavailable to users. Earlier this week, Yandex said it was struggling to maintain its services after two of its five data centres were hit in Ukrainian strikes. Both Russia and Ukraine have stepped up attacks on infrastructure in recent months as the war between them continues in its fifth year following Russia's full-scale invasion. Kyiv said it was targeting places that provide revenue streams for Moscow's war machine, and that the attacks could force Russia to divert its resources to repair the damage at Yandex. Sunday's attack came hours after US President Donald Trump warned that Ukraine should "damn well stop" attacking Russia's oil refineries so Moscow could release more diesel to the global market - a deal that has drawn criticism from Europe and sparked a diplomatic row with Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky. 'Time for Ukraine to get new president,' says Trump after Zelensky condemns diesel deal Published 1 day ago Analysis: Trump's shock Russia deal highlights mounting pressure to curb fuel prices Published 2 days ago Yandex confirmed on Telegram that its data centre in Vladimir had been damaged and that operations had been "completely suspended", although it said it was working to restore connectivity. The other strikes against Yandex facilities were on Thursday in Sasovo and Friday in Kaluga, south-west of Moscow, causing problems for some of its services, such as its AI chatbot and smart home devices. The tech company - which also runs a food-ordering and taxi app used by tens of millions of people - said at the time that its data centres were critical for the normal operation of its services, and that it was "very difficult to predict" when they would be back online. Meanwhile, Russian strikes on Ukraine have continued through the weekend. The State Emergency Service of Ukraine said six people were injured in Russian attacks overnight on four districts in its south-eastern Dnipropetrovsk region. On Saturday, at least 20 people including four children were killed in Russian attacks on Zaporizhzhia, local officials confirmed. Russia has previously also struck Ukrainian data centres, causing internet outages and prompting some firms to move their servers abroad. events.title: What to know about the landmark Warner Bros. Discovery sale
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Earlier this year, the streaming and entertainment industry witnessed one of its most high-stakes megadeals ever, stunning industry observers. Not only is it historic in its size, but it is also predicted to disrupt Hollywood and the media business as we know it. After years of Warner Bros. Discovery (WBD) struggling under the weight of billions of dollars in debt, compounded by declining cable viewership and fierce competition from streaming platforms, the company has been considering major strategic changes, including selling its entertainment assets to one of its rivals. Several major players saw the potential in acquiring the media giant, and in December, Netflix announced it would acquire WBD’s studios and streaming for $82.7 billion. But in a surprise eleventh-hour move in late February, the David Ellison-run Paramount became the winner of this bidding war, offering $111 billion to acquire all of WBD’s assets, including its studios, HBO, streaming platforms, games, and TV networks such as CNN and HGTV. Paramount was recently acquired by Ellison with significant support from his father, Larry Ellison — the Oracle chairman, world’s sixth-richest person, and major Trump donor. Paramount’s offer was approved by the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) in June. A federal judge then paused the deal after a lawsuit was filed on July 13 by a coalition of 12 state attorneys general. However, a judge approved it in late September, with the acquisition finally official as of October 6 . Let’s break down exactly what happened and what could come next. ​This all started back in October 2025 when Warner Bros. Discovery revealed it was exploring a potential sale after receiving unsolicited interest from several major players in the industry. ​The bidding process quickly became competitive, and Paramount and Comcast emerged as serious contenders, with Paramount initially viewed as the frontrunner. However, WBD’s board eventually determined that an offer from the streaming giant Netflix was the most attractive. Netflix offered $82.7 billion for just Warner’s film, television, and streaming assets. Thus began the bidding war. Paramount believed its bid of approximately $108 billion for all of Warner’s assets was superior to Netflix’s offer that focused on just the studios and streaming. To sweeten its deal, Netflix amended its agreement in January to an all-cash offer at $27.75 per share of Warner Bros. Discovery, further reassuring investors and paving the way for the deal to proceed. ​Paramount persisted in its attempts to acquire WBD . Still, the Warner board repeatedly rejected its offers, citing concerns about Paramount’s heavy debt load and the increased risk associated with its proposal, including concern over the suite of investors bankrolling Paramount’s bid, which includes Saudi, Qatari, and Abu Dhabi sovereign wealth funds. The board noted that Paramount’s offer would have left the combined company burdened with $87 billion in debt, a risk they were unwilling to take at the time. In January, Paramount filed a lawsuit seeking more information about the Netflix deal. A month later, the company sought to sweeten its deal by announcing it would offer a $0.25 per share “ticking fee” to WBD shareholders for each quarter the deal fails to close by December 31, 2026. It also said it would pay the $2.8 billion breakup fee if Warner backs out of its deal with Netflix. Then, in a final attempt to secure a deal, Paramount increased its offer to $31 per share in February. This prompted the WBD board to prolong discussions with Paramount regarding a potential agreement, considering it as a superior offer. Netflix declined to increase its bid and withdrew from the negotiations. “The transaction we negotiated would have created shareholder value with a clear path to regulatory approval,” Netflix co-CEOs Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters said in a statement on February 26. “However, we’ve always been disciplined, and at the price required to match Paramount Skydance’s latest offer, the deal is no longer financially attractive, so we are declining to match the Paramount Skydance bid.” In addition to the billions Paramount already holds in debt, the company is also set to assume the approximately $33 billion in debt Warner Bros. Discovery holds under the agreement . The deal will be backed by a $54 billion debt commitment from Bank of America, Merrill Lynch, Citi, and Apollo Global Management, as well as $45.7 billion in equity from Larry Ellison. Regulatory hurdles and other concerns In addition to the assumption of substantial debt posing a significant financial burden, Paramount faced several other hurdles in its deal with WBD. For one, Ellison has warned about significant job reductions that are expected in the near future.

events.title: These execs think voice AI hasn’t reached its ChatGPT moment yet
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. The theory of voice being the next big interface has picked up strong momentum, with investors pouring billions of dollars into voice AI startups working on areas ranging from model makers to enterprise customer service providers, and from meeting note-takers to AI-powered dictation. Every week there is a new model or a tool release that claims to sound human and converse like one. However, in reality, that might not be the case. Enterprise voice AI platform PolyAI’s CTO Shawn Wen thinks that despite the release of full-duplex models — which can speak while listening to you — voice AI doesn’t have its “ChatGPT moment” yet. “We have reached the milestone of developing full-duplex models. The next challenge is to make reasoning very fast, so that the models can fetch answers quickly and the conversation feels natural,” he told me on stage at the HumanX conference last month. He also said that AI agents in customer service should not sound robotic and should give callers enough confidence that they can solve problems. “I think the next stage will be slightly different because once the voice is good enough, like, and the customer is willing to engage with them for the first two or three turns, they start to build confidence, and over time, they will feel like I probably don’t have to talk to a human if the agent can solve my problem,” he said. Alex Gay, CMO for meeting notetaker Otter, opined that speaker identification, intent capture, and typing that up with organizational knowledge is a key step for enabling automation. The company is also working on digital twins that might represent people in meetings. For that technology, he said it’s paramount that the output voice gives the same emotive expressions of talking to a human in a meeting. “If you think about the meetings that you’re in right now, the best conversations that you have are where you can have debate, and strategic discussions, and when you feel like there’s a relationship that underpins it. If you aren’t able to have that with an avatar, then it’s just a q and a chatbot,” Gay noted. Voice AI’s understanding and transparency While voice AI models have improved, AI assistants often don’t understand users, or your meeting notetaker shows the wrong transcript or a summary. Wen thinks that ASR (Automatic Speech Recognition) models often miss important keywords, and that creates an issue in capturing the whole context. Otter’s Gay agreed with this, adding that the company keeps working on improving transcription. He also said that language is one area where voice models need to improve. “For Otter, you know, transcription was never the end point. It was just the layer that we could start to drive some of the productivity gains on the back of. But if your original transcription didn’t have the accuracy that you needed, all the follow-up actions that you have become flawed. And the minute that starts to take action, that is wrong. You lose trust in the platform. It is critical for us to continue to improve that ASR model because all of the downstream impacts are significant,” he said. With the new voice tools, there is also a question of transparency. Tools should declare to customers that they are being recorded or talking to AI. Otter said that it wants to instill trust in people who are in a meeting, so even for a meeting where the bot is not present, it wants to try methods like notifying everyone in the chat that the meeting is being recorded. PolyAI’s Wen also said that it’s important to establish that people are talking to an AI in enterprise calls. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Silicon Valley's horror shows
events.summary: Hollywood's hottest villain right now is the tech billionaire. Four films hitting theaters this fall put some of Silicon Valley's most powerful and controversial figures in the spotlight: Elon Musk , Mark Zuckerberg, Sam Altman and Elizabeth Holmes. Why it matters: Hollywood's portrayal of Silicon Valley and its leaders is getting darker as negative headlines about the tech industry seep into pop culture. Once portrayed as brilliant but flawed innovators, tech leaders are increasingly being cast as creepy villains whose ambitions may do more harm than good. Zoom in: This fall's tech billionaire films span genres, from documentaries to thrillers. 💻 "The Social Reckoning," Aaron Sorkin's follow-up to his 2010 hit, "The Social Network," opened Friday with Jeremy Strong portraying a more sinister Mark Zuckerberg during the 2021 Facebook whistleblower leak . Sorkin takes some cinematic liberties with chronology and other details. 🚀 "Musk," the four-hour documentary ( including a 10-minute intermission) about Elon Musk's rise, is playing in select theaters and opens nationwide on Friday. The roller-coaster rollout of the film, directed by Oscar-winning documentarian Alex Gibney, included critical acclaim at the Venice Film Festival and legal threats from Musk's team. 🩸 "You Can See Everything," out Friday, is an experimental documentary from Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim that follows ex-Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes in the weeks before she went to prison. The studio, A24, says an "intimate portrait of an enigmatic felon becomes a mind-bending three-year journey into the abyss." ( More on the film .) 🤖 "Artificial," a drama directed by Luca Guadagnino, stars Andrew Garfield as Sam Altman and hits theaters Christmas Day. In the film, "[Garfield] depicts Altman as a manipulative, power-hungry psychopath who lies as easily as he breathes and will use anyone, anytime, anywhere to get what he wants," The Verge reports . The studio, NEON, calls it "the story of OpenAI and a two-decade artificial intelligence arms race. ... As the technology becomes more powerful and more valuable than anyone ever imagined, a battle rages over who should control the tech that could change the fate of humanity." These projects represent a sharp turn away from some earlier movies and documentaries about Silicon Valley, like "Jobs" and "Something Ventured," which celebrated the ingenuity of founders and venture capitalists. "With tech, it was an ardent love affair," says Margaret O'Mara, a University of Washington historian who studies Silicon Valley. "And when you fall out of love, you fall out of love fast." "Our popular understanding of Silicon Valley and the products it makes has changed drastically." Zoom out: Hollywood is reflecting the public's growing disillusionment with the tech industry. Polls show Americans of all ages are quickly souring on AI and think it's moving too fast. Two in three Americans say social media has been bad for democracy, per Pew Research Center polling . "Popular movies hold up a mirror to current social anxieties," says writer and editor-in-chief of Film Quarterly J.M. Tyree. Right now, "people are thinking about power consolidating in the hands of the few at the expense of the many." The intrigue: Tech founders are compelling on-screen villains, Tyree says. They bring together two archetypes: the ruthless businessman who's corrupted by greed, as seen in movies like "Citizen Kane" and "The Wolf of Wall Street," and the mad scientist who's morally ambiguous and employs science and technology recklessly, like in "Metropolis" or "Frankenstein." Plus, their eccentricities make for good entertainment. The bottom line: O'Mara, the Silicon Valley historian, notes: "One thing I have learned from studying the history of rich people is that extreme wealth makes you weird."
