events.title: House Republican, invoking Reagan, moves to block Trump's Russia oil deal
events.summary: Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-Pa.) vowed Saturday to force a House vote to block Russian oil purchases, challenging President Trump's diesel deal with President Vladimir Putin. Why it matters: Trump has touted the deal as a way to lower fuel prices, but it could also provide revenue for Russia's war in Ukraine. Driving the news: Fitzpatrick, co-chair of the Congressional Ukraine Caucus, said he would introduce the "Ronald Reagan Peace Through Strength Act" and force a vote through a discharge petition. "It will be forced to the Floor via discharge and it will pass overwhelmingly," Fitzpatrick wrote on X . Retiring Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) tells Axios he has "already agreed" to sign the petition. Catch up quick: Trump said Friday Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to U.S. and global markets, with more shipments to follow. Energy analysts are skeptical the additional diesel will meaningfully lower prices. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called the deal "not fair and not honest," telling Axios it amounted to a gift to Putin. Trump called Saturday for Ukraine to replace Zelensky with a leader willing to reach a deal with Russia. The White House has not yet responded to Axios' request for comment about Fitzpatrick's bill. The big picture: Fitzpatrick is the latest Republican lawmaker to break with Trump in a high-profile way, as the party fights to keep control of Congress amid mounting disapproval of the president. Zoom out: Fitzpatrick is turning to a tactic lawmakers have increasingly used to bypass Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.): a discharge petition, which requires 218 signatures to bring legislation up for a vote without House leadership's approval. Fitzpatrick and Bacon forced a House vote on Ukraine aid and Russia sanctions earlier this year; it passed the House but stalled in the Senate. Reality check: Fitzpatrick has little time to pass the bill before this Congress ends in January. The House isn't scheduled to vote again until after the Nov. 3 midterm. Any legislation that passes the House would still need Senate approval and could face Trump's veto pen. What they're saying: Another House Republican, speaking anonymously to offer their candid thoughts, tells Axios: "Being that Congress won't be in session for another four weeks, any prudent lawmaker would probably not make a commitment to this prematurely." One House Democrat tells Axios that they will personally sign the petition and that "most" of their colleagues probably would as well, but unanimous support from Democrats is not guaranteed. "Leadership may not want people to help him," the Democrat said, though they added that may change after the midterms. Ben Geman contributed.

events.title: Attacks on Riyadh threaten Saudi confidence
events.summary: The News Several people were wounded in another likely Houthi attack on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport on Saturday, the third strike this week on the gateway to Saudi Arabia’s capital. Earlier attacks killed four people. Flights were canceled or diverted, and airport operations were suspended. Hours of silence and speculation in the aftermath added to a sense of fear in Saudi Arabia and across the region. Rumors of injuries circulated in the afternoon, flights were canceled, Canada’s embassy warned citizens to avoid the airport at 5:34 p.m. The US followed at 8:03 p.m. Al Arabiya TV, which usually switches to breaking news if firecrackers are heard in other countries, was airing reruns. Saudi authorities finally acknowledged the incident at 8:34 p.m. There are definitely security considerations to withhold information during an attack. But the insistence on projecting calm is starting to backfire. Firms in Riyadh were telling their employees to work from home tomorrow, and people have been spooked for weeks. Since the US-Iran war began on Feb 28, Gulf governments have restricted media coverage and criminalized social media posts, even as everyone living here could see and hear explosions themselves. For months, Riyadh seemed relatively insulated from the war (sorry, “conflict,” as many officials in the region prefer to call it). Its airport remained open as travelers fled attacks elsewhere in the Gulf, and Saudis rallied around the flag, deeming any expressions of concern as unpatriotic. The messaging also seemed coordinated, with official statements followed by a flood of pledges of allegiance on social media. Now this confidence appears to be fraying. And in a war that is as much about economics as explosives, this may be the vulnerability that the Houthis, and Iran, are banking on. Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces had pushed back the Houthi advances around Bab el-Mandeb, the Red Sea shipping chokepoint this week. But in a similar move to the substantial losses that Iran had been dealt by the US and Israel earlier in the war, the Houthis chose asymmetric targets. The Iran-backed group has escalated attacks on Saudi oil facilities and civilian aviation, declaring Saudi airspace a military operations zone. The timing matters. Riyadh hosts the World Petroleum Congress this week, with CEOs from ExxonMobil, Shell, TotalEnergies, and BP expected, followed later this month by the Future Investment Initiative and Wall Street’s billionaire financiers. Organizers insist both events will proceed , according to Reuters. But it’s certain that some of these executives — or their boards — will have second thoughts. Some US officials who were planning to attend the events in Riyadh this month are reconsidering. At stake is not just some meetings, but a questioning of the kingdom’s pitch as a safe home for trillions in financial assets, data centers, and new industries. The repeated airport attacks provide a sense that a major escalation is close. President Donald Trump said on Saturday that the US may join strikes on the Houthis and will decide quickly. If that happens, it’s likely the region will remain the punching bag for any Houthi or Iranian response. Notable Ambulances and helicopters were sent to collect the wounded from Saturday’s attacks. The kingdom may be short on missile interceptors or are “struggling” to take out the Houthis’ rockets, The Wall Street Journal reported .

events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts NSW small businesses contend with how to cover merchant fees after card surcharge ban Mr Barbaro says that annually his company pays about $150,000 in merchant fees. ( ABC News: Simon Amery ) NSW small businesses are looking at how to cover the cost of merchant fees after the ban on card payment surcharges took effect on October 1. Some owners have increased the price of items, while others have opted to absorb the cost. The consumer watchdog says businesses have the option of offering "discounts to consumers, who pay using a particular payment method, such as cash or PayID." Small businesses across New South Wales are grappling with how they will cover the cost of merchant fees. The Reserve Bank of Australia's (RBA) last week introduced a ban on business owners adding extra fees for credit or debit card payments on EFTPOS, Mastercard, Visa and American Express. The changes, according to the RBA, are in the "public interest", and designed to make the system more transparent and less confusing for both businesses and customers. The Reserve Bank of Australia says the changes are in the "public interest". ( ABC News: Simon Amery ) Sydney cafe owner Philip Barbaro said he had been forced to put prices up for some items, as his fees to the bank must still be paid for the use of cards. Mr Barbaro said the cafe business was tough in the Sydney market. "In my very competitive market in the city we have not touched the price of our coffee, but there were other items on the menu we had to increase this week, to offset the bank surcharge." Specialist baker and owner of the Jamaican Patty Bakehouse in Sydney's inner west, Chris Skuce, said he opened his shop a year ago as a nod to his Jamaican heritage. Mr Skuce says he will, at some stage, have to increase prices. ( ABC News: Simon Amery ) Mr Skuce said he had been absorbing the cost of the bank fee in order to keep making the patties that were part of his childhood. "I haven't passed the cost on yet, but I will increase my prices at some stage probably in the new year," he said. Businesses 'need to cover their cost' Executive director of advocacy group Business Sydney, Paul Nicolaou, said people were struggling. "There have been rising interest rates, energy costs and the subsequent drop in discretionary spending affecting both households and business," he said. Price rises were now being introduced across the board, he added. "Business owners need to cover their costs, and unfortunately someone has to pay, and it is going to be the consumer." Coffee prices at some cafes rise by 10pc The unintended consequence of the Reserve Bank's card surcharge ban, which was intended to lower prices for consumers. Mr Nicolaou said the banks should be doing something about merchant fees, along with other payment platforms. "It is all electronic now, does it require a fee?" A spokesperson for the Australian Competition & Consumer Commission (ACCC) said that while businesses were able to build the fee into their pricing structure, they "must not mislead consumers about their prices or the reasons for any price changes". "Businesses can also offer discounts to consumers, who pay using a particular payment method, such as cash or PayID," the spokesperson added in a statement. "Where a business offers a discount for a particular payment method, this should be clearly disclosed before consumers choose to book, order or pay. "Businesses should not display only the discounted price or make the discounted price more prominent than the full price." Mr Barbaro said he was now looking at alternatives for customers. The removal of card payment surcharges took effect on October 1. ( ABC News: Simon Amery ) Mr Barbaro said that could be an incentive. "There is the old saying that cash is king." Mr Skuce said, however, he was not looking at cash discounts. "Most people want to pay by card. It is just a hassle to handle cash." Mr Skuce said he did not see any net benefits to the consumer, as prices would increase. "I am befuddled with the change. Another hit to the bottom line and completely unnecessary in my opinion." Apple revealed in a regulatory filing that it has reached an agreement to bring on team members and technology from personalized audio startup Huxe, in what’s commonly known as a reverse acqui-hire deal. As first reported in MacRumors , Apple disclosed to the European Commission that it has agreed to make employment offers to “certain employees of Huxe AI,” and to “receive a non-exclusive license to Huxe’s intellectual property rights.” Reverse acqui-hires emerged in recent years as a way for larger companies to hire key team members and license technology from startups without acquiring the startups outright — presumably allowing them to build up AI talent and tech without drawing as much antitrust scrutiny. (Confusingly, these deals have both been referred to as “reverse acqui-hires” and as plain old “acqui-hires.” ) In the case of Huxe, the startup was founded by developers who’d previously worked on the AI-generated podcast features in NotebookLM (recently renamed Gemini Notebook ). But Huxe announced on May 21 that it was shutting down , with the team posting on the Huxe website that the company would be removing its app from the Apple and Google stores, halting service, and deleting user data. “The team is moving on to new things, and we won’t be continuing development of the product,” the company said. It also thanked its users, saying, “The fact that you used it, told friends about it, sent us your suggestions and your ideas, made it feel like we built it together.” On June 9, shortly after Huxe’s announcement, Apple notified the European Commission of its deal. The filing does not say who received employment offers or if they accepted. Nor does it disclose anything about Apple’s plans. Possibly related: Huxe’s shutdown announcement came just a day after Spotify unveiled AI-powered podcast generation features of its own , so Apple could be hoping to add similar functionality to its Podcasts app. Tech executives seem enamored with the idea that personalized audio can replace regular podcasts (and maybe even parent-child interaction ?), though it’s not clear how many normal listeners agree. events.title: Why we’re stuck with a Premier League in the clutches of the global mega-rich | Jonathan Wilson
events.summary: Why we’re stuck with a Premier League in the clutches of the global mega-rich There’s little prospect of the model changing in a country that welcomes wealthy international owners with open arms F ootball, the world’s most popular sport, played by laws drawn up in London in 1863. The Premier League is the UK’s greatest soft power export. Premier League clubs are owned by a deputy prime minister of Abu Dhabi, the public investment fund of Saudi Arabia, a billionaire based in Monaco for tax reasons and a disappointing assortment of investors and private equity funds. And what, really, could be more British than that? Football truly is the national game. What the Manchester City case has exposed is just how difficult it is to regulate some of the richest and most powerful bodies in the world. While the wait for the verdict was frustrating, it was perhaps unavoidable given the possibility of legal objection at every turn when a leaked email from City’s in-house lawyer during Uefa’s action against the club had threatened to “ spend 30 million on the 50 best lawyers in the world to sue them for the next 10 years”. You didn’t get that with Albert Alexander Sr or Peter Swales. Football clubs in England and Wales still represent their communities, a relationship that may be strained in certain cases by the pressures of a globalised entertainment economy, but remains broadly true. Arsenal can feel like the club of choice for the nouveau fan from across the world, but the scenes of celebration when they ended their 22-year wait for the league title last season were an undeniable expression of local pride. The idea that there was ever an idyll when clubs were run by benevolent potentates for the good of those communities is romantic nonsense. But just because there was no golden age is not to say that the situation has always been as bleak as this. How did we get into a situation in which clubs are flotsam on the swirling currents of geopolitics and the world economy? Chelsea alone in the past four years have had a Russian oligarch forced to sell the club after falling under UK government sanctions, while a subsequent American co-owner has been forced to sell his minority stake after his insurance business came under federal investigation in the US. It’s a curious world in which the professional gamblers feel like a welcome breath of fresh air. The days of the local businessmen, the owners of mines, shipyards and factories, the hauliers and scrap-metal dealers, are gone. Some invested because they genuinely wanted to give back to their communities or liked the sport. Others did so because it was easier to fund a local football club than to improve working conditions or pay a proper wage. And some did so because, wrongly in most cases, they thought there may be money to be made. But no one should think those were days of purity. The decrepitude of English stadiums in the 1980s should caution anyone who thinks football was uncomplicatedly better then. The contradiction has always lain at the heart of English football. Clubs represent their communities and for fans support becomes an aspect of identity, a link to family and place and past, a role that has only become more significant as the influence of traditional institutions – the church, the workplace, the social club – has faded. Yet fans in England have almost never owned their clubs, which in part underlies the present crisis. That is not to say fan ownership is a panacea. There is much to be admired about the German 50+1 model which, to oversimplify, ensures outside investors can never own a majority of the club. But it has not prevented Bayern Munich from winning 13 of the past 14 Bundesliga titles. Some sort of recognition that a club is not just a business, that it has a community function might, though, have prevented the free-for-all that has led to this mess. At least when most owners were local, there was some understanding of what the club meant to its area, and a recognition that exploitation or neglect could have direct consequences. No owner wanted demonstrations at the directors’ entrance, or to be jeered as he drove the streets in his Rolls-Royce, or to have his car showroom boycotted because he put up ticket prices then sold a popular centre-forward at a knockdown price. The distant majority shareholder in his boardroom in Los Angeles, his penthouse in Monte Carlo or his luxury villa on the Gulf feels the sting less keenly. Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Richard Scudamore, the former chief executive of the Premier League who did more to shape the modern competition, for good and for ill, than any other individual, always spoke of being “neutral about ownership models”. Essentially that meant taking the money without worrying too much about where it came from. The current Premier League is the consequence: a gleaming, world-leading edifice, but built on what?

events.title: Captains offered $US100,000 a month in the Strait of Hormuz
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Shipping companies offering captains $US100k a month to transit Strait of Hormuz Before the US-Israel attacks on Iran, well over 100 commercial ships passed through the strait each day. ( Reuters ) Oil tanker captains in the Persian Gulf are being paid up to $US100,000 (about $143,000) a month to navigate the Strait of Hormuz, industry insiders and maritime unions say, as Iran and the United States continue to impose separate blockades of the critical waterway. Gulf oil producers are increasingly desperate to get their oil out of the region and onto market after a recent step-up in attacks from Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) on tankers attempting to pass the dangerous choke-point. The new wave of assaults on vessels followed reports last month that crude shipments were edging back toward prewar levels, indicating Middle Eastern oil exports were recovering. Facebook ads seen by the ABC show some seafarers in Asia have been offered double or triple their pay as well as "danger money" bonuses worth tens of thousands to work in the Gulf. The vast sums of money are being used to persuade them to stay on vessels and continue running the strait despite the risk of attack. "Right now [the captains] are getting paid crazy," Indian marine engineer Harshal Singh told a podcast in late September. "A ship captain usually get 15 lakh Rupees per month (about $22,000). Right now in Strait of Hormuz they can make 1 crore rupees (about $143,000) in a month." The commercial tankers struck as they transited the Strait of Hormuz in recent weeks were "highly, highly targeted", according to marine traffic watchers. Captains receive pay increases while they are in the southern Red Sea and Gulf of Oman, and again during each Hormuz transit, according to Indian union representatives. But the journeys come with substantial risk, with at least 24 seafarers killed in 100 confirmed incidents since the war began, according to the UN's International Maritime Organization. In this month alone, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) has recorded nine incidents of attacks on tankers within the Strait of Hormuz. For many shipowners, the risks are being outweighed by revenues reaching levels rarely seen in the industry's recent history. "They are offering [seafarers] double, sometimes even five times the wages they will get during the transit of Hormuz," Manoj Yadav, the general secretary of the Mumbai-based Forward Seamen's Union of India, told the ABC. In India, where the vast majority of the world's seafarers are from, the salary bump is a huge draw. But unions have warned seafarers are at risk of being exploited and some have very little choice in performing a job that could cost them their lives. The strait's significance has been in the spotlight since Iran placed an effective chokehold on the shipping route, used for 20 per cent of the world's oil and gas trade, at the end of February. After months of gridlock, the US responded by implementing its own blockade on Iranian shipments through the critical energy artery. Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding in June that aimed to end the war. ( Reuters ) Sailing into the Gulf, loading and coming out again now carries great risk. While the US intercepts vessels attempting to trade with Iran, the IRGC targets ships sailing in the strait and harasses them, including through drone overflights and surveillance, the US Navy-led Joint Maritime Information Center said last weekend. It means fewer operators are willing to make the voyage, and transit remains below typical prewar traffic levels, when more than 100 commercial vessels crossed the strait each day. "I think the issue is less [to do with] insurance and more availability of crews that are willing to make that hazardous transit because of a significant amount of attacks," former Australian naval officer Jennifer Parker told the ABC. An increasing number of ships have attempted to get around Iranian controls by taking the south corridor route, which hugs the Omani coast, rather than the north corridor route, which sails close to Iran. Ships navigating the strait also take "dark journeys" by travelling at night with their GPS signalling equipment switched off. Marine intelligence companies previously told the ABC some of these dark transits have occurred with the knowledge and permission of Iran via diplomatic-level negotiations. Others have not.

events.title: Richard Morecroft had a furry studio companion viewers never knew about
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Late veteran presenter Richard Morecroft's foster journey with grey-headed flying fox Archie Late veteran presenter Richard Morecroft is best known for his decades of news reading, but unbeknownst to viewers, he was sometimes joined at the desk by a furry companion. Morecroft, who died this week aged 70, was a familiar presence as an ABC 7PM NSW anchor, BTN presenter and host of Letters and Numbers on SBS. But if you were to peek under his shirt as he read particular news bulletins in late 1987, you would find another passion. Wrapped inside a handkerchief was a baby grey-headed flying fox. Current medical advice recommends bats should not be handled due to the risk of disease. Morecroft adjusting Archie before presenting the NSW 7PM news bulletin. ( ABC News ) Archie was considered well-versed in current affairs. ( ABC News ) Morecroft originally thought it was a boy and named it Archie. "I think probably of its species, that little flying fox ... was probably the best educated in terms of knowledge of news and current affairs," he said in late December, 2001. "Thousands of people watching at home wouldn't have known that there was a small furry animal wrapped in a handkerchief stuffed inside my shirt." The presenter said the handkerchief was used to keep the pup warm. Morecroft fostered two-week-old Archie, who he believed belonged to the Ku-ring-gai Chase National Park colony, after completing a Wildlife Information and Rescue Service (WIRES) training course in the late 1980s. Archie and Morecroft recorded their journey together in a 30-minute Wildscreen episode with ABC TV's natural history unit, titled Raising Archie. "This is a young grey-headed flying fox which came from a colony not very far from Sydney," he explained during the program. "His mother died and so I'm the new foster parent for a few months. "What we're hoping is that eventually he will be able to rejoin the colony and get back into the wild." Morecroft encouraging Archie to fly. ( ABC News ) He said pups needed lots of attention. "They have to have nappies changed, their fur cleaned and be wrapped up as they would be in their mother's wings." At one point, Morecroft encouraged an older Archie to fly. The documentary also highlighted threats facing colonies, including overdevelopment and the impact of flying foxes raiding orchards. Morecroft also interviewed iconic naturalist, David Attenborough, with an older bat named Gollum. A letter Morecroft sent to his trainer in November 1987 reveals more about how he cared for Archie. "It's been a delight (and occasionally quite a challenge) to have the opportunity to raise a young flying fox," he wrote. "According to weight and forearm measurements (90 grams and 60 millimetres) a couple of days after receiving her, she must have been very young when orphaned. "However, she seems to be progressing well (now 107g and forearm 71mm) and is enjoying exercise sessions." Baby Archie, the grey-headed flying fox. ( ABC News ) He said Archie "took particular delight" in being groomed. "Warm, damp cotton buds are great for the armpits and the 'hip pits!'" the letter read. "And a soft baby's toothbrush grooming the fur produces either a relaxed ecstasy or a vigorous cooperative effort with tongue and one foot." John George, whose late wife Helen trained hundreds of people to care for native animals, including Morecroft, said the presenter was "totally committed". "She loved it, loved him and she could rely on him totally," he said. Morecroft was an active member of the wildlife rescue, as seen here with the founder Mikla Lewis (centre) at the 1991 Christmas party. ( Supplied: WIRES ) WIRES founder Mikla Lewis still remembers being surprised by Morecroft's call. "One day I picked up the phone and this voice on the other end said, 'Hello, I'm Richard Morecroft and I'd like to join'," she said. She said he was "really besotted" with Archie. WIRES bat unit coordinator Storm Stanford said bats these days did not stay with carers as long, and incubators were used for warmth to reduce disease risks. "Back when Richard was doing it, we didn't know about lyssavirus," Ms Stanford said, referring to Australian bat lyssavirus or ABLV. Archie was fostered at two weeks old. ( ABC News ) The disease is spread by saliva through a cut or a bite, or via the eyes, nose or mouth. It causes fever, fatigue, seizures and likely death, the Australian Centre for Disease Control warns. There is a vaccine, but no cure. People are told not to handle bats, even while wearing gloves, and seek urgent medical help if bitten.

events.title: Decades-old exemption tweaked to give cruise ship workers more rights
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Cruise ship crews still vulnerable to exploitation as government announces updated protections A decades-old exemption to Australian labour law for cruise ships has been extended with some new protections for workers. ( ABC News: Jasper Wells ) A legal exemption for cruise ships from Australian labour law has been altered to allow some new protections for crew. Critics say the legal loophole that left them vulnerable shouldn't have existed in the first place and allows for worker exploitation. The exemption was due to expire at the end of the year but has been extended to 2028. The union that represents cruise ship workers has warned that the exploitation of staff will become "embedded" in the industry after the federal government extended a decades-old exemption that allowed cruise ships to circumvent Australian labour law. The government has announced new protections for cruise workers following an ABC News investigation that revealed allegations of shocking conditions among the crew on some Carnival Cruise vessels. It includes the ability to collectively bargain and make complaints to the maritime safety regulator. Punishing conditions face Carnival crew Passengers boarding a Carnival cruise ship are promised a world of endless food, relaxation and oceanic luxury. But for the crew, life is vastly different. But the government has decided to continue the practice of allowing cruise ships an exemption to labour laws, extending the long-standing exemption until 2028. The ABC revealed in August that workers were accusing the company of 12-hour work days for seven days a week, medical neglect, not providing safe drinking water and wages less than $3 an hour. Carnival denied the allegations. Transport Minister Catherine King called the allegations "horrifying". Catherine King said the new conditions on the exemption would help draw tourists as well as protect workers. ( ABC News ) In response to the investigation Australia's anti-slavery commissioner said: "I think some change in this area is long overdue." Exemption should never have existed: union Maritime Union of Australia national secretary Jake Field said the exemption should never have existed in the first place and did so at the expense of Australian jobs. Introduced in 1998, the exemption lets cruise ships avoid Australian labour law and instead follow the looser international Maritime Labour Convention. The new obligations are the first time cruise operators have had conditions attached to their exemption. Originally expiring at the end of this year, it was extended until 2028 with the new conditions that ship operators cannot restrict crews rights to collective bargaining, and complaints about working conditions must to be reported to the maritime regulator, the Australian Maritime Safety Authority. Under the new conditions, cruise operators can no longer restrict crews' rights to collective bargaining. The ABC has seen letters from Carnival that warned crew against the presence of Maritime Union of Australia representatives at ports and reminded staff that they were under no obligation to stop. Carnival corporation operates over 90 ships globally, with around 100,000 crew on their ships at any one time. ( ABC New: Pete Garnish ) Transport Minister Catherine King said in a statement that the changes would protect workers while supporting Australia's maritime industry. Carnival and Royal Caribbean Cruises did not comment when asked if they would begin bargaining with crews. Carnival said it was considering the details of the announcement. Carnival operates three ships full-time in Australia: Adventure, Encounter and Splendor. ( ABC News: Pete Garnish ) Regulator to have more oversight of complaints The changes also mean that all crew complaints regarding the Maritime Labor Convention must be reported to the Australian regulator. It is intended to give the government a better understanding of the types of complaints being made about conditions and how they are managed. The government has said it will be the last time the exemption is renewed and it is considering a review of the laws, the findings of which are not yet public. Carnival operates three ships full-time from Australia, with roughly 1,000 crew on each, mostly flown in from South-East Asian and African countries. In a previous statement to the ABC, Carnival rejected the allegations made by crew and said the maritime authority had carried out "surprise inspections of our three ships in recent weeks and cleared Carnival on each occasion". It said that the company followed international standards.

events.title: Anthropic's Claude AI submits a false tip on a Philadelphia unsolved homicide case
events.summary: An Anthropic artificial intelligence model submitted a false tip to Philadelphia police about an unsolved homicide case, authorities and Anthropic said NEW YORK -- An Anthropic artificial intelligence model submitted a false tip to a Philadelphia police website about an unsolved homicide case, authorities and Anthropic said. It's the latest example of AI models acting in unintended ways and manipulating government and other websites during tests. In a report Friday , Anthropic also disclosed a separate incident when its AI model submitted forms to an undisclosed government website instead of stopping before submission. The incident in Philadelphia occurred on July 18 when the AI model Claude Haiku 4.5 was tasked with generating and performing example tasks on randomly selected webpages, Anthropic said. Claude filled out a form on police site PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com indicating it might have information regarding an unsolved murder listed on the site. Philadelphia Police said in a statement they were unaware of the incident until Anthropic notified them on Wednesday. Then they found the submission in the website’s tip records and confirmed it was marked spam and never forwarded to police. There are rising concerns about AI companies’ unchecked AI agents meddling with everything from U.S. government websites to healthcare data. Critics have been calling for more regulation. In September, another AI company, OpenAI, disclosed six reports of “unexpected or concerning” behavior in artificial-intelligence models. events.title: Petra Power looks to modernize energy for data centers and defense vehicles
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. As AI gobbles up an ever larger amount of energy, the hunt is on for efficient and cost-effective power sources. One of the companies leading the charge is Petra Power . Petra, which was founded in 2017, sells solid oxide fuel cells — ceramic devices that convert fuel, like natural gas, into electric power without burning it. The company markets them as a more efficient and environmentally friendly way to operate data centers and large vehicles. Petra’s founder, Aaron Goodman, told TechCrunch that his company’s product has significantly lower fuel costs and emissions than traditional power sources, and that they have much less of a physical footprint, too, because they’re more compact and lightweight. The efficiency, and the cost savings that come with it, is what makes the fuel cells attractive. “Combustion takes fuel and creates explosions,” Goodman said, describing how traditional power generation works. “Those explosions create heat. That heat creates motion. The motion powers an electromotive force, which eventually creates electricity. It’s a lot of steps, and they all have so much loss in them that you end up with a really inefficient system.” Petra’s fuel cells skip most of these steps. “What fuel cells do is they take the electrons directly off of the fuel, so they strip the fuel of its electrons, which creates electricity,” he explained. “It’s one step, no loss, and subsequently, in theory, at least, they’re much, much more efficient.” As a result, companies that run off fuel cells stand to save a significant amount on fuel costs, Goodman said. Although it may offer an innovative product, the customer base is still emerging for Petra. Goodman said that his company is targeting two different types of customers: data centers and the Defense Department. Goodman doesn’t want to reveal specific agreements just yet, but said Petra is currently working with neoclouds and other infrastructure providers that were a few steps down from the hyperscaler crowd. The target for first deployment with these customers is 2028, with full-scale production for the company hopefully set for 2029, Goodman said. “Hyperscalers are an ICP [ideal customer profile] for us, and we talk a lot to them, but we don’t have anything firm with them yet,” said Goodman. “We’re still kind of working in that direction. Obviously, they’re the largest consumers of power. They’re the ones that we can make the biggest impact with, so that’s where we’d like to go.” The other customer — the government — is also still taking shape. The idea is that Petra’s fuel cells will be able to provide auxiliary power for land vehicles, meaning electricity for onboard equipment when the main engine is off. Petra is a small team — some 15 people — but the company is growing, Goodman said. Petra has so far received nearly $9 million in contracts from the Defense Department, and the hope is to scale that work significantly in the coming years, he said. events.title: Christa Pike left the hospital and returned to Tennessee prison after failed lethal injection
events.summary: Tennessee inmate Christa Pike was released from the hospital and is back in prison more than a week after she survived the state's attempt to execute her by lethal injection , her attorneys said Saturday. The big picture: The failed execution was unprecedented. Pike, 50, got two doses of the deadly drug pentobarbital on Sept. 30 and was still breathing. The state called an ambulance and Pike got life-saving care at a local hospital. Pike's attorneys said they believed she was "brain dead" and on life support. It shocked them and her doctors when she woke up and began talking earlier this week . What they're saying: Pike's attorneys said she had returned to Debra K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center, where she had been housed for decades. "She is grateful to the first responders and her medical team for their care in these extraordinary circumstances," the attorneys said in a statement. "She is continuing to receive medical care at the prison, and we will continue to track her recovery." Catch up quick: Gov. Bill Lee ordered an independent review to determine how Pike was able to survive the attempted lethal injection. Another execution set for December was called off while that investigation plays out. Pike was sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer.

events.title: Trump announces deal for Russian diesel as Zelensky calls it a gift to Putin
events.summary: Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin met in Alaska last year Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has condemned Donald Trump's announcement of a deal to import Russian diesel into the US. Zelensky called it a gift to Russian President Vladimir Putin that amounts to "an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged", a position quickly backed by Ukraine's European allies. Trump said Putin had agreed to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel immediately "to the American and global marketplace" followed by 500,000 tonnes in November and a further one million after that. It is understood that the US Treasury is suspending sanctions on Russian diesel exports until 7 April as part of the deal, but other assets like those in American banks are still frozen. Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform that a further three million tonnes of Russian diesel would be delivered "within a short period", dependent on the condition of its refineries, which have been attacked by Ukraine. Putin later said that Russia, which introduced a ban on diesel exports earlier this year, was willing to supply both the US and global markets with oil and petroleum products, but his statement did not specify amounts. Zelensky said Russia would repay the diesel with "further terror". "We count on America's fair support for our defence of life, for our defence of people in Ukraine – and on the United States having a correspondingly strong conversation with Russia. A strong one, not a weak one," he wrote. He later pointed to deadly overnight strikes on Zaporizhzhia and Kyiv as Russia expressing "its thanks" for the agreement. Analysts have questioned whether Russia is capable of providing that quantity of diesel and the extent to which doing so will ease prices for American consumers. Analysis: Trump's shock Russia deal highlights mounting pressure to curb fuel prices Published 2 days ago Russian glide bomb attack on Zaporizhzhia kills at least 15 people Published 1 day ago Tim Armitage, an investment strategist at Quilter Cheviot, said the numbers mentioned by Trump were "relatively small". He said the first tranche equated to approximately 2.25 million barrels, and daily US consumption was around 3.8 million barrels, "so it won't make a material difference to pump prices in the US". "Granted, there are then two more releases to come, but it does appear to be a slightly desperate move by President Trump to try to lower inflation ahead of the midterms," he said. Paul Johnson, former director of the Institute of Fiscal Studies think tank and provost of The Queen's College, Oxford, said: "What would make a difference, of course, is sorting out what's happening with Iran. "Let's be clear, President Trump has created this problem himself," he told Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg. "This is a problem not created because of Ukraine and Russia in terms of diesel prices at the moment, this is created by the war in the Middle East." The BBC has asked the White House what Russia will get from the US in return for the commitment. The agreement with Russia also opens Trump up to criticism from European allies and pro-Ukraine politicians in the US that the American president is now helping to fund Moscow's war machine. The EU's foreign affairs chief Kaja Kallas said suspending sanctions "provides Moscow with more revenues to wage war", adding: "This is not the time to ease pressure on Russia, and Europe won't." She said European foreign ministers intended to approve the biggest set of sanctions on Russia since the start of its full-scale invasion on Monday. Meanwhile, a UK government spokesperson said its position "could not be clearer" and that it would continue working with international partners to support Ukraine and bring about sustained peace. "We will also maintain pressure on Russia through the toughest sanctions regime ever imposed by the UK, increasing the cost of Putin's aggression and supporting efforts to secure a just and lasting peace." Friday's announcement is the latest effort from Trump to lower fuel prices in the US ahead of the midterm elections, after months spent grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war. That conflict, which began in February, has sent the cost of petrol and in particular diesel skyrocketing, which has soured his standing with the American public who have been stung by the higher pump prices and knock-on effects that led to across-the-board inflation. Ukraine's President Volodymr Zelensky said Russia would repay the diesel with "further terror" The average diesel price in the US is currently $6.28 (£4.74) a gallon, according to the AAA, down from the record high of $6.53 recorded at the end of September. Shortly after Trump's announcement, the US Treasury formally issued a temporary licence allowing Russian diesel into the market.

events.title: Here are the top AI agents that can live in your text messages
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Rather than downloading another app, a growing number of agents can simply be texted like an ordinary person. You text it what you need, and it can remember context, connect to the apps and services you already use, and complete tasks on your behalf. That can mean scheduling an appointment, organizing a calendar, researching a trip, sending an email, making a reservation, shopping online, or reminding you about something days later. While Instinct is one of the buzziest AI agents at present, thanks to its $10 billion valuation after its latest funding round of $1 billion, there are many others also making a play for this space. Below are the most notable options so far, from general-purpose personal assistants to agents designed for families, travel, and work. Caddy is an AI assistant that turns the information scattered across your phone into things you can actually act on. It lives in iMessage for iPhone users and RCS for Android users, so there’s no separate app or inbox to constantly check. For instance, an email contains an appointment that needs to be added to your calendar or a friend sends a list of things to pick up. Instead of worrying about all the details getting buried, Caddy connects to your calendars and conversations, then identifies things that may require action. It can add events to your calendar, set reminders, keep track of follow-ups, and even do research for you. Caddy has been available in public beta since April 2026. Comma is designed to manage tasks across both work and everyday life. Comma carries tasks through to completion, checking its own work and determining when a task is finished. Completed work is surfaced for review when a decision or approval is needed. It also proactively notifies users and recommends the next steps. It can work across a user’s browser, computer, and files, while remaining accessible remotely through messaging apps such as Signal, Telegram, and WeChat. Comma maintains context and memory across devices and conversations, and can deliver daily briefings, flag urgent matters, and summarize recorded calls. Comma is free to start and open source. Fambot is an AI-powered “chief of staff” for families, designed to bring together the many moving parts of family life, including school communications, sports activities, meal planning, calendars, and other day-to-day responsibilities, and turn them into an organized plan. The service is designed to work across both an app and text messages. Fambot is available on iOS devices, Android devices, and the web, and families can also interact with it directly over SMS. Every night, Fambot automatically sends a summary of the following day, including upcoming events, to-dos, and details such as school uniform or packing requirements. Parents can reply to those messages to ask questions, check information, or make changes to their calendar. Fambot currently connects to Gmail, Google Calendar, Outlook, and WhatsApp, with support for Apple Calendar planned for the future. The company launched in beta in early September 2026 and has raised $3.5 million in pre-seed funding. The service is currently free during the beta period, but Fambot expects to eventually charge roughly the equivalent of a Netflix subscription. Folk is designed to be an AI assistant you can reach through iMessage, WhatsApp, and Telegram. It can remember personal context, manage reminders, research topics, track flights, handle email, and perform real-world tasks such as restaurant reservations. One distinction is that Folk runs on its own private cloud computer. It can also run code and execute multi-step tasks rather than merely responding conversationally. Folk launched its beta in May 2026, and it’s available for free but also offers a Pro subscription for $8.33/month if you want unlimited tasks running in the background. Instinct first made headlines after raising $350 million at a $2.5 billion valuation. In September 2026, it raised $1 billion , valuing it at $10 billion. The always-available agent can take actions on your behalf, rather than simply answer questions. Users can communicate with Instinct by text or voice and connect it to the apps and services they already use, such as email, calendar, Google Workspace, and more. The company says early users have used Instinct for tasks ranging from planning trips and buying groceries to booking tickets and canceling subscriptions. In September, Instinct began giving users dedicated email addresses for their assistants. The idea is to let Instinct create and manage accounts on a user’s behalf without filling the user’s personal inbox. The agent can use its address to sign up for services, contact businesses, follow up on requests, and handle tasks that require an email account.

events.title: UAW tries to reassert political power in Michigan despite internal divisions
events.summary: Membership is divided over which party best represents working-class interests. SHELBY TOWNSHIP, Mich. -- Walter Usakowski was mowing his lawn in a northern suburb of Detroit when three canvassers from the United Auto Workers approached. “I don’t even need to talk to you,” Usakowski said. As a retired member, he was already supporting the union’s slate of Democratic candidates in the Nov. 3 midterms. But he is not sure how many of the other “guys in the shop” will vote for Democrats. He worked at Ford Motor Co.’s Sterling Axle Plant for more than 45 years, and he knows many members who backed Republican President Donald Trump . The election-year canvassing was one part of the UAW’s efforts to reassert its political power in Michigan, a premier political battleground. Although the union generally backs Democrats, its membership is more divided over which party best represents working-class interests. It also is reckoning with past corruption scandals , a drop in membership and a lack of transparency that has eroded trust within its ranks. “It’s not going to be an overnight thing,” said JJ Jewell, who is part of the UAW’s Community Action Program executive committee. “Even if this election goes fantastically, that’s not mission accomplished. That means we’re 1% of the way done.” Jewell and others made the rounds on a recent sunny Saturday in Macomb County, where Trump won by nearly 14 percentage points in 2024. Many of the union members they met in a neighborhood of well-kept suburban houses were retirees, and while most said the cost of living was their top concern , they did not agree on whether Democrats or Republicans would better address it . One resident, who said she blamed billionaires for the country’s problems, planned to vote for Democrats. Another street over, a couple said they both supported Trump and declined to take a flyer of the UAW-endorsed candidates. In a microcosm of broader political rifts , union voters remain politically divided. Union voters have traditionally been seen as a Democratic-leaning constituency, but Trump made direct appeals to them with his anti-elite rhetoric and promises to overhaul international trade agreements that sapped factory jobs. In 2024, voters who were union members or were in a household with a union member split between Trump and Democratic nominee Kamala Harris , with more than half voting for the then-vice president and 44% for Trump. Betty Anderson, a UAW member, thinks the organization is on the right track, but she is not confident about bridging internal political divisions. She said she is angry with members who voted for Trump, whom she sees as selling out the working class. “I don’t think those people are ever going to be on our side,” Anderson said. “They think they have an opportunity to be in an elite class.” Since 2017, more than 10 UAW officials have pleaded guilty in a corruption investigation that found millions of dollars of union dues were stolen. Members also faulted leaders for closed-door contract negotiations that they said destroyed trust in the UAW. Shawn Fain was elected UAW president in 2023 on a platform of transparency, and victories in labor disputes with Detroit's three major automakers bolstered member support. Leaders hope this will translate into votes for its candidates. “I think the UAW members now are starting to fall a little more in line,” said Usakowski, the retired axle plant worker. On Friday, Fain said he won reelection to lead the union for four more years. The results have not yet been certified. Fort Hood survivors speak out on Pentagon's decision to livestream Hasan's execution 8 people, including 2 kids, pregnant woman, killed at home: Police Hasan execution will be live-streamed, Pentagon official says Mark DePaoli, director for one of the UAW’s southeast Michigan regions, said the union hosted forums with candidates where any member could ask questions. The UAW endorsed progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed in the U.S. Senate primary even though rival Haley Stevens , a four-term congresswoman, worked as chief of staff on an auto bailout task force during the Great Recession, a position she frequently cited while campaigning. “I don’t think anybody expected us to endorse him,” DePaoli said. In its announcement, the union referenced El-Sayed’s support for universal healthcare and criticism of corporate money in politics. El-Sayed wore a UAW pin during the first Senate debate with his Republican opponent, former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers . “The UAW’s backing of Abdul was critical in winning a historic primary despite being outspent by tens of millions of dollars, and will be just as critical in winning" next month, El-Sayed spokesperson Cole Wozniak said in a statement. Rogers is emphasizing his opposition to controversial federal regulations under Democratic President Joe Biden that would have required automakers to ramp up production of electric vehicles, which some feared would lead to factory closures.

events.title: The big unknown behind Democrats' polling leads
events.summary: Poll after poll spells trouble for GOP candidates — in purple states and deep-red ones alike — but while Democrats see a blue wave coming, some Republicans see a polling mirage. Why it matters: Pollsters worry they're flying partly blind. Even a modest polling error could mean the difference between Republicans retaining control of Congress and President Trump facing Democratic majorities in both chambers. The big picture: Polling Trump voters has long been notoriously difficult. The polls underestimated Trump's support in 2016, 2020 and 2024. Midterm polling has been more accurate, though some still underestimated Republican support in 2022, notes Scott Keeter, senior survey adviser at Pew Research Center. Catch up quick: With less than a month until the midterms, the polls paint a bleak picture for Republicans. The House: Democrats lead Republicans 49.8%-41.9% in the RealClearPolling generic congressional ballot average. Cook Political Report projects Democrats will gain nine to 19 seats, enough to win a narrow majority. The Senate: Cook now sees a potential Democratic net gain of two to six seats. Democrats need four to take control, and Cook just moved the Kansas Senate race into its toss-up column. Trump: The president's approval rating stands at 37.6% in Cook's polling tracker . A recent Economist/YouGov poll found 35% approving and 60% disapproving of his performance. State of play: Research suggests Republicans have become somewhat less likely than Democrats to participate in telephone surveys, and response rates overall have plummeted since the late 1990s, per Pew . "We definitely have more people answering surveys who voted for [former Vice President Kamala] Harris than who voted for President Trump," says Brent Buchanan, a Republican pollster and founder of Cygnal. "But if you're a good pollster, you still get the other people." Pollsters can compensate by giving greater weight to Trump voters or adjusting samples to better reflect the Republican electorate, which skews male, white and working class. Advanced statistical modeling tools can also take a poor sample and make it look like the true electorate, though results may be inaccurate for subgroups like young people or Hispanic voters, Pew's Keeter says. But that has risks: "The adjustment assumes that the Republicans who respond to a poll are similar to the Republicans who don't respond to the poll," Rice University political science assistant professor Matthew Tyler tells Axios. Tyler said weighting GOP respondents more heavily can backfire if those willing to answer polls are also more willing to vote Democratic than the Republicans who never respond. That could inflate the apparent size of a Democratic wave. Between the lines: Predicting who will actually vote can dramatically change the results. YouGov chief scientist Douglas Rivers found Democratic leads ranging from six to 16 points depending on how likely voters were identified in a September survey — and called the 16-point margin "almost certainly an overstatement." The bottom line: Even with the questions about the accuracy of recent polls, most pollsters believe Democrats have the edge heading into Election Day. " I think it's telling that we're hanging our hopes on, 'The polls are wrong,'" Buchanan says. "That's not very strong."

events.title: Hegseth's public execution plan meets the age of viral violence
events.summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's announcement that the Fort Hood shooter's execution will be livestreamed reflects a shift toward putting raw, real-world violence on display for unlimited audiences. Why it matters: The Trump administration has made a show of flexing American power, sometimes with grisly footage. Now, it's preparing to make the government's ultimate punishment available for all to see. The big picture: Americans are increasingly encountering shocking images on their phones, often without warning. Graphic footage of Charlie Kirk's assassination spread widely across social media, searing in the brains of social media users — often young ones. Since Oct. 7, 2023, footage from the Hamas attacks and Israel's military campaign in Gaza has circulated online. Some videos have spread from Telegram to social platforms like X , where clips are easy to find. Footage of the August 2025 killing of Ukrainian refugee Iryna Zarutska on a Charlotte train went viral across X, stirring debate about crime and public safety. President Trump later said he had watched the video and wished he hadn't. A livestream of Nidal Hasan's execution would be the first known public broadcast of a lawful execution, according to death penalty experts interviewed by Reuters. Public executions are increasingly rare worldwide. In recent years, most have taken place in Iran and Taliban-run Afghanistan, according to Amnesty International. Friction point: Tech companies are now facing the question of whether they would allow the Pentagon to livestream the execution on their platforms. Hasan, who killed 13 people in 2009 at the Fort Hood Army base in Texas, is scheduled to be executed on Dec. 3. TikTok and Kick said that livestreaming the event would violate their policies, The Verge reported. YouTube, Meta, X and Twitch did not respond to The Verge's requests for comment. Yes, but: Elon Musk has positioned X, in particular, as a bulwark against internet censorship in the name of free speech. Hegseth's plan is putting the limits of that free-speech philosophy to a new test. The platform defended its decision to keep graphic content of the Kirk shooting on the platform, saying: "We will continue to stand against violence and censorship, ensuring this platform amplifies truth and open dialogue for everyone." After a bishop was stabbed during a livestreamed church service in Australia in 2024, X defied government demands to remove footage of the attack worldwide. Zoom out: Hegseth's announcement raises the prospect of reversing America's nearly century-long retreat from public executions. He justified making the execution public, saying that "people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things." The 1936 hanging of Rainey Bethea in Kentucky, which drew 20,000 spectators, is widely considered America's last public execution. A modern-day livestreamed execution could reach billions. The intrigue: Vice President JD Vance questioned Friday whether the execution would actually be livestreamed and said he wouldn't watch if it were. Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah) posted : "A civilization erodes when it cultivates an appetite for executions as a form of entertainment. ... Broadcasting a death diminishes us and is not an effective deterrent." Trump told reporters he had approved the decision to livestream the execution. The bottom line: America spent nearly a century moving away from public executions. Now, with real-world violence just a click away, the U.S. government is preparing to show one to the world.

events.title: Trump rages over Nobel Peace Prize loss
events.summary: President Trump lashed out late Friday night after he once again did not win the Nobel Peace Prize he has openly coveted . Why it matters: The award is Trump's white whale, an honor he talks about frequently and believes he deserves. This year's prize went instead to a former judge of a court Trump has sanctioned and called "rogue" and "evil." Navi Pillay, the winner, reacted to the award by saying world leaders have a "legal obligation to protect human rights and refrain from war," according to the AP . What he's saying: " I know nothing about this woman, and neither does anyone else! In fact, to the best of my knowledge, no one ever heard of her other than the fact that she, very obviously, hates Israel. I don't know what the woman has done," Trump said in a Truth Social post of nearly 600 words that went up just before midnight on Friday. "I settled 8 Wars, with letters being sent from every President and Prime Minister from the countries that I helped to the Norwegian Nobel Committee, and I'm about to settle, or win, two more, Iran and, Russia/Ukraine," Trump wrote. "They're both happening at breakneck speed but, forget them, it's the 8 that I've already settled, any one of which, in particular, Pakistan and India, would be far more than necessary to win the Nobel Prize. In actuality, I should have won 8 Nobel Peace Prizes, not just 1." Between the lines: Pillay, this year's winner, is a former judge of the International Criminal Court and also the former UN High Commissioner for Human Rights. Nobel officials said she received the honor "for her efforts to promote peace and international law." Originally from South Africa, Pillay, 85, also served as chair of the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory. Zoom in: Trump took aim at that UN association as well. "In all of the Wars that I have settled, I never spoke to the United Nations—they were of no help. The United States of America, represented by me, as your President, should have received the Nobel Peace Prize, but didn't," he said. The intrigue: Trump also blasted Norway, as he's previously done over Nobel snubs, though the country doesn't award the prize. "This is an indelible stain on Norway, one that will never be forgotten. The Nobel 'Peace' Prize has been forever discredited by a handful of Radical Ideologues who are Anti-Democracy, and Enemies of Civilization!" The bottom line: The president didn't hold back making his case for why he should have won — and why his loss was a personal snub.

events.title: As Trump’s Wall Closes in, DHS Intimidates a Border Tribe With Surveillance, Masked Agents and Drones
events.summary: A border patrol vehicle drives past the Tadai Me:i prayer camp on the Tohono O’odham nation on Sept. 5. Cam Mackey At 4:59 a.m. on Aug. 25, Verlon Jose, the chairman of the Tohono O’odham Nation in Southern Arizona, received an email from the head of the U.S. Border Patrol’s Tucson Sector. Government contractors were en route to conduct soil tests for construction of a 62-mile wall along the Nation’s southern boundary, wrote acting chief patrol agent Henry N. Laxdal. If the tribe wished to have cultural monitors observe the work, they were welcome to, but they could not interfere with the government’s operations. The work would begin in exactly one minute. Jose, 59, was already aware of the contractors’ arrival. An hour earlier, a tribal member had called to report a caravan heading south through the reservation, and Facebook was lighting up with similar accounts. The convoy included not only work trucks and drilling rigs, but Border Patrol vehicles as well. Dozens of border wall contractor and Border Patrol vehicles pass the Tadai Me:i prayer camp on the morning of Aug. 27. Nate Sosa For months, the O’odham had maneuvered to avoid such a scene, taking their case to federal court. Their homeland straddles the border, and thousands of tribal members live in Mexico. A wall would disrupt routine border crossings for ceremonies and family visits and destroy landscapes they consider their duty to protect, members and leaders say. Their lawsuit argued that the Trump administration’s efforts to build it despite their opposition constituted an historic attack on tribal sovereignty. But administration attorneys gave assurances that the government was engaging with the O’odham in good faith, and a judge in Washington, D.C., denied the tribe’s request for a preliminary injunction. In his Aug. 25 email providing Jose a 60-second heads up, the Border Patrol chief said his agency’s willingness to accommodate cultural monitors underscored its “commitment to ongoing coordination” with the Nation. As daylight broke, Jose learned the contractors were guarded by federal agents in masks and tactical gear, drawn from a special operations cadre that participated in citywide sweeps in Minneapolis and Chicago the previous year, which left three people dead, including two U.S. citizens. When the tribe’s chief of police tried to reach the worksite, he was stopped at a roadblock set up by the agents. Merrian Felix Davy Cross Border Patrol tactical team members amass around the Tadai Me:i prayer camp on Aug. 26. Jose issued a statement on the Nation’s website declaring the incursion illegal and revealing that the Department of Homeland Security had deployed a surveillance blimp and enlisted Mexican security forces to help protect the work crews. For a quarter-century, Tohono O’odham leaders have staved off a border wall by allowing DHS to use the reservation as a testing ground for some of the government’s most aggressive homeland security measures — from vehicle barriers on the reservation’s southern boundary, to state-of-the-art surveillance towers , to law enforcement partnerships with the Border Patrol and Immigration and Customs Enforcement . Despite the collaborations, and assurances from the Trump administration, ProPublica found that DHS has turned its vast apparatus on tribal members, with 24-hour surveillance directed at an ongoing border prayer ceremony and tribal members being questioned outside the reservation about their ceremonial activities. ProPublica’s account is based on photos, videos, court filings, interviews with tribal leadership, firsthand observations and more than 1,000 contemporaneously written observations compiled by tribal members. The battle over a border wall on the Nation has broken along familiar partisan lines in Arizona. While GOP legislative leaders have filed briefs in support of the project, Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs has done the same in support of the tribe. Progressive U.S. Rep. Adelita Grijalva, whose district includes the reservation, has said she is crafting legislation to rein in the Department of Homeland Security’s sweeping powers to waive federal laws in order to expedite wall construction. The Trump administration has used those authorities to circumvent environmental and cultural preservation statutes on 60 occasions across its two terms. For Deshane Gregg, whose vehicle was forced off the road by a convoy of contractors and federal agents, the recent show of force on the reservation has felt like a government siege, not cooperation. “You just feel helpless. You see these people, and they’re just so aggressive. They want you to react. They want you to show them that we could be ugly too,” she said. “We’re just here doing prayer. We’re just here, not trying to bother them, but it gets to you when it’s constantly being like that.” “The drones flying over us all day,” she added, “it’s a lot.” A drone hovers over the Tadai Me:i camp during morning prayer songs on Aug. 27. Ryan Devereaux/ProPublica ProPublica sent DHS, U.S. Customs and Border Protection, and the Border Patrol nearly 30 questions about the government’s surveillance and interactions with tribal members and leaders. The agencies answered none of those questions. Instead, CBP pointed to a statement Commissioner Rodney Scott made in August, in which he described the reservation’s southern boundary as “one of the most dangerous smuggling and trafficking corridors on the Southwest border” and a “remote desert that has facilitated decades of drug loads, migrant deaths, and cartel activity.” Regarding construction of a wall, Scott said, “Congress funded this work, a Federal court has affirmed it, and CBP is carrying it out under the legal authorities that apply. Under President Trump’s leadership, we are securing the border and giving our agents the tools and support they need to protect the American people.” A post on X from James Percival, general counsel of the Department of Homeland Security, celebrates the denial of a request for an emergency injunction against border wall construction filed by Tohono O’odham leadership in August. Screenshot of X With no sign the White House or the O’odham government is backing down, DHS has cast off any pretense that the agency will work cooperatively with the Nation. Within hours of the judge’s denial of the emergency injunction, on Aug. 14, the department’s general counsel, James Percival, posted a celebratory meme depicting one of the cybernetic Star Trek supervillains known as “the Borg.” “RESISTANCE IS FUTILE,” it read. “We respect tribal sovereignty but not to the detriment of border security,” he wrote. “This wall is getting built. Our authority is beyond dispute.” The O’odham have inhabited the Sonoran Desert, from what is now Southern Arizona to Mexico’s Sea of Cortez, for thousands of years . events.summary: Illustration by Mauricio Rodríguez Pons/ProPublica. Source images by Angela Weiss/AFP via Getty Images. Earlier this year, we heard that reporter Jake Pearson planned to ask our editors at ProPublica for more than $20,000 so he could spend the NBA playoffs betting like a problem gambler .  We told him we wanted in on the action.  For 10 weeks, our documentary team at ProPublica filmed Jake as he dove ball-cap-first into DraftKings and FanDuel, the country’s largest online sportsbooks. Jake bet early, late and often, ramping up the amounts and frequency of his wagers, chasing his losses with even bigger bets.  He wanted to flagrantly wave the red flags of a gambler descending into addiction. Would the apps serve up speed bumps as he careened into the red, or would they push him to keep betting?  Since 2018, the year the Supreme Court opened the door for states to legalize sports betting, the number of people staking money on games has exploded. It’s now legal in 39 states and Washington, D.C. The apps don’t just offer straight action on the outcome of a “Sunday Night Football” game — you can put money on myriad sports events and outcomes, including who will score the next point in a tense contest of Czech table tennis. Every month, millions do.  More than $600 billion has sloshed through the legal sportsbooks in wagers — and brought billions in state tax revenue — in the last eight years. But between the ever-present ads featuring celebrities from LeBron James and Charles Barkley to Kevin Hart and Kendall Jenner, cracks in the system have started to show.  About a quarter of active sportsbook account holders surveyed by the Siena Research Institute this year said that they’d lost enough on a bet that they’d have trouble meeting their financial obligations . Other studies and public health experts warn of rising cases of bankruptcy, addiction and self-harm. ProPublica reporter Jake Pearson at a Manhattan bar this spring, testing DraftKings’ and FanDuel’s guardrails. More than a quarter of people in the U.S. say they have an active account with an online sportsbook, according to a poll by the Siena Research Institute. Gerardo del Valle/ProPublica DraftKings and FanDuel say that they don’t want to profit off bettors who can’t control themselves, and they provide a range of what the industry calls “responsible gaming” tools to help users stay in check.  Jake received pop-up notices, reminders and emails noting his time on the app and nudging him to “take a beat” after a loss. He opted into some of the tools DraftKings makes available. But he was struck by user design choices and promotions that encouraged him to keep betting, some of which he was served right after setting limits on his play.  In a statement, DraftKings told ProPublica that it trains its more than 5,000 employees on responsible gaming and has more than 50 full-time staff dedicated to its “responsible engagement” program. A FanDuel spokesperson wrote that the company’s program is “designed to identify potential risk early and empower customers with real-time information about their play.”  Even so, regulators and lawmakers from Colorado to Massachusetts have begun to question whether sportsbooks have sufficient protections in place. Those concerns have risen with the popularization of prediction markets, which are even less regulated than sports betting apps like DraftKings.  We were behind the camera back in April when Jake opened his DraftKings account to place his first bet, a $100 Hail Mary wager for the New York Knicks to win the chip. We had no idea what a ride it would be.   Watch our new documentary that follows Jake as he intentionally descends into problem gambling — and see how the apps react.  Have you used apps like DraftKings or FanDuel to place sports bets? ProPublica is looking for at least 250 people who use these apps to share their data with us. Your transaction history will help us better understand how the apps respond to user behavior. You can also reach Jake Pearson and the reporting team at 917-512-0276 or sportsbetting@propublica.org . The post Watch: Inside Our $22K Sports Betting Experiment appeared first on ProPublica .

events.title: 2 Inflation reports, retail sales and big bank profits all arrive in the coming week
events.summary: The upcoming week promises to deliver notable updates on inflation, a topic sure to dominate the U.S. midterm elections now less than a month away NEW YORK -- The upcoming week promises to deliver notable updates on inflation, a topic sure to dominate the U.S. midterm elections now less than a month away. A separate report will show how retailers are faring in an inflationary environment, while the nation's biggest banks roll out financials details from the most recent quarter. The price of oil will be front and center as the U.S. war with Iran drags into its eighth month. Renewed violence has sent oil prices back above $100 per barrel and average gasoline prices remain well above $4 per gallon, while diesel remains just below the record high prices reached in September. That has all fueled inflation, putting more pressure on household budgets and businesses. Here's a look at some of the events that will be front and center in the week ahead. No news is good news lately in the U.S. housing market. On Tuesday, the National Association of Realtors reports existing home sales for September, and economists believe sales held steady from August. But August was awful , with sales declining to their slowest annual pace in more than a year. Prospective home buyers are being thwarted by rising mortgage rates which, as Freddie Mac reported Thursday , marched higher for the seventh consecutive week. The average long-term U.S. home loan rate is now higher than it's been in nearly three years. The housing sector has been in a slump since 2022 and sales of previously occupied homes were essentially flat last year, stuck at a 30-year low. The U.S. reported last month that inflation accelerated in August as gas prices spiked in the wake of renewed fighting in the Middle East. More of the same is expected for September with all sides in the Iranian conflict unwilling to concede ground. The Labor Department is expected to report Wednesday that its consumer price index rose by two-tenths of a percent month over month and rose 3.6% compared with a year ago at this time. A day later, the department will release its producer price index — which captures inflation before it reaches consumers. Same story there. Economists expect an increase from the 5.4% registered in August , which was up from 4.8% in July . Last week, PepsiCo said it was raising prices on Doritos and other favorites, citing rising costs for fuel, aluminum and commodities. Economists believe that Americans pulled back on shopping in September with the holiday shopping season just around the corner. Most expect a 0.65% bump. That said, consumers surprised just about everyone in August . As they griped about higher prices at the pump and at the grocery store, Americans spent heartily, expanding retail sales by 1.2%, nearly twice what forecasters had expected. Also next week, the National Retail Federation releases its forecast for the holidays. Pakistan provides fuel aid to 9 million low-income people as Middle East war drives up prices UN human rights office slams racist abuse of Coco Gauff Park service could remove more than 500 trees at historic golf course Trump wants to redesign Banks have notched record profits this year as their trading desks benefit from a volatile stock market while the U.S. war with Iran drags on. Big swings in markets tend to increase activity on trading desks, leading to higher commissions and fee revenue for the banks. Meanwhile, consumers keep spending despite pressure from high prices, and that helps boost fee and lending revenue. Wall Street expects more of the same from the third-quarter updates. Analysts expect JPMorgan Chase to report a 47% boost in profits and Citigroup to report a 61% profit jump when both release earnings Tuesday. Bank of America is expected to tally a profit gain of 36% when it announces results Wednesday. Several other banks and financial institutions, including Morgan Stanley, will also report results during the week. Households and businesses are also facing high interest rates that allow banks to charge more for loans and that won't likely change anytime soon. The Federal Reserve recently raised its benchmark interest rate in an effort to cool inflation and is leaning toward another rate hike by the end of the year. 8 people, including 2 kids, pregnant woman, killed at home: Police 24/7 coverage of breaking news and live events
